thematicGuides.title: Abram and the Stars He Couldn't Count
thematicGuides.hook: Abram believed God and, almost in the same breath, asked how he could be sure. God answered with a covenant.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Now faith is confidence in what we hope for and assurance about what we do not see.
thematicGuides.intro: Some of what you trust God for can't be checked, and may not be settled for years: whether the thing you've prayed about will ever come, how the people you love will turn out. The New Testament keeps going back to one chapter, Genesis 15, to say what faith is. It's an odder chapter than its reputation suggests. The man of faith spends part of it shooing birds off carcasses, and is fast asleep for the important part.
story: God had promised Abram a great nation. Genesis 15 opens some time later with no child in sight, and Abram's first recorded words to God are a complaint. Whatever God gives him, he points out, he has no child to leave it to. He has already worked out who will inherit instead, a servant, Eliezer of Damascus. God's answer is to take him outside and tell him to count the stars, "if indeed you can count them." Abram's offspring, He says, will be like that. Sarai was no younger, and the stars had been there every night of his life. All that had happened was that God had said it again, and Abram believed Him.

Genesis says God counted that belief as righteousness, meaning Abram was right with Him because he trusted Him. Two verses later, promised the land as well, Abram asks, "Sovereign LORD, how can I know that I will gain possession of it?" God sends him for a heifer, a goat and a ram, with a dove and a young pigeon. Abram cuts the larger animals in two and lays the halves facing each other. Jeremiah 34 describes people sealing a solemn agreement this way, by walking between the pieces. Then Abram waits, driving birds of prey off the carcasses. At sunset he falls into a deep sleep, and in the dark a smoking firepot with a blazing torch passes between the halves. Nothing else is said to go through. Genesis calls it the LORD making a covenant, a binding promise, with Abram.

What God tells Abram in that sleep is not what anyone would choose to hear. His descendants will be strangers in a country not their own, enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years before they are brought out. Then, about Abram himself: "You, however, will go to your ancestors in peace and be buried at a good old age." He has just been told he'll be dead centuries before his descendants have the land. So it proved. Isaac was born when Abram (by then renamed Abraham) was a hundred, twenty-five years after he left Harran. When he died, all he is recorded as owning in the promised land was a field with a burial cave in it, bought at the asking price. Hebrews says people like him were still living by faith when they died, having seen what was promised only from a distance.

keyVerses.text: He took him outside and said, 'Look up at the sky and count the stars, if indeed you can count them.' Then he said to him, 'So shall your offspring be.' Abram believed the LORD, and he credited it to him as righteousness.
Yet he did not waver through unbelief regarding the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God, being fully persuaded that God had power to do what he had promised.

All these people were still living by faith when they died. They did not receive the things promised; they only saw them and welcomed them from a distance, admitting that they were foreigners and strangers on earth.

insights: You can believe God and still ask Him how you can be sure. Abram did both inside three verses, and what he got back was a covenant with no rebuke attached. His part in the ceremony, as far as Genesis records, was to fetch the animals, keep the birds off and fall asleep.

Abram was promised a son. You may have no such promise about the job or the diagnosis, and it's better to be honest about that. What you do have is what God has said about Himself, including that He will never leave you. Trusting that, with nothing new in your hands, is the same act Abram made under the stars.
reflectQuestions: Where in your life right now are you trusting God with nothing new to go on, only what He has already said?
If you were as blunt with God as Abram was about having no child, what would you say to Him about the situation that looks least likely to change?
thematicGuides.practice: One clear night this week, go outside for five minutes and look up, even if street lights leave you only a handful of stars. Take one line, written beforehand, naming the thing you find hardest to trust God with. Say it to Him as bluntly as Abram did, and ask Him how you can know. Then read Genesis 15:5-6 aloud before you go back in.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I would like more to go on than I have. You know what I keep asking You about, and how long it has been. I've made my own arrangements in case nothing happens, and You know about those too. Help me today to trust what You've said, as Abram did with nothing in his hands. If the answer is further off than I want, keep me trusting You, and let me bring You my questions without fear. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Anchor Behind the Curtain
thematicGuides.hook: Hebrews calls hope an anchor, and the anchor is lodged behind a curtain that Jesus has already gone through.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain.
thematicGuides.intro: 'Hope' is mostly a word for things that may not happen. You hope the weather holds or the interview went well, and you say it because you can't be sure. The letter to the Hebrews, written to tired Christians, means something sturdier by it. Near its start it warns them not to drift, and in chapter 6 it tells them they have an anchor.
story: God tested Abraham by telling him to offer his son Isaac on a mountain in Moriah. With Isaac already bound on the altar, the angel of the LORD called from heaven and stopped him, and a ram was offered instead. Then the angel called a second time: "I swear by myself, declares the LORD." What followed was a promise of blessing, and of descendants as numerous as the stars. Abraham had first been promised a great nation when he left Harran at seventy-five. This time God swore to it. Hebrews 6 goes back to that oath. People swear by someone greater than themselves, and that settles the argument. God had no one greater, so He swore by Himself, for the sake of those who would inherit the promise. The writer counts his readers among them.

Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest went behind the curtain that hung in front of the Most Holy Place, the inner room of the tent where Israel worshipped. He carried in burning coals and incense, then blood for his own sins and the people's. He went alone, and until he came out nobody else was allowed in the tent at all. Hebrews says our hope goes in behind that curtain like an anchor, into God's own presence, where Jesus has already entered on our behalf. He went in as a forerunner, someone who goes ahead of others who are coming after. No high priest had been that. Four chapters later the writer tells his readers to draw near themselves, by a way Jesus has opened through the curtain.

Paul is drawing his letter to the Christians in Rome to a close when he writes that everything in the old Scriptures was "written to teach us, so that through the endurance taught in the Scriptures and the encouragement they provide we might have hope." He tells the Jews among them and the Gentiles, the non-Jews, to accept one another as Christ accepted them. He quotes Isaiah on a ruler who will arise over the nations: "in him the Gentiles will hope." Then he prays for them, a church he has never visited, and uses a name for God found nowhere else in the Bible, the God of hope.

keyVerses.text: Because God wanted to make the unchanging nature of his purpose very clear to the heirs of what was promised, he confirmed it with an oath. God did this so that, by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be greatly encouraged.
We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where our forerunner, Jesus, has entered on our behalf.
May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you trust in him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

insights: In Hebrews 6 it's the anchor that is called firm and secure. Nothing of the kind is said about the soul it holds. This hope doesn't get weaker when you do.

Paul used the word the ordinary way too. He hoped to see the Romans on his way to Spain, and arrived under guard after a shipwreck in which the crew cut four anchors loose and left them in the sea (Acts 27). The job or the test result is that kind of hope. Pray for it, but it hasn't been promised. What Hebrews calls sure is Jesus, in God's presence on your behalf.

In Paul's prayer, hope is something God gives, so you can ask Him for it when you have none. You can ask a friend to pray for you as well. Paul himself asks the Romans to pray for him later in the same chapter.
reflectQuestions: Where is it hardest for you to feel hopeful at the moment?
What has God said that you most need to be sure of in what you're facing now?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, when you're on your own, say out loud the thing you're hoping for most, in one sentence beginning with the words 'I hope'. Then read Romans 15:13 aloud as a prayer for yourself. The second hope doesn't depend on whether the first comes true.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, when I say I'm hoping, I usually mean I've got my fingers crossed. I'll keep asking You for the thing I want most just now, and I'll need Your help to bear it if the answer is no. I can't see behind the curtain, but Jesus is there, and He went in for me. On days when I feel no hope, keep hold of me, and give me the hope I can't work up for myself. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Bought Back for Fifteen Shekels
thematicGuides.hook: Moses says God loved Israel because He loved them, and Hosea and John each show what a love like that costs.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.
thematicGuides.intro: Ask anyone why they love their oldest friend and you'll get reasons. She's funny, and she stayed when things were bad. So we tend to assume God loves us for something too, because we try hard, or because of what we might become. Moses told Israel the opposite to their faces, and centuries later the prophet Hosea was given a marriage to show the same thing.
story: Israel was camped east of the Jordan, about to enter a land held by seven nations larger and stronger than they were. In Deuteronomy 7 Moses tells them why God chose them out of every people on earth. It wasn't their size, since they were the fewest of all peoples. What he gives instead goes round in a circle. The LORD set His affection on them because He loved them, and because He was keeping an oath sworn to their ancestors. In chapter 9 he rules out their goodness as well. Three verses running he says the land is not coming to them for their righteousness, and he ends by calling them a stiff-necked people.

By Hosea's time Israel was giving its worship to other gods, and God had Hosea's own marriage stand for it. He told him to marry a promiscuous woman, and Hosea married Gomer. Two of the children she bore were given names meaning 'not loved' and 'not my people'. Later his wife took up with another man, and God told Hosea to go and love her again, as He loves the Israelites while they turn to other gods. So Hosea bought her back, in silver and barley. He told her she was to live with him for many days and give herself to no one, and that he would behave the same way towards her. Hosea tells this part himself. He doesn't say who took the payment, or how his own wife came to have a price on her.

Probably the best-known sentence in the Bible comes in John's account of a night-time talk between Jesus and a Jewish teacher called Nicodemus. God loved the world, it says, and gave His one and only Son. John has already said what kind of world that was. The one through whom it was made came into it, and it did not recognise Him. The verdict that goes with the famous sentence is no kinder: light has come, "but people loved darkness instead of light because their deeds were evil." God loved the world, and the people in it loved the dark. It was to them that the Son was sent, and not, John adds, to condemn them.

keyVerses.text: The LORD did not set his affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples. But it was because the LORD loved you and kept the oath he swore to your ancestors that he brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the land of slavery, from the power of Pharaoh king of Egypt.

The LORD said to me, 'Go, show your love to your wife again, though she is loved by another man and is an adulteress. Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods and love the sacred raisin cakes.' So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and about a homer and a lethek of barley.

For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him.

insights: If you look inside yourself for the reason God loves you, you're looking where Moses says it isn't. He told Israel they were few and stubborn, and loved.

Hosea's marriage was a sign God had one prophet act out, a picture of Him and Israel, and never advice about marriage. Nothing in it asks anyone to stay with a partner who is unfaithful or who is harming them. If that is your situation, your safety comes first, and it is right to ask for help.

On a day when God's love seems like a theory, you can look at what it cost. Hosea paid in silver and barley, and God gave His Son. Even the word Moses chose for the rescue from Egypt, "redeemed", is one the Law also uses for buying a person back.
reflectQuestions: If a friend asked you why God loves you, what reason would you find yourself reaching for first?
What would it cost you, in time or money, to do one kind thing for the person who has done least to deserve it?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick someone who has given you no particular reason to be generous lately, perhaps the neighbour who never says hello or the cousin who only rings when he wants something. One day this week, cook or buy them something to eat and take it round yourself. If they ask why, say you were thinking of them.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I keep a list of reasons You might love me and a longer list of things that might make You stop, and I go on adding to both. Loving me cost You Your Son, and I've mostly treated that as a verse I know by heart. Help me believe You love me on the days I've brought You nothing. And when loving someone this week costs me something, make me willing to pay. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Abraham, Isaac and the Ram in the Thicket
thematicGuides.hook: The Bible's hardest story about obeying ends with God stopping Abraham's hand and providing the ram Himself.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: So Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide. And to this day it is said, 'On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.'
thematicGuides.intro: Most people hear the word obedience and think of doing as you're told without being told why, and people following orders have done a good deal of harm. So it makes sense to be wary when the Bible praises someone for obeying. The chapter where it praises Abraham, Genesis 22, is a painful one to read. God asks him for his son.
story: Genesis 22 tells the reader in its first line what Abraham isn't told, that God was testing him. God said, "Take your son, your only son, whom you love, Isaac," and told him to offer the boy as a burnt offering in the region of Moriah. Genesis records no reply to the command, and nothing of what Abraham felt. Early next morning he loaded his donkey, cut the wood and set out with Isaac and two servants. On the third day he told the servants to wait, saying that he and the boy would worship and come back. He laid the wood on Isaac and carried the fire and the knife himself. Isaac asked where the lamb was. His father said God would provide one, and the two of them went on together.

At the place, Abraham built an altar and arranged the wood. He bound Isaac, laid him on it and took the knife. The angel of the LORD called his name twice from heaven, and Abraham answered, "Here I am," as he had when God spoke his name in the chapter's first verse. "Do not lay a hand on the boy," he was told. Abraham had not held back his only son, the angel said, and that showed he feared God. A ram caught in a thicket took Isaac's place on the altar. The angel called to Abraham a second time with God's oath to bless him, and only there, in the last words from heaven, does the chapter use the word 'obeyed'. Abraham returned to the servants he had told to wait.

On the night He was arrested, Jesus went out as usual to the Mount of Olives. He withdrew about a stone's throw from His disciples, knelt and prayed. He asked His Father, if He was willing, to take the cup from Him, the suffering that was coming, and put His Father's will ahead of His own. Luke says an angel from heaven appeared and strengthened Him, and He prayed on in anguish, His sweat falling like drops of blood. On Moriah the angel of the LORD had called out to stop the knife. Here an angel came to give strength, and nothing was stopped. Jesus rose, went back to His disciples, and was still speaking to them when Judas arrived with the crowd.

keyVerses.text: Abraham answered, 'God himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.' And the two of them went on together.
Abraham looked up and there in a thicket he saw a ram caught by its horns. He went over and took the ram and sacrificed it as a burnt offering instead of his son.
Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done.

insights: God does not ask anyone to harm a child. His command to Abraham was a test, He stopped it Himself, and His law names child sacrifice among the things He hates (Deuteronomy 12:31). If a thought ever tells you to hurt someone for God, it is not from Him, and you should tell a doctor or someone you trust.

Abraham named the mountain after what God did there and left his own part out. Christians have long heard the angel's words, that he had not held back his son, in Paul's line that God "did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). That is the God who asks things of you.

Abraham's command was for him alone, once. The things God asks of you are mostly written down already and look ordinary beside Moriah: tell the truth, forgive, keep your promises, give. Obeying usually means doing the next one of those you've been avoiding.
reflectQuestions: Which part of your life do you keep coming back to with a sense that God wants something there to change?
What is the one thing you know God is asking of you right now that you'd rather He hadn't?
thematicGuides.practice: Find a card that fits in your wallet or your Bible. On it write the thing you've been putting off that you know God wants done. Under it write the name Abraham gave the mountain, The LORD Will Provide, and today's date. When you've done the thing, add that date beside the first.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, Your Son told You what He wanted before He put Your will first, so I'll say it. I don't want to do the thing You're asking, and I've been finding reasons why it can't be this week. I'd like to see the ram before I start up the hill, and I know that isn't how it went for Abraham. Get me as far as setting out. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: What Solomon Asked For at Gibeon
thematicGuides.hook: Offered anything he wanted, Solomon asked God for a discerning heart, and two women with one baby soon put it to work.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: So give your servant a discerning heart to govern your people and to distinguish between right and wrong. For who is able to govern this great people of yours?
thematicGuides.intro: A decision is usually hard because you can't see enough to make it. Two people give you opposite accounts and both sound sure, or the job is plainly bigger than you are and nobody has left instructions. Solomon was in that position at the start of his reign, when God came to him in a dream and told him to ask for whatever he wanted. He was new to the job and said so.
story: Solomon had gone to Gibeon and offered a thousand burnt offerings there. The temple wasn't built yet, and Gibeon was the most important of the hilltop shrines Israel used. During the night the LORD appeared to him in a dream and said, "Ask for whatever you want me to give you." Before asking for anything, Solomon spoke about the kindness God had shown his father David in giving him a son to sit on his throne. He was a married man and a king, and he said, "I am only a little child and do not know how to carry out my duties."

Solomon asked for a discerning heart, to govern the people and to tell right from wrong. The Hebrew behind 'discerning' is the everyday word for hearing, so his request was for a heart that listens. Three times in the prayer he calls the nation God's people, and never his own. God was pleased, and named what Solomon had left out: long life, wealth, the death of his enemies. He would be given a wise heart, and wealth and honour with it. Long life came with a condition, that he walk in obedience as David had. Solomon woke, and realised it had been a dream.

The next story 1 Kings tells is of two prostitutes standing before the king. They lived in the same house and each had a newborn son. One baby had died in the night, and each woman said the living one was hers. By the first woman's account nobody else had been in the house. Solomon began by saying back what each of them had claimed. Then he sent for a sword and ordered the living child cut in two, half for each. One woman begged him to give the baby to her rival and not to kill him. The other said neither of them should have him, and to cut him in two. Solomon gave the boy to the one who was ready to lose him. She, he ruled, was his mother.

keyVerses.text: So give your servant a discerning heart to govern your people and to distinguish between right and wrong. For who is able to govern this great people of yours?

Since you have asked for this and not for long life or wealth for yourself, nor have asked for the death of your enemies but for discernment in administering justice, I will do what you have asked. I will give you a wise and discerning heart
When all Israel heard the verdict the king had given, they held the king in awe, because they saw that he had wisdom from God to administer justice.

insights: Solomon began by admitting he was out of his depth, and God was pleased with the prayer that followed. If you feel the same in a new job, a marriage or the care of a parent, you can say so to God and make the same request.
The wisdom he was given worked by listening. With no witness to call, he repeated each woman's claim, then found a way to hear which of them loved the child. Most of us reach a verdict much sooner.

You haven't been told to ask for whatever you want, and nothing here promises the wealth and honour that came with Solomon's answer. The thing he chose is open to you, though. James tells anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God for it (James 1:5).
reflectQuestions: What are you facing at the moment where the right thing to do isn't yet clear to you?
Solomon asked for a heart that listens. Whose side of a story have you been slowest to hear properly this year?
thematicGuides.practice: Some time in the next few days, walk to a park bench or an open church where you can be alone for ten minutes. Solomon made his request away from home, at Gibeon, and he began it with the job he'd been given and what he didn't know about doing it. On your way there, tell God the same things about your own situation. When you arrive, ask Him for a discerning heart.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, You know the responsibility I've been handed and how little I know about carrying it. If You had made me Solomon's offer I think I'd have asked for the money, or for the problem to go away. I'm asking for what he asked for. Give me a heart that listens, to You first and then to the people involved, including the one I've already made up my mind about. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Not Treated as Our Sins Deserve
thematicGuides.hook: Joseph's brothers and the criminal crucified beside Jesus knew what they deserved, and were promised something they hadn't earned.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: He will not always accuse, nor will he harbor his anger forever; he does not treat us as our sins deserve or repay us according to our iniquities.
thematicGuides.intro: What makes forgiving hard is that the wrong was real, and letting it go can feel like agreeing it didn't matter. Being forgiven is hard to take in for much the same reason. You know what you did, and some part of you keeps waiting for the bill. In the last chapter of Genesis, Joseph's brothers are still waiting for theirs.
story: Joseph's brothers sold him to passing merchants for twenty shekels of silver. Years later, as governor of Egypt, he wept over them, kissed them and fed their families through a famine. Their father Jacob lived another seventeen years, in Egypt, and when he died they said to each other, "What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrongs we did to him?" They sent word that Jacob had left instructions for Joseph to forgive them, and Joseph wept. When they came and offered to be his slaves, he told them not to be afraid and asked, "Am I in the place of God?" They had meant to harm him, he said, and God had meant it for good. He promised to provide for them and their children, and spoke kindly to them.

Moses climbed Mount Sinai carrying two stone tablets, cut to replace the pair he had smashed at the sight of Israel's golden calf. There the LORD proclaimed His name and what He is like: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love. Psalm 103 opens with David telling his own soul not to forget what the LORD has done, beginning with the forgiveness of all its sins. A few lines on he names Moses and repeats those words from Sinai. Then he adds that the LORD will not harbour His anger for ever, and does not pay us back according to our sins.

Jesus was crucified between two criminals at the place called the Skull. There He said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." The next thing Luke records is His clothes being shared out by lot. Nobody had asked to be forgiven. The rulers sneered, the soldiers mocked, and one of the men hanging beside Him joined in. The other criminal rebuked him. He said, "We are punished justly, for we are getting what our deeds deserve," and added that Jesus had done nothing wrong. Then he asked Jesus to remember him when He came into His kingdom, and Jesus answered that he would be with Him in paradise that very day.

keyVerses.text: You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good to accomplish what is now being done, the saving of many lives.
For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his love for those who fear him; as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.
Be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you.

insights: Joseph didn't call the wrong small. He told his brothers they had meant to harm him, and he would not take God's place and collect. Forgiving like that doesn't mean you have to trust someone again, and nobody is being told to go back to a person who is hurting them.

Joseph's brothers lived in Egypt for seventeen years after he wept over them, and still expected to be paid back. David tells his own soul not to forget that it is forgiven. If you believe it on Sunday and doubt it by Wednesday, the psalm is there to be said to yourself again.

In Ephesians 4:32 God's forgiveness of you in Christ comes first, and your forgiving of someone else is modelled on it. Your forgiveness of them may need saying more than once. Joseph had to reassure his brothers twice, years apart, and he wept both times.
reflectQuestions: Who has wronged you in a way that still feels unpaid?
What have you done that you half expect God to bring up again one day?
thematicGuides.practice: On a slip of paper write, in a few words only you would understand, what the person who came to mind did to you. Under it copy Joseph's question about the place of God. If the wrong was yours, write that and put Psalm 103:10 under it instead. Keep the slip in your wallet or your Bible. Each time the old anger or guilt comes round this week, take it out, read both lines, and tell God the judging is His.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, You haven't treated me as my sins deserve, and I thank You for that more easily than I believe it. I still expect You to bring some things up again. And there is someone I've kept an account against, more carefully than I keep most things. What they did mattered, and I won't pretend to You that it didn't. But I am not in Your place. Take the judging off my hands, and show me what kindness would be wise here. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Hannah's Prayer That Made No Sound
thematicGuides.hook: The priest who watched Hannah pray told her to sober up, and she answered that she was pouring out her soul.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Trust in him at all times, you people; pour out your hearts to him, for God is our refuge.
thematicGuides.intro: The hard thing about prayer is that you're talking to someone you can't see, who doesn't answer the way a person in the room would. So it's natural to suspect you're doing it wrong and that other people know how. The Bible's reply is mostly to show people at prayer, and one of them, Hannah, prayed without making a sound.
story: Elkanah had two wives. Every year he took the household up to Shiloh, and every year Peninnah, who had children, goaded Hannah, who had none, until Hannah wept and wouldn't eat. One year, after the meal, Hannah got up and prayed, crying bitterly, asking for a son and vowing to give him back to the LORD for life. Eli the priest sat on his chair by the doorpost, watching her mouth. Her lips were moving and he could hear nothing, so he told her to put away her wine. Hannah answered that she hadn't touched a drink and had been pouring out her soul to the LORD. Eli told her to go in peace, and asked that the God of Israel would give her what she had prayed for. Then the woman who had been refusing food went off and ate, and the misery had gone from her face. In time she had a son and named him Samuel, saying, "Because I asked the LORD for him."

Moses used to pitch a tent some distance outside the camp and call it the tent of meeting. When he went in, the pillar of cloud would come down and stay at the entrance while the LORD spoke with him face to face, the way one friend talks to another. One of their conversations follows. The people had just made the golden calf, and God had told them to go on to the land without Him. Moses points out that God has told him to lead these people and hasn't said who will go with him. If God's Presence isn't going, he says, then don't send us. God answers, "I will do the very thing you have asked."

As the crowds around Jesus grew, He often withdrew to lonely places to pray, and before choosing the twelve apostles He spent a whole night praying on a mountainside. The disciples saw some of it. They were with Him once when He was praying in private, and three of them went up a mountain with Him to pray. Then one day He was praying in a certain place, and when He had finished, one of them asked Him to teach them to pray, as John the Baptist had taught his own disciples.

keyVerses.text: I am a woman who is deeply troubled. I have not been drinking wine or beer; I was pouring out my soul to the LORD.
The LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend.
One day Jesus was praying in a certain place. When he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.'

insights: If you suspect you're praying wrongly, you're in the company of disciples who had watched Jesus pray and still had to ask how. Hannah brought the state she was in, and Psalm 62 tells everybody to do what she said she was doing: "pour out your hearts to him".

Many people have asked God for a child with as many tears as Hannah, over as many years, and have not been given one. Samuel was God's answer to Hannah. Her story sets no rule that enough tears bring a baby, and their prayers were no worse than hers.

You may get up from praying with nothing you could call an answer. Hannah did. Moses was answered in words, but all she took home that day was the blessing of a priest who had misjudged her, asking God to grant what she'd prayed for. She ate and her face lifted before there was any sign of a baby.
reflectQuestions: If someone had watched you pray over the past month, the way Eli watched Hannah, what would they have seen?
Hannah's trouble went on year after year. What have you never quite said to God about the thing you've waited for longest?
thematicGuides.practice: One evening this week, take a sheet of paper and write to God about the thing that weighs on you most. Write it as Hannah prayed it, with no effort to sound proper: how long it has gone on and what you want from Him. Date it, fold it, and keep it somewhere only you will look.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I can't see You, and half the time I'm not sure any of this gets through. I've given You tidy prayers because I thought that was what You wanted, and kept the real thing to myself. So here is the real thing, untidy as it is. You heard Hannah when no sound came out of her. Hear me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Lion, the Bear and Goliath
thematicGuides.hook: Before David fought Goliath he had to answer an angry brother and a doubtful king, and he told the king why he could win.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.
thematicGuides.intro: David came to the Valley of Elah to deliver bread to his brothers and ten cheeses to their commander. The army he found there, in 1 Samuel 17, had been hearing the same challenge for weeks and had not answered it. You may know something of that from the phone call you keep not making, or the letter that has sat unopened since last month.
story: For forty days Goliath of Gath came out morning and evening, shouting for one man to come down and fight him, and each time the Israelites ran. He was shouting again when David, talking to his brothers, asked the men nearby what would be done for whoever killed this Philistine, and who he was to defy the armies of the living God. Eliab, his oldest brother, burned with anger. He asked who was minding David's few sheep, called him conceited and wicked at heart, and said he had only come to watch the battle. "Now what have I done?" said David. "Can't I even speak?" Eliab got no more answer than that. David turned to someone else and asked again.

Saul sent for David, who offered to fight Goliath. He was only a young man, the king told him, and Goliath had been a warrior from his youth. David answered with his father's sheep. When a lion or a bear carried one off he went after it and pulled the sheep from its mouth, and when it turned on him he caught it by its hair and killed it. He had killed the lion and the bear himself, and he called it a rescue. The LORD who rescued him then, he told Saul, would rescue him from this Philistine. Saul dressed him in his own tunic and a coat of armour. David tried walking in them, said he wasn't used to them and took them off. He went out with a staff, a sling and five smooth stones from the stream.

Goliath saw that David was little more than a boy, and despised him. "Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?" he asked. David's answer took longer than the fight did. The LORD would hand Goliath over that day, he said, and everyone there would learn that He does not save by sword or spear. As Goliath moved in, David ran to meet him and slung one stone into his forehead, and he fell face down. The Philistines ran, and the men who had run from Goliath for forty days went after them with a shout.

keyVerses.text: The LORD who rescued me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will rescue me from the hand of this Philistine.
You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD Almighty, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

But the Lord stood at my side and gave me strength, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. And I was delivered from the lion's mouth. The Lord will rescue me from every evil attack and will bring me safely to his heavenly kingdom.

insights: David's courage rested on two rescues he could name, both from days spent minding sheep. You can get that kind of courage ready on a quiet day, before you need it.

The first person in David's way was his brother. A chapter earlier Samuel had taken Eliab for the LORD's choice of king and been told that the LORD looks at the heart, and here Eliab claims to know David's. If someone close to you has already decided what your motives are, you don't have to change their mind before you start.

David told Goliath how the day would end, which is more than you know about yours. Paul, expecting to die soon, argues the way David did: delivered once from the lion's mouth, he is sure the Lord will rescue him again. The rescue he means is being brought safely to God's heavenly kingdom, and that is promised to you as well.
reflectQuestions: What has been in front of you every morning and evening for weeks that you still haven't moved towards?
Whose opinion of you, like Eliab's of David, do you feel you have to change before you can make a start?
thematicGuides.practice: This evening, find a card that fits your wallet or phone case and copy 1 Samuel 17:37 at the top. Under it write your own lion and bear, two times God brought you out of something you thought would finish you. If you can only think of one, write one. Keep it on you, and read it the next morning you wake up dreading something.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've listened to the same threat for so long that I know it by heart. I could describe it in more detail than anything You've done for me, and I'm not proud of that. Bring back to my mind the times You got me through. Give me strength for the one step in front of me. However this turns out, bring me safely to You in the end. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Mephibosheth at the King's Table
thematicGuides.hook: David sent for Saul's grandson and gave him a seat at his table for life, because of a promise made to the man's father.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I will surely show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table.
thematicGuides.intro: David asks his question before he knows whether there is anybody to ask it about: "Is there anyone still left of the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for Jonathan's sake?" The kindness and the reason for it were settled before he had a name to attach them to. Grace is the Bible's word for kindness of that sort. If you doubt that God would go out of His way for you, notice whose house David was asking after. Saul had tried to kill him.
story: Mephibosheth first appears in a single bracketed verse. He was five when news came from Jezreel that his grandfather King Saul and his father Jonathan were dead. His nurse picked him up and fled, and in her hurry he fell. After that he was lame in both feet. The verse sits inside the account of how two men killed his uncle Ish-Bosheth, Saul's son, and carried the head to David, telling him the LORD had avenged the king "against Saul and his offspring". David had them put to death. When Mephibosheth is next mentioned he is a man with a young son, living in another man's house in Lo Debar.

Ziba, a servant from Saul's household, told David that a son of Jonathan was still alive, and added that he was lame in both feet. David asked only where he was, and had him brought. Mephibosheth came in and bowed down. David said his name and told him not to be afraid. Years earlier David's friend Jonathan had made him swear never to cut off his kindness from Jonathan's family. Now David told Jonathan's son that Saul's land was his again, and that he would always eat at the king's table. Mephibosheth bowed again and asked, "What is your servant, that you should notice a dead dog like me?" David's next recorded words are to Ziba, about the land.

Mephibosheth moved to Jerusalem and ate at David's table like one of the king's sons. Years later a revolt drove David out of the city, and Ziba told him Mephibosheth had stayed behind hoping for Saul's kingdom. David gave Ziba the land. As the king came home, Mephibosheth went down to meet him, not having taken care of his feet, trimmed his moustache or washed his clothes since the day David left. He had been slandered, he said. His family had "deserved nothing but death" from the king, he went on, and after a place at the king's table he had no right to ask for more. David ruled that the land be divided. Mephibosheth said Ziba could have all of it, now that the king was home safe.

keyVerses.text: But show me unfailing kindness like the LORD's kindness as long as I live, so that I may not be killed, and do not ever cut off your kindness from my family, not even when the LORD has cut off every one of David's enemies from the face of the earth.

'Don't be afraid,' David said to him, 'for I will surely show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table.'
He has saved us and called us to a holy life, not because of anything we have done but because of his own purpose and grace. This grace was given us in Christ Jesus before the beginning of time

insights: David calls what he is offering God's kindness. Paul says God's grace was given us in Christ Jesus before the beginning of time, and not for anything we have done. Your place with God rests on Jesus, as Mephibosheth's rested on Jonathan.

David never tells Mephibosheth why he is worth noticing, and doesn't argue him into a better opinion of himself. He gives him a seat at dinner, and the man who called himself a dead dog eats there. You can accept what God gives before you've worked out why He would give it.

God hasn't promised that what you've lost will come back in this life, as Saul's land did. Grace gives a place with Him. Looking back on David's kindness, Mephibosheth mentioned only the table, and he let the land go.
reflectQuestions: What, if anything, makes it hard to believe that God's kindness to you was settled before you had done a thing to earn it or lose it?
David went looking for someone to be kind to. Who could you seek out this month with a kindness they have no reason to expect from you?
thematicGuides.practice: Before you eat this evening, take five minutes by yourself and read the thirteen verses of 2 Samuel 9. Tell God the thing about yourself that makes you least sure He wants you near, and thank Him that for Jesus's sake He does. Then go and eat.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, the Father's kindness to me rests on You, and most days I forget it. I come with my defence ready, as if You had sent for me to settle a score. I can't say why You would notice me. I'm coming anyway, and I'm grateful. This week I'll go looking for someone to be kind to for Your sake, as David did for Jonathan's. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Manna That Wouldn't Keep Overnight
thematicGuides.hook: God fed Israel one day at a time, and the portion some of them kept overnight was full of maggots by morning.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I will rain down bread from heaven for you. The people are to go out each day and gather enough for that day.
thematicGuides.intro: Exodus gives the date. Israel reached the Desert of Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month, a month to the day after marching out of Egypt, and there the whole community told Moses and Aaron they wished they had died in Egypt beside their pots of meat. God answered with bread, but in a form nobody could stockpile. If you only relax once next month is covered, you'll recognise the people in this chapter.
story: The LORD told Moses He would rain down bread from heaven, a day's worth at a time. He called it a test of whether they would follow His instructions. Next morning, once the dew had gone, thin flakes like frost lay on the desert floor. "What is it?" the Israelites asked each other. Moses said it was the bread the LORD had given them, and told them to take an omer, a set measure, for each person in the tent. Some gathered a lot and some a little, and it measured out at exactly what each needed. Moses' other instruction was to keep none of it until morning. Some kept part of theirs anyway. By morning it was full of maggots and had begun to smell, and Moses was angry with them.

Forty years later, on the edge of the promised land, Moses told Israel what the manna had been for. God had led them through the wilderness to humble and test them, he said, and had caused the hunger before He sent the bread. Both were to teach them that bread by itself doesn't keep a person alive. What the LORD says does. Moses also warned them about the land ahead. It had wheat and barley, and once they had eaten their fill and built fine houses they might say to themselves, "My power and the strength of my hands have produced this wealth for me." After Moses' death, when Israel had crossed the Jordan and eaten the land's grain for the first time, the manna stopped the next day.

Jeremiah, speaking for God to Judah, sets two plants side by side. The person who trusts in human strength, he says, and whose heart has turned away from the LORD, is like a bush in the wastelands, in a salt land where no one lives. When prosperity does come, the bush never sees it. The one whose confidence is in the LORD is like a tree planted by the water. Psalm 1 has a tree by the water too, but Jeremiah adds what the psalm leaves out. Heat comes, and a whole year of drought. The tree gets through both with green leaves and fruit, because it has sent its roots out to the stream.

keyVerses.text: Then Moses said to them, 'No one is to keep any of it until morning.' However, some of them paid no attention to Moses; they kept part of it until morning, but it was full of maggots and began to smell.

He humbled you, causing you to hunger and then feeding you with manna, which neither you nor your ancestors had known, to teach you that man does not live on bread alone but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.

But blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD, whose confidence is in him. They will be like a tree planted by the water that sends out its roots by the stream. It does not fear when heat comes; its leaves are always green. It has no worries in a year of drought and never fails to bear fruit.

insights: Joseph stored so much grain in Egypt that he stopped keeping count, and it fed the country through the famine, so saving is not what the overnight rule was against. What it ruled out was a supply that made tomorrow's trip unnecessary, so the next morning began with going out to collect what God had put there.

The prayer Jesus taught asks for bread the way the manna came: "Give us today our daily bread." And when He was hungry Himself, after forty days in the wilderness, and was tempted to turn stones into bread, He answered with Moses' sentence about the manna.
None of this promises you'll never go short. Israel went hungry before the bread came, and Jeremiah's tree gets the heat and the drought like every other plant.
reflectQuestions: What are you having to trust God with one day at a time just now, because you can't see any further ahead?
What were you given, on a day you had been dreading, that you didn't have the night before?
thematicGuides.practice: Starting tomorrow, for five mornings, go without asking God for anything beyond that day. Before you eat, name what the day ahead will need from you, perhaps a hard conversation or a long afternoon on your own, and ask Him for enough for that. When next month's worry pushes in, tell Him it isn't today's and leave it there. After the five mornings, pray as you normally do.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, You taught me to ask for bread for today, and most of what I bring You is about next year. I'd rather have a full store than have to come back to You every morning, and when I do have plenty I mostly stop asking. Give me what today needs, and bring me back tomorrow to ask again. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Peace Jesus Left at the Table
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus left His friends His own peace on the night He was arrested, and greeted them with the word twice on the evening He rose.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives.
thematicGuides.intro: Peace is hard to get by trying. The harder you work at feeling it the further off it gets, as with falling asleep, and a week by the sea is no help if the trouble has come with you. The Hebrew word for it is shalom, from a root that means whole, and it covers how things stand between you and God and between you and other people.
story: About a year out of Egypt, while Israel was camped at Sinai, God gave Moses a blessing to pass on to Aaron and his sons, the priests. They were to say it over the people, and He supplied the wording Himself. It is three lines long. Each line begins with His name, the LORD, and asks Him to do something for the people listening, and the last thing asked for is peace. God finished with this: "So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I will bless them."

Judas had already left the supper table and gone out into the night when Jesus told the others He was going away. Peter was told he would disown Jesus three times before the cock crowed, and Jesus Himself had been troubled in spirit when He spoke of being betrayed. At that table He told them He was leaving them peace, and He called it His own: "my peace I give you." The same evening He told them they would scatter and leave Him on His own, and that in this world they would have trouble. Then He crossed the Kidron Valley with them to a garden that Judas knew.

On the evening of the day Jesus rose, His disciples had shut themselves in behind locked doors, afraid of the Jewish leaders. He came and stood in the middle of them and said, "Peace be with you!" It was the everyday greeting, what anyone might say on coming into a house. Then He showed them His hands and His side. He gave the greeting a second time and went straight on to say, "As the Father has sent me, I am sending you." He breathed on them, told them to receive the Holy Spirit, and gave them a charge about forgiving sins. Three nights earlier these men had scattered and left Him on His own.

keyVerses.text: The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the LORD turn his face toward you and give you peace.
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled and do not be afraid.

On the evening of that first day of the week, when the disciples were together, with the doors locked for fear of the Jewish leaders, Jesus came and stood among them and said, 'Peace be with you!' After he said this, he showed them his hands and side. The disciples were overjoyed when they saw the Lord.

insights: In Numbers and in John, peace reaches people as words somebody else says to them. Many churches still end a service with the blessing God gave Aaron's sons to say. By His own account the priests supplied the voice and He did the blessing.

The peace Jesus gave was His own, and He gave it on an evening when He was troubled in spirit. At the end of that evening's talk He told His friends that in Him they could have peace and that in this world they would have trouble. He said both to the same people. If you feel troubled most days, tell a doctor and someone you trust as well as God.

Between His two greetings on the evening He rose, Jesus showed His friends His hands and His side. Isaiah had written of one whose punishment would bring us peace and whose wounds would heal us. Being whole, in the Bible's sense, starts with being put right with God. It goes on to other people. With the second greeting He sent these men out and spoke of forgiving sins.
reflectQuestions: How would you describe the state of your heart over the past month to someone who wouldn't judge the answer?
Of the things that keep taking your peace away, which one would you most like to hand over to God?
thematicGuides.practice: This week, tell one Christian you trust, a friend or the minister after a service, what has been troubling you. Then ask them to read Numbers 6:24-26 aloud over you, with your name at the start, the way the priests said it over Israel. It takes under a minute and will feel a little odd for both of you.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, most of what I call peace is a closed door and nobody asking me for anything. I can arrange that myself. I can't arrange being whole, with You or with the people I'd rather not name. Give me the peace Your Son had at that table, with Judas already on his way. I lock myself in when I'm afraid. Let Him come in anyway, and say peace to me twice. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: James and John Ask for the Best Seats
thematicGuides.hook: Peter twice heard Jesus say His followers were not to lord it over anyone, and the phrase is there in his own letter.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
thematicGuides.intro: Being in charge is generally taken to mean being looked after. Whoever carries the responsibility usually does get the last word and somebody to fetch the coffee. The men closest to Jesus wanted their share of it. More than once the Gospels catch them jostling for rank, and one of those times is the last supper.
story: Jesus was leading the Twelve up to Jerusalem when He told them, for the third time, that He would be killed and rise again. This time He spoke of being mocked, spat on and flogged. Mark's next sentence has James and John coming to Him. "Teacher," they said, "we want you to do for us whatever we ask." What they wanted was the seats at His right and left in His glory. Jesus asked whether they could drink His cup, meaning what He was about to suffer. "We can," they answered. They would, He told them, but those seats weren't His to give. The other ten were indignant when they heard, and Jesus called all twelve together. Gentile rulers lord it over their people, He said, and it was not to be like that among the Twelve.

At the Passover meal on the night of His arrest, Jesus gave the Twelve bread and a cup and told them that one of the men at the table would betray Him. They began asking each other who it could be, and they also fell to arguing over which of them was considered the greatest. Jesus said again that the kings of the Gentiles lord it over their subjects, and added that such rulers call themselves Benefactors. The Twelve were not to be like that. He asked them who is greater, the one sitting at the table or the one waiting on him. The one at the table, He said. Then He told them that He was among them as the one who serves. John's Gospel records that during this meal He got up, wrapped a towel round His waist and washed their feet.

Peter was one of the ten on the road, and he was at the table that night. In time he wrote to Christians scattered across five provinces. The first line of the letter calls him an apostle of Jesus Christ, but when he comes to their elders he appeals to them as "a fellow elder". He tells them to shepherd God's flock, and he uses a phrase he had twice heard from Jesus when he says they are not to go lording it over those entrusted to them. Then he tells all of them, elders included, to clothe themselves with humility towards one another.

keyVerses.text: Not so with you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all.
For who is greater, the one who is at the table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who is at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.

Be shepherds of God's flock that is under your care, watching over them, not because you must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to be; not pursuing dishonest gain, but eager to serve; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.

insights: Jesus let the wish to be great stand, and gave it a different job to do. If you want your work to count, a fair test is whether the people under you are better off for having you over them.

Further along the road to Jerusalem, outside Jericho, a blind beggar shouted for Jesus while many told him to be quiet. Jesus stopped and asked him, word for word, what He had asked James and John: "What do you want me to do for you?" Serving can begin with that question, put to someone who has nothing to offer you.
reflectQuestions: What would the people who have to go along with your decisions say it's like to have you in charge?
What do you still remember about the way one particular boss, teacher, parent or church leader used their position to look after you?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick one place where you have some say over other people, whether that's a team, a household or a committee. Work out which job there always falls to whoever is most junior, like washing the mugs or putting the chairs away. Within the week, do it with your own hands and don't mention it to anyone.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I would have asked for one of those seats. I like it when people wait for me to decide, and I notice when my name is left off the list of thanks. Thank You that Your Son served me before He asked me to serve anybody. Where I'm in charge this week, let me see the job nobody wants before it lands on whoever is newest, and let me do it without telling anyone. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Prisoner Who Broke Bread in the Storm
thematicGuides.hook: By the fourteenth night of the storm, soldiers were cutting a lifeboat adrift on the word of a prisoner nobody had listened to.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: So keep up your courage, men, for I have faith in God that it will happen just as he told me.
thematicGuides.intro: Steadying other people in a crisis would be easier if you weren't in it as well. You're as tired and frightened as they are, and often you aren't the one in charge. Acts 27 is a fortnight in a storm at sea, told by someone who was on board. The man who holds the ship's company together through it is one of the prisoners.
story: Paul was being taken to Rome for trial, one of several prisoners under a centurion named Julius. At Fair Havens in Crete it was already past the Day of Atonement, the autumn fast, and sailing had become dangerous. Paul told them he could see the voyage ending in disaster, with "great loss to ship and cargo, and to our own lives also." The centurion went with the pilot and the ship's owner instead, and the majority decided to try for a better winter harbour. A gentle south wind came up and they set off. Before long a wind of hurricane force swept down from the island, and all they could do was let the ship be driven. They threw the cargo overboard, and then the ship's tackle.

Many days into the storm, when nobody on board had eaten for a long time, Paul stood up in front of them. He began, "Men, you should have taken my advice not to sail from Crete." Then he told them to keep up their courage. An angel had stood beside him in the night, he said, and everyone sailing with him was going to live, though the ship would not survive. He had one more thing to tell them. "Nevertheless," he said, "we must run aground on some island."

On the fourteenth night the sailors sensed land, dropped anchor and tried to slip away in the lifeboat. Paul told the centurion and the soldiers they couldn't be saved unless those men stayed. This time he was listened to, and the soldiers cut the boat adrift. Just before dawn he urged everyone to eat. "You need it to survive," he said. He took bread, thanked God for it where everyone could see, broke it and started eating. There were 276 people on board, and they all ate as much as they wanted. At daylight the ship ran onto a sandbar and began to break up. The soldiers meant to kill the prisoners rather than let any swim away, but the centurion, who hadn't listened to Paul at Fair Havens, wanted to spare his life and stopped them. Everyone reached land.

keyVerses.text: When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days and the storm continued raging, we finally gave up all hope of being saved.

But now I urge you to keep up your courage, because not one of you will be lost; only the ship will be destroyed. Last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me and said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand trial before Caesar; and God has graciously given you the lives of all who sail with you.'
After he said this, he took some bread and gave thanks to God in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat. They were all encouraged and ate some food themselves.

insights: By the end the soldiers were acting on what Paul said. He had been right at Fair Havens, and being ignored there hadn't made him go quiet. He was still a prisoner when they cut the ropes.

At Fair Havens Paul warned that lives would be lost. Days later, in the thick of the storm, he said nobody would die, and the only reason he gave was what an angel had told him the night before. He told them the worst when that was what he could see, and the best only when it had been told to him.

Nobody has told you how the takeover at work or your sister's illness will end, so don't tell people it will be fine. You can still make sure everyone eats, yourself included, and say who you belong to, as Paul did.
reflectQuestions: When something goes badly wrong at work or at home, what do you tend to do in the first hour?
In the hardest situation you're in right now, what would be your version of getting everyone to eat something?
thematicGuides.practice: Each day for the next seven, stop before your main meal and thank God for the food in one sentence, as Paul did on a ship that was about to break up. Add one thing from that day that didn't go wrong. Say it aloud if the people you're eating with won't mind, and keep doing it on the bad days.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, when things go badly and I'm not the one steering, I want to say I told you so and leave them to it. Keep me from walking off. I belong to You and I serve You, whatever happens. Stop me promising anyone an ending You haven't told me. Give me one true thing to say, and the sense to see what the people around me need next. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Cloak Elijah Threw and Elisha Picked Up
thematicGuides.hook: The one job Kings records for Elisha, in all his time as Elijah's servant, is pouring water on his master's hands.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: And the things you have heard me say in the presence of many witnesses entrust to reliable people who will also be qualified to teach others.
thematicGuides.intro: When Elijah told God he was the only one left, part of the answer he got was the name of his successor, Elisha son of Shaphat. Whatever work you do, someone will have to do it after you, and somebody once made room for you. The prophet who said he was the last one was sent back the way he had come, and found the next one behind a plough.
story: Elijah came down from Horeb with an instruction to anoint Elisha as his successor. He found Elisha ploughing, driving the last of twelve pairs of oxen, went up to him and threw his cloak around him. Kings gives Elijah nothing to say as he does it, and Elisha left the oxen and ran after him. He asked to kiss his father and mother goodbye first. He went back, slaughtered his pair of oxen, burned the ploughing gear to cook the meat and gave it to the people. Then he set out after Elijah and became his servant. What that service involved is mentioned once, later on, by an officer of the king of Israel: "He used to pour water on the hands of Elijah."

On the day the LORD took him, Elijah told Elisha three times to stay behind, and three times got the answer, "As surely as the LORD lives and as you live, I will not leave you." At the Jordan Elijah struck the water with his rolled-up cloak and they crossed on dry ground. He asked what he could do for Elisha before he was taken. Elisha asked for a double portion of his spirit. A double share was what the law gave an eldest son, so he was asking to be Elijah's heir, and Elijah didn't promise it. It would be his, he said, only if Elisha saw him go. As they walked on, a chariot and horses of fire came between them, and Elijah went up in a whirlwind. Elisha saw it. He cried out, "My father! My father!" and tore his garment in two. Then he picked up the fallen cloak, went back to the river and struck the water, and it parted again.

Paul was in chains in Rome when he wrote his second letter to Timothy, saying that the time for his departure was near. Elisha had called Elijah his father. Paul addresses Timothy, who had worked beside him for years, as "my dear son". He asks him to come before winter and to bring the cloak he left at Troas. One instruction looks past Timothy altogether. What he has heard Paul say in front of many witnesses is to be handed on to reliable people who can teach others in their turn.

keyVerses.text: So Elijah went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat. He was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, and he himself was driving the twelfth pair. Elijah went up to him and threw his cloak around him.

When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, 'Tell me, what can I do for you before I am taken from you?' 'Let me inherit a double portion of your spirit,' Elisha replied. 'You have asked a difficult thing,' Elijah said, 'yet if you see me when I am taken from you, it will be yours, otherwise, it will not.'

Elisha then picked up Elijah's cloak that had fallen from him and went back and stood on the bank of the Jordan. He took the cloak that had fallen from Elijah and struck the water with it. 'Where now is the LORD, the God of Elijah?' he asked. When he struck the water, it divided to the right and to the left, and he crossed over.

insights: Elijah could leave a cloak behind. When Elisha asked for a double share of his spirit, Elijah called it a difficult thing, and at the river it was the God of Elijah that Elisha called on. You can hand over what you know and the place you hold, but the power for the work is God's to give.

On Horeb, Elijah was told to anoint three men, and the only one we see him reach is Elisha. It was Elisha who later told Hazael he would be king of Aram, and a prophet sent by Elisha who anointed Jehu. Some of what you were given to do may be finished by the person who comes after you.
reflectQuestions: What did you pick up from the person you learned most from, just by being around them, that they never sat you down to teach?
Who is already hard at work in their own field, as Elisha was at his plough, that you could ask to join you in something you do?
thematicGuides.practice: This week, ask one person to do a job with you that you normally do alone and that someone will need to do after you. It might be keeping the accounts or cooking the family Christmas dinner. Ask them in person, tell them why you thought of them, and agree a date.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, You gave me people who let me tag along when I knew nothing, and I'm grateful. I'd rather be missed than replaced, and it suits me to be the only one who knows how it's done. The work was Yours before it was mine. Show me who to ask, and give me the patience to let them get it wrong beside me, as someone once let me. When the time comes, help me put it down and be glad. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Cry That Reaches God's Ears
thematicGuides.hook: God heard slaves groaning in Egypt, and James says the cries of unpaid harvesters reach the same ears.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: And now the cry of the Israelites has reached me, and I have seen the way the Egyptians are oppressing them.
thematicGuides.intro: It's natural to think God's attention is mostly on prayer and singing, and that pay, rent and court cases belong to another department. There's something in that, since He does ask to be worshipped. But Exodus, Amos and James each describe a sound rising to Him from earth, and none of the three keeps those departments apart.
story: Early in Exodus, under a new king, Egypt put slave masters over the Israelites, who built Pharaoh's store cities and worked in brick and mortar. It went on for a long period, long enough for a king to die. The Israelites groaned and cried out, and their cry "went up to God". Here the book gives God four verbs in two verses. He heard, He remembered His covenant (His binding promise) with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, He looked, and He was concerned. In the next chapter He tells Moses so Himself, names the slave drivers as the cause, and adds that He has come down to rescue His people. When the slaves were later told that the LORD had seen their misery, they bowed down and worshipped.

Centuries later Israel had kings and law courts of its own, and God sent Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa in Judah, north to preach there. In one chapter Amos mentions stone mansions and lush vineyards alongside a tax on the poor man's grain and bribes in the courts. Religion was thriving too, with festivals, burnt offerings, choice fellowship offerings and harps. God's verdict, through Amos, is "I hate, I despise your religious festivals; your assemblies are a stench to me." He will not accept the offerings, and He calls the songs noise. The God who heard groaning from the brickfields of Egypt is here refusing to hear music from the descendants of those slaves.

Deuteronomy told employers to pay a poor hired worker each day before sunset. Otherwise, it warned, "they may cry to the LORD against you". In the letter of James that cry arrives. Near the end James goes for the rich landowners. The wages they kept back from the workers who mowed their fields are crying out against them, he says, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty. In Exodus God said the same of the slaves' cry, that it had reached Him. Then James turns to his brothers and sisters and tells them to be patient until the Lord's coming, as a farmer waits for the autumn and spring rains.

keyVerses.text: I have indeed seen the misery of my people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their slave drivers, and I am concerned about their suffering. So I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians
Away with the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps. But let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream!
Look! The wages you failed to pay the workers who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty.

insights: Perhaps you're the one being cheated, and nobody in power has noticed. Exodus and James both say that kind of cry is heard. Neither promises it will be put right quickly, and in Exodus things got worse first, when Pharaoh took away the brickmakers' straw. Speak up anyway, as the slaves did, and tell someone who can act, such as a manager, a union rep or an advice service.

Amos's hearers were regular, generous worshippers, and the charge against them was about grain taxes and courtrooms. Ask who might have a fair complaint against you. It could be a tenant still waiting for their deposit, or a cleaner or babysitter you pay less than you'd accept yourself.
reflectQuestions: Who near you is being underpaid or pushed around so routinely that it has come to seem normal?
Which unfairness, close to home or far away, still bothers you after everyone else has stopped talking about it?
thematicGuides.practice: On the back of a receipt, write the name of one person you know who is being treated unfairly at work or over money they're owed, and under it God's words from Exodus 3:7, "I have indeed seen the misery of my people". Keep it in your wallet or phone case for a month. Each time you pay for something, ask God whether there's anything He wants you to do for that person.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, hear the one whose name I've written down, as You heard slaves groaning over bricks and harvesters who were never paid. Send me if I'm the one to send. I'm on the other side of this too. I like a low price and I don't ask who made it low. If anyone has cause to cry out to You because of me, show me who, and help me put it right before I next sing to You. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Abram Lets Lot Choose First
thematicGuides.hook: Abram gave his nephew first pick of the land, and Isaac walked away from two wells his own men had dug.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.
thematicGuides.intro: When Genesis reports that Abram's herders and Lot's had started quarrelling, it adds a sentence that seems to belong somewhere else: "The Canaanites and Perizzites were also living in the land at that time." The two men were newcomers in a country that already had people in it. Plenty of quarrels start because something is short, and whoever moves first to end one usually comes away with less.
story: Abram came back from Egypt rich, and his nephew Lot had flocks and herds of his own. The land couldn't support both, and their herders began to quarrel. Abram was the elder, and God had promised this land to his offspring. He told Lot that close relatives shouldn't quarrel, and gave the choice away: whichever way Lot went, he would go the other. Lot looked around, saw that the plain of the Jordan was well watered, and chose it for himself. After he had gone, the LORD told Abram to look around as well, and said that all the land he could see would be given to him and his offspring.

Abram was later renamed Abraham, and his son Isaac farmed among the Philistines at Gerar and grew so rich that they envied him. Their king, Abimelek, told him to go: "you have become too powerful for us." Isaac went. His servants dug in the valley and struck fresh water, and the herders of Gerar said it was theirs. He named the well Esek, meaning dispute, and his men dug another. That was quarrelled over too, so he called it Sitnah, opposition, and moved on. Nobody contested the third. Later Abimelek came with two of his officials, wanting a treaty. Isaac asked them, "Why have you come to me, since you were hostile to me and sent me away?" They answered that they had always treated him well. Isaac made them a feast, and in the morning they swore an oath and left in peace.

In the sermon where Jesus said peacemakers would be called children of God, He described someone at the altar with a gift, who remembers there that a brother or sister has something against them. Leave the gift in front of the altar, He said, go and be reconciled first, then come back and offer it. The altar was in Jerusalem, and He was speaking on a hillside in Galilee, days away on foot. In His example it is the other person who has the grievance, so the one He sends is the one in the wrong, or thought to be. He doesn't say what to do if the brother refuses.

keyVerses.text: So Abram said to Lot, 'Let's not have any quarreling between you and me, or between your herders and mine, for we are close relatives. Is not the whole land before you? Let's part company. If you go to the left, I'll go to the right; if you go to the right, I'll go to the left.'

Therefore, if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and offer your gift.
Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, since as members of one body you were called to peace. And be thankful.

insights: Abram was the elder and held the promise, and Abimelek himself said Isaac had grown too powerful for his people. Each gave way from the stronger position. Abram's reason was that he and Lot were close relatives, and Paul later gave Christians much the same one, that they were called to peace as members of one body.
Isaac made peace without pretending. He named the lost wells Dispute and Opposition, and he told Abimelek to his face that he had been hostile. Then he fed him.

Paul wrote, "If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone." Sometimes it isn't possible, and part of it depends on the other person. None of this means giving way to someone who is harming you. If that's where you are, getting safe comes before making peace. Tell someone who can help you do that.
reflectQuestions: When you think of the person you most need to make peace with, what has kept you from making the first move?
In a quarrel going on around you at home, at work or among friends, what could you give up or say that might help end it?
thematicGuides.practice: Think of a small running dispute with someone you're safe with, such as whose turn it is to host or who gets the car on Saturday. Before the week is out, go to that person, say you'd sooner not quarrel over it, and give them first choice. Don't point out that you've done it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I like the idea of peace, and I like winning more. You know the quarrel I mean, and that I've been waiting for them to come to me. Give me the courage to go first and let them have the pick. Let Your peace rule in my heart before I open my mouth. If the other person won't have peace however I come, show me when to move on. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Faith as Small as a Mustard Seed
thematicGuides.hook: The disciples asked Jesus for more faith, and He told them a seed's worth would do.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I do believe; help me overcome my unbelief!
thematicGuides.intro: Take a message in a group chat: a friend's scan has come back clear, and she thanks everyone for praying. You're glad, and you also think of the person you prayed for just as hard who didn't get better.
