Sooner or later the thought comes that the difference was faith, and behind it is Jesus' line about faith that moves mountains. He said it to disciples who had just failed in public, and what He told them was how little faith it takes.
story: The Twelve had already driven out many demons with authority Jesus gave them. But while He was up a mountain with Peter, James and John, a man brought the other disciples his son, who had seizures and often fell into fire or water, and they couldn't heal him. Jesus came down to find teachers of the law arguing with them. The father asked Him to help if He could. Jesus picked up the 'if' and said that everything is possible for the one who believes, and the man exclaimed, "I do believe; help me overcome my unbelief!" Jesus rebuked the demon, it came out, and the boy was healed. Indoors afterwards, the disciples asked Him why they couldn't drive it out. He said it was because they had so little faith, and then that faith as small as a mustard seed could move a mountain.

Another time Jesus told His disciples that if a brother or sister wronged them they were to tell them so, and if that person came back seven times in one day saying they repented, they must forgive every time. The apostles' answer was to ask Him for more faith. He said faith the size of a mustard seed could send a mulberry tree into the sea. He also described a servant who comes in from ploughing and still has his master's supper to cook, and gets no thanks, because he has only done what he was told.

In the week before the cross, Jesus went up to a fig tree in leaf, found no fruit on it and said that no one would eat from it again. The next morning they passed it and it had withered from the roots. Peter remembered and pointed it out. Jesus answered, "Have faith in God." He went on to speak of telling a mountain to throw itself into the sea, and of asking in prayer and believing you have received it. And anyone who stands praying while holding something against someone, He said, must forgive them.

keyVerses.text: Then the disciples came to Jesus in private and asked, 'Why couldn't we drive it out?' He replied, 'Because you have so little faith. Truly I tell you, if you have faith as small as a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move. Nothing will be impossible for you.'

The apostles said to the Lord, 'Increase our faith!' He replied, 'If you have faith as small as a mustard seed, you can say to this mulberry tree, 'Be uprooted and planted in the sea,' and it will obey you.'

Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. And when you stand praying, if you hold anything against anyone, forgive them, so that your Father in heaven may forgive you your sins.

insights: Jesus told those disciples their faith was too small and, in the next sentence, that the smallest faith would be enough. Both can be true if the faith that counts is the kind that asks. In Mark, His answer is that a spirit like this one comes out only by prayer, and prayer is asking God to do it.

Jesus said "so little faith" to men He had already given authority for this very work, on a day when they failed at it, and that gives no rule for why your prayer went unanswered. Jesus Himself asked in Gethsemane to be spared and was not, and Paul left his friend Trophimus ill at Miletus and blamed nobody's faith. If you're ill, keep asking and keep seeing your doctor.

In Luke the seed sits between a command to forgive and a servant who just does what he was told. In Mark a command to forgive follows the mountain. Sometimes the thing that won't move is a grudge, and the faith you have is enough to start on it.
reflectQuestions: What in your life looks as fixed as a mountain right now, the thing you've almost given up praying about?
What problem have you been working at by yourself for a long time without asking God to act in it?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, on your own, think of the one request you've quietly stopped making because you doubted it would do any good. Ask God for it once, out loud, in a plain sentence, and add the father's prayer from Mark 9:24, that you do believe and need help with your unbelief. Don't try to feel surer than you are.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I've been treating faith as something I have to produce before You'll listen, and I can't produce it. What I have is small, and some days I'm not sure it's there at all. I stopped asking You about this because I didn't want to be disappointed again. I'm asking again now, knowing You may still say no. And show me who I'm still holding something against. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: By Faith, and Still Not Rescued
thematicGuides.hook: Hebrews 11 commends those who escaped the sword and those who died by it, and says none received what was promised.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: For we live by faith, not by sight.
thematicGuides.intro: You've kept praying and kept doing what you believe is right, and so far there is nothing to show for it. Paul's line about living by faith and not by sight is usually quoted to keep people going until things come right. He wrote it in a paragraph about dying. Hebrews 11, the Bible's list of people who lived by faith, is just as sober once you're past Noah and Abraham, and kinder to someone in your position than a promise of a happy ending would be.
story: Abraham and Sarah, the writer of Hebrews says, died still living by faith, having only seen what was promised and welcomed it from far off. They could have gone back to the country they came from, and didn't. Further on he says he has no time to tell the rest one by one. Through faith, people shut the mouths of lions and escaped "the edge of the sword". Women received their dead back, raised to life. The same verse goes on to others, who were tortured and refused release. Some were sawn in two, some were killed by the sword, and some went about in sheepskins and lived in caves and holes in the ground. He commends every one of them for their faith, the ones in the caves along with the ones who escaped.

Moses grew up as the son of Pharaoh's daughter. As a grown man, Hebrews says, he refused the title and chose to be mistreated with God's people, counting disgrace for the sake of Christ as worth more than the treasures of Egypt. In Exodus he went out to his own people, killed an Egyptian who was beating one of them, and fled from Pharaoh to Midian, where he sat down by a well. Everything he had given up could be seen and counted. What he had instead comes in a phrase that contradicts itself: "he persevered because he saw him who is invisible." At Sinai Moses asked to see God's glory and was told that no one could see His face and live.

Paul had earned his living in Corinth making tents. Writing to the church there, he calls the body "the earthly tent we live in" and says that if it is destroyed a building from God is waiting, a house no human hands built. Meanwhile, he says, we groan in this tent and are weighed down. For now, being at home in the body means being away from the Lord. The famous line comes straight after, and in this paragraph it just states a fact. We can't see Him yet. What Paul does have is the Spirit, given as a deposit on what is coming, and one aim that holds whether he lives or dies, which is to please the Lord.

keyVerses.text: Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.
These were all commended for their faith, yet none of them received what had been promised, since God had planned something better for us so that only together with us would they be made perfect.
Therefore we are always confident and know that as long as we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord. For we live by faith, not by sight.

insights: Hebrews 11 never ranks its people. How things ended is no measure of how well someone trusted God. If your rescue hasn't come, this chapter gives you no grounds for deciding you believed too little.
God planned that the people of Hebrews 11 would be made complete only together with us. Abraham and Moses are still waiting too, and for the same day you are.
Paul's aim held however things went for him. He meant to please the Lord whether he lived or died, and that aim is open to you on a day when nothing seems to be happening.
reflectQuestions: Which part of your life are you waiting to see settled before you'll trust God with it?
Looking back at a time that made no sense while you were in it, what, if anything, can you see now that you couldn't see then?
thematicGuides.practice: This week, write one sentence about yourself in the form Hebrews 11 uses. Begin 'By faith', add your name, then the thing you're keeping on with this year without being able to see how it ends. Date it and leave the outcome off the page, as the chapter often does. Keep it somewhere you'll come across it again, in a paper Bible at Hebrews 11 if you have one.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I keep a private tally of the prayers that worked and the ones that didn't, and I use it to decide how far to trust You. I'd like to stop. I don't know how this will end, or whether I'll be one of the rescued. Keep me going anyway, and let me do today what pleases You and leave the tally alone. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Flaming Arrows and the Shield of Faith
thematicGuides.hook: Peter's resolve didn't last the night, and a psalm of David names a better shield.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one.
thematicGuides.intro: The man who told Christians to take up the shield of faith was a prisoner when he wrote it. The flaming arrows Paul writes of might reach you as an old accusation, or as the suspicion that God has stopped listening. So it's worth knowing what that shield is, and whether it depends on how hard you can believe on a bad day.
story: Near the end of his letter Paul tells the Ephesians to be strong in the Lord's power and put on the full armour of God, so that they can stand, a word he uses four times in four verses. Two of the pieces were God's own first. In Isaiah 59 He puts on righteousness as a breastplate and the helmet of salvation. The shield, Paul says, is faith, and with it his readers can put out every flaming arrow the evil one sends. His word for the shield is the one for the long kind a Roman foot soldier carried, which covered most of his body. Then the man who calls himself "an ambassador in chains" asks them, twice, to pray that he will speak without fear.

Psalm 28 carries David's name and opens with him in trouble. He lifts his hands towards God's Most Holy Place and asks Him not to turn a deaf ear. If God stays silent, he says, he will be like those who go down to the pit. At verse 6 the psalm turns to praise, because the LORD has heard his cry for mercy. Next he calls the LORD his strength and his shield. By the last two verses he has stopped saying 'my' and is praying for the whole people, that God would be their shepherd and carry them for ever.

At the Last Supper Jesus told Simon Peter that Satan had asked to sift all the disciples like wheat. He had prayed for Simon by name, He said, that his faith would not fail, and once Simon had turned back he was to strengthen his brothers. Peter replied that he was ready for prison and death. Before the rooster crowed he had sat by a fire in the high priest's courtyard and denied three times that he knew Jesus, the first time to a servant girl. He went outside and wept bitterly. In his first letter he tells churches suffering for their faith to resist the devil, standing firm, and calls them people "who through faith are shielded by God's power".

keyVerses.text: The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in him, and he helps me.
Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you as wheat. But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.

Be alert and of sober mind. Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour. Resist him, standing firm in the faith, because you know that the family of believers throughout the world is undergoing the same kind of sufferings.

insights: David calls the LORD his shield and, in the same sentence, says his heart trusts in Him. God does the shielding, and faith gets you behind Him, so Paul's shield of faith doesn't depend on how hard you can believe. Peter's own resolve lasted a few hours. Jesus had prayed for him before it gave way, and Romans 8:34 says He is interceding for us now.

The shield of faith didn't keep Paul out of chains. One verse after telling his readers they are shielded by God's power, Peter adds that they may have had to suffer grief in all kinds of trials. His promise is that their inheritance is kept in heaven, and that God will guard them until they come into it.

Paul and Peter both treat the devil as real, and neither asks you to work out which troubles are his doing. Doubt can come from grief or an honest question. Whatever the source, both letters say to stand firm.
reflectQuestions: Which fear or accusation has come back at you most often in the past few weeks?
What are you facing that you already know your own resolve won't be enough for?
thematicGuides.practice: David prayed Psalm 28 with his hands lifted. The next time a fear or an accusation comes at you this week, go somewhere you can be alone for two minutes, even the bathroom. Stand, hold your hands out, palms open, and tell God what has hit you. Keep them open while you say David's words, "The LORD is my strength and my shield".
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I've been trying to hold my faith up by effort, and it isn't working. More than once I've gone quiet about You in front of people whose good opinion I wanted. Be my strength and my shield, as You were David's. You knew Simon would give way, and You had already prayed for him. I'm counting on the same. When I've given way, turn me back, and make me some use to someone else. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Faith Without Deeds: Rahab and the Two Spies
thematicGuides.hook: James says faith without deeds is dead, and one of his two proofs is a woman in Jericho with spies hidden under flax on her roof.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.
thematicGuides.intro: Ask most people what faith is and they'll describe something that goes on inside you, what you hold to be true about God and what you'd say if somebody asked. There's sense in that, since nobody can act on what they don't believe. James asks what use the belief is if nothing ever comes of it, and he calls two people as evidence. One is Abraham, the father of Israel. The other is a prostitute from Jericho, the city Israel was about to attack.
story: James puts a case. A brother or sister is without clothes and without food for the day. Someone in the church says, "Go in peace; keep warm and well fed," and does nothing about either need. James asks what good that is. Even the demons believe there is one God, he adds, and shudder. He goes on to Abraham, who believed God and, many years later, was ready to offer his son Isaac on the altar until God stopped him. James says his faith was made complete by what he did. Then, in a single sentence, he adds Rahab, who gave lodging to Israel's spies and sent them off another way.

Joshua sent two spies across the Jordan to look over Jericho, and they stayed at the house of a prostitute named Rahab. The king was told that same night and sent word to her to bring the men out. She had already taken them up to her roof and hidden them under stalks of flax laid out there. She told the king's men that the strangers had left at dusk, and that if they hurried they might catch them. The book of Joshua reports the lie and passes no comment on it. The pursuers set off for the fords of the Jordan, and the city gate was shut behind them.

Before the spies lay down, Rahab went up to the roof and told them she knew the LORD had given Israel the land. All Jericho had heard how He dried up the Red Sea, forty years before, and everyone's courage had failed, hers included. She asked the men to swear that her family would be spared. They agreed, on condition that she tied a scarlet cord in her window and gathered her family indoors. Her house was part of the city wall, so she let them down through that window by a rope. Once they had gone she tied the cord there. When Jericho fell, the same two men went in and brought out Rahab, her parents, her brothers and sisters and all who belonged to her.

keyVerses.text: When we heard of it, our hearts melted in fear and everyone's courage failed because of you, for the LORD your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below.

In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute considered righteous for what she did when she gave lodging to the spies and sent them off in a different direction? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.
By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies, was not killed with those who were disobedient.

insights: Everyone in Jericho had heard what Rahab had heard, and all of them were afraid. James says the demons believe too, and shudder. What marked Rahab out from her neighbours was that she took the spies in and tied a cord in her window.

Hebrews 11 says Rahab welcomed the spies by faith. James says she was considered righteous for what she did. They are describing the same night. Paul, who insists we are saved by grace and not by works, also writes that what counts is faith expressing itself through love.

The person in James's scene says nothing wrong, and wishing someone warmth and a full stomach is kind. The trouble is that the speaker is near enough to do something about it and doesn't. The deed James has in mind is that close to home. You can see the need, and you already have what would meet it.
reflectQuestions: If someone could see only how you spent your time and money this past week, what would they conclude you believe?
Where, this month, would acting on what you believe cost you something?
thematicGuides.practice: Notice one moment each day this week when you wish somebody well, even a passing 'hope it goes all right'. Before you go to bed, do one small thing to back it up, such as texting the offer of a lift with a day and a time, or putting the thing you said you'd lend by the front door.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, show me who is near enough for me to help this week. Most days what I believe about You gets no further than my head, and I've told people I would pray for them and then forgotten to. Rahab was as frightened as everyone else in Jericho, and she still took two strangers up to her roof. Let what I believe get as far as my hands. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Engraved on the Palms of His Hands
thematicGuides.hook: God tells a ruined city she is engraved on His hands, and Paul's list of what can't separate us is mostly his own history.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: See, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are ever before me.
thematicGuides.intro: The hard part of believing God loves you without conditions is that almost nothing else works that way. Your job and a fair few friendships depend on how you're doing, so after a bad week it seems natural that God has cooled as well. When trouble comes and stays, it can look like proof that He has let go. Isaiah has Jerusalem say it out loud, and Paul answers it with a list drawn from his own life.
story: Isaiah 49 promises a ruined people that they are coming home. Captives are told to come out, and heaven and earth are told to shout for joy because the LORD comforts His people. Zion, meaning Jerusalem, answers with something else: "The LORD has forsaken me, the Lord has forgotten me." God replies that a mother might forget the baby at her breast, and He will not. He has engraved Zion on the palms of His hands, He says, and her walls are always in front of Him. In the same speech He speaks of her as ruined and made desolate, with her people still to return. Those are the walls He means.

Acts first mentions Paul as Saul, the young man who had coats laid at his feet while Stephen was being stoned. He approved of the killing. Then he went from house to house in Jerusalem, dragging men and women off to prison. This is the man who asks, in his letter to Rome, who will bring any charge against those God has chosen. His answer is that God has already declared them in the right, and that Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at God's right hand speaking up for them.

Five times Paul was given thirty-nine lashes, and once he was stoned. When he set it all down for the church in Corinth he used the word danger eight times, and added hunger, cold and going without clothes. So when he asks the Romans what could separate us from Christ's love, and names trouble, hardship, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger and sword, he is mostly reading from his own record. Then he quotes a line from Psalm 44 about facing death all day long. The people who first sang it said they had kept faith with God and were suffering anyway, and the psalm's next words tell God to wake up. Paul's next words are, "in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us."

keyVerses.text: Can a mother forget the baby at her breast and have no compassion on the child she has borne? Though she may forget, I will not forget you! See, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are ever before me.

Who will bring any charge against those whom God has chosen? It is God who justifies. Who then is the one who condemns? No one. Christ Jesus who died, more than that, who was raised to life, is at the right hand of God and is also interceding for us.

For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

insights: The promise that her people were coming back was Zion's. Paul's is the one you can take as your own. Hunger and danger had come to him and may come to you, and he says that when they do they are no sign God has stopped loving you.
Paul deals with the charge sheet before the hardships. If what makes God feel far off is something you've done, start with verses 33 and 34, written by a man who had dragged Christians to prison.
Zion said out loud that the LORD had forgotten her, and Isaiah kept it in, so you can say it too when that's how things look.
reflectQuestions: The last time God felt a long way off, what had you done, or what had happened, that made you assume He had pulled back?
If you were as convinced as Paul that nothing can separate you from God's love, how would you come to Him after a bad week?
thematicGuides.practice: Paul told the church in Corinth what he had done and what had been done to him. One evening this week, ring a friend who prays, or go and see them, and tell them the thing that most makes you think God has let go of you, whether you did it or it happened to you. Two sentences will do. Then ask whether they've ever thought the same.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, when I've let You down I keep away for a few days, as if You needed time to calm down. When things go badly I assume You've lost interest. Zion said she was forgotten, so I'm telling You that some days I feel forgotten too. I find it easier to picture Jesus keeping a record than speaking up for me. I can't talk myself into feeling loved, so keep hold of me when I don't. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Lawyer Who Asked About His Neighbour
thematicGuides.hook: A lawyer asked Jesus who counted as his neighbour, and the Law he had just quoted told Israel to love the foreigner among them.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The expert in the law replied, 'The one who had mercy on him.' Jesus told him, 'Go and do likewise.'
thematicGuides.intro: Luke says why the lawyer asked Jesus who his neighbour was: he wanted to justify himself. He had just quoted the command to love his neighbour as himself and been told to go and do it. We ask his question too, when we wonder whether loving our neighbour has to cover the colleague nobody likes or the man asleep in the shop doorway, and it's easy to ask it for the same reason.
story: An expert in the Jewish law stood up to test Jesus, and asked what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus asked him what the Law said and how he read it. So it is the lawyer who gives the well-known answer, joining two commands from different books. Loving God with everything you have comes from Deuteronomy, and loving your neighbour as yourself from Leviticus 19. They are the same two commands Jesus names in Mark 12 when He is asked which matters most. Jesus said the lawyer had answered correctly and told him, "Do this and you will live." The lawyer's next question was who his neighbour was.

In the story Jesus told, a man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho was attacked by robbers, who stripped him, beat him and left him half dead. A priest happened to be going down the same road, saw the man and passed by on the other side. A Levite, from the tribe that served in the temple, came to the place, saw him and did the same. The third man on the road was a Samaritan. Only a chapter earlier in Luke, a Samaritan village had refused to take Jesus in because He was heading for Jerusalem, and James and John had asked whether to call fire down on it. This Samaritan saw what the other two had seen, took pity on the man and went to him.

The Samaritan bandaged the man's wounds, pouring on oil and wine, put him on his own donkey, brought him to an inn and took care of him. The next day he gave the innkeeper two denarii, about two days' pay for a labourer, asked him to look after the man, and promised to cover any extra cost on his way back. Then Jesus asked the lawyer which of the three had been a neighbour to the man who was robbed. The lawyer said it was the one who had mercy on him, an answer that leaves out the word Samaritan. Jesus told him to go and do the same.

keyVerses.text: 'Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind' and, 'Love your neighbor as yourself.'

When a foreigner resides among you in your land, do not mistreat them. The foreigner residing among you must be treated as your native-born. Love them as yourself, for you were foreigners in Egypt. I am the LORD your God.
'Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?' The expert in the law replied, 'The one who had mercy on him.' Jesus told him, 'Go and do likewise.'

insights: The verse the lawyer quoted, Leviticus 19:18, is about how to treat "anyone among your people". Further down the same chapter Israel is told to love the foreigner living among them 'as yourself' too, since they had been foreigners in Egypt. The Law he was quoting had already carried those two words past his own people.
You can't work out in advance who you owe help to. In the story Jesus told, that gets settled on the road, by who happens to be lying there.

'As yourself' on that road came to bandages, a ride on the Samaritan's own donkey and a paid bed. He also went on with his trip, having paid someone better placed to carry on and promised to come back. You don't have to be the whole answer to someone's trouble.
reflectQuestions: On an ordinary day, who do you see between your front door and the shops, or your desk, and walk straight past?
What is one thing you could do for the person you find hardest to like because they're so unlike you?
thematicGuides.practice: Most of us have someone we see nearly every day and have never properly spoken to, like the man who waits at the same bus stop. This week, go over, ask how things are, and stay for the answer even if it takes ten minutes. If something comes up that you could help with, offer one thing and name the day.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I'm good at seeing people and carrying on. I usually have a reason, and it usually sounds sensible. Show me who I'm about to walk past this week. Get me across the road, and give me the sense to fetch someone else when the need is bigger than I am. Thank You for the people who came over to me when I needed it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: David, Saul and Loving Your Enemy
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus names small things to do for an enemy. David spared Saul in a cave, and then kept well out of his reach.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be children of your Father in heaven.
thematicGuides.intro: There may be a car you look for outside your mother's house or the church hall, and when it's there you come back later. Most people have someone they avoid like that. For some it's a falling-out that was never mended, and for some the reason is real harm. Jesus told His followers to love their enemies, and Matthew 5 records what He asked them to do about it.
story: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus quoted a saying His hearers knew: love your neighbour and hate your enemy. The first half is in the law of Moses. The second isn't. The law says that when you see the donkey of someone who hates you fallen under its load, you must stop and help them with it. Jesus told them to love their enemies and pray for the people persecuting them, and His reason was the weather. Their Father sends sun and rain on good people and bad, and His children should take after Him. Then He asked them about saying hello. "And if you greet only your own people, what are you doing more than others?"

Paul had once gone from house to house in Jerusalem, dragging believers off to prison. Years later he told the church in Rome to bless those who persecuted them. He went on, "If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone." Peace also depends on the other person, and Paul allowed for that. Revenge he ruled out altogether, since avenging belongs to God, who has said He will repay. In its place he quoted a proverb about giving a hungry or thirsty enemy food and drink. The proverb goes on to speak of heaping burning coals on the enemy's head. Nobody is sure what that picture meant, but the food and drink are clear.

King Saul had more than once thrown a spear at David, and was now hunting him near En Gedi with three thousand men. Saul stepped into a cave to relieve himself. David and his men were far back inside it, and the men said the LORD had handed him his enemy. David crept forward and cut a corner off Saul's robe, and afterwards even that troubled his conscience. He would not let his men attack. When Saul had gone, David followed him out, bowed to the ground and held up the piece of cloth. He told Saul to his face that he had done him no wrong and was being hunted for his life. Saul wept aloud and said, "You have treated me well, but I have treated you badly." Then Saul went home, and David went back up to the stronghold. Two chapters later Saul was after him again.

keyVerses.text: But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be children of your Father in heaven. He causes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.

Do not take revenge, my dear friends, but leave room for God's wrath, for it is written: 'It is mine to avenge; I will repay,' says the Lord. On the contrary: 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals on his head.' Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
May the LORD judge between you and me. And may the LORD avenge the wrongs you have done to me, but my hand will not touch you.

insights: Everything Jesus and Paul name here is something to do, whether a prayer, a greeting or a meal. Each can be done while you're still angry. Neither Jesus nor Paul asks you to feel differently first.

Loving an enemy doesn't mean going back within their reach. David spared Saul, heard him weep, and still went up to the stronghold. If someone is hurting you, get to safety and tell a person who can help.
Going to the police is not revenge. A few verses after ruling revenge out, Paul calls the authorities God's servants, there to punish wrongdoing.
reflectQuestions: When you think of praying by name for someone who has wronged you, what happens in you?
David spared Saul and still kept his distance. What good could you do the person you find hardest without going nearer than is safe for you?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose someone you've been avoiding who is no danger to you, such as the neighbour you fell out with over a hedge. The next time you see them this week, greet them first, by name, and ask one ordinary question. Leave out anyone who has harmed you or frightens you, and pick someone easier.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, there's a name I'd rather not say to You. I can't feel kindly towards this person yet, and I'm not sure I want to. You were good to me while I was still against You. Please be good to them today. Keep me from the revenge I've rehearsed. Judge between me and them, as David asked, because I can't judge it fairly myself. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Errand That Nearly Killed Epaphroditus
thematicGuides.hook: The greatest love, Jesus said, lays down its life for friends, and Epaphroditus came close to that on an errand for his church.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one's life for one's friends.
thematicGuides.intro: Nobody is likely to ask you to die for them. What you will be asked for is an evening, or money you had other plans for, usually when it doesn't suit. So it's fair to wonder what Jesus' words about laying down your life have to do with a week like yours. Paul's letter to the Philippians has an answer in it.
story: Judas had gone out into the night when Jesus told the eleven who were left that He had loved them as the Father had loved Him. He gave them one command, to love each other the same way. The greatest love, He said, is to lay down your life for your friends, and He went straight on to call them His friends. He no longer called them servants, because He had told them everything He had learned from His Father. Of His own life He had said, "No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord." By the next afternoon He had done it.

Paul asked the church at Philippi to do nothing out of selfish ambition. He had already told them about people who were preaching Christ out of exactly that, supposing they could stir up trouble for him while he was in chains. The Philippians were to value others above themselves, and each to look to the interests of the others. In their dealings with one another, he wrote, they should have the mindset of Christ Jesus, who was in very nature God and did not use that for His own advantage. He made Himself nothing and humbled Himself as far as death on a cross. Every step down is His own doing, and only after the cross does Paul write that God exalted Him.

The Christians at Philippi had sent one of their own, Epaphroditus, to Paul in prison, carrying their gifts and charged with looking after him. While he was away he fell ill and almost died. What distressed Epaphroditus, Paul wrote, was that the people at home had heard he was ill. He recovered, and Paul called that God's mercy, on Epaphroditus and on himself as well. Paul decided to send him home, and told the church to welcome him with great joy and to honour people like him, because he had risked his life doing for Paul what they could not do themselves. Everyone, he had just written, looks out for their own interests. He named two men who didn't, Timothy and Epaphroditus.

keyVerses.text: My command is this: Love each other as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one's life for one's friends.

Who, being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness. And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross!
So then, welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honor people like him, because he almost died for the work of Christ. He risked his life to make up for the help you yourselves could not give me.

insights: Jesus said no one takes His life from Him. What someone takes from you by fear or force is a different thing from what you give, and if you're being mistreated, say so to someone you trust.
Jesus' command to love each other was given to everyone in the room. It runs both ways, so somebody is meant to be looking out for you too.

We have no sermon from Epaphroditus and no letter. He carried a gift and looked after a prisoner, and Paul sets him in the same chapter as Christ's obedience to death and says to honour people like him. You probably know one or two.
reflectQuestions: What has someone given up for your sake that you only understood the cost of later?
Among the people closest to you, where do you usually get your own way?
thematicGuides.practice: For the next seven days, go without one small thing you normally keep for yourself, such as lunch out or the hour on your phone after supper. Spend the money or the hour on one particular person, and don't tell them what you went without. If you're already worn thin from looking after someone, skip this, and say yes the next time somebody offers to help.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I like the thought of laying down my life more than I like being asked for a lift at a bad time. I notice what I give, and I want it noticed. Thank You for the people who carried things to me at a cost I never saw. Show me whose interests I've been stepping over, and help me do one thing for them this week that nobody hears about. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Love Is Patient: Paul to a Quarrelling Church
thematicGuides.hook: The words read at weddings were first sent to a church whose members were suing each other and competing over gifts.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud.
thematicGuides.intro: Paul was in Ephesus when word reached him from Chloe's household that the church in Corinth, which he had spent a year and a half starting, was quarrelling. The letter we call 1 Corinthians is his reply to that news and to questions the church had sent him, and nearly every line of its thirteenth chapter answers something they were doing to each other. Read that way, it has something to say about a family row or a difficult colleague, and about a marriage too.
story: The church in Corinth had lined up behind its favourite teachers, some members saying they followed Paul and others Apollos. Paul told them he had planted the seed, Apollos had watered it, and the two of them were co-workers. Believers were taking each other to court. At the Lord's Supper some went ahead with their own meals, so that one went hungry while another got drunk. Even the gifts of the Spirit, such as prophecy and speaking in tongues, had become something to compete over, and Paul gave three chapters to them. Partway through he said he would show them "the most excellent way", and chapter 13 follows.

Paul began chapter 13 with himself. He wrote that if he spoke with the tongues of angels, understood every mystery and gave away everything he owned, but had no love, he would be a clanging cymbal and gain nothing. Line after line of the list that follows has its opposite earlier in the letter. Love does not envy, and he had already named the jealousy among them. It does not boast, and he had asked why they boasted of what they were only given. About a scandal they had put up with he had written, "And you are proud!" Now he told them love is not proud. The people who ate their private suppers heard that it is not self-seeking, and the people with lawsuits that it keeps no record of wrongs.

Prophecy, tongues and knowledge, Paul wrote, all belong to a time of knowing in part, and will stop when completeness comes. The Corinthians were proud of what they knew. He had warned them that "knowledge puffs up while love builds up", and now he said that even he knew only in part. Faith, hope and love remain, and love is the greatest. Then he went straight back to how their meetings should run, telling them to follow the way of love and keep eagerly desiring the Spirit's gifts. Near the end of the letter he put it in four words: "Do everything in love."

keyVerses.text: If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have a faith that can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. If I give all I possess to the poor and give over my body to hardship that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It does not dishonor others, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no record of wrongs. Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres.

For now we see only a reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.

insights: The lines about keeping no record of wrongs and always persevering were written to church members keeping score against each other. In the same list love takes no delight in evil, is glad of the truth and always protects. The chapter can't be used to keep you quiet about harm, or to keep you with a person who is harming you.

Giving all you own to the poor is on Paul's list of things that can be done without love, and so is knowing a great deal. Whatever you're good at, his question is whether it is doing the people around you any good.
reflectQuestions: Which one line of Paul's list in verses 4 to 7 would the people you live or work with say you find hardest?
If you stopped adding to the running count you keep of someone's small wrongs, what would change between the two of you?
thematicGuides.practice: Before you go to bed tonight, think back to your most recent disagreement, however small. With 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 open in front of you, go down the list asking only about your own part in it, such as whether you were patient or brought up something old. Pick the one line you'd want to get right if you had that conversation again. Leave the other person's lines to them.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I've heard these words at so many weddings that I stopped thinking they were about me on an ordinary weekday. I'm more patient with strangers than with the people I live with, and I keep a list I know by heart. Show me which entries are small enough to cross out, and give me the courage to speak to the right person about anything that isn't. Thank You for knowing me fully and loving me anyway. Make me a little easier to live with by this time next week. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Miners of Job 28 and the Fear of the Lord
thematicGuides.hook: Job 28 says miners can reach almost anything except wisdom, and Solomon's old age shows a clever man without it.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
thematicGuides.intro: One of the Bible's best-known sayings about wisdom comes at the end of a poem about mining. Job 28 spends eleven verses underground before it asks where wisdom can be found. We tend to treat wisdom as one more thing to be got hold of, given enough experience or good advice. In the poem people can get hold of nearly anything, and this is the exception.
story: Job 28 opens with miners. They cut a shaft far from where anyone lives, and dangle and sway in it. They tunnel through rock, put an end to the darkness down there and bring up silver and gold, iron, copper and lapis lazuli. No falcon has seen the path they open, and no lion has walked it. Then the poem asks, twice, where wisdom comes from and where understanding lives. The deep says it isn't there, and so does the sea. It can't be bought with gold, silver or lapis lazuli, which are the very things the miners brought up. Death has heard only a rumour of it.

In Job 28 God alone knows the way to wisdom, because He sees everything under the heavens. When He set the force of the wind and marked a path for the thunderstorm, He looked at wisdom and tested it. He speaks once in the whole poem, to the human race, and tells them that wisdom is the fear of the Lord and understanding is to shun evil. The book's first verse had used both phrases of Job himself. In chapter 31 Job describes what that looked like when a servant, man or woman, had a grievance against him. He did not deny them justice, because he would be called to account by the God who had made both him and them in the womb.

Solomon's name stands at the head of Proverbs, the book that says wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD. Israel's law told its kings not to gather great numbers of horses or wives, or large amounts of silver and gold, and to read that law daily so they would learn to revere God. Solomon ended up with twelve thousand horses, a thousand wives and concubines, and silver as common in Jerusalem as stones. In his old age his wives turned his heart after other gods. The king who had built the temple built a high place for Chemosh and for Molek on a hill east of Jerusalem. The LORD was angry because Solomon's heart had turned from the God "who had appeared to him twice."

keyVerses.text: But where can wisdom be found? Where does understanding dwell? No mortal comprehends its worth; it cannot be found in the land of the living.
And he said to the human race, 'The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to shun evil is understanding.'
As Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and his heart was not fully devoted to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father had been.

insights: To fear the Lord is to give His word more weight than your own wishes or anyone's opinion of you, because He is God and you will answer to Him. That is different from cowering before someone cruel. In Deuteronomy 10:12 Moses asks Israel to fear the LORD and to love Him in a single sentence.

When 1 Kings sums up Solomon's reign, it still speaks of "the wisdom he displayed" (1 Kings 11:41), while its account of his old age is that his heart turned. You can keep the skill 1 Kings calls wisdom and slowly lose the fear of the LORD that Job 28 calls wisdom.

Job 28 has wisdom hidden from every living thing. Paul tells the Colossians where it is kept, in Christ, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). So a Christian looking for wisdom starts with what Jesus said and did.
reflectQuestions: When you last faced a big decision, where did you go first for help in making it?
Where in an ordinary week does someone else's opinion of you carry more weight than what God has said?
thematicGuides.practice: Each morning for the next seven days, before you look at your phone, read Psalm 111 aloud. It takes about a minute. Most of the psalm's ten verses are about what God has done, and the last is the one about the fear of the LORD being the beginning of wisdom. Daily reading is the method Israel's kings were given for learning to revere God.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, teach me to give what You say the weight it has. I'm more careful around the people who can affect my week than I am around You. I notice their moods and weigh their opinions, and Yours often comes into it late. I don't want to end up old, still clever and facing the wrong way. Where my heart has started to turn, show me, and turn it back. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Proverbs: Straight Paths and Gentle Answers
thematicGuides.hook: Mouldy bread fools Joshua, Gideon talks an angry tribe down and David is told no, each beside the proverb it fits.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.
thematicGuides.intro: Say a sharp message arrives, and you've typed a sharper one back before you've finished reading theirs. Proverbs was written for that half-minute. The book is framed as a father's advice to his son ("My son, do not forget my teaching") and most of it concerns ordinary days: whom to believe, what to say, what to do about tomorrow.
story: A delegation came to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal, asking for a treaty and saying they had travelled from a distant country. The Israelites suspected they might live nearby and said so. The visitors showed their patched sandals and cracked wineskins, and bread they said had been warm when they packed it, now dry and mouldy. Joshua's men "sampled their provisions but did not inquire of the LORD." The treaty was made. Three days later they heard that the visitors were Gibeonites and lived close by. Israel had sworn to it by the LORD, and kept its word.

Gideon had just put the Midianite army to flight with three hundred men when the men of Ephraim, called in after the main battle, challenged him hard over why they hadn't been sent for at the start. Exhausted and still in pursuit, he asked what he had done compared with them, since they had captured two Midianite leaders, and said the gleanings of Ephraim's grapes were better than his own clan's whole harvest. "At this, their resentment against him subsided." Later in Judges, Ephraim brings the same complaint to Jephthah, with a threat to burn his house down. He answers with a grievance of his own, and it ends in a battle with forty-two thousand Ephraimites dead.

David was living in a house of cedar while the ark of God sat in a tent, and he planned to build a temple. The prophet Nathan told him, "Whatever you have in mind, go ahead and do it, for the LORD is with you." That night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, and it was different. David would not build the house. His son would, and God would establish a house for David, meaning a line of kings. Nathan reported it all, and David went in, sat before the LORD and asked who he was that God had brought him this far. Before he died he gathered gold, silver, timber and stone for the temple and handed Solomon the plans for a house he himself had been told not to build.

keyVerses.text: Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
In their hearts humans plan their course, but the LORD establishes their steps.

insights: The chapter that says not to lean on your own understanding calls the person who gains understanding blessed, a few verses later. So you're meant to think. The warning is against putting your full weight on your own reading of things, which is easiest to do when, as with the mouldy bread, the evidence looks good.

A proverb tells you how things usually go and doesn't promise they will. A gentle answer cools most anger and sometimes cools none, and Proverbs 26:4-5 sets two sayings side by side that give opposite advice about answering a fool, leaving you to judge which one the day needs.

Even Nathan, a prophet, told David to go ahead before the word of the LORD had come to him, much as Israel's leaders swore without asking. A plan can be good, and backed by good people, and still not be yours to carry out. Some part of it may be, as the timber and stone were David's.
reflectQuestions: Which decision in front of you are you most sure you've already worked out, without having asked God or anyone else about it?
Looking back over your conversations this past week, which one would have gone differently if your first reply had been gentler?
thematicGuides.practice: This week, pray about a decision you're facing, then take it to one person who knows you well and has nothing to gain from it. Face to face or on the phone, lay out what you plan to do and why. Then ask what you might be missing, and let them finish before you answer. Proverbs 15:22 says plans fail for lack of counsel.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I mostly ask You about a decision once I've made it. I check the bread, like Joshua's men, and then I sign. Slow me down before I answer the next person who annoys me, and give me a kinder answer than the first one that comes. I've grown fond of my plans for this year. Do what You want with them, and when You change my path, help me take it without sulking. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: God's Will: A Night of Prayer, Then a Choice
thematicGuides.hook: Most of God's will is already written down, and for the rest Scripture shows people praying and then choosing.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you.
thematicGuides.intro: You have a decision to make and you want to know what God wants. It might be a job, a relationship, or what to do about a parent who can't manage alone any more. You've prayed, and nothing has come that you could call an answer. The New Testament offers no technique for this, which may be a relief if you've tried a few. It lets you watch Paul plan a journey and Jesus choose the Twelve.
story: Paul had never been to Rome when he wrote Romans, his letter to the Christians there. He had planned many times to visit, he writes, and been prevented every time so far. In chapter 12 he tells them not to be shaped by the world around them but to let their minds be made new, and then they'll be able to test and approve what God's will is. Near the end he sets out his own plan, which is to take a gift to the poor among the believers in Jerusalem and then call at Rome on his way to Spain. He asks them to pray that he'll come "with joy, by God's will". He did arrive, some years later, as a prisoner with a soldier to guard him.

James wrote to believers scattered among the nations, and the first thing he raises is their trials. A few lines in he tells anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God, who gives generously to all and doesn't find fault, so you needn't start by explaining why you ought to know already. But whoever asks must believe and not doubt, he says, because the doubter is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind, and shouldn't expect to receive anything from the Lord. James calls that person double-minded and "unstable in all they do". That describes someone who lives divided, which is a long way from being nervous while you pray.

Jesus had twice clashed with the Pharisees, a strict religious party, over what was allowed on the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest. The second time they were furious and began to discuss what they might do to Him. Around then He went out to a mountainside and spent the night praying to God. When morning came He called His disciples to Him and chose twelve of them to be apostles. Luke then gives their names, from Simon, whom Jesus named Peter, down to the twelfth, "Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor."

keyVerses.text: Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God's will is, his good, pleasing and perfect will.
If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you.
Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus.

insights: Twice in 1 Thessalonians Paul says what God's will is, and neither time is it about a decision. It is that you should be holy (4:3), and that you rejoice, pray and give thanks in all circumstances (5:16-18). That much is settled, and it goes with you whichever way you choose.

James promises wisdom, which is the sense to choose well. He doesn't promise that the choice will be made for you. None of these passages promises a sign or an inner voice, and Christians hold different views on how much God guides in those ways.

A decision can be prayed over and still turn out hard. Paul reached Rome under guard, and the twelve Jesus chose after a night of prayer included Judas. If something you decided with care has gone badly, that alone doesn't show you misread God.
reflectQuestions: In the decision you keep putting off, what exactly are you afraid will happen if you get God's will wrong?
Paul warns against being shaped by the world around you. Whose expectations have the strongest pull on the choices you make?
thematicGuides.practice: Before the week is out, ask one person who knows you well and takes God seriously to give you half an hour. Lay out the decision and every option, including the one you're privately hoping for. Ask what they see that you can't, and whether any option goes against something Scripture makes clear. The choice stays yours.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, You spent a whole night praying before You chose twelve men, and I've been asking for a sign so that I wouldn't have to choose at all. Part of me wants someone to blame if it goes badly. I'm asking for wisdom instead, and for You to stop me if I'm about to choose something You've forbidden. Then give me the courage to decide, and stay with me whatever comes of it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Church Where Not Many Were Wise
thematicGuides.hook: Paul answered a church that prized impressive teachers by pointing at the cross, at himself and at them.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: For the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than human strength.
thematicGuides.intro: Paul was in Ephesus when people from Chloe's household brought him news from Corinth. The church he had started there had split into camps, each claiming a name, Paul's or Apollos's or Peter's, and one claiming Christ's. The camps were proud of their teachers, and Paul's reply, which opens 1 Corinthians, treats the whole quarrel as boasting about wisdom and fine speaking. You may know the instinct behind it as the faint embarrassment about what you believe when the cleverest person in the room is listening.
story: Jesus was crucified at nine in the morning, between two rebels. The chief priests and teachers of the law mocked Him among themselves, saying that He had saved others and couldn't save Himself, and that if He came down from the cross now they would see and believe. He stayed where He was, and that afternoon He died. About twenty years later Paul wrote that Jews demanded signs and Greeks looked for wisdom, and that to them a crucified Messiah looked like neither. To Jews it was a stumbling block, because the law of Moses put anyone hung on a pole under God's curse, and to Gentiles it was simply foolish. But to those God has called, Paul says, the same Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

Paul arrived in Corinth from Athens and made tents with Aquila and Priscilla, a couple who shared his trade. Every Sabbath he argued his case in the synagogue until the opposition turned abusive, and then he moved next door, to the house of Titius Justus. One night the Lord told him in a vision not to be afraid and to keep on speaking. In 1 Corinthians Paul tells it from his side: "I came to you in weakness with great fear and trembling." He had resolved, he says, to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and Him crucified. Some in Corinth later said his letters were weighty and that in person he was unimpressive.

"Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were influential; not many were of noble birth." That is Paul's description of the church in Corinth, written to the church in Corinth. He says not many, and there were a few. Crispus had been leader of the synagogue, and Erastus was the city's director of public works. Others were slaves, whom Paul addresses directly later in the letter, and at the church's shared meal some had nothing. The three things on Paul's list echo Jeremiah 9, where the wise, the strong and the rich are told not to boast, and he closes with that passage's next line: anyone who boasts should boast in the Lord.

keyVerses.text: For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.

But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong. God chose the lowly things of this world and the despised things, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are, so that no one may boast before him.
My message and my preaching were not with wise and persuasive words, but with a demonstration of the Spirit's power, so that your faith might not rest on human wisdom, but on God's power.

insights: The sign the chief priests asked for would have undone what the cross was for. Had Jesus come down, they'd have had their proof and nobody would have been saved. The power Paul sees in Christ crucified was at work in His staying there.
A synagogue leader and a city official sat in the same church as its slaves, and Paul gives one reason for any of them being there: "It is because of him that you are in Christ Jesus."
God chose this way, Paul says, so that no one could boast. That deals with pride, and with the opposite feeling that you're too ordinary to be any use, since your ability was never why He wanted you.
reflectQuestions: In which part of your life does doing what Jesus says look least sensible to the people around you?
What have you held back from because you assumed God would want someone better qualified for it?
thematicGuides.practice: For the next seven days, go without the small boasts. Leave out what you've achieved, who you know and how busy you've been, unless someone needs the information. When you catch one on its way out, let it go, and thank God silently for whatever you were about to take the credit for. At the end of the week, tell Him which was hardest to leave unsaid.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I'd have done it differently. I'd have had You come down from the cross while they were watching, and I'd have chosen cleverer, better-connected people for Your church than the ones in mine, me included. Forgive me for the times I've kept quiet about You so as not to look stupid. Thank You that I'm Yours because of what You did, with no standard to reach first. When I count myself out as too ordinary, bring Corinth to mind. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Lord's Prayer Behind a Closed Door
thematicGuides.hook: Only one line of the prayer Jesus taught gets an explanation from Him, and it is the line about forgiving.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: When you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen.
thematicGuides.intro: Just before the Lord's Prayer, Jesus tells His hearers to pray in a room with the door closed, and the words He gives them next say 'our' and 'us' throughout. If you've known the prayer since childhood, you can probably get from one end of it to the other, in church or half asleep, without a word of it registering.
story: Partway through the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus came to prayer and began with two ways of getting it wrong. Some people loved to pray standing in the synagogues and on street corners, where they would be seen, and being seen, He said, was all the reward they'd get. Others kept on babbling, thinking that many words would get them heard. His answer to the first was a room with the door closed, where only the Father sees. To the second He said, "your Father knows what you need before you ask him." Then came the prayer itself, which is fifty-three words long in the NIV and takes less than half a minute to say.

Go into a room and shut the door, as Jesus said, and the first word of the prayer He gives you is 'Our'. It begins with God's concerns: that His name be hallowed, which means treated as holy, that His kingdom come and His will be done. Then it asks for bread, and only for today's. Israel had been fed like that in the desert, where each morning the ground was covered with thin flakes that Moses said were bread from the LORD. He told them to gather an omer, a set measure, for each person in the tent. Some gathered a lot and some only a little. When it was measured out, whoever had gathered a lot had nothing left over and whoever had gathered little had enough.

When Jesus finished the prayer He went back to one line of it. Those who forgive other people will be forgiven by the Father, He said, and those who will not forgive will not be. It is the only line of the prayer He stops to explain. Matthew's wording speaks of our own forgiving as already done, "as we also have forgiven our debtors". Luke records a shorter form of the prayer, with sins where Matthew has debts. The lines about God's will and about the evil one are missing from it. The bread is still there, and so is the forgiving: "for we also forgive everyone who sins against us."

keyVerses.text: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.
For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins.

insights: The prayer can be short because nothing has to be explained. The Father knows what you need before you ask, and Jesus tells you to ask for bread anyway, the way a child asks a parent who already knows.

You can't pray this prayer for yourself alone. Ask for bread and you've asked for your neighbour's as well. Ask to be forgiven and the person who wronged you has come into the room. Jesus sends you in by yourself and hands you words full of other people.

The line about forgiving is the hard one, and Jesus makes no exception to it. Forgiving someone is still a different thing from trusting them again, or from going back within reach of a person who harmed you. If you can't yet say the line and mean it, you can say it as a request for help.
reflectQuestions: If you said the Lord's Prayer slowly tonight and meant each line, which line would be the hardest to say honestly?
Think of the person who comes to mind when you reach the line about having forgiven your debtors. What stands between you and saying that line about them?
thematicGuides.practice: Before you next shop for food this week, go into a room, shut the door and say the Lord's Prayer once, slowly, listening for each 'us' and 'our'. Then buy a second loaf or a few extra tins and take them to a food bank or a supermarket collection point.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've said Your prayer so often that I can reach the end without having meant a word of it. Slow me down. When I ask for bread, bring to mind who else is asking. When I get to the line about forgiving, there's a name I hurry past, and I need Your help with that one. Thank You that the Father knows what I need before I've found the words for it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Widow Who Kept Coming Back
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus told two stories about asking, and in both the one being asked is nothing like God.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Then Jesus told his disciples a parable to show them that they should always pray and not give up.
thematicGuides.intro: Say you've rung your landlord four times about a broken boiler and nobody has come. By the fifth call you're wondering whether to bother. Praying for the same thing month after month can start to feel like that, and then it's a short step to picturing God as the landlord, not much interested and needing to be nagged. Luke has two stories from Jesus about someone asking, one at a locked door at midnight and one in front of a judge.
story: Jesus had just given His disciples the Lord's Prayer, with its request for daily bread, and He followed it with a story about bread. Suppose, He said, a friend arrives at your house from a journey, you have nothing to give him, and at midnight you go to another friend to borrow three loaves. The answer comes from inside: "Don't bother me. The door is already locked, and my children and I are in bed." Even if friendship won't get him out of bed, Jesus goes on, your "shameless audacity" will, meaning the nerve it takes to stand at a locked door at midnight asking for bread for somebody else. He'll give you as much as you need.

After the story of the midnight loaves, Jesus told His disciples to ask, to seek and to knock. The door in the story had been locked. To the one who knocks, He now said, it will be opened. Then He turned to the fathers among them and asked which of them, if his son wanted a fish, would hand him a snake, or a scorpion if the boy asked for an egg. His next words call those same fathers evil, and still able to give their children good gifts. The Father in heaven, He said, will do much more than that, and the gift He named was the Holy Spirit.

Seven chapters on, Luke introduces another story by saying what it is for, that the disciples should always pray and not give up. A widow wanted justice against an opponent, and the judge in her town was a man with no fear of God and no interest in what anyone thought of him. He turned her away. She came back, and kept coming back. In the end he gave in for his own sake, telling himself that she was a nuisance and might finish by attacking him. Jesus said God will see that His chosen ones get justice, and quickly. He ended with a question He left unanswered, whether the Son of Man will find faith on the earth when He comes.

keyVerses.text: So I say to you: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened.
If you then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!

And will not God bring about justice for his chosen ones, who cry out to him day and night? Will he keep putting them off? I tell you, he will see that they get justice, and quickly. However, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?

insights: The neighbour and the judge are in these stories because God is unlike them. If even those two give in, a Father who is awake and does care will do more. God doesn't have to be worn down, and the answer is never a set number of prayers away.

Jesus says everyone who asks receives, and the gift He goes on to name is the Holy Spirit. The widow asks for justice. Neither passage says you'll be given whatever you ask for if you ask for long enough, and people pray for years for a healing or a reconciliation that doesn't come. What the father in Jesus's picture never does is hand over a snake.

God will see to it quickly, Jesus says, and yet He told the story to stop people giving up, which only makes sense if the wait can feel long. If you feel like stopping, you are one of the people it was told for.
reflectQuestions: Think of something you used to pray for and have let drop. What was it that made you stop asking?
When you've asked God for the same thing many times, what do you find yourself assuming about why He hasn't given it?
thematicGuides.practice: Each night this week, when you lock your door before bed, stop and ask God again, in a single sentence, for the thing you've nearly stopped asking for. Then say 'Father in heaven' aloud, so that you remember who you've just asked.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, this is the same request as last week and the month before. I've started to mumble it, and some days I leave it out because not asking hurts less. I don't know why the answer hasn't come, and I won't pretend I don't mind. You are nothing like that judge, and You were never asleep behind a locked door. So here it is again. Give me Your Spirit while I wait, and keep me asking until You answer or until You come. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Paul Prayed for People He Had Never Met
thematicGuides.hook: From prison Paul asked a church he had never met to pray for him, and release was not what he asked for.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you.
thematicGuides.intro: Someone you care about is in trouble you can't fix. They're ill, or their marriage is coming apart, and you've told them you'll pray. Then you don't know what to ask for, you're not sure it does anything, and by Thursday you've forgotten. People in the Bible who pray for each other go about it more openly than we tend to, and Paul's letter to the church at Colossae shows how.
story: Paul was a prisoner when he wrote to the Christians at Colossae. Epaphras, one of their own, had brought him news of them, and in chapter 2 Paul counts them among those who had not met him personally. He tells them he has prayed for them constantly from the day that news came, and he writes out what he asks: that God would fill them with the knowledge of His will and make them strong enough to endure and be patient. Near the end of the letter he turns it round and asks for their prayers. With the chains still on, what he wants is an open door for the message.

When the Amalekites attacked Israel at Rephidim, Moses sent Joshua to pick men and fight, and told him where he himself would be the next day, up on the hill holding the staff of God. He climbed it with Aaron and Hur. From then on the battle followed his hands. While they were raised Israel had the better of it, and each time they dropped the Amalekites did. He couldn't keep them up. So the other two got a stone under him to sit on and stood one on each side, holding a hand apiece, and kept his hands steady until the sun went down. Joshua beat the Amalekite army.

In the last chapter of his letter James tells anyone in the church who is sick to call for the elders, who are to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord. The sick person does the asking and other people do the praying. Then he widens it to the whole church, telling them to pray for each other. To show what prayer can do he points to Elijah, who prayed that it would not rain and, three and a half years later, that it would. The first thing James says about him is that "Elijah was a human being, even as we are."

keyVerses.text: Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful. And pray for us, too, that God may open a door for our message, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains.

When Moses' hands grew tired, they took a stone and put it under him and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on one side, one on the other, so that his hands remained steady till sunset.
Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective.

insights: You'd expect a man in chains to ask for his release. Paul asked for an open door for the message. You can't always guess what someone wants prayed for, so ask, and tell them what you've prayed as well. In Luke 22, at the Last Supper, Jesus said to Peter, "I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith may not fail."

If praying for someone month after month is wearing you out, ask one or two others to pray for that person with you. Exodus describes only raised hands on that hill, though readers have long seen prayer in them, and Moses couldn't keep them up alone. He needed two men and a stone.

James is confident that the Lord will raise the sick person up, and Christians read that in more than one way. Churches that pray like this have seen some recover and others not. Praying for someone ill goes alongside their treatment, never in place of it. Paul prayed for people constantly, and his letter to Colossae carries greetings from "our dear friend Luke, the doctor".
reflectQuestions: Name the two or three people whose trouble has been most on your mind this week. What would each of them most want you to ask God for?
What happened in the days after you last told someone you'd pray for them?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose a day this week and somewhere fifteen minutes away on foot, a hill if you have one. Tell someone you've promised to pray for that you'll spend that walk praying for them, as Moses told Joshua a day ahead that he'd be on the hill. Ask what they most want prayed for, and ask God for it as you go.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, You told Peter what You had prayed for him. I'm bringing You someone now. I can't fix this for them and I'm not sure what to ask, so give them strength and patience, and healing if You will. I've promised to pray more often than I've prayed. Bring them back to my mind tomorrow, and when I next see them, let me ask what they want prayed for instead of guessing. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Singing in the Stocks at Midnight
thematicGuides.hook: Paul and Silas sang hymns after a flogging, with their feet in the stocks, and Acts never says the singing got them out.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.
thematicGuides.intro: The jailer at Philippi was handed two men who had just been flogged, with orders to guard them carefully. He put them in the inner cell and fastened their feet in the stocks, and that was where they sang. Most praying is asking. Praise is the part of prayer that asks for nothing and says what is true about God, and it's the hardest part to mean when things are going badly.
story: Paul had ordered a spirit out of a slave girl in Philippi whose fortune-telling earned her owners a great deal of money. With that income gone, the owners dragged Paul and Silas into the marketplace and told the magistrates that these Jews were throwing the city into an uproar, and a crowd joined in. The two were stripped, beaten with rods and thrown into prison with their feet in the stocks. Nobody washed their wounds. Around midnight they were praying, and singing hymns to God.

In the middle of the night an earthquake shook the foundations of the prison at Philippi where Paul and Silas were held. Every door flew open and everyone's chains came loose. The jailer woke, saw the doors open and drew his sword to kill himself, thinking his prisoners had escaped. Paul shouted, "Don't harm yourself! We are all here!" Before the night was over the jailer had come to believe, washed their wounds and set a meal in front of them. In the morning the magistrates sent word to let them go. Paul told the officers that Roman citizens had been beaten publicly without a trial, and that the magistrates could come and escort them out in person, which they did.

On the night He was arrested, Jesus ate the Passover meal in Jerusalem with His twelve disciples. At the table He told them that one of them would betray Him.
