Peter puts anxiety straight after humility. Handing a worry to God is an admission that you can't carry it alone. If your anxiety rarely lets up, or you can't sleep or work for it, the same admission is a good reason to see a doctor or a counsellor, and to tell someone you trust.
reflectQuestions: Jesus named food, drink and clothes. If He were naming your worries from this past week, which would come first?
What has already been provided for you that worry has kept you from noticing?
thematicGuides.practice: Find the date of the thing you're dreading in your diary or phone calendar, an appointment perhaps, or the day a bill is due. Write there: 'Father, You know what I need here.' Under it, name the worry in one line. Each time it comes back before that day, say the first line again and remind yourself which day it belongs to. If the worry has no date, write it in the diary a month from today.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I'm worn out with worrying about tomorrow. I've lost sleep over it for days, and it's still there every morning. You said my Father feeds the birds and knows what I need, and I find the first easier to believe. Here is the thing I keep going over. I can't carry it, so I'm giving it to You. Help me with today's trouble, and help me leave tomorrow's where it is. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Nehemiah and the Wall He Wouldn't Leave
thematicGuides.hook: A king's cupbearer rode out by night to inspect Jerusalem's ruined wall, then stayed with the work for the fifty-two days it took.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I am carrying on a great project and cannot go down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and go down to you?
thematicGuides.intro: Take the front door of a block of flats that hasn't locked properly since the spring. Everyone in the building has complained about it, and nobody has rung the landlord. It will stay broken until one person decides the job is theirs. For Jerusalem's wall that person was Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia, and he tells the story himself.
story: Nehemiah was in the citadel of Susa, in the month of Kislev, when his brother Hanani arrived from Judah with news. The survivors of the exile were in disgrace, Jerusalem's wall was broken down and its gates had been burned. Nehemiah sat down and wept, and for days he fasted and prayed. When he confessed Israel's sins he said 'we', and added "including myself and my father's family". In Nisan, four months after the news came, he was serving the wine when the king asked why he looked so sad. He was very much afraid, he writes, but he asked to be sent to rebuild the city where his ancestors were buried, and the king agreed.

In Jerusalem he told nobody what he had come to do. After three days he went out at night with a few men and a single mount, and examined the wall from the Valley Gate on towards the King's Pool, where there wasn't room for the animal to get through. Only then did he speak to the priests, nobles and others who would do the work, and he called the ruin "the trouble we are in". He told them how God's hand had been on him, and they agreed to start. Chapter 3 lists the builders. A goldsmith took one stretch and a perfume-maker the next, one ruler worked with his daughters, and several men repaired the piece in front of their own house.

When the wall stood at half its height, the people of Judah said the labourers' strength was giving out and there was too much rubble. Warnings of an attack came ten times over. Nehemiah posted families with swords and spears behind the lowest points and kept the trumpeter at his side. Later, with every gap closed and only the gate doors still to hang, his opponents Sanballat and Geshem, scheming to harm him, asked him to meet them on the plain of Ono. He sent word that he couldn't leave the work. Four times they sent the same message and got the same answer. Another day a prophet in Sanballat's pay warned that men were coming to kill him and urged him to hide in the temple. He would not go.

keyVerses.text: Then I said to them, 'You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace.'
I am carrying on a great project and cannot go down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and go down to you?

So the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days. When all our enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and lost their self-confidence, because they realized that this work had been done with the help of our God.

insights: Before Nehemiah asked anyone to lift a stone, he had put himself inside the problem twice. In Susa he confessed his people's sins as his own, and in Jerusalem, fresh from a palace, he called the ruin our trouble.

Jesus' picture of counting the cost of following Him was a builder who sits down first and works out whether he can finish. Nehemiah did some of his working out on a night ride, before he'd asked anyone in Jerusalem for help.

The first messages about Ono were civil, and the prophet's warning sounded like concern for his safety. One would have taken Nehemiah off the wall while the gates still had no doors. The other had been paid for, to frighten him into a sin and leave him with a bad name. Near the end of a long job, ask of any reasonable request what saying yes would cost.
reflectQuestions: Which broken thing near you do you keep coming back to, the one you suspect may be partly yours to rebuild?
What is your plain of Ono this month, the reasonable-sounding request that would take you away from work you ought to be finishing?
thematicGuides.practice: Within three days, go and look properly at one shared job that's been left undone. Then ask one person to take the part nearest their own door, as several people did in Nehemiah 3. It might be the room they already use or the relative they already ring. Offer to do the first hour alongside them.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, there's a thing I keep saying somebody should sort out. I've talked about it far more than I've looked at it. Teach me to count myself among the people who let it get this bad. You haven't promised me fifty-two days or a finished wall. Keep me at my own stretch of it, and when a good reason to walk away arrives, help me see it for what it is. Strengthen my hands. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Work Was Too Heavy for Moses
thematicGuides.hook: Moses judged every dispute himself until his father-in-law watched for one day and told him it was not good.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: What you are doing is not good. You and these people who come to you will only wear yourselves out. The work is too heavy for you; you cannot handle it alone.
thematicGuides.intro: If everything at home, at work or at church has to come through you, it probably happened one job at a time, and each one made sense when you took it on. By now you're tired and the people waiting on you are tired of waiting, and you still can't see which part you could put down. Exodus 18 finds Moses in that position, and the person who points it out is a relative on a visit.
story: Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law, came out to the camp in the wilderness with Moses' wife and two sons. Moses bowed down and kissed him, and in the tent told him everything the LORD had done to Pharaoh. Jethro was delighted. He praised the LORD and ate a meal with Aaron and the elders. The next day Moses took his seat as judge, and the people stood round him from morning till evening. Jethro saw all of it and asked why he sat alone while everyone else stood. Moses explained that the people came to him to seek God's will. Whenever they had a dispute he decided between them and told them God's decrees.

Jethro told him that what he was doing was not good. The work was too heavy for one man, and it would wear out the people who came to him as well as Moses himself. Then he divided it. Moses was to go on standing before God for the people, bringing Him their disputes and teaching them how to live. For the rest he should choose capable men who feared God, could be trusted and hated dishonest gain, and set them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. They would decide the simple cases and bring him the difficult ones. Jethro offered it as advice, to be followed only if God commanded it. Moses did everything he said, and Jethro went back to his own country.

Sharing out the cases didn't lift the whole weight. In Numbers 11 the people were wailing at the entrances to their tents for meat, sick of manna and remembering the fish and cucumbers of Egypt. Moses told the LORD the burden was too heavy to carry by himself, and that he would sooner be killed than go on like this. The LORD had him bring seventy elders to the tent of meeting, and put on them some of the Spirit that was on Moses. Two on the list, Eldad and Medad, had stayed in the camp, and they prophesied there. Joshua wanted them stopped. Moses answered, "I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!"

keyVerses.text: Moses' father-in-law replied, 'What you are doing is not good. You and these people who come to you will only wear yourselves out. The work is too heavy for you; you cannot handle it alone.'
If you do this and God so commands, you will be able to stand the strain, and all these people will go home satisfied.

I will come down and speak with you there, and I will take some of the power of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them. They will share the burden of the people with you so that you will not have to carry it alone.

insights: Jethro saw two lots of people being worn out. Moses was one, and the other was everyone who stood from morning till evening for a hearing. If everything has to go through you, the queue is paying for it too, and that is harder to see from the judge's seat than from where Jethro stood.

The words "not good" come only twice in the Bible's first five books. God says them in Genesis 2 about the man being alone, and Jethro says them here about a man working alone. Both times what follows is help.
What Jethro said to Moses, Moses later said to God in nearly the same words, and God answered as Jethro had, with other people to share the load.
reflectQuestions: Where in your life does everything have to come through you, so that other people end up standing and waiting?
Who knows your ordinary days well enough to tell you, as Jethro told Moses, that what you're doing isn't good?
thematicGuides.practice: For seven days, starting tomorrow, stop deciding one thing that somebody capable and trustworthy could decide without you, such as what's for dinner or whether a colleague's routine work is ready to go. Tell them it's theirs for the week and that they can bring you anything hard. Then leave it alone, which includes not quietly redoing it afterwards.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I've been sitting where Moses sat, and I've told myself that's because nobody else can do it. Some of it I keep because I like being the one people need. You sent the Twelve out two by two while they still had a great deal to learn. Show me which part is mine to keep. And when someone who loves me says that what I'm doing is not good, help me listen as Moses did. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: David, Taken from the Sheep Pens
thematicGuides.hook: Anointed king, David went back to his father's sheep, and years later at Ziklag he was still leading like a shepherd.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: He chose David his servant and took him from the sheep pens; from tending the sheep he brought him to be the shepherd of his people Jacob, of Israel his inheritance.
thematicGuides.intro: On the morning David set out for the army camp where he would fight Goliath, he first left his father's sheep with another shepherd. He had already been anointed king. Psalm 78 sums up his reign as a change of flock. God took him from the sheep pens to be the shepherd of His people. If anyone depends on you, the years between the anointing and the throne show what that meant.
story: The prophet Samuel came to Bethlehem with a horn of oil, sent to anoint one of Jesse's sons as king. He saw Jesse's eldest, Eliab, and thought he must be the one, but the LORD told him not to go by appearance or height. Seven sons passed and none was chosen. Asked if there were any more, Jesse said there was still the youngest, out tending the sheep, and Samuel wouldn't let anyone sit down until he was fetched. David was anointed in front of his brothers, and went back to the flock. When King Saul later sent for him, the message asked for "your son David, who is with the sheep."

Years later David was hiding from Saul in the Philistine town of Ziklag, with six hundred men. They came back from a march to find it burned by Amalekite raiders and their wives and children carried off. David and his men wept until they had no strength left, and the men talked of stoning him. He "found strength in the LORD his God", asked Him whether to give chase, and was told to pursue. At the Besor Valley two hundred men were too exhausted to cross, so he went on with four hundred. In a field they found an Egyptian slave whose Amalekite master had abandoned him when he fell ill. They gave him water, figs and raisins, and he led them to the raiders. David brought back everyone and everything that had been taken.

On the way home David came to the two hundred who had been too exhausted to cross the Besor Valley, and asked them how they were. The troublemakers among the four hundred wanted to hand them their wives and children and none of the plunder. David said, "No, my brothers, you must not do that with what the LORD has given us." Everyone was to share equally, and that stayed the rule in Israel. Within days word came that Saul was dead. Judah made David king at Hebron, and seven and a half years later all the tribes of Israel came there to do the same. They quoted what the LORD had said to him, "You will shepherd my people Israel, and you will become their ruler."

keyVerses.text: But the LORD said to Samuel, 'Do not consider his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him. The LORD does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.'
The share of the man who stayed with the supplies is to be the same as that of him who went down to the battle. All will share alike.

He chose David his servant and took him from the sheep pens; from tending the sheep he brought him to be the shepherd of his people Jacob, of Israel his inheritance. And David shepherded them with integrity of heart; with skillful hands he led them.

insights: 1 Samuel 30 sets two men side by side. An Amalekite left his slave in a field when the man fell ill. David came back to two hundred men who had been too tired to keep up, asked how they were and gave them a full share.
David's reason for sharing alike was that the LORD had given them the plunder. If you see a good result as something you were given, it gets harder to argue that the tired ones deserve less.

At Bethlehem God said He looks at the heart, and Psalm 78's verdict on David's reign is integrity of heart, with skilful hands beside it. Being upright and being good at the job both count, and the psalm starts its account of both at the sheep pens.
reflectQuestions: What are you looking after at the moment that nobody sees, the way David's sheep were out of sight on the day Samuel came?
Before Goliath, David had rescued sheep from a lion and a bear. Which smaller responsibility in your past taught you most about looking after people?
thematicGuides.practice: Before the weekend, go in person to whoever kept things going in the background the last time you were thanked or paid for something, and hand them a share of it. Half the thank-you gift will do, or a meal you pay for. David gave those who stayed with the supplies a fighter's share.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, You took David from the sheep pens, and I would rather skip the sheep. I notice the people who make me look good and lose track of the ones who've fallen behind, some of whom I haven't asked after in weeks. Give me a shepherd's eye for whoever in my care is too tired to cross the valley. If nobody ever sends for me from the fields, let me do the work well where I am. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Red Sea Took All Night
thematicGuides.hook: A wind blew until there was dry ground, and a cloud kept Pharaoh's chariots away from Israel while it did.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land.
thematicGuides.intro: In the films the Red Sea opens in seconds. Moses lifts his staff, the water leaps apart, and the people hurry through. Exodus 14 tells it more slowly. The sea takes all night to open, and most of the chapter is about what happened before anyone set foot on the seabed. That is the stretch you're in when something has you cornered and no way out has appeared.
story: When Pharaoh let Israel go, God did not take them by the short road through Philistine country, in case they met war and turned back. He led them by the desert road, and then had Moses turn them round to camp beside the sea. Pharaoh, He said, would think they were wandering in confusion, hemmed in by the desert, and would come after them. Pharaoh came with six hundred of his best chariots and all the others in Egypt. The Israelites looked up, saw the army and cried out to the LORD in terror. To Moses they said, "Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us to the desert to die?"

Moses told the people not to be afraid, because the LORD would fight for them and they had only to be still. The LORD's next words to Moses were, "Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to move on." Before the water moved, the cloud did. The pillar of cloud that had been travelling in front of Israel went round behind them and stood between the two armies all night. Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and through that whole night the LORD drove it back with a strong east wind. The Israelites went through on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left.

The Egyptians followed them in. In the last watch of the night the LORD looked down from the pillar of fire and cloud and threw their army into confusion. He jammed their chariot wheels, and the Egyptians said, "The LORD is fighting for them against Egypt," which is nearly what Moses had told Israel. At daybreak the sea went back to its place, and not one of the army that had gone in survived. Seeing it, the people feared the LORD and put their trust in Him and in Moses. Three days into the desert, at Marah, the water was too bitter to drink and they grumbled against Moses.

keyVerses.text: Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the deliverance the LORD will bring you today. The Egyptians you see today you will never see again. The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.

Then the angel of God, who had been traveling in front of Israel's army, withdrew and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from in front and stood behind them, coming between the armies of Egypt and Israel. Throughout the night the cloud brought darkness to the one side and light to the other side; so neither went near the other all night long.
Your path led through the sea, your way through the mighty waters, though your footprints were not seen.

insights: Being cornered is not, by itself, proof that you took a wrong turn or that God has lost track of you. Israel's campsite, between Migdol and the sea, was God's choice.

Moses said to be still and God said to move on, and that night needed both. The cloud moved first and the wind took hours, so Israel was kept safe well before there was ground to walk on. Then the walking was theirs. Hebrews 11 calls it faith, in people who had just asked about graves and would be grumbling again within days.

Moses could tell Israel they would never see that army again, and no one can promise you that about your own trouble. Psalm 77 was written by someone awake at night, asking whether God had forgotten to be merciful. He steadies himself on the Red Sea, where, he says, God's path ran through the water and left no footprints. Nobody saw where God walked then either.
reflectQuestions: What has you hemmed in at the moment, with something closing in behind you and no way forward you can see?
When has a way opened for you that you could not have opened yourself?
thematicGuides.practice: The order to move on came while the sea was still in the way. Before you sleep tonight, do the one part of your own trouble that is yours to do, even if it's only drafting the email or looking up the number of someone who could help. Then stop, and leave the rest with God. Israel never did deal with the chariots.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I can't see a way through this, and what's behind me is getting closer. On bad days I'd go back to Egypt if it would make this stop. Stand between me and what I can't fight, and if it takes all night, keep me until morning. Tell me which part of this is mine, and get me walking. I can't see You anywhere in it yet. Be at work where I'm not looking. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Water Into Wine and the Servants Who Knew
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus' first sign was over a hundred gallons of wine for a wedding in Cana, and the bridegroom got the credit.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: What Jesus did here in Cana of Galilee was the first of the signs through which he revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
thematicGuides.intro: Very little was at stake at the wedding in Cana, which makes it hard reading when you're waiting on something serious. Nobody was ill or in danger. A party had run out of wine, and the worst that could follow was an embarrassed family. Jesus' first miracle went on drink for a wedding, and John still calls it the first of the signs by which He revealed His glory.
story: Jesus and His disciples, who had been with Him only a few days, were invited to a wedding at Cana in Galilee. His mother was there too. When the wine ran out she told Him so in one short sentence and asked for nothing. He asked why she was involving Him, and said that His hour had not yet come. He hadn't said He would do anything, and she told the servants to do whatever He said. Those are the last words of hers that John records anywhere in his Gospel.

Nearby stood six stone jars of the kind used for Jewish ceremonial washing, each holding twenty to thirty gallons. Jesus told the servants to fill them with water, and they filled them to the brim. Then He told them to draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet. Nobody prayed over the jars or said a word to them, as far as we're told. The master tasted wine. With no idea where it had come from, he called the bridegroom aside and complimented him on keeping the best until now, when most hosts bring out the cheaper wine once the guests have had plenty. The servants who had filled the jars knew.

Two chapters on, Jesus came to Cana again, the place where He had turned the water into wine. A royal official had travelled there from Capernaum, where his son was close to death, and begged Jesus to come down before the child died. Jesus didn't go. He told him to go, and said his son would live, and the official set off with no more than that sentence. He was still on the road when his servants met him with news that the boy was alive. The fever had left him at one o'clock the previous afternoon, the time at which Jesus had spoken. John calls it the second sign.

keyVerses.text: When the wine was gone, Jesus' mother said to him, 'They have no more wine.' 'Woman, why do you involve me?' Jesus replied. 'My hour has not yet come.' His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'
The master of the banquet tasted the water that had been turned into wine. He did not realize where it had come from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew.
'Go,' Jesus replied, 'your son will live.' The man took Jesus at his word and departed.

insights: John says this sign revealed Jesus' glory and that His disciples believed in Him. One thing it shows about Him is that He gives far more than the need and lets another man be thanked for it.

Nothing here explains why this wedding and that child, and not others, and neither sign promises that what you've asked for will come the way you asked. Between them the two signs at Cana cover a drinks shortage and a deathbed, and Jesus attended to both.

At Cana Jesus said His hour had not yet come. Days before His death He said, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified." His mother, who had heard Him say it hadn't, was standing near the cross. If you're waiting on something far graver than a wedding, the cross is where to see how much the one who saw to the wine was prepared to do.
reflectQuestions: Which everyday needs, your own or other people's, do you tend to leave out when you pray?
What has run out for you, as the wine did at Cana, so that something you relied on is finished and you can't replace it yourself?
thematicGuides.practice: Jesus' mother needed one short sentence: "They have no more wine." On a card, write one need the same way, as a bare statement with nothing about how it should be fixed. Date it, read it to Jesus once, and keep it in your Bible or your wallet. A month from now, write underneath what has happened since, even if all you can honestly put is 'nothing yet'.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I've read about the wine at Cana and felt put out, because what I'm asking You for matters more than a party and I'm still waiting. I don't understand how You choose, and I'm asking anyway. Here is my need, said as briefly as Jesus' mother said hers. Whatever Your Son tells me to do meanwhile I'll do, even if it's only carrying water. When I start to think You don't care, point me back to the cross. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: How Many Loaves Do You Have?
thematicGuides.hook: Twelve tired disciples were told to feed a crowd, asked what food they had, and given it back to hand round.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: 'How many loaves do you have?' he asked. 'Go and see.' When they found out, they said, 'Five, and two fish.'
thematicGuides.intro: The feeding of the five thousand began as an attempt to get some rest. Mark says so many people were coming and going that the disciples hadn't had a chance to eat, and Jesus was taking them somewhere quiet when the crowd turned up. So the men He told to feed everyone had come there needing food and rest themselves, which is about the state you're usually in when somebody needs something from you.
story: By Matthew's account, Jesus had just been told that John the Baptist was dead when He and the Twelve set out by boat. People saw them leaving, ran ahead on foot from all the towns and were waiting when the boat landed. Jesus had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and began teaching them. Late in the day the disciples made a reasonable suggestion, that He send the people off to the villages to buy food. He answered, "You give them something to eat."

The disciples did the sum and made it more than half a year's wages. Jesus asked, "How many loaves do you have?" and sent them to look. Andrew reported a boy with five small barley loaves and two small fish, and asked how far they would go among so many. Jesus had the people sit down on the green grass, took the loaves and the fish, looked up to heaven, gave thanks, broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to hand round. About five thousand men ate as much as they wanted. Then He had the disciples gather what was left so that nothing was wasted, and they filled twelve baskets.

The next day the crowd crossed the lake in boats and found Jesus at Capernaum. He told them they had come because they had eaten the loaves and had their fill. No second meal followed. Jesus said that He was the bread of life, and that whoever fed on Him would live because of Him. Many of His own followers called it a hard teaching and turned back. He asked the Twelve whether they wanted to leave as well. Peter said, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."

keyVerses.text: Then, because so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat, he said to them, 'Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.'

When Jesus looked up and saw a great crowd coming toward him, he said to Philip, 'Where shall we buy bread for these people to eat?' He asked this only to test him, for he already had in mind what he was going to do.
I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never go hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.

insights: The disciples' arithmetic was right, and Jesus never disputed it. He asked how many loaves they had, which is a better question when you're spent, because it has an answer you can go and find. John adds that He already had in mind what He was going to do, so nothing was resting on their having enough.

John mentions twice that the loaves were barley. In 2 Kings 4 Elisha is brought twenty barley loaves, his servant asks how he can set that before a hundred men, and they eat and have some left over. By the lake a quarter as many loaves fed fifty times as many people, with twelve baskets over. Afterwards the crowd began to say Jesus was the Prophet who was to come.

The crowd came back the next day and got no second meal, so the story doesn't promise that money or energy you give away will come back to you. Jesus offered them Himself as the bread of life. A hungry person can go to Him, and that includes the one who has been handing out the bread.
reflectQuestions: What do you have at the moment (a free hour, a little money) that you've written off as too small to be worth offering?
Where do you keep counting up and deciding there won't be enough?
thematicGuides.practice: One day this week, share your own lunch. Ask one person to sit down and eat with you, perhaps a colleague who eats at their desk or a neighbour on their own. Don't lay on anything special. Divide what you'd have eaten yourself, and give thanks for it before you start, as Jesus did on the grass.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I'd planned on some rest and it hasn't worked out that way. Someone needs something from me, and my honest wish is that You'd send them off to the villages. I've done the sum and I haven't enough. So I've gone and looked, and what I do have is not much time and less patience. It's Yours. Take it and put it back in my hands to pass on. I'm hungry too, so feed me while You're feeding them. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: A Touch in the Crowd, Mud on the Eyes
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus healed a woman in a crowd and a man born blind, and in both stories He would not leave it at the cure.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Jesus kept looking around to see who had done it.
thematicGuides.intro: A neighbour asks how you are and you say fine, because the true answer is long and they were only being friendly. People who have been ill for years get used to that, and so do those who look after them. In Mark 5 a woman who has been ill for twelve years is healed in a moment, and Jesus holds up a crowd until He has heard the whole of it.
story: Jesus was on His way to the dying daughter of Jairus, a synagogue leader. In the crowd pressing round Him was a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years. She had been through a great deal under many doctors, had spent everything and was worse. She came up behind Jesus and touched His cloak, and at once felt that the bleeding had stopped. She was well before He said a word. He turned and asked who had touched His clothes, and went on looking until she came, fell at His feet shaking with fear and told Him the whole truth. With Jairus waiting, He called her "Daughter" and sent her away in peace. As He spoke, word came that the girl had died. Jesus went on to the house, took the twelve-year-old by the hand, and she got up.

Jesus saw a man who had been blind from birth. His disciples asked whose sin was behind it, the man's own or his parents'. Jesus answered, "Neither this man nor his parents sinned," and said it had happened so that God's work could be seen in him. Then He spat on the ground, made mud, put it on the man's eyes and told him to go and wash in the Pool of Siloam. He went, washed, and came home seeing. When his neighbours asked where Jesus was, he didn't know.

The Pharisees, a strict religious group, questioned the healed man twice. Some objected that Jesus had healed him on the Sabbath, when no work was allowed. His parents, afraid of being put out of the synagogue, left him to speak for himself. The man kept to what he knew, argued that Jesus must be from God, and was thrown out. As far as John tells it, he had still never set eyes on Jesus. Then Jesus heard what had happened and found him, and asked whether he believed in the Son of Man. The man asked who that was. "You have now seen him," Jesus said. The man believed, and worshipped Him.

keyVerses.text: Then the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell at his feet and, trembling with fear, told him the whole truth. He said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be freed from your suffering.'
Whether he is a sinner or not, I don't know. One thing I do know. I was blind but now I see!

Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and when he found him, he said, 'Do you believe in the Son of Man?' 'Who is he, sir?' the man asked. 'Tell me so that I may believe in him.' Jesus said, 'You have now seen him; in fact, he is the one speaking with you.'

insights: The woman was well before Jesus turned round, and He had a dying child to get to. The man could already see, and had already been thrown out, when Jesus found him. Both cures were finished, and both times He went looking for the person anyway.

Jesus told the woman her faith had healed her. In John 9 the man never asks to be healed, and at first knows his healer only as "the man they call Jesus". So illness is no measure of anyone's faith, yours included. Mark mentions the woman's doctors to say how long and how hard she had tried. It's no reason to stop seeing yours.

The disciples gave Jesus two answers to choose from, the man's sin or his parents', and He turned both down. He spoke about that one man, and gave no general reason why people are ill or disabled. Neither story promises a cure, and many faithful people have prayed and stayed ill.
reflectQuestions: What have you carried for so long that you've stopped mentioning it, even to God?
If you had to keep to one thing you're sure of about God, however small, as the man born blind did, what would it be?
thematicGuides.practice: Each evening this week, give God the long answer to how you are. Take two minutes before bed and tell Him the whole truth about that day, including what you kept from the people who asked. If one of them could be trusted with more of it, tell them too. On the seventh evening, read Mark 5:33-34 and notice what Jesus called her when she had finished.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, this has gone on a long time, and I've got used to saying I'm fine. The whole truth is that I'm tired, that I've wondered whose fault it is, and that some nights I've decided it's mine. I'm asking You to heal what is wrong, and I don't know what You will do. Don't let me slip off into the crowd. Turn round and look for me, as You looked for her. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Easter Morning: Afraid Yet Filled with Joy
thematicGuides.hook: In Matthew, the two women who hear that Jesus has risen run from the tomb frightened and glad at once.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: He is not here; he has risen, just as he said. Come and see the place where he lay.
thematicGuides.intro: You've probably heard it so often that 'Jesus rose from the dead' no longer sounds like news. It was news to everyone in Matthew's account. The only people who had acted on His words about rising were His enemies, who had the tomb guarded. Matthew's ten verses about that morning mention fear four times, which may be nearer to how you feel at a graveside than the hymns are.
story: On the Friday evening Joseph, a rich disciple from Arimathea, wrapped the body of Jesus in clean linen, laid it in his own new rock tomb, rolled a big stone across the entrance and went away. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there, opposite the tomb. Next day the chief priests and Pharisees went to Pilate. They remembered Jesus saying He would rise after three days, and wanted the tomb secured in case His disciples stole the body and claimed He had. Pilate gave them a guard, and they sealed the stone. The disciples themselves, Matthew has already said, had all deserted Jesus and fled on the night of the arrest.

At dawn on the Sunday the two Marys went back to look at the tomb. There was an earthquake, and an angel of the Lord came down, rolled the stone back and sat on it. He looked like lightning, and the guards set over a dead man's tomb shook with fear and "became like dead men". Matthew never describes Jesus coming out. When the angel told the women not to be afraid and to come and see where He had lain, the place was already empty. Then he sent them to tell the disciples that Jesus had risen and was going ahead of them into Galilee. They ran, frightened and full of joy together.

Jesus met them on the road with an ordinary word of greeting. They took hold of His feet and worshipped Him. He too told them not to be afraid, and sent them on the same errand. The angel had said to tell His disciples. Jesus said, "Go and tell my brothers." These were the men who had run. On the night of His arrest He had told them they would all fall away, and straight afterwards that once He had risen He would go ahead of them into Galilee. So the eleven went to Galilee, and when they saw Jesus they worshipped Him, Matthew says, "but some doubted". He came to them and promised to be with them always.

keyVerses.text: The angel said to the women, 'Do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified. He is not here; he has risen, just as he said. Come and see the place where he lay.'

So the women hurried away from the tomb, afraid yet filled with joy, and ran to tell his disciples. Suddenly Jesus met them. 'Greetings,' he said. They came to him, clasped his feet and worshiped him. Then Jesus said to them, 'Do not be afraid. Go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me.'
But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

insights: In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits, the first sheaf cut from a harvest. The rest of the harvest is the people who belong to Him, who will be raised when He comes. So the picture is about people who have died. Paul doesn't stretch it to cover a marriage or a business that has ended.

The angel told the women not to be afraid, and they ran with the news still afraid. Jesus met them and said it again. Paul calls death an enemy, the last to be destroyed, so a death is allowed to hurt. If you believe Jesus rose and still dread a funeral or a scan result, you're where those two women were when He met them.
reflectQuestions: Whose death, or what other loss, do you keep going back to, as the two Marys went back to look at the tomb?
If Jesus is alive, which fear or grief of yours looks different this week, even if it doesn't go away?
thematicGuides.practice: Sometime this week, ask a Christian you trust what the resurrection has meant to them beside a grave. Choose someone who has buried a parent, a husband or wife, or a close friend, and for whom the loss is no longer raw. Give it twenty minutes over tea or on the phone, and mostly listen.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I've said that You are risen so many times that I stopped hearing it. I do believe it, and I'm still afraid of dying, and of the funerals I'll have to stand through before my own. You called the men who ran away Your brothers. I've run from You too, so count me in with them. And be there when I stand at the next grave. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Rain, Crops and the Crowd at Lystra
thematicGuides.hook: When a crowd at Lystra took a miracle the wrong way, Paul and Barnabas talked to them about rain and harvests.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: He has shown kindness by giving you rain from heaven and crops in their seasons; he provides you with plenty of food and fills your hearts with joy.
thematicGuides.intro: At Lystra a priest of Zeus brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, ready to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas. A man who had never walked was on his feet, and the crowd had decided the two visitors were gods. If you've been wishing God would do something unmistakable for you, it's worth seeing how that went.
story: Paul was in the middle of speaking at Lystra when he looked straight at a man who had been lame from birth and called to him to stand up. The man jumped up and walked. The crowd shouted in Lycaonian that the gods had come down in human form. They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes because he did most of the talking. When the priest of Zeus brought bulls to sacrifice to them, the two tore their clothes and ran into the crowd, shouting that they were only human and had come with good news about the living God, who made heaven, earth and sea. He had never left Himself without testimony, they said, and the testimony they named was the rain and the crops. Even then they could hardly stop the sacrifice.

The writer of Psalm 104 goes through the land noting what God keeps supplied. Springs run down the ravines, and the wild donkeys drink. Cattle get their grass, and people their bread and wine. Then come creatures no farmer has a use for, the stork at home in the junipers and the hyrax sheltering in the crags. At night the lions roar and "seek their food from God". At sunrise they slip back to their dens, and people go out to their work until evening. From the springs to the moon the writer has been saying 'He'. When night falls he says 'You', and a few lines later he breaks off to say, "How many are your works, LORD!"

David starts Psalm 19 with the sky. Day and night, he says, it tells of God's glory without a word, and it is heard everywhere on earth. The sun comes out like a bridegroom from his room, and nothing is left without its warmth. Halfway through he turns from the sky to the law of the LORD, God's own words, and calls them sweeter than honey. Then he asks forgiveness for faults he can't see in himself, and his last line is a prayer that the words of his own mouth will please God. Paul's complaint in Romans 1 is about people who saw God's power in what He had made and "neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks to him".

keyVerses.text: Yet he has not left himself without testimony: He has shown kindness by giving you rain from heaven and crops in their seasons; he provides you with plenty of food and fills your hearts with joy.

He makes grass grow for the cattle, and plants for people to cultivate, bringing forth food from the earth: wine that gladdens human hearts, oil to make their faces shine, and bread that sustains their hearts.

The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands. Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge. They have no speech, they use no words; no sound is heard from them. Yet their voice goes out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.

insights: Lystra was given a miracle nobody could miss, and misread it on the spot. Later the same crowd was won over by Paul's opponents, and he was stoned and left for dead. The testimony he and Barnabas named has been there every day of your life.

The sky gets the first six verses of Psalm 19, and it tells David about God's glory. He calls God "my Rock and my Redeemer" only after turning to what God has said. At Lystra the rain was the evidence. The good news still had to be said aloud.

Three chapters before Lystra, Barnabas and Paul were carrying famine relief to Judea, so they knew not everyone has enough. When rain does fall and there is food in front of you, they called that a kindness from God.
reflectQuestions: What small thing in the last few days, a meal or a change in the weather, made you stop for a moment, if anything did?
Psalm 104 says God makes the grass grow and the springs run, in the present tense. What would be different about an ordinary Tuesday if you thought of your food and your work that way?
thematicGuides.practice: Share one meal this week with one other person. Before you eat, ask what they were glad of today, and tell them one thing you'd call a kindness from God, such as the food in front of you. Then thank Him for both, aloud if they don't mind, in one sentence.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I ate today and thanked You for none of it. While I waited for You to do something I couldn't miss, it rained, the shops had bread and somebody made me laugh. Thank You that the wild donkeys and the lions get fed without any help from me, and that my working day is in Your psalm too. Teach me to say thank You while the plate is still warm. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Who the Prophets Were Talking About
thematicGuides.hook: The chief priests quoted Micah to Herod, and a traveller reading Isaiah 53 had to ask who it was about.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: We all, like sheep, have gone astray, each of us has turned to our own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
thematicGuides.intro: If you were taught the Old Testament promises about the Messiah, it was probably as a proof, a column of predictions matched against a column of events. There's something in that, and the first Christians did argue from the Scriptures. But when Matthew and Acts show people with the old words in front of them, most of them don't see what they're looking at. You may know these verses by heart or never have made sense of them. The New Testament has people in both positions.
story: Magi, wise men from the east, arrived in Jerusalem asking where the child born king of the Jews was. King Herod, disturbed, called in the chief priests and teachers of the law and asked where the Messiah, God's promised king, was to be born. They answered from the prophet Micah: in Bethlehem, the small town a ruler of Israel was to come from. Herod sent the Magi there. They found the child with His mother Mary, and bowed down and worshipped Him. Matthew mentions no priest or teacher going with them. The only other person he shows acting on Micah's words is Herod, who gave orders to kill every boy of two and under in and around Bethlehem.

A few days before His death, Jesus reached Bethphage and sent two disciples into the village ahead to untie a donkey and her colt and bring them. The two did not know what they were part of. John says the disciples understood only after Jesus had died and risen that the prophet Zechariah's words, about Jerusalem's king coming to her on a donkey, had been written about Him. On the day itself they put their cloaks on the animals and Jesus rode in. A very large crowd spread cloaks and branches on the road and shouted Hosanna to the Son of David. When He entered Jerusalem the whole city was stirred and asked, "Who is this?"

An angel sent Philip, one of the early church's preachers, to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. There he met an Ethiopian eunuch, the official in charge of his queen's treasury, heading home from worship in Jerusalem and reading the prophet Isaiah in his chariot. Philip ran up, heard what he was reading and asked if he understood it. The official said he couldn't unless someone explained it, and invited Philip up beside him. The lines he had reached were about someone led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent, denied justice, his life taken from the earth. He asked Philip, "Tell me, please, who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?" Philip began with that passage and told him the good news about Jesus. When they came to some water, the official asked what was to stop him being baptised. Philip baptised him, and he went on his way rejoicing.

keyVerses.text: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times.
Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout, Daughter Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
But he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.

insights: If two disciples could untie the donkey with their own hands and not recognise a promise being kept, it's no surprise when parts of the Old Testament stay closed to you. They understood it looking back from the cross and the empty tomb, which is still the place to read it from.

The official asked who the passage was about. Just before the lines he was reading, the same chapter says who the suffering was for: the LORD "has laid on him the iniquity of us all". That 'us' had room in it for a court official from Ethiopia, and it has room for you.
reflectQuestions: Take whichever of these stays with you most: Micah on Bethlehem, Zechariah on the donkey or Isaiah on the silent servant. Why that one?
The disciples only understood the ride into Jerusalem afterwards. Looking back over your own life, what can you now see God was doing that you couldn't see at the time?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick one stretch of your day when you'd normally be scrolling or listening to something, like the bus to work or the half hour after supper. For the next five days, go without it and read Isaiah 53 in the gap. It's twelve verses. If a line makes no sense, do what the official did and ask someone who knows the Bible better.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, thank You that Your Son was pierced for what I've done wrong. I can say those words without giving them a thought, so let them be news to me again. I don't want to be right about Bethlehem and never make the trip. Where I can't follow what I'm reading, send me a Philip, and make me willing to ask. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Job Isaiah Volunteered For
thematicGuides.hook: The five verses after Isaiah's 'Send me' tell him what the job is, and it's one nobody would have chosen.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying, 'Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?' And I said, 'Here am I. Send me!'
thematicGuides.intro: Isaiah's vision is usually read out as far as verse 8, where he has been forgiven and offers to go, and that leaves out the difficult half. In the verses that follow, God tells him what he has just offered to do, which is to keep speaking to people who will hear every word and take none of it in. If you've said yes to something for God and found it slower and heavier than you expected, read all thirteen verses.
story: King Uzziah had reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-two years and ended them as a leper, banned from the temple after he walked into it to burn incense, which was the priests' work. In the year he died, Isaiah saw the Lord seated on a throne. Of what the Lord looked like he says almost nothing, only that the train of His robe filled the temple. Above Him were seraphim, heavenly beings with six wings each, and with two of them they covered their faces. They were calling to one another, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD Almighty", and at the sound the doorposts and thresholds shook and the temple filled with smoke. Isaiah cried out that he was ruined, a man of unclean lips who had seen the King.

One of the seraphim above God's throne flew to Isaiah holding a live coal, taken with tongs from the altar. He touched Isaiah's mouth with it and told him his guilt was taken away and his sin dealt with. Isaiah hadn't asked for that. All he had done was say what was true about himself. Then he heard the Lord ask, "Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?" The question wasn't put to Isaiah by name. He answered it anyway, and what came from his cleaned lips was "Here am I. Send me!" He said it before anyone had told him where he would be going or what he would have to say.

Isaiah had offered to go, and the job God gave him, which he went on to do under three more kings, was to tell his people to keep on hearing and never understand. He was to make their hearts hard, their ears dull and their eyes closed. His reply was to ask how long. Until the cities lay ruined and empty, God said, and even the tenth still left in the land would be laid waste again. The last thing God told him was about trees. A terebinth or an oak leaves a stump when it is cut down, and God said the land would be left with one too: "the holy seed will be the stump in the land." In chapter 11 Isaiah writes of a shoot coming up from a stump.

keyVerses.text: Then one of the seraphim flew to me with a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with tongs from the altar. With it he touched my mouth and said, 'See, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away and your sin atoned for.'

Make the heart of this people calloused; make their ears dull and close their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed.

Then I said, 'For how long, Lord?' And he answered: 'Until the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, until the houses are left deserted and the fields ruined and ravaged, until the LORD has sent everyone far away and the land is utterly forsaken.'

insights: Isaiah was told beforehand that the people would not take in what he said, so their response could never be the test of whether he had done his job. A poor response doesn't prove you're doing right, but it doesn't prove you've failed either.

John writes that the glory Isaiah saw that day was Jesus' glory (John 12:41). When He came, Jesus stood in Isaiah's place, telling parables to crowds who heard and did not understand, and He quoted God's words to Isaiah about them. He knows what it is to speak and not be heard.
reflectQuestions: Isaiah saw the Lord and cried out about his own lips. In his place, what is it about yourself that you would expect to come to mind?
Where have you said 'send me' to something, for God or for other people, that has cost more, or gone on longer, than you bargained for?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, when you're on your own, read the whole of Isaiah 6 out loud. It takes a couple of minutes. Then, still aloud, name the thing you've already said yes to that has gone on longer than you thought it would, and ask God Isaiah's question about it: how long. Then stop talking and stay where you are for a minute. You don't have to add anything.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I like verse 8 better than verse 9. I'd rather offer to go than hear where. I've said yes to things and I'm tired of seeing so little come of them. I can't make my own lips clean, so do for me what You did for Isaiah. Keep me at the work You've given me for as long as You mean it to last, and when I ask You how long, help me stay for the answer. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Daniel, the Statue and the Son of Man
thematicGuides.hook: Daniel told a king his empire would end, then saw the kingdom that won't, given to one like a son of man.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and his kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.
thematicGuides.intro: Daniel 2 begins with the most powerful man of his day lying awake. Nebuchadnezzar, the king who had carried Daniel off from Jerusalem, went to bed with his mind on "things to come", and the dream that followed left him too troubled to sleep. When the news makes whoever is in charge look permanent, it's worth knowing that this king lost sleep over the future too, and what he and Daniel were shown about it.
story: King Nebuchadnezzar demanded that his magicians and astrologers tell him what he had dreamed as well as what it meant, or be cut into pieces. They protested that only the gods could do that, "and they do not live among humans." So he ordered every wise man in Babylon put to death. Daniel and his three friends were on the list, and Daniel had to ask Arioch, the officer carrying out the order, why it had been given. He went in to the king and asked for time, the very thing the king had accused the astrologers of playing for. Then he went home and urged his friends to plead with the God of heaven for mercy. That night the mystery was revealed to him in a vision.

Daniel's first request, once God had shown him the dream, was that the other wise men be spared. He told the king no wise man could have done what was asked, but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries. The king had seen a statue with a head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with baked clay. A rock cut out by no human hand struck the feet, the whole statue broke to pieces and blew away like chaff, and the rock became a mountain that filled the earth. Daniel told him, "You are that head of gold." Other kingdoms would follow, and in their time God would set up one that would last for ever. Nebuchadnezzar fell face down in front of the young exile.

Years later Daniel had a dream of his own. Four great beasts came up out of a churning sea, and he was told they were four kings who would rise from the earth. Then the Ancient of Days, God Himself, took His seat, and "one like a son of man", a human figure after all the beasts, came with the clouds of heaven and was given a kingdom that would never be destroyed. Centuries on, Jesus was brought as a prisoner before the high priest and asked if He was the Messiah. He said He was, and that they would see the Son of Man seated at God's right hand and coming on the clouds of heaven. The high priest tore his clothes, and the court condemned Him as deserving death.

keyVerses.text: In the time of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people. It will crush all those kingdoms and bring them to an end, but it will itself endure forever.
In my vision at night I looked, and there before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into his presence.

Again the high priest asked him, 'Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?' 'I am,' said Jesus. 'And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Mighty One and coming on the clouds of heaven.'

insights: 'Son of Man' is the name Jesus used for Himself more than any other, and it can sound like the modest one. In Daniel it belongs to the figure handed authority over every nation. The astrologers had said the gods do not live among humans, and this figure looks like a human being.

Only one kingdom in these two dreams is identified, Nebuchadnezzar's own, and Christians don't agree on which empires the others are. Both dreams are clear that every human kingdom is temporary, including the one you live under. Daniel knew that and still served at court until King Cyrus's first year (Daniel 1:21).
reflectQuestions: When something frightening lands on you, as the death sentence landed on Daniel, what do you tend to do before anything else?
Think of the news story that weighs on you most. What changes about it, if anything, when you set it beside what Daniel saw?
thematicGuides.practice: The last verse of Daniel 2 has him asking the king for posts for the three friends condemned with him. Someone you know is as worried by the news as you are. One evening this week, go round and take one job off their hands, the cooking or an errand they've put off.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, You called Yourself the Son of Man in front of a court that wanted You dead. I believe the kingdom was given to You, though most days I can't see it. I read the news as if the people in it will be in charge for ever, and it frightens me more than I let on. Help me live and work under whoever is in power, as Daniel did, without being ruled by fear of them. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Joel's Promise at Nine in the Morning
thematicGuides.hook: Joel said God would pour out His Spirit on sons, daughters, old men and servants, and at Pentecost Peter said it had come.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, for all whom the Lord our God will call.
thematicGuides.intro: Someone at your church prays aloud, easily, as if God were in the next chair, and you conclude that whatever they have was given out on a day you missed. Plenty of Christians sort the church this way, into the few the Holy Spirit works through and the rest who look on. The prophet Joel was given a promise with no such division in it, and Peter quoted it to a crowd in Jerusalem.
story: When Israel was in the wilderness, the Spirit rested on seventy elders chosen to share Moses' load, and they prophesied. Two men listed among the elders, Eldad and Medad, had stayed behind, and they prophesied in the camp. Joshua wanted them stopped. Moses refused, and said he wished the LORD would put His Spirit on all His people. Centuries later the prophet Joel spoke to Judah after locusts had eaten the fields and stripped the fig trees to bare white branches. Through him God promised grain, wine and oil again, and after that something more. He would pour out His Spirit on all people, on sons and daughters, old men and young men, and on servants, both men and women.

Jesus had told His apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the gift His Father had promised. They prayed with the other believers, about a hundred and twenty in all, Mary the mother of Jesus and other women among them. On the day of Pentecost, a Jewish harvest festival, they were all together when a sound like a violent wind filled the house. What looked like tongues of fire separated and came to rest on each of them, and all were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues. Jews from every nation were staying in Jerusalem, and a crowd of them gathered, bewildered, because each one heard these Galileans declaring the wonders of God in their own language. Some made fun of them and said they'd had too much wine.

Peter stood up with the other eleven apostles and dealt with the joke first, pointing out that it was only nine in the morning. This, he said, was what the prophet Joel had spoken of. As Peter quoted it, the line about the servants ended with four words that aren't in Joel, "and they will prophesy." Then he told the crowd about Jesus, whom they had crucified and God had raised, and said it was Jesus who had poured this out. Cut to the heart, people asked what they should do. Peter told them to repent and be baptised, and said the gift of the Holy Spirit was promised to them, their children and all who are far off. About three thousand were baptised that day.

keyVerses.text: Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!

And afterward, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions. Even on my servants, both men and women, I will pour out my Spirit in those days.

Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, for all whom the Lord our God will call.

insights: Joel's list takes in sons and daughters, old and young, and then, with the word 'Even', the servants. The young, the old and the people nobody notices are each named, so being one of them is no reason to count yourself out.

In Joel the servants receive the Spirit. As Peter quoted the line, they prophesy too, like the sons and daughters. The people at the bottom of the household are given something to say as well as something to receive.

Peter gave Joel five verses and Jesus most of the rest of his sermon. For him, what the crowd could see and hear was evidence that God had raised Jesus and exalted Him, and that the Spirit had been poured out by His hand.
reflectQuestions: There's someone you'd say the Holy Spirit is clearly at work in. What do they have that you assume you don't?
If the promise Peter spoke of that morning has you in it, where this week would you most want the Holy Spirit's help?
thematicGuides.practice: Next Sunday, get to church five minutes early and sit still in your seat, phone away. Look round at who has come: the teenagers, the oldest person there, whoever put the chairs out. At Pentecost every person in the house was filled with the Holy Spirit. Ask God silently to fill each one you notice, ending with yourself. If you have no church, five minutes on a bench in a busy street will do.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I've long assumed Your Spirit was for other people, the confident ones. I'd like to believe Your promise includes me. I've also decided who else in my church You're unlikely to use, and I'd be glad to be wrong about them too. Fill me with Your Spirit today. I'm asking as one of the people on Joel's list. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Tree of Life at the End of Revelation
thematicGuides.hook: The Bible ends with God living among His people and the tree of life back within reach, in a city that never shuts its gates.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.
thematicGuides.intro: There are things in your life that won't be put right this year, and some that won't be put right in your lifetime: the death of someone you love, or a body that isn't going to mend. Much of Revelation is hard to follow, and people argue over what it means. Its last two chapters are clearer about what God intends to do in the end.
story: The book begins like a letter. Its writer calls himself John, "your brother and companion in the suffering", and says he was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. A voice tells him to write what he sees and send it to seven churches, from Ephesus to Laodicea. Near the end he sees a new heaven and a new earth, and a city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God. A loud voice from the throne announces that God's dwelling place is now among the people and that He will live with them. Then it says that God will wipe away every tear, and that death and pain will be over.

Then the One seated on the throne speaks. He is making everything new, He says, and John is to write that down. "It is done," He goes on, and He calls Himself the Beginning and the End. The thirsty will be given water from the spring of the water of life, at no cost, and those who are victorious will inherit all this and be His children. The same voice then warns that some will have no share in it. The offer of water is made once more on the Bible's last page, to whoever wishes to take it.

In the new Jerusalem John sees no temple, because the Lord God and the Lamb, his name for Jesus, are its temple. The city's gates are never shut. An angel shows him a river, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne down the middle of the great street. On each side of it stands the tree of life, bearing fruit every month, its leaves for the healing of the nations. That tree stood in Eden at the start of Genesis, and when God drove the man out He set cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to it. Here it is again, with every gate standing open. In the same chapter of Genesis the ground was cursed. John writes that there will be no more curse, and that God's servants will see His face. Moses once asked to see God's glory and was told, "you cannot see my face, for no one may see me and live."

keyVerses.text: Look! God's dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.
He who was seated on the throne said, 'I am making everything new!' Then he said, 'Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.'
No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his servants will serve him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.

insights: The first thing the voice from the throne announces is that God will live with His people. The end of death and crying comes second, and it follows from His being there.
Genesis 3 ends with the ground cursed and a guard on the way to the tree of life. What was shut in the Bible's third chapter is open in its last two, and the curse is gone.

The tears are wiped away when God comes to live with His people, and nothing in these chapters says they stop before then. John is given no date, and no promise that the illness will lift or the grief will ease this year. If your grief is heavy, tell God, tell a friend, and see a doctor if it's wearing you down.
reflectQuestions: What are you living through at the moment that is hardest to set beside the ending John describes?
Which tears, your own or someone else's, do you most want God to wipe away?
thematicGuides.practice: Send one message today, from wherever you're reading this, to someone who is grieving or whose illness won't mend. Say only that they came to mind and that you're asking God to stay close to them. John introduced himself as a brother and companion in the suffering before he described anything he had seen.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, some days I believe this ending and some days it sounds too good to be true. There are people I miss, and things in me and around me that I don't expect to see mended. You sent this vision to the churches Yourself, and on the days I doubt it I'm going on that. Until the last tear is wiped away, stay close to the people I'm thinking of now. I'm not good at waiting, so I'll pray the prayer on the Bible's last page. Come, Lord Jesus. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Test Them All: Prophecy From Amos to Paul
thematicGuides.hook: A shepherd ordered out of Bethel and Paul's rule for Corinth show how to weigh the words 'God told me'.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Do not quench the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt but test them all; hold on to what is good, reject every kind of evil.
thematicGuides.intro: A man called Amos, who kept sheep and looked after sycamore-fig trees, turned up at Bethel, the king of Israel's own sanctuary, saying that the king's house would fall and that God had sent him. People still tell each other that God has told them something, about a job or a marriage or about you, and it's hard to know what to do with a sentence like that. The Bible has prophets in it, and it also has instructions for the people who had to listen to them.
story: God showed Amos locusts stripping Israel's land, and then fire, and both times Amos pleaded with Him for Israel, because the nation was so small. Both times God relented. In a third vision He said He would spare Israel no longer and would rise with the sword against the house of King Jeroboam. Amos was prophesying at Bethel, the king's own sanctuary, and Amaziah, the priest there, reported him to the king for conspiracy, then told him to go back to Judah and earn his bread prophesying there. Amos answered that he had been neither a prophet nor a prophet's son. "But the LORD took me from tending the flock and said to me, 'Go, prophesy to my people Israel.'" Told to stop, he prophesied again on the spot, about Amaziah's own family and land.

Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain, and in front of them His clothes turned dazzling white, whiter than anyone in the world could bleach them. The prophet Elijah appeared, and Moses, through whom God had given Israel the law, and they talked with Him. Peter, as frightened as the others and not knowing what to say, offered to put up three shelters, one each for Jesus, Moses and Elijah. Then a cloud covered them and a voice from the cloud said, "This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!" When they looked round, they no longer saw anyone with them except Jesus.

When the church in Corinth met, people came with a hymn, a word of instruction, a revelation, a tongue. Paul, who told the Thessalonians not to treat prophecies with contempt, told the Corinthians to eagerly desire the gifts of the Spirit, prophecy especially, because the one who prophesies builds up the church. He also wrote to them, "Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said." All of them could prophesy in turn, he said, and if something was revealed to a person sitting down, the first speaker was to stop.

keyVerses.text: In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets at many times and in various ways, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom also he made the universe.
But the one who prophesies speaks to people for their strengthening, encouraging and comfort.
Do not quench the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt but test them all; hold on to what is good, reject every kind of evil.

insights: Amaziah took prophecy for a trade and told Amos to earn his bread at it somewhere else. Amos already had a living, and his message got him reported to the king. When someone brings you a word in God's name, it's fair to ask what they stand to gain by it.

Moses once told Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him. "You must listen to him," he said. On the mountain the voice from the cloud said the same of Jesus. So anything claimed as a word from God can be measured against what the Son said and did, as Scripture records it. A message that draws you away from Him fails, however sure the speaker sounds.

Churches disagree about whether prophecy still happens as it did in Corinth. Paul's instruction to Thessalonica can be kept on either view: don't sneer at what is said in God's name, and don't swallow it whole.
reflectQuestions: When you want to know what God is saying to you, where do you go first?
Think of a time someone said they had a word from God for you, or you felt sure of one yourself. What did you do with it?
thematicGuides.practice: Over a coffee this week, ask a Christian you trust, someone older if you can, how they weigh it when a person says God has told them something. Read 1 Thessalonians 5:19-22 together first, which takes half a minute, then ask for one time they held on to what was said and one time they let it go.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, You've spoken through prophets like Amos, and most fully in Jesus, and I'd still rather have a private message than read what You have already said. When someone tells me they have a word from You, give me the patience to weigh it and someone sensible to weigh it with. Where I've been quick to say 'God told me', make me slower. And give me something to say this week that strengthens somebody. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Job Did Not Suffer Quietly
thematicGuides.hook: Job said bitter things to God, chapter after chapter, and afterwards God said he had spoken the truth about Him.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I will not keep silent; I will speak out in the anguish of my spirit, I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
thematicGuides.intro: The usual idea of bearing suffering well is bearing it quietly, and Job is held up as the proof. That holds for two chapters. Then come forty more, Job does the talking in about half of them, and little of it sounds patient. If what you'd like to say to God just now doesn't sound like faith, look at what God said about Job once the speeches were over.
story: The book's first verse calls Job blameless and upright. In one day four messengers reached him, three of them while the one before was still speaking. Raiders had taken his oxen, donkeys and camels, fire had burned up the sheep, and a wind from the desert had brought the eldest son's house down on all ten of his children. Job tore his robe, shaved his head, fell to the ground and worshipped. "The LORD gave and the LORD has taken away," he said. Later his skin broke out in sores from head to foot, and he sat among the ashes, scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery.

When Job next spoke at length, it was to curse the day he was born. He argued with three friends who were sure he must have sinned, and what he said to God, and about Him, was blunter still. He told God to look away and leave him alone, and said that if God ever did answer, He wouldn't listen and would crush him with a storm. Even his best-known line of trust, that he will hope in God though God slay him, ends with a promise to defend his ways to God's face. His last long speech has him signing his defence and saying, "let the Almighty answer me."

Then the LORD spoke to Job out of the storm, the very thing Job had said would crush him. For four chapters God asked questions: who feeds the raven's young, who sends rain on a desert where nobody lives. He gave Job no reason for what had happened, and told him he had used "words without knowledge". Job took back what he had claimed to understand, and said that until then he had only heard of God, and now his eyes had seen Him. Then God told the friends He was angry with them, because they had not spoken the truth about Him as His servant Job had. Afterwards Job's brothers and sisters came, ate with him in his house and consoled him over all his trouble. The LORD gave him twice the livestock he had owned before. Job had seven sons and three daughters again, ten as before.

keyVerses.text: I will not keep silent; I will speak out in the anguish of my spirit, I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Though he slay me, yet will I hope in him; I will surely defend my ways to his face.
I am angry with you and your two friends, because you have not spoken the truth about me, as my servant Job has.

insights: James later held up Job's perseverance as an example. Job held on to his integrity and kept talking to God. He complained, accused and demanded a hearing, and much of it he said straight to the One he was complaining about.

God corrected Job for talking as if he understood more than he did, and kept His anger for the friends, who had been so sure why he suffered. If someone explains your suffering to you with the same confidence, you're free to doubt them.

Job was answered from a storm and saw his fortunes restored. You're promised neither, and nothing in the last chapter says the new children made up for the ten who died. The book leaves you with God's verdict on a man who brought Him his bitterest words.
reflectQuestions: What have you held back from saying to God because it didn't sound like something a believer should say?
Job said he had only heard of God before, and now had seen Him. How has trouble changed the way you think about God?
