thematicGuides.practice: Ask an old friend, or one of your family, to come and eat with you one day this week, as Job's brothers and sisters did with him. Tell them beforehand that you don't want advice or reasons, only a hearing. Then give them the true version. If part of it is that you've been wishing you weren't alive, as Job did, tell your doctor as well.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I've been tidying up what I say to You and keeping back what's underneath. So here it is. This hurts, and some days I'm angry with You. I want to know why it happened, and You may tell me no more than You told Job. Keep me talking to You when all I have is complaint, and send me someone who will sit and eat with me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Groaning Before Romans 8:28
thematicGuides.hook: Paul's promise that God works in all things for good comes at the end of a passage about groaning.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose.
thematicGuides.intro: Being told that God works for good in all things is hard to take when you're the one in pain. Someone quotes Romans 8:28 kindly, at a bedside or after a funeral, and what you hear is that the thing that happened must somehow be good. Before you decide what the verse means, read the ten verses that lead up to it and the one that follows. Paul takes his time getting to that sentence, and he doesn't stop at it.
story: In his second letter to Corinth Paul set out what his work had cost him. He had been given thirty-nine lashes five times and beaten with rods three times. He had been stoned once, shipwrecked three times, and had spent a night and a day in the open sea. That is the man who tells the Christians in Rome that our present sufferings aren't worth comparing with the glory that is coming. The whole creation, he goes on, has been groaning like a woman in labour, waiting to be set free from decay. Then he adds himself and his readers. We groan as well, he says, we who have the Spirit, while we wait for the redemption of our bodies.

Paul once pleaded with the Lord three times to take away what he called a thorn in his flesh, and was told instead that God's grace was enough for him. So when he writes in Romans 8 that we don't know what we ought to pray for, the 'we' includes an apostle. In that weakness, he says, the Spirit helps. The Spirit Himself intercedes for us, which means He asks on our behalf, "through wordless groans". It's the third groan in five verses, after creation's and ours. And God, who searches our hearts, knows what the Spirit means, because the Spirit asks in line with His will.

Two verses after saying what we don't know, Paul writes "And we know". He is sure that in all things God works for the good of those who love Him. He still calls the things what they are, and a few lines later he names some, famine and the sword among them. Verse 29 starts with the word 'For', and it says what the good is. God's purpose for His people is that they be made like His Son. Whatever happens to them, that is what He is working towards. Paul then lists what God has done for them, and the last item is that He glorified them, in the past tense, as though it were finished.

keyVerses.text: We know that the whole creation has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth right up to the present time. Not only so, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption to sonship, the redemption of our bodies.
In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us through wordless groans.

And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose. For those God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.

insights: Nobody can tell you, on the strength of Romans 8:28, what your pain is for, and you don't have to work that out before you can trust God in it.

The people who groan in verse 23 are the people verse 28 describes as loving God. You can do both at once. And on a day when a sound is all you can manage, Paul's claim is that the Spirit is asking for you anyway, and asking for the right thing.

Paul calls our condition weakness, and counts himself in. If what you're carrying has made you ill, or your mood has been low for weeks, see a doctor as well as praying, and tell someone close to you how bad it is.
reflectQuestions: Looking back at a hard time that's now some way behind you, what, if anything, is different in you because of it?
What makes it hard for you to tell God that something still hurts and, in the same prayer, that you trust Him with it?
thematicGuides.practice: Until Sunday night, stop trying to find the right words when you pray about the hardest thing in your life. Each time it comes to mind, tell God, 'I don't know what to pray about this,' and leave it there, even if all that follows is a sigh. Don't go back and improve on it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I don't know what to pray about this, and I'm relieved to read that Your Spirit does. I've spent a long time trying to make sense of it, and I'm no nearer. I can't call it good, and Your word doesn't ask me to. I will believe that You are at work in it, making me more like Your Son. Until I can see that, please take my groaning as prayer. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Comforted by the Coming of Titus
thematicGuides.hook: Paul was worn down and afraid in Macedonia, and God's comfort reached him as a friend arriving with news.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God.
thematicGuides.intro: When Paul says God comforts us so that we can comfort others, he says the others may be in "any trouble", which is wider than the kind we've been through ourselves. That matters if you've kept your distance from someone who is suffering because you've never faced what they're facing, or because you're hardly on top of your own difficulties. Later in the same letter Paul describes a day when God comforted him, and how.
story: Paul wrote his second letter to Corinth after things had gone badly between him and the church there. He mentions a painful visit, and an earlier letter he had written in tears. He had also come through trouble in Asia so severe that he had expected to die. Yet he opens by praising God as the Father of compassion. God comforts us in all our troubles, he says, so that we can comfort people in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have had from Him. In five verses the word comfort, in one form or another, comes nine times.

Titus, one of Paul's fellow workers, had been in Corinth, and Paul expected to meet him at Troas. Paul went there to preach and found that the Lord had opened a door for him. But Titus wasn't there, Paul had no peace of mind, and he said goodbye and went on to Macedonia. There he was harassed at every turn, with "conflicts on the outside, fears within." Then, he writes, God "comforted us by the coming of Titus". Titus brought news that the Corinthians longed for Paul and were sorry for what had happened. He also brought the comfort they had given him while he was with them. So some of the comfort Paul had to pass on began in Corinth, went to Titus, then to Paul, and now came back to Corinth in a letter.

A few years before he saw Rome, Paul had written to the Christians there that he longed to visit, so that he and they could encourage each other. When he came, it was as a prisoner in the charge of a centurion, after a shipwreck and three months on Malta. The believers in Rome heard he was coming and came out along the road to meet him, as far as the Three Taverns and the Forum of Appius, the nearer of them about thirty miles from the city. Luke records nothing they said. At the sight of them, he writes, Paul thanked God and was encouraged. The encouragement he had hoped to share in Rome reached him first, on the road.

keyVerses.text: Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God.

For when we came into Macedonia, we had no rest, but we were harassed at every turn, conflicts on the outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus, and not only by his coming but also by the comfort you had given him.

The brothers and sisters there had heard that we were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of these people Paul thanked God and was encouraged.

insights: Paul was comforted before the trouble ended. Writing after Titus came, he speaks of "all our troubles" in the present tense, and on the road to Rome he was a prisoner under guard. You needn't wait until you're through your own trouble before you can be of use to someone in theirs.

Both times the help was somebody arriving, and both times it is put down to God. If a visit, a lift to the hospital or a message at the right moment once got you through a bad week, Paul would call that God's comfort. So you already know what comfort is made of, and it's the same whatever trouble the other person is in.
reflectQuestions: Who do you know at the moment who could do with the kind of help that got you through a hard time of your own?
When you were at your lowest, what did the person who helped most do that others didn't?
thematicGuides.practice: This evening, when you're by yourself, write down the names of the people who helped you through the hardest stretch you've had, and next to each name what they did. Thank God for each of them. Then add one name at the bottom, someone you know who is in trouble now, and pick one thing from the sheet that you could do for them.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, people came when I was low, and I didn't always see at the time that You had sent them. Thank You for each one. There's someone I've been avoiding because I don't know what to say, and because I've troubles of my own. I may still have nothing to say when I get there. Get me to their door anyway, and let my coming be some comfort to them, as the coming of Titus was to Paul. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: What the Refiner's Fire Is For
thematicGuides.hook: Peter told insulted Christians their faith was worth more than gold, years after his own was tested in a courtyard.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: These have come so that the proven genuineness of your faith, of greater worth than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire, may result in praise, glory and honor.
thematicGuides.intro: A friend you've known for years says you were better company before you got religious, and the rest of the table laughs. It's a small thing, and it can stay with you for days. Peter wrote his first letter to Christians under that kind of pressure, and worse. To help them he borrowed a picture from the prophets, metal in a refiner's fire.
story: In Malachi's day the priests in Jerusalem were putting blind and lame animals on the altar and calling the work a burden. God told them to try offering animals like that to their governor. He said He wished one of them would shut the temple doors, so that they would stop lighting useless fires on His altar. Two chapters on, Malachi says the Lord will come suddenly to His temple and sit as a refiner of silver, purifying the Levites, the tribe the priests came from, until their offerings are right again. Three verses later God says, "I the LORD do not change. So you, the descendants of Jacob, are not destroyed."

After the Last Supper, out on the Mount of Olives, Jesus quoted Zechariah, "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." In Zechariah, those who are left are then put into the fire and refined like silver. Jesus told the disciples they would all fall away, and Peter said that even if all the others did, he would not. Luke adds that Jesus had prayed for Peter's faith not to fail, and had told him to strengthen his brothers once he had turned back. That night Peter sat down by a fire in the high priest's courtyard, where a servant girl looked closely at him in the firelight, and three times he denied knowing Jesus. Then he went outside and wept bitterly.

Years afterwards Peter wrote to Christians scattered from Pontus to Bithynia. By the letter's own account their neighbours accused them of doing wrong, and old companions heaped abuse on them for no longer joining in. Peter grants that it hurts. Then he turns to gold, which is put through fire to refine it and perishes anyway. Their faith, he tells them, is worth more than that, and the trials are showing it to be real. Near the end of the letter he promises that God Himself will make them strong. Strengthening his brothers was what Jesus had asked of him on the night of the denial.

keyVerses.text: In all this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in all kinds of trials. These have come so that the proven genuineness of your faith, of greater worth than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire, may result in praise, glory and honor when Jesus Christ is revealed.

But who can endure the day of his coming? Who can stand when he appears? For he will be like a refiner's fire or a launderer's soap. He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver; he will purify the Levites and refine them like gold and silver.

This third I will put into the fire; I will refine them like silver and test them like gold. They will call on my name and I will answer them; I will say, 'They are my people,' and they will say, 'The LORD is our God.'

insights: Peter's certainty that he would never fall away was gone before morning, and the faith Jesus had prayed for was still there. If pressure has shown up a weakness in you, it has not shown your faith to be fake.

In Peter's letter the fire is there to show the metal is real, which is why his word is genuineness. Malachi's fire was for priests who had gone wrong, and even there God tells His people they are not destroyed. Neither passage calls every illness or cruelty a furnace God has lit to purify you, and neither asks you to stay where someone is harming you.
reflectQuestions: Peter's confidence in himself didn't survive the courtyard. What has pressure shown you about yourself that you hadn't seen before?
When you're under pressure for what you believe, where do you picture God while it's happening?
thematicGuides.practice: On a small card, write down one time in the past year when your faith cost you something. It can be as minor as an invitation that stopped coming. Under it copy five words from 1 Peter 1:7, "of greater worth than gold". Keep the card in your wallet or purse beside your bank card, where you'll come across it when you pay for things.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I don't like being the odd one out, and more than once I've kept quiet about You so that I wouldn't be. Peter did worse beside a fire, and You kept hold of him. Keep hold of me. The next time someone laughs at what I believe, don't let me go quiet again. I'd take being thought well of over almost anything, so I'm asking You to make my faith worth more to me than that. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Why Paul Wanted to Share Christ's Sufferings
thematicGuides.hook: Paul wanted a share in Christ's sufferings, and he had once heard Jesus say 'me' about the Christians he was jailing.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I want to know Christ, yes, to know the power of his resurrection and participation in his sufferings, becoming like him in his death.
thematicGuides.intro: Following Jesus is costing you something. Perhaps your family went quiet when you were baptised, or you live where the price is far higher. Paul and Peter call this sharing in the sufferings of Christ. They mean trouble that comes because you belong to Him, and neither man went looking for it. Both wrote as if Christ were in it with them. On the road to Damascus, Paul had heard Jesus say as much.
story: Saul of Tarsus, the man we know as Paul, had been going from house to house in Jerusalem, dragging off men and women who followed Jesus and putting them in prison. He was on his way to do the same in Damascus when a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" He asked who was speaking, and was told it was Jesus, whom he was persecuting. Saul was led into the city blind. The Lord sent a disciple named Ananias to him, and said of Saul, "I will show him how much he must suffer for my name."

In Philippi Paul and Silas were beaten with rods and locked in the inner cell with their feet in the stocks. The jailer washed their wounds that night and was baptised. Later, in chains again, Paul wrote to the church there. In the third chapter he lists what he once counted in his favour, and one item on the list is "as for zeal, persecuting the church". He now counts all of it as loss beside knowing Christ. A few lines after naming himself a persecutor of the church, he says he wants a share in the sufferings of the one he had persecuted.

Before Saul ever set out for Damascus, Peter and the other apostles had been arrested in Jerusalem for teaching about Jesus and brought before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council. The council wanted them dead, until Gamaliel, the Pharisee who was Saul's teacher, argued for letting them go. He persuaded the council, but first it had them flogged and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus. Then it released them. They left rejoicing, Acts says, because they had been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the Name. In his first letter Peter tells churches insulted for the name of Christ not to be surprised, and to rejoice in so far as they share Christ's sufferings. He adds that if any of them suffers, it should not be as a murderer or a thief, "or even as a meddler".

keyVerses.text: He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?' 'Who are you, Lord?' Saul asked. 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,' he replied.
I want to know Christ, yes, to know the power of his resurrection and participation in his sufferings, becoming like him in his death, and so, somehow, attaining to the resurrection from the dead.

But rejoice inasmuch as you participate in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed when his glory is revealed. If you are insulted because of the name of Christ, you are blessed, for the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.

insights: Jesus said 'me' about believers Saul had put in prison. Whether being known as His has cost you your freedom or a friendship, He counts it as done to Him. The man who heard that 'me' is the one who later wrote of sharing in Christ's sufferings.

Paul's sentence begins and ends with resurrection, with the sufferings in between. Pain is not where he is heading, and nothing here is a reason to stay where someone is hurting you. He left Damascus in a basket through the city wall, and in Jerusalem he stopped a flogging by saying he was a Roman citizen. He got out of harm's way when he could, and so may you.
reflectQuestions: When being a Christian last cost you something, how near or far did Jesus seem to you while it was going on?
Paul wrote off his old advantages as loss beside knowing Christ. Whose good opinion would it hurt you most to lose for being known as His?
thematicGuides.practice: Think of one person you know who is paying a price for belonging to Christ. It may be someone at your church who had to leave their own country over it. This week go and see them, take a meal with you, and tell them you've noticed. The Philippians did this for Paul by sending Epaphroditus with their gifts, and Paul wrote back that they had shared in his troubles.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I want to know You without it costing me anything, and that isn't what Paul wanted. Most of what I've paid so far is embarrassment, and I've resented even that. Thank You that You said 'me' about people in a prison cell, and would say it about me. When being Yours next costs me something, let me remember You are in it. And keep me from calling it Your cross when the trouble is my own doing. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Weeping May Stay for the Night
thematicGuides.hook: David sang of joy in the morning in a psalm that never says how long the night will be.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Weeping may stay for the night, but rejoicing comes in the morning.
thematicGuides.intro: David wrote Psalm 30 after he had nearly died. It has the line people say at funerals, that weeping may stay for the night but rejoicing comes in the morning. It tends to be said too soon. David sang it once his own night was over. If yours isn't, you're hearing the line from a man on the far side of his.
story: When he felt secure, David had said, "I will never be shaken." Then, as he tells it in Psalm 30, God hid His face and he was dismayed. He was close to the grave, and his prayer from that time argues with God, asking what He would gain if David went down to the pit. God healed him. David says He took off his sackcloth, the rough cloth of mourning, and clothed him with joy. He calls on God's faithful people to sing with him, and the verse about night and morning is the reason he gives them.

The singers of Psalm 126 look back to the day God restored the fortunes of Zion, most likely the exiles' return from Babylon. They were like people dreaming, they say, with mouths full of laughter. Two verses on they are asking God to restore their fortunes again. The psalm ends with a sower who goes out weeping, carrying his seed, and comes home singing with sheaves in his arms. Ezra 3 describes a day from that homecoming. When the foundation of the new temple was laid, the people gave a great shout of praise, but many of the old men who had seen the first temple wept aloud. No one could tell the sound of the joy from the sound of the weeping.

Jesus told His disciples, the night before He died, that soon they would not see Him, and then after a little while they would see Him again. They kept asking one another what He meant by "a little while". He told them they would weep and mourn while the world rejoiced. Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb, and later she stood outside it crying. Two angels asked her, "Woman, why are you crying?" Jesus, whom she took for the gardener, asked the same and then said her name. That evening He came to the disciples behind locked doors and showed them His hands and His side, and they were overjoyed. The marks had not gone.

keyVerses.text: For his anger lasts only a moment, but his favor lasts a lifetime; weeping may stay for the night, but rejoicing comes in the morning.
Those who sow with tears will reap with songs of joy. Those who go out weeping, carrying seed to sow, will return with songs of joy, carrying sheaves with them.
So with you: Now is your time of grief, but I will see you again and you will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy.

insights: Psalm 30:5 sets a moment against a lifetime and a night against a morning. David is saying which of the two lasts, and he gives no hour for the dawn. For some losses the morning may be the one in Isaiah 25:8, when God swallows up death and wipes the tears from all faces.

David linked his night to his own complacency. Mary wept because her Lord was dead and now His body was gone. Scripture doesn't trace every grief to a fault, so the word 'anger' in David's verse is no verdict on yours.

Twice at the tomb Mary was asked why she was crying, and both times she answered. If your sorrow has gone on for months and is taking your sleep or your will to get up, your doctor should hear about it, and so should the next friend who asks how you are.
reflectQuestions: If you're in the middle of a grief now, how does David's line about the morning sound from where you are?
Looking back at a sorrow that did ease in time, what do you remember about the first day you noticed joy had come back?
thematicGuides.practice: Each day this week, do one small ordinary job that sorrow has made hard to face, such as opening the curtains. Do it whether or not you feel any better, as the sower in Psalm 126 goes out with his seed, weeping as he goes. Then pray the psalm's own request once, "Restore our fortunes, LORD, like streams in the Negev." If the grief is someone else's, pray it for them.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I've been told that joy comes in the morning so often that I've stopped hearing it. It's still night here. You know what I've lost. I don't altogether want to feel better, because that feels like letting go of what I loved. I won't ask You to hurry me. Stay with me while it's dark, and when morning comes, here or on the day You wipe every face dry, let me know Your voice as Mary did when You said her name. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Question Micah 6:8 Was Answering
thematicGuides.hook: To act justly and to love mercy was the answer given to a worshipper offering God rams, rivers of oil and, last of all, a child.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: He has shown you, O mortal, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you? To act justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God.
thematicGuides.intro: There's no finishing Micah 6:8, and that's what is hard about it. A gift to God, however large, can be handed over and ticked off, and something in us would rather be told the amount and allowed to get on. Acting justly, loving mercy and walking humbly with God has no last payment. The verse is the closing line of a court scene, and the person it answers was trying to settle up.
story: The scene opens with God telling the prophet to stand up and plead His case before the mountains, because He is bringing a charge against Israel. Then, where you expect the charge, God asks, "My people, what have I done to you? How have I burdened you? Answer me." His evidence is a list of what He has done for them. He brought them up out of Egypt, the land of slavery. He sent Moses to lead them, and Aaron and Miriam too. When Balak king of Moab hired Balaam to curse them, Balaam blessed them instead. God took them from Shittim, east of the Jordan, to Gilgal on the far bank, with the river stopped in between. The mountains had been there for all of it.

A voice replies, speaking as a single worshipper, and it doesn't answer the question. It asks what to bring, and the offers climb. Burnt offerings come first, with calves a year old, which the law of Moses itself provided for. Thousands of rams follow, and then ten thousand rivers of olive oil. The last offer is a firstborn child, given for the parent's sin. Israel's law forbade the sacrifice of a child, and yet it was being done. Micah's years as a prophet included the reign of Ahaz of Judah, and 2 Kings records that Ahaz sacrificed his son in the fire.

Micah's reply begins, "He has shown you, O mortal, what is good." God's question had been put to His own people, and the answer is addressed to anyone alive. It asks for three things, to act justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with God, none of which can be carried to an altar and left there. The law commanded burnt offerings, and Micah leaves that standing. He supplies what the list of offers left out. In the verses that follow God speaks of dishonest scales, a bag of false weights and a measure made short. In the city Micah was speaking to, acting justly began at the market stall.

keyVerses.text: Hear, you mountains, the LORD's accusation; listen, you everlasting foundations of the earth. For the LORD has a case against his people; he is lodging a charge against Israel.
Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousand rivers of olive oil? Shall I offer my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?
He has shown you, O mortal, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you? To act justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God.

insights: Micah says you have already been shown. Most of the time you do know what the fair thing and the kind thing would be, and asking what God wants from you can be a way of putting it off.
The verse asks you to act justly but to love mercy. You can be fair to someone while resenting every minute of it. Mercy is the one Micah wants you to be fond of.

God's case opened with what He had already done, so the three requirements were never a price. The question about sin is real, though, and verse 8 doesn't answer it. The New Testament does. Paul writes that God "did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all".
reflectQuestions: Which of Micah's three, acting justly, loving mercy or walking humbly with God, do you find hardest to keep up when nobody is checking?
What are you most likely to offer God, such as extra giving or more time at church, in place of being fair to the people you deal with all week?
thematicGuides.practice: Micah goes straight on to scales and weights, so begin with what you owe. Find one thing you've been slow to pay or give back, such as money a friend lent you, a tradesman's bill or a borrowed tool. Take it to them within the next few days, in person if you can. Keep the handover short, and skip the speech about why it's late.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I would sooner pay You than change. I've offered You busier Sundays and bigger promises, hoping You'd overlook how I treat the people who can do nothing for me. You have already shown me what is good, and I keep asking as though You hadn't. Make me fair in the dealings I'd like to keep vague, and glad to show mercy without keeping count. Thank You for giving Your own Son for my sin, since I could never pay for it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: God of Gods, Defender of Widows
thematicGuides.hook: Unasked, Jesus stopped the funeral of a widow's only son, and the first church had to be told it was overlooking its own widows.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.
thematicGuides.intro: Deuteronomy 10 calls God the God of gods and Lord of lords, and by the next verse He is taking up the case of a widow and a fatherless child. You may have lost a husband or a wife, or grown up without a parent. If so, these passages are about you, and they say who is on your side. If not, they're specific about what is asked of you.
story: In the fortieth year after Israel left Egypt, Moses was telling the people what the LORD is like. The great God, he said, shows no partiality and accepts no bribes, which matters most to someone with nothing to offer a judge. Later in the book the people are given laws to match. Nobody was to take a widow's cloak as security for a loan. A sheaf overlooked at harvest was to stay where it lay, and olive trees and vines were to be gone over only once, with the rest left for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. Moses gives the reason twice. They had been slaves in Egypt themselves.

Jesus was coming up to the gate of a town called Nain when a dead man was carried out, his mother's only son, and she was a widow. Nobody had asked Jesus for anything. He saw her, and He felt for her. He told her not to cry, touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. He told the young man to get up. The dead man sat up and began to talk, and "Jesus gave him back to his mother". The first book of Kings says almost the same of Elijah at Zarephath, when a widow's son came back to life and the prophet "gave him to his mother". The crowd said that a great prophet had appeared among them.

The church in Jerusalem was growing fast and gave out food every day. The Greek-speaking Jewish believers complained against the Hebrew-speaking ones that their widows were being overlooked. The twelve apostles called everyone together, and Luke records no argument. They asked the whole group to choose seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom to take charge of the food. Luke gives all seven names, and every one is Greek, so the job may well have gone to men from the side that had complained. The apostles prayed and laid their hands on them, and the next sentence says the word of God spread.

keyVerses.text: For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great God, mighty and awesome, who shows no partiality and accepts no bribes. He defends the cause of the fatherless and the widow, and loves the foreigner residing among you, giving them food and clothing.
When the Lord saw her, his heart went out to her
Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.

insights: If you've been widowed or lost a parent, you won't be given back in this life what the widow at Nain was given. The Lord who noticed her before anyone asked is the one you pray to, and Psalm 68 calls God "a father to the fatherless, a defender of widows".
The widow at Nain wasn't on her own at the gate. A large crowd from the town was with her. If you don't know what to say to someone who is grieving, start where her neighbours did and turn up.

James says the religion God accepts looks after widows and orphans. The Jerusalem church, full of the Spirit, still missed its own. What put it right was a complaint that was listened to and seven people given the job. Anyone being missed today has Acts 6 as grounds for saying so.
reflectQuestions: Thinking of someone you know who has been widowed or has lost a parent, what do you know about how they are managing day to day?
In the months after a funeral, whether you were the one who was left or one of those looking on, what has your faith led you to do?
thematicGuides.practice: Think of one person who has been widowed, or one household missing a mother or a father, and every day for a week do one small thing for them, like a text in the morning or a meal left on the step. If you are the one who has been left, turn it round. Each day accept one small thing someone offers, or ask one person for one small thing, and don't apologise for it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, You saw a widow at a town gate before anyone said a word to You. I'm good at funerals and poor at the months afterwards. Bring to mind the people I know who are grieving on their own, and get me to their door with food and time. If I am the one who has been left, see me as You saw her, and help me say so when I'm being missed. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Two Halves of God's Name
thematicGuides.hook: On Sinai God called Himself compassionate, and with His next words said the guilty do not go unpunished.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Love and faithfulness meet together; righteousness and peace kiss each other.
thematicGuides.intro: Your brother borrowed money from your mother, never paid it back, and is coming to dinner on Sunday. Half the family wants it said to his face, and the other half wants it left alone for one evening. We each know which half we'd be in, and assume God is in it too. When God describes Himself in Exodus, He takes both sides.
story: Israel made a golden calf while Moses was up Mount Sinai, and when he came down he smashed the two stone tablets of God's law. Later God told him to chisel out two more, and early in the morning he climbed alone with the blank stones in his hands. The LORD came down in the cloud and proclaimed His own name. He called Himself compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, full of love and faithfulness, and forgiving. He went straight on to say that He does not leave the guilty unpunished, and that the punishment reaches the third and fourth generation. Moses bowed to the ground at once and asked God to "forgive our wickedness and our sin". He counted himself in, though he had been up the mountain when the calf was made.

Psalm 85 is sung by people God had already forgiven once, now in trouble again and asking whether He will be angry with them for ever. Then the asking stops. Up to here the psalm has said 'us'. Now one voice says, "I will listen to what God the LORD says". He hears a promise of peace for God's people, with a warning not to turn to folly. After that the psalm brings back the pair from the name God gave on Sinai. Love and faithfulness meet, and righteousness and peace greet each other with a kiss.

Jesus called Matthew away from his tax collector's booth, and at dinner in Matthew's house many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with Him. Some Pharisees, a group strict about keeping God's law, asked His disciples why their teacher ate with such people. Jesus heard, and answered that it is the sick who need a doctor. Then He sent them to learn the meaning of a line from Hosea, where God tells His people He would rather have mercy from them than offerings burnt on an altar: "I desire mercy, not sacrifice". Mark and Luke describe this dinner too, calling the host Levi. Only Matthew's Gospel keeps the line from Hosea. The people round that table were, by Jesus' own account, the sick and the sinners, and He was eating with them.

keyVerses.text: The LORD, the LORD, the compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness, maintaining love to thousands, and forgiving wickedness, rebellion and sin. Yet he does not leave the guilty unpunished; he punishes the children and their children for the sin of the parents to the third and fourth generation.
Love and faithfulness meet together; righteousness and peace kiss each other. Faithfulness springs forth from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven.
It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. But go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice.' For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.

insights: The second half of the name is hard to take, and two things belong beside it. Ezekiel 18 says a child will not share a parent's guilt. And the numbers are lopsided, love to thousands against punishment to three or four generations. What that half rules out is a wrong that simply evaporates, which matters if you were the one wronged.

Mercy in Moses' prayer doesn't skip the truth about what was done. He called his people stiff-necked while he was asking for their pardon. Letting something go because you can't face the conversation leaves the debt exactly where it was.

Exodus says God does not leave the guilty unpunished. Paul says that in His patience He had "left the sins committed beforehand unpunished". The cross, he writes in Romans 3, shows God to be just while He puts right those who trust in Jesus. However that is explained, sin was not shrugged off there and sinners were not turned away.
reflectQuestions: When someone has done wrong, what makes you lean towards holding them to it, or towards letting it go?
Who do you need to be honest with about what they did, without walking away from them?
thematicGuides.practice: Ask someone you've fallen out with, or quietly written off, to eat with you this week, even just a sandwich at lunchtime. Be honest about what went wrong, and tell them what you'd like from here. If the person has abused you or isn't safe to be near, choose someone else, and talk the harder situation over with someone you trust.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, You called Yourself compassionate and said You don't leave the guilty unpunished, and I mostly want the first half for myself and the second for other people. Thank You that Jesus sat down to eat with the sick, because I'm one of them. Teach me to tell the truth about what's wrong and then stay at the table. Where I've called it mercy and only wanted a quiet life, make me honest. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Speaking Up for the Man in the Cistern
thematicGuides.hook: A foreign official went to the king about a prophet left to die in a pit, then fetched old rags to pad the ropes.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all who are destitute.
thematicGuides.intro: You can usually get a hearing when something is wrong. Complain about a bill or a missed delivery and, sooner or later, somebody answers. Some people around you can't get one. The man in the care home rings his bell and nobody comes, and the agency cleaner would lose her shifts if she complained. Proverbs 31 tells a king to open his mouth for people in that position, and the book of Jeremiah has a palace official who did.
story: The last chapter of Proverbs begins with what a king named Lemuel was taught by his mother. She calls him the son of her womb and the answer to her prayers, then warns him off the things that ruin kings, drink among them. Her reason is that a king who drinks may "forget what has been decreed, and deprive all the oppressed of their rights". Then she tells him twice to speak up, first for those who cannot speak for themselves and then, as a fair judge, for the poor and needy. She has the king's ear, and she spends it on people who will never get near him.

Jerusalem was under siege, and Jeremiah kept saying the city would fall to Babylon. Four officials told King Zedekiah that Jeremiah should be put to death for it. The king answered that he could do nothing to oppose them. So they lowered Jeremiah on ropes into a cistern in the courtyard of the guard. It held no water, only mud, and he sank into it. Ebed-Melek, a foreigner from Cush who served in the palace, heard about it. He went out to the Benjamin Gate, where the king was sitting, and said that these men had acted wickedly, and that Jeremiah would starve to death down there once the city's bread ran out. This time the king gave an order. Ebed-Melek was to take thirty men and lift Jeremiah out before he died.

Ebed-Melek went with the thirty men himself. On the way he stopped at a room under the palace treasury for old rags and worn-out clothes. He let them down on ropes and told Jeremiah to put them under his arms as padding. Jeremiah did, and they hauled him up out of the mud. He stayed a prisoner in that courtyard until the day Jerusalem was captured, and while he was there God gave him a message for Ebed-Melek by name. The city would fall before his eyes, God said, but "you will not be given into the hands of those you fear". The book never says who they were, only that Ebed-Melek had people he was afraid of.

keyVerses.text: Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all who are destitute. Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy.

My lord the king, these men have acted wickedly in all they have done to Jeremiah the prophet. They have thrown him into a cistern, where he will starve to death when there is no longer any bread in the city.

Rescue those being led away to death; hold back those staggering toward slaughter. If you say, 'But we knew nothing about this,' does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who guards your life know it? Will he not repay everyone according to what they have done?

insights: Ebed-Melek already had the king's order when he stopped for the rags. Speaking for someone includes caring how the help reaches them, down to what a rope does under a man's arms.

Proverbs 24 expects the excuse "we knew nothing about this", which plenty of us have used, and says God sees through it. But it is written as a command, and a command is about the next time. The one who weighs your heart is called, in the same verse, the one who guards your life.
reflectQuestions: Who do you know by name who can't get a hearing in a place where you could get one?
When you think of a time you kept quiet about something you knew was wrong, what were you afraid would happen if you spoke?
thematicGuides.practice: Think of one person you know who isn't being heard. If you can, ask them first whether they want it raised. Then work out two sentences like Ebed-Melek's, one saying what has been done to them and one saying what will happen if it's left. Before next weekend, say them face to face or by phone to whoever can change it, a manager or a landlord.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, You speak to the Father for me when I've nothing to say for myself. There is someone I could speak for, and I've been hoping somebody better placed would do it. You know who I'm afraid of and what it might cost me. Give me two plain sentences and get me as far as the gate. Make me careful about how the help reaches them. Forgive the times I knew and kept quiet, and don't let them be my reason for keeping quiet now. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Year of the Lord's Favour in Nazareth
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus went home to Nazareth and read Isaiah's lines about good news for the poor, and the visit ended at a cliff edge.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.
thematicGuides.intro: In the synagogue at Nazareth, where He had been brought up, Jesus was handed the scroll of Isaiah. He read a few lines about good news for the poor and told His neighbours the words had come true that day. They liked what they heard. It's easy to like until it costs you something you're holding, or goes to someone you'd have left off the list. The last phrase He read, the year of the Lord's favour, looks back to a year in Israel's law when land was handed back.
story: At Sinai God gave Moses a law for a land Israel had not yet entered. After every forty-nine years a trumpet was to sound across the country on the Day of Atonement, the day each year when the people's sins were dealt with. The fiftieth year was the jubilee. Liberty was to be proclaimed to everyone in the land, and a field that had been sold was to come back to its family. The law even set the price of land by it. A buyer paid for the harvests left before the next jubilee, since what was really being sold was the number of crops.

Centuries later the book of Isaiah echoed the jubilee. Its speaker says God's Spirit is on him and that he has been sent to proclaim freedom for captives and the year of the Lord's favour. On a Sabbath in Nazareth, Jesus found that place in the scroll and read it. In Isaiah the sentence runs on to "the day of vengeance of our God". The reading Luke records stops just short of those words. Jesus rolled the scroll up, handed it back to the attendant and sat down, and everyone in the synagogue kept their eyes on Him. His first word was 'Today'. This scripture, He said, was fulfilled as they listened.

Everyone in the Nazareth synagogue spoke well of Him at first, and they asked, "Isn't this Joseph's son?" Jesus told them no prophet is accepted in his home town. Then He reminded them that during the famine in Elijah's time Israel had many widows, yet Elijah was sent to a widow in Zarephath, a foreign town in the region of Sidon. In Elisha's time Israel had many people with leprosy, and the only one cleansed was Naaman, a Syrian general whose wife was served by an Israelite girl captured in a raid. Everyone in the synagogue was furious. They drove Him out of the town to the brow of the hill it stood on, to throw Him off the cliff. He walked straight through the crowd and went on His way.

keyVerses.text: Consecrate the fiftieth year and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you; each of you is to return to your family property and to your own clan.

The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim freedom for the prisoners and recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.
Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.

insights: The jubilee trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, so the year when land went back began on the day sins were dealt with. Being put right with God and putting things right with a neighbour were set for the same day.

Between Nazareth's praise and its fury came two foreigners, a widow near Sidon and a Syrian general. The congregation welcomed God's favour and could not bear hearing where it had gone before. You may have people you'd rather it didn't reach.

The jubilee law was given to Israel for its own land, and the Gospels never show Jesus handing back a field. Acts, which Luke also wrote, does show His followers selling land and houses so that "there were no needy persons among them".
reflectQuestions: The lines Jesus read name the poor, prisoners and the oppressed. Where do they come into an ordinary week of yours?
What would a jubilee, a real way back, look like for someone near you who is stuck with a debt, a record or a bad name?
thematicGuides.practice: Stop chasing one thing you're owed and can afford to lose, such as money lent to a friend or an apology you've been waiting for. Don't mention it or hint at it until a week from today. When the week is up, decide whether to let it go for good. At the jubilee, land that people had been holding went back to the family it came from.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I'm as much an outsider to Nazareth as the widow in Zarephath was, and Your favour reached me anyway. I still keep a list of the people it shouldn't go to. I'd have sat in that synagogue nodding, and I know the names that would have brought me to my feet. When You are kind to them, keep me in my seat. And show me what I'm holding that I could hand back. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Iron Sharpens Iron: Jonathan and David
thematicGuides.hook: Jonathan went out to David in the wilderness and, in four short sentences, gave him courage and gave up his claim to the throne.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another.
thematicGuides.intro: Most people who quote "iron sharpens iron" mean that a real friend tells you the truth even when it stings. That's fair, and the same chapter of Proverbs says wounds from a friend can be trusted. The Bible's best-known friends, Jonathan and David, show a different kind of sharpening. Another pair, Paul and Barnabas, fell out so badly that they parted, and the Bible records that too.
story: Jonathan was King Saul's son and in line for the throne, and he loved David as himself. On the second day of a New Moon feast David's seat at the king's table was empty again. Jonathan made excuses for him, and Saul turned on his son. He said that as long as David lived neither Jonathan nor his kingdom would be established, and told him to send for David, who must die. Jonathan answered, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?" Saul hurled his spear at him. Jonathan left the table and ate nothing that day, grieved at the way his father had treated David. In the morning he went out to the field where David was hiding and warned him to get away.

Later David was hiding in the Desert of Ziph. Saul searched for him day after day, but God did not give David into his hands. When David learned that Saul had come out to take his life, Jonathan went to him at Horesh. He told him not to be afraid, because Saul would not lay a hand on him. Then he said what his father had warned him of at the table: "You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you. Even my father Saul knows this." The two made a covenant, a solemn promise, before the LORD. Jonathan went home and David stayed at Horesh. It is the last time the story shows them together. Jonathan was killed in the same battle as his father, before David became king.

When Paul first came to Jerusalem as a believer, the disciples were all afraid of him. Barnabas took him to the apostles and told them his story. Later Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for him and brought him to Antioch, and from there the two were sent out to preach together. Some time after their return, Paul proposed going back to the towns where they had preached. Barnabas wanted to bring John Mark, who had left them part-way through the first trip and returned to Jerusalem. Paul didn't think that wise, and Acts says they "had such a sharp disagreement that they parted company." Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, and Paul chose Silas and went through Syria and Cilicia.

keyVerses.text: And Saul's son Jonathan went to David at Horesh and helped him find strength in God.
David was greatly distressed because the men were talking of stoning him; each one was bitter in spirit because of his sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.
As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another.

insights: At Horesh Jonathan helped David find strength in God. Seven chapters later, at Ziklag, the town had been burned and David's own men were talking of stoning him. Nobody came out to him this time, and he found that strength in the LORD his God on his own.

The proverb uses iron for both friends, so neither gives way easily. Acts reports that two people who loved God quarrelled and parted, and it gives no verdict, which is a mercy to anyone who has had a quarrel like it.
reflectQuestions: What has someone said or done, at a time when you were low, that helped you find strength in God?
Think of a friendship you've kept at a safe distance. What would you be risking if you let that person get closer?
thematicGuides.practice: On your next free evening, go to a friend who's under pressure and has little fight left, or ring if they live too far away. Ask how things are and listen until they've finished. Then tell them, in a sentence or two, one thing about God that has kept you going. Jonathan said what he had to say and went home, so you needn't stay late or solve anything.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I know what it is to go quiet and hope someone will come looking. Show me who is doing that now, and give me something true to say about You when I get there. I'm quicker with advice than with the trip out to where they are. There's a friendship of mine that ended in a row I still think I was right about. Keep me from writing that person off. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Ruth, Who Was Better Than Seven Sons
thematicGuides.hook: Ruth tied her life to a grieving woman who kept telling her to go home, then went out to find them both food.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God.
thematicGuides.intro: Loyalty is hardest when the person you're staying with has nothing to give back and can't see what you're giving them. Grief can do that to someone for years. In the book of Ruth a young widow from Moab refuses to leave a woman in that state, her mother-in-law Naomi, and follows her to Bethlehem, where Ruth is a foreigner among people she doesn't know.
story: Naomi had buried her husband and both her sons in Moab. On the road home to Bethlehem she told her sons' widows, Orpah and Ruth, to turn back. She had no more sons to give them, and she said the LORD's hand had turned against her. Orpah kissed her goodbye and went, and the book has no word of blame for her. Ruth clung to Naomi, and her answer went as far as the grave: "Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried." She swore it in the name of the LORD, the God Naomi had just said was against her. Naomi saw that Ruth was determined and stopped urging her.

When they reached Bethlehem the women asked if this could be Naomi. She told them to call her Mara, which means bitter. "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." She said it with Ruth beside her. The next thing Ruth says is a request to go and glean, picking up what the harvesters left behind. When the field's owner, Boaz, arrived, she had worked since morning with one short rest. He told her to stay in his field and drink from his men's water jars. She asked why he would notice a foreigner, and he answered that he had been told all she had done for her mother-in-law. That evening she carried home her barley and gave Naomi what was left of her own midday meal.

Boaz was one of the family's guardian-redeemers, relatives with the right to buy back its land and keep a dead man's name alive. Ruth asked him to act, and he agreed. A nearer relative had first claim, so Boaz met him at the town gate in front of ten elders. The man was ready to buy Naomi's field until he heard that Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's widow, came with it. "I might endanger my own estate," he said, and took off his sandal to hand the right over. Boaz married Ruth and she had a son, Obed, the grandfather of King David. The women who had heard Naomi call herself empty now told her that her daughter-in-law loved her and was better to her than seven sons.

keyVerses.text: Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God.

I've been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, how you left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before. May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.
He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.

insights: Naomi came home saying she was empty. When Boaz later filled Ruth's shawl with barley, he told her not to go back to her mother-in-law empty-handed. Naomi had said 'empty' with Ruth standing next to her, and it was Ruth who came home carrying the barley.
Ruth made her promise with no Boaz in sight. Her vow looked no further ahead than a grave beside Naomi's. You aren't promised that your loyalty will end in a wedding, or that anyone will notice it.

Naomi was bitter, but she never mistreated Ruth, and she told her to go for Ruth's own good. The story honours staying with someone who is hurting. Staying with someone who is hurting you is a different matter, and Ruth's vow shouldn't be used to keep anyone there.
reflectQuestions: Who in your life is having a hard enough time to need you close, even if they keep saying you needn't bother?
Which part of what Ruth did for Naomi would be hardest for you to do for someone in your own family or circle of friends?
thematicGuides.practice: Offer one person a small, regular thing for the next four weeks: a phone call every Sunday evening, or a lift to the shops on Fridays. Pick someone who is grieving or worn down and has stopped asking. Tell them today, then keep to it, including the week you'd sooner not.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, there's someone I'm finding it hard to stay close to. They're low, they push me away, and I mind that they never seem to notice I'm there. Give me Ruth's kind of loyalty, which went out to the field in the morning and didn't wait to be thanked. And when I'm the one saying I'm empty, let me see who is standing beside me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Marriage, With God as Witness
thematicGuides.hook: Men in Malachi's day wept over offerings God would not accept, and were told it was because of how they had treated their wives.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.
thematicGuides.intro: Paul tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her. Twenty-three verses earlier he says almost the same thing to every Christian in Ephesus, married or not. So that love is asked of all of us. Marriage adds a promise, made to one person with God as witness, and the Bible's word for that promise is covenant.
story: In Genesis 2 God makes a woman from one of the man's ribs while he sleeps and brings her to him. The man's first words in the Bible are about her: "This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." Genesis adds that this is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh. Long afterwards some Pharisees asked Jesus whether a man might lawfully divorce his wife. He took them back to that sentence and added that it is God who has joined the two together, and no one should separate them.

The Bible's plainest use of the word covenant for marriage is in the prophet Malachi. Men were flooding the LORD's altar with tears because He no longer accepted their offerings, and they asked why. The answer was about their wives. The LORD, Malachi said, was the witness between each man and the wife of his youth, the wife of his marriage covenant, and each had been unfaithful to her. God had been there when the promise was made. He added that the man who hates and divorces his wife "does violence to the one he should protect". Nobody in the passage speaks for the wives except God.

Paul's letter to the church in Ephesus comes to marriage late. By then he has told them all to walk in the way of love, as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us, and to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. He gives wives three verses. They are to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, and the husband is called the head of the wife. Christians read those lines in different ways. Husbands get most of the next nine, which open with what the whole church has already heard, almost word for word: love her as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.

keyVerses.text: It is because the LORD is the witness between you and the wife of your youth. You have been unfaithful to her, though she is your partner, the wife of your marriage covenant.
walk in the way of love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us as a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.

insights: How you treat the person you made a promise to can get in the way of your prayers. Malachi's men found that out at the altar, and Peter tells husbands to treat their wives with respect so that nothing will hinder theirs.

Paul quotes the one-flesh verse and says he is talking about Christ and the church. Marriage is the picture, and what it pictures belongs in full to the person who never married, as Jesus never did, and to the one whose marriage ended or who has buried a husband or wife.

Christians reach different conclusions about when a marriage may be ended, but Malachi calls a wife the one her husband should protect. If you aren't safe at home, tell a friend, your GP or a domestic abuse helpline, and get to safety. Nothing in these passages asks you to stay in danger.
reflectQuestions: Married or not, you have made promises to people. Take one of them. What changes when you think of God as its witness?
In the relationship that matters most to you, what are you keeping a running count of?
thematicGuides.practice: Paul asked the whole church for a love that gives itself up. For one week, go without keeping score with the person you're closest to, whether that's a husband or wife, a parent, a housemate or a friend. Don't mention, out loud or with a look, who cooked last or whose turn it is to ring. When the tally starts up in your head, do the next small job that needs doing and say nothing about it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, You gave Yourself up for people who had given You nothing, and I'm one of them. I keep careful accounts with the people I love, and could tell You who apologised last. Help me keep the promises I've made, and keep them without the ledger. You were the witness to any that were made to me and broken, and I ask You to heal what that left. On the days I'm on my own, let me know I'm not outside the love that marriage is a picture of. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: One Another Means Someone in Particular
thematicGuides.hook: The command to love one another was given on the night Jesus washed feet, and in Romans it comes with a list of names.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.
thematicGuides.intro: A message goes round asking whether anyone could drive an older member of the church to a hospital appointment on Thursday, and you wait a while to see whether somebody else answers first. It costs nothing to be in favour of loving one another so long as nobody in particular is meant. The New Testament keeps using the phrase, and the verbs that go with it need a person on the other end: wash, honour, greet, carry.
story: The evening meal was under way, just before the Passover, when Jesus got up from the table and wrapped a towel round His waist. He poured water into a basin and began to wash His disciples' feet. Judas had not yet left the table. When Jesus had finished, He told them that since He, their Lord and Teacher, had washed their feet, they should wash one another's. After Judas had gone out into the night, He gave the rest a new command, to love one another, and the measure He set for it was "As I have loved you". He had washed the feet of every man who heard it, earlier that evening.

Paul wrote to the Christians in Rome before he had ever been there. He told them to honour one another above themselves, and to rejoice with those who rejoice and mourn with those who mourn. Towards the end of the letter he greeted more than twenty of them by name, many with a word about what they had done. Mary had worked very hard for them. Priscilla and Aquila had risked their lives for him, and a church met in their house. He greeted Rufus along with his mother, "who has been a mother to me, too." The list ends with "Greet one another with a holy kiss", a greeting he leaves them to give.

Paul first preached in Galatia because he was ill. His illness was a trial to the people there, he reminds them in his letter, but they welcomed him, and would have torn out their own eyes and given them to him if they could. Later in the same letter he says that when one of them is caught in a sin, those who live by the Spirit are to restore that person gently, and to watch themselves, because they may be tempted too. Then he tells them to carry each other's burdens, and says that is how the law of Christ is kept. Three verses later he adds, "each one should carry their own load."

keyVerses.text: A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.
Be devoted to one another in love. Honor one another above yourselves.
Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

insights: Paul knew who in Rome had worked hard, who had risked their lives and whose mother had been a mother to him. You can't honour people, or carry much for them, when you only know them by sight.

The first burden Paul has in mind in Galatians 6 is another person's failure. Carrying it means helping someone who has done wrong to get back on their feet, gently, and remembering that you could fall the same way.

The load Paul says each person must carry is their own actions, which nobody else can answer for. Burdens are different, and he expects them to be shared. That includes yours, so letting somebody help you is part of keeping the command.
reflectQuestions: Wash, honour, greet, rejoice with, mourn with, carry: which of these are you slowest to do for the people you see every week?
What would the Christians you see most often need to know about your life before they could help you carry any of it?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, on your own, read Romans 16:1-16 aloud, names and all. Then go through the coming week in your head and say to God the name of each person you expect to see, with one thing you know they're carrying. Sooner or later you'll reach a name and have nothing to say. That's the person to ask how things are at home, or at work, the next time you meet, and to wait for the answer.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I'm better at being friendly than at being any use. I know where some people went on holiday and nothing about what keeps them awake. Thank You for the ones who have carried things for me, whose names I could list the way Paul listed his. Show me whose burden I've walked past this week. I'd sooner help than be helped, and I suspect that's pride. Let me tell someone what I'm carrying too. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Just Between the Two of You
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus' steps for dealing with a wrong come straight after His story of a shepherd who goes looking for one sheep.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: If your brother or sister sins, go and point out their fault, just between the two of you. If they listen to you, you have won them over.
thematicGuides.intro: A friend or someone at church has wronged you. It's a person you could sit down with as an equal, and so far you've either said nothing and been carefully polite, or you've talked it over with people who weren't there. Jesus gave short instructions for exactly this in Matthew 18, and where they come in the chapter says a good deal about what they're for.
story: Jesus was still answering the disciples' question about who was greatest in the kingdom of heaven when He told them about a man with a hundred sheep. One wanders off, and the man leaves the ninety-nine on the hills to look for it. If he finds it, he's happier about that one than about all the others. "In the same way your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish," Jesus said, and went straight on to a brother or sister who sins. Go, He told them, and point out their fault, just the two of you. If they listen, you have won them over.

If the person won't listen, Jesus said, take one or two others along. His reason is a rule from Deuteronomy, that a matter has to be established by two or three witnesses. The rule protected the accused, since one witness was never enough to convict anyone. Whoever you bring is there to establish what happened, and might well not take your side. If that fails, tell it to the church, and if they won't listen even to the church, treat them as you would a pagan or a tax collector, someone outside the community. Then Peter came and asked how many times he had to forgive a brother or sister who sinned against him, and whether seven would do. Jesus told him seventy-seven.

Two women in the church at Philippi, Euodia and Syntyche, had fallen out. Paul's letter doesn't say what it was over or which of them was right. He pleads with each by name: "I plead with Euodia and I plead with Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord." Then he asks a third person, whom he calls his true companion, to help them, because both women had worked alongside him for the gospel. By the time the quarrel reached Paul it was past being private, and in a letter addressed to the whole church he blames neither woman.

keyVerses.text: If a man owns a hundred sheep, and one of them wanders away, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go to look for the one that wandered off?

If your brother or sister sins, go and point out their fault, just between the two of you. If they listen to you, you have won them over. But if they will not listen, take one or two others along, so that 'every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.'
Yes, and I ask you, my true companion, help these women since they have contended at my side in the cause of the gospel

insights: Jesus sets this instruction beside a shepherd looking for a sheep, so the point of going is to get the person back. Waiting for the other one to apologise feels fair, but He tells the one who was hurt to go. He also makes the person who did it the first to hear about it.

Philippi shows what the one or two others in Jesus' second step are for. Paul asks his companion to help both women and takes neither side himself. That is a long way from collecting people who'll agree with you.

All this is for a wrong between equals. If someone is hurting, frightening or controlling you, Jesus is not asking you to meet them alone. Your safety comes first, so tell a friend you trust, a church leader, a doctor or the police. When Saul tried to pin David to the wall with a spear, David fled that night through a window, and Scripture doesn't fault him.
reflectQuestions: One person will have come to mind as you read this. What is holding you back from speaking to them directly?
When someone upsets you, what do you usually do in the first day or two, before you've said a word to them?
thematicGuides.practice: If this is someone you can talk to as an equal, then before you go to them, write down what happened in three or four plain sentences: what they did or said, when, and what you'd like to be different. Leave out your guesses about why. Keep the page in your Bible at Matthew 18. It's what you'll say when the two of you talk, and what you'll show anyone you have to bring in.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I've told this story to several people, but never to the person who did it. I know my side of it by heart. You went after the one sheep, and part of me would rather this one stayed lost. I don't want to have this conversation. Help me start it. If I've got some of it wrong, I need to hear that. And if they won't listen, keep me from writing them off. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Timothy and the People Who Taught Him
thematicGuides.hook: Near the end of his life Paul told Timothy to keep going, and the reason he gave was the people Timothy had learned from.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it
thematicGuides.intro: When Paul came to Lystra he found a disciple there called Timothy, whose mother was a Jewish believer and whose father was a Greek. Paul's letters show what passed between the two of them over the years that followed, and by Paul's own account he wasn't Timothy's first teacher. If you've kept going as a Christian, there is probably someone older you watched at close quarters, as Timothy watched Paul.
story: The believers at Lystra and Iconium spoke well of Timothy, and Paul wanted to take him along on the journey. From then on Timothy went with him from town to town. Long afterwards, writing to Timothy, Paul looked back to before they met. The faith Paul saw in Timothy, he wrote, had lived first in Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. It is the only time in the Bible that either woman is named. Timothy had known the Scriptures since he was a small child. Of his own part Paul mentions that he had laid his hands on Timothy, and that he remembered him in his prayers night and day.

Some years into their work together Paul wrote to the church at Philippi. The letter opens with two names under one description, "Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus". Paul couldn't come to Philippi himself yet, so he hoped to send Timothy soon. He had no one else like Timothy, he told them. Everyone else looked out for their own interests, but Timothy would care about the Philippians. They knew how he had worked beside Paul, the way a son works with his father. Now the younger man was to go on ahead and bring back news.

Paul was chained like a criminal when he wrote his second letter to Timothy, and he said the time for his departure was near. Timothy, he wrote, knew all about his teaching, and also his way of life, his purpose, faith, patience, love and endurance, and "what kinds of things happened to me in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra". Lystra was Timothy's own town. Paul had been stoned there and dragged outside the city for dead. Then he told Timothy to carry on in what he had learned, because Timothy knew the people he had learned it from. And he asked for something himself. "Do your best to come to me quickly", he wrote, and bring the cloak left with Carpus at Troas, and the scrolls.

keyVerses.text: I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, now lives in you also.
But you know that Timothy has proved himself, because as a son with his father he has served with me in the work of the gospel.

But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.

insights: Paul gave the first credit for Timothy to a grandmother and a mother. Whoever taught you most may be someone nobody else would think to name. If you're teaching the faith to a child or a grandchild at home, that is the work Paul traced Timothy's faith back to.

Of the things Paul lists in 2 Timothy 3:10-11, only the first is teaching. The rest is how he lived and what he went through. If someone younger is watching you, much of what they take from you will be how you behave when things go badly.
reflectQuestions: Think of the person who taught you most about living as a Christian: what did you pick up from watching them that they never put into words?
If someone younger in the faith had travelled with you through last week, as Timothy did with Paul, what would they have learned from watching you?
thematicGuides.practice: Paul asked Timothy to come, and to bring a cloak. This week, go and see someone older who helped you believe, a grandparent or the person who sat beside you in church for years. Take something they'd use, a cake or an hour's help in the garden, and tell them one thing you learned from watching them. If they've died or live too far away, do the same for someone in your church who is doing that work now, and tell them who they remind you of.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I can see the faces of the people I learned You from, and I'm thanking You for them now. Most of them I've never thanked. What I believe was handed to me, though I like to think I worked it out myself. Keep me going in what they taught me. Someone is probably watching how I live, and on my worse days I'd prefer they weren't. Make what they see worth copying. And when I need help from someone younger, let me ask for it as Paul did. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Daniel: Neither Corrupt nor Negligent
thematicGuides.hook: Daniel's rivals searched his work for a charge to bring, found nothing, and made a crime of his prayers.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: They could find no corruption in him, because he was trustworthy and neither corrupt nor negligent.
thematicGuides.intro: Integrity is usually pictured as one big moment, the bribe pushed across the table or the lie that would save your job. Daniel had a night like that, with lions in it. But he had served at court in Babylon since his youth, and most of what tested him there was dull, starting with what was on his plate. Most of what tests you will be dull too.
story: Daniel was among the young men taken from Judah to Babylon to be trained for the king's service. That meant a new name, three years of Babylonian schooling and a daily ration from the king's table. As far as we're told, he took the name and the lessons. The food was another matter.
