He resolved not to defile himself with it or with the wine. When he asked to be excused, the chief official, whom God had made well disposed to him, was still afraid for his own head. So Daniel asked the guard to try him and his three friends on vegetables and water for ten days and judge by what he saw. Ten days later they looked healthier than the young men on the royal food, and the guard took their wine and choice food away.

King Belshazzar gave a banquet for a thousand nobles, and they drank from the gold goblets taken from the temple in Jerusalem. The fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall, and none of the king's wise men could read it. Daniel, who had served the king's father, was sent for and offered purple clothing, a gold chain and the third highest place in the kingdom for doing what they could not. He told the king to keep his gifts and give his rewards to someone else. Then he read the writing. God had brought Belshazzar's reign to an end, and the king had been weighed on the scales and found wanting. Belshazzar had him dressed in purple anyway. That very night the king was killed, and the kingdom Daniel had just been made third in passed to Darius the Mede.

Darius appointed 120 officials called satraps to rule the kingdom, with three administrators over them so that the king would not suffer loss. Daniel was one of the three, and did so well that Darius planned to put him over the whole kingdom. At that, the other administrators and the satraps went through his handling of government business for grounds to bring a charge, and found none. Finally they said, "We will never find any basis for charges against this man Daniel unless it has something to do with the law of his God." So they went to the king with a law against praying to anyone but him for thirty days.

keyVerses.text: But Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the royal food and wine, and he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself this way.
Then Daniel answered the king, 'You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else. Nevertheless, I will read the writing for the king and tell him what it means.'

At this, the administrators and the satraps tried to find grounds for charges against Daniel in his conduct of government affairs, but they were unable to do so. They could find no corruption in him, because he was trustworthy and neither corrupt nor negligent.

insights: When the chief official said Daniel's request could cost him his head, Daniel didn't press him. He offered the guard ten days and agreed to go by what the guard saw. A conviction can be held in a way that asks very little of other people.

Jeremiah's letter told the exiles in Babylon to "seek the peace and prosperity of the city". Daniel's working life is what that looks like. When his rivals went through it, they couldn't show that he had helped himself to anything or left a job half done.
A clean record didn't keep Daniel safe. It left his rivals one thing to use, his obedience to God, and they used it. Honest work comes with no guarantee that people will be fair to you.
reflectQuestions: If your harshest critic went through your work, your money and your messages, where would they look first?
Which small matter could you make up your mind about now, before any pressure comes?
thematicGuides.practice: Before this week is out, tell one person a polite no. Pick something small you go along with and wish you didn't, such as covering for a friend. See or ring whoever expects it of you, and say in two sentences that you'd rather not, and what you can do instead. Daniel's request to the guard began, "Please test your servants for ten days".
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, if someone went over my week the way those men went over Daniel's work, they'd find something, and I could tell them where to start. Forgive me for the corners I've cut because nobody was checking. Show me the thing I shouldn't accept, and help me say so early and politely, as Daniel did. If honest work goes unnoticed, or gets held against me, keep me at it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Joseph Did Right and Went to Prison
thematicGuides.hook: The cupbearer whose dream Joseph explained walked free and forgot him for two full years.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But while Joseph was there in the prison, the LORD was with him; he showed him kindness and granted him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.
thematicGuides.intro: Doing the right thing can make your life worse, and it can stay worse for a long time. You own up to a mistake and find you're the only one who pays for it. The usual comfort is that it works out in the end. For Joseph it did, but not for years. Genesis 39 says four times that the LORD was with him, twice while he is a slave and twice while he is in prison.
story: Joseph was sold in Egypt to Potiphar, the captain of Pharaoh's guard, who came to trust him with everything he owned. Then Potiphar's wife told Joseph to come to bed with her. He refused. His master had kept back nothing from him except her, he told her, and it would be a sin against God. She asked day after day, and he kept away from her. One day he went in to do his work when none of the other servants was inside, and she caught hold of his cloak. He left it in her hand and ran. The cloak stayed beside her until her husband came home, and then she told him his Hebrew slave had come in to make sport of her. Potiphar burned with anger and put Joseph in the prison where the king's prisoners were held.

The prison warden did what Potiphar had done and put Joseph in charge. Later Pharaoh's chief cupbearer and chief baker were locked up there. One morning Joseph saw that they were dejected, and when he asked why, they said each had dreamed in the night and there was no one to interpret it. Joseph said that interpretations belong to God and asked to hear the dreams. The cupbearer's meant he would be back at his post within three days. The baker's meant he would be put to death, and Joseph told him so. To the cupbearer he added a request: "mention me to Pharaoh and get me out of this prison." He had done nothing, he said, to deserve a dungeon. The third day was Pharaoh's birthday, and it all happened as Joseph had said. The cupbearer went back to work and forgot him.

Two full years after the cupbearer was released, Pharaoh had dreams that none of Egypt's magicians and wise men could interpret. Only then did the cupbearer speak up: "Today I am reminded of my shortcomings." Joseph was brought quickly from the dungeon. He shaved, changed his clothes and came before Pharaoh, who had heard that he could interpret dreams. Joseph's first words to him were "I cannot do it." God, he said, would give Pharaoh the answer. Then he explained the dreams, seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine, and Pharaoh put him in charge of all Egypt. Joseph was thirty years old. When his story opens in Genesis 37, tending the flocks with his brothers, he is seventeen.

keyVerses.text: My master has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How then could I do such a wicked thing and sin against God?
They bruised his feet with shackles, his neck was put in irons, till what he foretold came to pass, till the word of the LORD proved him true.
'I cannot do it,' Joseph replied to Pharaoh, 'but God will give Pharaoh the answer he desires.'

insights: Twice Joseph turned down something that wasn't his. In Potiphar's house it was the one thing his master had kept back. In front of Pharaoh, the man who could free him, it was the credit for an ability that was God's.

Psalm 105 adds what Genesis leaves out, the shackles on Joseph's feet and the irons on his neck. Genesis says of those same days that the LORD was with him. Neither promises you a better job or a cleared name for an honest choice. If doing right has left you worse off, that is where Joseph was when God was with him.
reflectQuestions: What has doing the right thing cost you lately that the easier option would have spared you?
When you hold back from something that tempts you, what usually stops you?
thematicGuides.practice: Find a friend this week who can keep a confidence, and tell them, in a few sentences, where doing the right thing has gone badly for you. Ask them for one specific thing, even if it's only that they ask you about it again in a month. Joseph asked the cupbearer to mention him to Pharaoh. The man forgot, and two years later he did it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I did what I believed was right and it has cost me. I've been keeping a tally ever since, and waiting for You to settle it. Joseph was still in that prison long after the cupbearer walked out, and You were with him there. Be with me. Keep me from grabbing what isn't mine to make up for what I've lost. And if someone has forgotten me as the cupbearer forgot Joseph, I trust that You haven't. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Son Who Said No and Went
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus told of a son who said yes and never went, and James of a man who looked in a mirror and forgot his own face.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says.
thematicGuides.intro: In Jesus's story of the two sons, the only one who calls his father "sir" is the one who never gets to the vineyard. We're often nearer that son than we'd like, with our 'I'll pray for you' and our 'leave it with me', said warmly and meant at the time. Jesus had more to say about what a yes is worth, and so does the letter of James.
story: The chief priests and elders came to Jesus in the temple courts to ask who gave Him His authority. He asked them first whether John's baptism was from heaven or of human origin. They worked out what each answer would cost them and said, "We don't know." So He told them about a man who asked his two sons to work in the vineyard that day. The first refused, then later changed his mind and went. The second said he would, and did not go. Asked which of the two did what his father wanted, the leaders said the first. Then Jesus told them that tax collectors and prostitutes, who had believed John, were entering the kingdom of God ahead of them. They had watched that happen and had still not changed their minds.

The old rule said an oath made to the Lord must be kept, and Jesus took it up in the Sermon on the Mount. By His day there were teachers ruling that an oath by the temple meant nothing, while an oath by its gold was binding. Jesus went through the things people swore by. Heaven is God's throne, the earth is His footstool and Jerusalem is the city of the Great King. Even your own head is not yours to pledge, since "you cannot make even one hair white or black." There was no oath small enough to leave God out of it. His instruction was not to swear at all, and to let a yes or a no be all they said.

James, who calls himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, wrote to believers scattered among the nations. Anyone who hears the word and doesn't do what it says, he tells them, is like someone who looks at his face in a mirror and, after looking at himself, goes away and at once forgets what he looks like. James doesn't accuse him of never looking. Beside the man at the mirror he sets someone who looks intently into that same word, which he calls the perfect law that gives freedom, and who stays with it and does what they have heard. That person, he says, will be blessed in what they do.

keyVerses.text: 'I will not,' he answered, but later he changed his mind and went. Then the father went to the other son and said the same thing. He answered, 'I will, sir,' but he did not go.
All you need to say is simply 'Yes' or 'No'; anything beyond this comes from the evil one.
Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says.

insights: Nothing in the parable says the second son was lying. He said yes, and then the day went by. A warm yes can leave you feeling you've done something, and so can a sermon you agreed with. James calls that deceiving yourself.
If you've said no to God, or said yes and done nothing about it, you can still go. The first son changed his mind and went, with no speech that we're told of, and that was what his father wanted.

Near the end of his letter James repeats Jesus's rule about yes and no almost word for word. If yes is all you're allowed to say, with nothing to swear by, you'll say it less often. Telling someone you can't is more honest than a yes you half expect to break.
reflectQuestions: Of the things you've told people lately that you would do, which one are you least likely to get round to?
What is one thing you have heard from the Bible many times, and agree with, that hasn't yet changed anything you do?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose one person you've promised something to and not delivered, perhaps the call you said you'd make or the prayer you said you'd pray. Do it within the next three days. Then tell them it's done, or if it's too late to do, tell them that and say sorry. Keep it short, and don't promise anything new while you're there.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I say yes too easily. I like how it sounds, and how people look at me when I say it, more than I like doing the thing. There are promises I made and haven't kept, and things I've heard You say so often that I nod and move on. Bring one of them to mind now, and get me to do it today. Teach me to say no when no is the truth. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: A Lamp on Its Stand
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus called His disciples the light of the world, then pictured a lamp that lights one house.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden.
thematicGuides.intro: Say the talk at the table turns to someone who isn't there. Everyone adds a little, and you add a little too, because sitting silent would be noticed. Jesus told His disciples they were the light of the world, and Paul picked the image up in two letters he wrote as a prisoner. Most of what they say about it comes down to moments about the size of that one at the table.
story: Jesus went up a mountainside, sat down and taught the disciples who came to Him. He called them the light of the world. A town on a hill can't be hidden, He told them, and nobody lights a lamp and then covers it with a bowl. It goes on its stand, where everyone in the house can see by it. Their good deeds were to be seen in the same way, and the praise was to go to their Father in heaven. Later in the same sermon He told them to be careful not to practise their righteousness in front of others "to be seen by them", and to give without the left hand knowing what the right is doing.

Paul spent more than two years in Ephesus. Many who believed there came and openly confessed what they had done. Some who had practised sorcery burned their scrolls in public, fifty thousand drachmas' worth, a drachma being about a day's pay. Some years on, Paul wrote to that church as a prisoner. Once, he told them, they were darkness, and now they were light in the Lord. They were to have nothing to do with the deeds of darkness and to expose them instead. Everything exposed by the light becomes visible, he wrote, and "everything that is illuminated becomes a light."

Paul was also in chains when he wrote to the church at Philippi. They had always obeyed, he told them, "not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence", and he asked them to carry on that way. Then he told them to do everything without grumbling or arguing, so that they would shine like stars in the sky among what he called a warped and crooked generation. That phrase comes from the song of Moses, where it describes Israel itself, the people who grumbled their way through the wilderness. Early in the letter Paul says the whole palace guard has learned he is in chains for Christ. Its last greetings include some from believers who belong to Caesar's household.

keyVerses.text: Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a bowl. Instead they put it on its stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven.
For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Live as children of light (for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness and truth)

Do everything without grumbling or arguing, so that you may become blameless and pure, 'children of God without fault in a warped and crooked generation.' Then you will shine among them like stars in the sky

insights: Jesus started with the world and finished on a lamp that lights one house. What happened in Ephesus and what Paul wrote to Philippi are that size too: believers owning up to what they had done, and a church told to get through its days without grumbling. The people who see it first are the ones who see you most days.

In Matthew 5 Jesus wants the good deeds seen, and a chapter later He warns the same people against doing good in order to be seen. The difference is who you're hoping gets the credit, you or your Father.

When Paul told the Ephesians to expose the deeds of darkness, he was writing to people who had begun with their own. If there's something you'd dread anyone finding out, the place to start is telling God, and then saying it out loud to one close friend.
reflectQuestions: In whose company do you most often go along with things so that you won't stand out?
Paul ties shining like stars to doing everything without grumbling or arguing. Where would the people around you notice it soonest if you did that this week?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick the one place where you complain most easily, whether that's work, home or a group chat. For three full days, starting tomorrow morning, go without grumbling there about anything or anyone. Paul also wanted wrong things brought into the light, so if something needs putting right, say so to the person who can do it. When you catch a complaint half out, stop and leave the sentence unfinished.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, in some rooms I've arranged things so that nobody could tell I belong to You, because I'd rather be easy company. Make me the same person in those rooms as I am alone with You. Whatever good people do see in me, I want the credit to go to You, and I know I usually keep some back for myself. I complain more than I'd noticed, so help me stop for three days and find out what else I have to say. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Trusted With Very Little
thematicGuides.hook: By very little, Jesus meant other people's money, and 2 Kings has foremen who handled it with nobody checking.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much.
thematicGuides.intro: Most of what you're trusted with this week is small, and most of it belongs to somebody else, like an hour your employer is paying for or the change from a neighbour's shopping. Hardly anyone will check what you do with it. Jesus had a saying about this, and long before He said it the men in charge of repairs to the temple in Jerusalem had lived up to it.
story: Jesus told His disciples about a rich man's manager who was accused of wasting his master's possessions and told he couldn't stay on. Before he was out of the job he called in his master's debtors and cut their bills, nine hundred gallons of olive oil down to four hundred and fifty, so that somebody would take him in afterwards. It's a puzzling story, because the master ends up commending the manager for his shrewdness, but the saying Jesus hung on it is clear enough: whoever can be trusted with very little can be trusted with much. He went on to say what He meant by very little. First He called it worldly wealth, which He set against true riches, and then "someone else's property". The Pharisees, who loved money, heard all this and sneered at Him.

King Joash of Judah wanted the temple repaired and told the priests to see to it out of the money people brought. By the twenty-third year of his reign it still hadn't been done. So the priest Jehoiada took a chest, bored a hole in its lid and stood it beside the altar. Whenever it held a large amount, the royal secretary and the high priest counted the money into bags and gave it to the foremen in charge of the work, who paid the carpenters and builders, masons and stonecutters, and bought timber and stone. Nobody asked these foremen to account for what they were handed, because, 2 Kings says, they acted with complete honesty. Not one of them is named.

In another of Jesus' stories, a man going on a journey leaves his money with three servants: five bags of gold to one, two to another and one to the third. A bag was a talent, about twenty years' pay for a labourer. The first two put the money to work and double it. When the master returns, a long time later, the servant with five bags is told he has been faithful with a few things and will be put in charge of many. The servant with two bags hears the same reply, word for word. The third had dug a hole and hidden his bag. He says he was afraid, and hands back exactly what he was given. The master calls him wicked and lazy, and says he should at least have put it in the bank.

keyVerses.text: So if you have not been trustworthy in handling worldly wealth, who will trust you with true riches? And if you have not been trustworthy with someone else's property, who will give you property of your own?
They did not require an accounting from those to whom they gave the money to pay the workers, because they acted with complete honesty.
Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Come and share your master's happiness!

insights: Jesus calls money very little, and the master in His story calls five bags of gold, about a hundred years' pay, a few things. On that scale your small job and somebody else's large one sit close together, and the same thing is asked of you both.

Jesus doesn't promise that honesty in small things leads to a bigger job. The bigger thing He names in Luke 16 is true riches, and in the story of the bags nothing is settled until the master comes back. In the meantime some careful people get noticed and plenty don't, and when he does come, two bags doubled get the same words as five.
reflectQuestions: Which small responsibility of yours, one that nobody is likely to check, have you been treating as if it didn't count?
Where are you holding back your full effort until something bigger, or more worth your while, comes along?
thematicGuides.practice: Jesus spoke of someone else's property, so begin there. Before you go to bed tonight, go round your home on your own and find one thing that isn't yours or isn't settled, such as a borrowed book or a tenner you owe. Put it by the front door, or send the money there and then. One thing is enough for tonight.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, You called money a very little thing, and I think about it most days. I'm careful where someone will check and careless where nobody will. I've rounded things in my own favour and told myself it was nothing. Show me what's in my hands that belongs to somebody else, and make me a person whose accounts don't need checking. If no one ever notices, let it be enough that You do. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: How Nathan Told David the Truth
thematicGuides.hook: Sent to tell a king what he had done, Nathan began with a story about a poor man's lamb.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will grow to become in every respect the mature body of him who is the head, that is, Christ.
thematicGuides.intro: By the time Nathan the prophet went to see King David, the baby had been born. David had taken another man's wife, arranged for the husband to die in battle and married her, and 2 Samuel records nobody saying a word to him about it. Paul's phrase for what was needed is speaking the truth in love. You may know a smaller version of Nathan's position, where something true needs saying to someone you care about and you could swallow it or say it badly.
story: The LORD sent Nathan to David, and Nathan began with a story. A rich man had a great many sheep and cattle. A poor man in the same town had nothing except one little ewe lamb, which he raised with his children. It shared his food, drank from his cup and slept in his arms. When a traveller came, the rich man spared his own animals and cooked the poor man's lamb. David, who had kept his father's sheep when he was young, burned with anger. He swore that the man must die, and must pay for the lamb four times over.

Nathan answered in one short sentence: "You are the man!" Then, speaking for God, he began with what David had been given. He had been anointed king, rescued from Saul and handed all Israel and Judah. The message went on, "if all this had been too little, I would have given you even more." Only after that came the charge, with Uriah the Hittite named, and the wife David had taken. David admitted it, without an excuse. Nathan's next words were that the LORD had taken away his sin and he was not going to die. He didn't take back what he had said a moment before, that the sword would never leave David's house.

When David and Bathsheba's next son, Solomon, was born, Nathan was sent again, with a second name for the baby, Jedidiah, which means loved by the LORD. After that he isn't heard of until David is very old. By then another son, Adonijah, was gathering chariots and supporters and saying he would be king. His father, the writer notes, had never rebuked him by asking, "Why do you behave as you do?" Nathan sent Bathsheba in to David first and arrived while she was still speaking. He bowed with his face to the ground and asked whether the king had declared Adonijah his successor without letting his servants know. David acted that day, and Nathan was among those he sent to anoint Solomon.

keyVerses.text: Then David said to Nathan, 'I have sinned against the LORD.' Nathan replied, 'The LORD has taken away your sin. You are not going to die.'
Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will grow to become in every respect the mature body of him who is the head, that is, Christ.
Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building others up according to their needs, that it may benefit those who listen.

insights: The charge against David came with God's generosity stated before it, and His forgiveness as soon as David owned up. Neither softened the charge, and Uriah was still named. When you have something hard to tell someone, the good you can honestly say on either side of it belongs to the truth as well.

Later in Ephesians 4 Paul gives a test for anything you're about to say: is it helpful for building the other person up? A true remark made to win, or to get something off your chest, fails it. You can be completely honest without being harsh, and Nathan was.
Saying nothing has a cost too. David had been told a hard truth and forgiven, yet he never asked Adonijah why he behaved as he did, and that son ended up reaching for the throne.
reflectQuestions: When something hard needs saying, which way do you more often go wrong, by keeping quiet as David did with Adonijah or by saying it with more force than care?
What true thing does someone close to you need to hear from you that you have so far kept to yourself?
thematicGuides.practice: One evening this week, take a card and write on it, as one plain sentence, the true thing you've been putting off saying. Under it, write what you hope for that person once it's said. If you can't fill in the second line honestly, or you're afraid of how they'll react, wait and talk to a level-headed friend or pastor. Keep the card in your Bible or wallet, and read it again just before you speak.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I've kept quiet and called it kindness, when really I wanted to avoid an awkward half hour. I've been sharp with people too, mostly because I wanted to be right. You sent Nathan to David with forgiveness ready. Give me that much care for the person I need to speak to. And if someone comes to me with a truth I don't want, help me answer as David did. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Moses Asks God to Send Someone Else
thematicGuides.hook: Moses pushed back five times at the burning bush, and each time God answered with help, never with a compliment.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But Moses said to God, 'Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?' And God said, 'I will be with you.'
thematicGuides.intro: The natural assumption is that if God wanted you for something you'd feel ready for it, or at least keen, and sometimes that is how it goes. It didn't go that way for Moses. In Exodus 3 and 4 the man God sends to Pharaoh is about eighty and minding another man's sheep, and he spends most of two chapters trying to get out of it.
story: Moses had fled Egypt years before, after killing an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew. When Exodus 3 opens he is at Horeb, on the far side of the wilderness, with his father-in-law's flock. He goes over to look at a bush that is on fire and not burning up, and when the LORD sees him go over He calls him by name, twice. Moses hides his face, afraid to look. God tells him He has seen the misery of His people in Egypt and has come down to rescue them. Then He says He is sending Moses to Pharaoh to bring them out.

Moses' first answer is to ask who he is to do such a thing. God's reply says nothing about who Moses is. He says He will be with him, and offers an odd sort of sign. When Moses has brought the people out, they will worship God on this mountain. Moses asks what name to give the Israelites, and God gives it. Then, although God has just said the elders will listen to him, Moses asks what happens if they don't. God answers with a question: "What is that in your hand?" It's a staff. Thrown on the ground it becomes a snake, and Moses runs from it. Told to take it by the tail, he does, and it is a staff again.

The fourth objection is about his speech. Moses says he has never been eloquent, "neither in the past nor since you have spoken to your servant." Talking with God has not made him a better talker, and he points this out. God promises to help him speak and to teach him what to say. The fifth time, Moses gives no reason and asks God to send someone else. Only now does the LORD's anger burn against him, and even then the answer is more help. His brother Aaron speaks well, God says, and is already on his way to meet him. Moses goes back to Jethro and asks leave to return to his people in Egypt. He puts his wife and sons on a donkey and takes the staff, which Exodus now calls the staff of God.

keyVerses.text: But Moses said to God, 'Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?' And God said, 'I will be with you. And this will be the sign to you that it is I who have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.'
Now go; I will help you speak and will teach you what to say.

But Moses said, 'Pardon your servant, Lord. Please send someone else.' Then the LORD's anger burned against Moses and he said, 'What about your brother, Aaron the Levite? I know he can speak well. He is already on his way to meet you, and he will be glad to see you.'

insights: To a man who says he can't do it, God gives His own company, the staff already in his hand, and a brother already on the road. Feeling equal to the task was never part of what he was offered.

The first sign God offered could only be seen after Moses had obeyed. Moses would know he had been sent when he stood at the same mountain again with the people, as he does in Exodus 19, where it is called Sinai. You may have to act on what God has said before you can see it was right.

The promise Moses was given is the one Jesus tied to the task He left His followers, to make disciples: "surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age." The bush and the signs were Moses' own.
reflectQuestions: Which of Moses' objections is closest to your own reason for thinking God couldn't use you?
What have you been putting off because it looks too big for you, though you suspect it is yours to do?
thematicGuides.practice: Moses' first move after the bush was to walk back to Jethro and ask for leave. Think of one thing you believe is yours to do and haven't started. This week, go in person to the place where it begins, which might be a neighbour's front door or the desk where volunteers sign up. Say why you've come and ask what happens next.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I keep giving You the same reasons. I'm no good with words, and nobody would listen to me anyway. Some of that may be true. Underneath it is the thing Moses said last: I'd like You to send someone else. I'm sorry. I don't feel ready, so help me go without waiting until I do. Show me what's in my hand that You can use, and let me notice the help You've already put on the road. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jeremiah, Known Before He Was Sent
thematicGuides.hook: God's first words to Jeremiah were about knowing him, and the job that followed was one nobody would choose.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart; I appointed you as a prophet to the nations.
thematicGuides.intro: The line about being set apart before you were born is hard to apply to yourself honestly. It's quoted as though every reader has an assignment waiting, yet it was said to one man about one task, and it leaves you no wiser about your own. Jeremiah 1 still has something for people who were never appointed prophets, and it lies in what God says to him first.
story: Jeremiah came from a family of priests at Anathoth. When the word of the LORD first came to him, it began with what God had done before Jeremiah could do anything. He had known him, set him apart and appointed him a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah said he didn't know how to speak and was too young. God's only answer about his age was to tell him not to say it. Then, though Jeremiah had said nothing about fear, God told him not to be afraid of the people he'd be sent to. He reached out His hand, touched Jeremiah's mouth and said He had put His words in it. The task came in six verbs, and four of them pull things down: "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and to plant."

In a vision that followed, Jeremiah saw a boiling pot tilting from the north, and was told that peoples from there would come against Jerusalem and every town in Judah, because the nation had left God for other gods. God said He had made Jeremiah a fortified city, an iron pillar and a bronze wall against the whole land, from the kings of Judah to the priests and the people. Jeremiah's own family were priests, and in chapter 11 it is the people of Anathoth, his home town, who threaten to kill him if he keeps prophesying. God had told him at his call that they would fight against him and not overcome him.

In chapter 20 Pashhur, the priest in charge of the temple, had Jeremiah beaten for his prophesying and left in the stocks at a temple gate until the next day. In the prayer that follows, Jeremiah told God he was mocked all day long, and that when he tried to keep quiet the word burned in him until he couldn't hold it in. He said the LORD was with him like a mighty warrior, and called for praise. His very next words were "Cursed be the day I was born!" He went on to ask why he had ever come out of the womb. Womb was the word God had used when He called him. The chapter ends on that question. Jeremiah was still prophesying when Jerusalem fell, some forty years after his call.

keyVerses.text: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart; I appointed you as a prophet to the nations.
You must go to everyone I send you to and say whatever I command you. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you and will rescue you.
But if I say, 'I will not mention his word or speak anymore in his name,' his word is in my heart like a fire, a fire shut up in my bones. I am weary of holding it in; indeed, I cannot.

insights: God tells Jeremiah that He knew him, and only then that He appointed him. Jeremiah was known before he was any use to anyone. If you measure your worth to God by what you get done for Him, that order runs the other way.

The appointment was Jeremiah's, and Jeremiah 1:5 doesn't hand every reader a task chosen before birth. The New Testament says of everyone who trusts Christ that they are known by God and "called to belong to Jesus Christ".

If you ever find yourself wishing you had not been born, say so to God as Jeremiah did, and tell a doctor or a close friend as well. More than once the rescue God had promised him arrived through other people, in chapters 26 and 38.
reflectQuestions: How would you see yourself differently if being known by God came before anything you do for Him?
Jeremiah said he was too young. What has your own 'too old' or 'too inexperienced' kept you from doing?
thematicGuides.practice: Before you get out of bed on each of the next seven mornings, say the opening line of Psalm 139 aloud: "You have searched me, LORD, and you know me." Then name to God one thing about today that He knows and nobody else does. It takes under a minute.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I've read that You set Jeremiah apart before he was born, and wondered what I was meant for and whether I've missed it. I still don't know. But You knew me before I'd done one useful thing, and You haven't gone off me on the days I get nothing done. When I say I'm too young or too old, You can tell how much of that is fear. Stay with me when the work goes badly. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Night Samuel Heard His Name
thematicGuides.hook: Samuel's first message from God was bad news about Eli, the man who had just taught him how to answer.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The LORD came and stood there, calling as at the other times, 'Samuel! Samuel!' Then Samuel said, 'Speak, for your servant is listening.'
thematicGuides.intro: On the morning after God first spoke to him, Samuel got up and opened the doors of the house of the LORD. He hadn't told Eli what he had heard, because he was afraid to. Asking God to speak is a riskier prayer than it sounds. We tend to pray it hoping for comfort, or for directions, and Samuel was given neither.
story: Samuel had lived at Shiloh since his mother, Hannah, brought him there as a small child. He served under Eli the priest in days when the word of the LORD was rare. One night he was lying down in the house of the LORD, where the ark was, and the LORD called him. He ran to Eli and said, "Here I am; you called me." Eli sent him back to lie down, and it happened twice more. Samuel had served in that house for years and did not yet know the LORD. Eli was the priest who had once watched Hannah pray without a sound and taken her for a drunk. On the third visit he realised who was calling, told the boy to lie down again and gave him the words to answer with.

The fourth time, the LORD came and stood there and called his name twice. Samuel repeated Eli's words, leaving out only the name of the LORD. Then God said He was about to do something in Israel that would make the ears of everyone who heard of it tingle. He would carry out everything He had spoken against Eli's family. Eli's sons were priests who took the worshippers' meat under threat of force and slept with the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting. Eli knew, and had failed to restrain them. No sacrifice or offering, God said, would ever atone for it or put it right. Samuel was given no task that night, and wasn't told to pass any of it on.

The next morning Eli did call Samuel, and the boy answered as he had in the night. Eli asked what God had said and left him no room to soften it: "May God deal with you, be it ever so severely, if you hide from me anything he told you." Samuel held nothing back. Eli, who had already heard this judgement from an unnamed man of God in chapter 2, answered that it was for the LORD to do what seemed good to Him. Samuel grew up, and the LORD was with him, and what he said came true. In time all Israel knew him for a prophet.

keyVerses.text: The LORD came and stood there, calling as at the other times, 'Samuel! Samuel!' Then Samuel said, 'Speak, for your servant is listening.'
So Samuel told him everything, hiding nothing from him. Then Eli said, 'He is the LORD; let him do what is good in his eyes.'
The LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, and there he revealed himself to Samuel through his word.

insights: Eli misjudged Hannah and failed with his own sons. He is still the one who taught Samuel what to say, and who got the truth out of him next morning. The person who helps you hear God doesn't have to be impressive, or even doing well themselves.

Samuel heard his name said aloud. The chapter itself calls that kind of thing rare, and promises it to nobody else. It ends with the LORD revealing Himself to Samuel through His word, spoken to a prophet and passed on to all Israel. That word, and what God has since "spoken to us by his Son", is now written down. For a Christian, listening starts with the Bible open.
reflectQuestions: What is the last thing you read in the Bible that you'd have been happier not to find there?
Which older Christian could you go to, as Samuel went to Eli, with something you can't make sense of alone?
thematicGuides.practice: Ask someone who has been a Christian longer than you to give you twenty minutes this week, over tea or on the phone. Take them the Bible passage you least want to hear and read it to them. Ask how they've learned to live with it, and let them finish before you answer. If you know nobody like that, a local minister will be used to being asked.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, when I ask You to speak, what I mostly want is to be told I'm right. Let me hear what is there in the Bible this week, including the parts I usually hurry past. I learned to listen to You from other people, and I thank You for every one of them. If someone asks me for the truth, as Eli asked Samuel, help me to tell all of it, kindly. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: David and the House He Didn't Build
thematicGuides.hook: David offered to build God a house, was told he wasn't the one, and spent his last years getting it ready for someone else.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Many are the plans in a person's heart, but it is the LORD's purpose that prevails.
thematicGuides.intro: A plan you've told people about can end with one short email. The place on the course went to someone else, or the church has asked another person to run the thing you'd offered to start. Then come weeks of wondering whether the plan was wrong, or you were, or God had stopped it. King David had a plan turned down too, a generous one, and it was God who turned it down.
story: David was settled in his palace when he remarked to the prophet Nathan that he was living in a house of cedar while the ark of the covenant, the chest that stood for God's presence, sat under a tent. Nathan told him to do whatever he had in mind, because God was with him. That night God spoke to Nathan, and the prophet had to go back and tell David, "You are not the one to build me a house to dwell in." Since Egypt, God said, He had moved from one tent site to another, and had never asked any of Israel's leaders for a house of cedar.

God had more to say to David than no. He turned the offer round: "I declare to you that the LORD will build a house for you." This house was a royal line, and one of David's sons would build the house for God. David went in, sat before the LORD and prayed, "Who am I, LORD God, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far?" The prayer runs for twelve verses and never asks God to think again. Solomon said later, at the dedication of the temple, that God had also told his father he did well to have the plan in his heart.

Late in his reign David was still busy with the house he had been told not to build. He set stonecutters to work and laid in iron for the nails of the gateway doors and more cedar logs than could be counted. Solomon was "young and inexperienced", he said, so he would get everything ready himself before he died. Explaining to his son why he hadn't built it, he gave a reason the account of the refusal leaves out. The LORD had told him, he said, that he had shed much blood and fought many wars. He handed Solomon written plans, down to the weight of gold for each lampstand. David died before the building began.

keyVerses.text: But the LORD said to my father David, 'You did well to have it in your heart to build a temple for my Name. Nevertheless, you are not the one to build the temple, but your son, your own flesh and blood, he is the one who will build the temple for my Name.'
Many are the plans in a person's heart, but it is the LORD's purpose that prevails.
For we are God's handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.

insights: God refused David's plan without calling the wish a mistake. Whether you were right to want something and whether it was yours to do are separate questions, and David got a different answer to each.

David heard his no from a prophet, with a reason, and you'll rarely get either. Plans also fail through other people's decisions, your own mistakes, or nothing you can identify, and you aren't asked to work out which failures were God saying no. Proverbs 19:21 says only that whatever becomes of the plans in a heart, the LORD's purpose stands.

David spent his last years getting work ready for someone else. In Ephesians 2:10 Paul says God has good works ready for us, and he says works, in the plural. Nothing in the verse points to one hidden assignment you could miss. Whatever good you find to do this month counts.
reflectQuestions: Looking at your life as it is this month, and not as you'd planned it, what good work is already in front of you?
Think of a plan you had your heart set on that came to nothing. What did you do afterwards with the wish behind it?
thematicGuides.practice: Once this week, walk to somewhere you can sit for ten minutes, an open church or a bench in a park. When David was told he wasn't the one to build, he went in and sat before the LORD. Sit down and tell God about the plan that came to nothing, as plainly as you'd tell a friend. Before you get up, tell Him, as David did, how far He has brought you already.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, there was something I was sure I would do, and it isn't going to happen. I can't tell whether You stopped it or it just fell through. If the wish was a good one, let me believe You saw it, as You saw David's. I'm still sore that someone else may get to do it. Show me the good in front of me this week, and make me willing to get things ready for a house I won't see finished. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Some Doubted: The Great Commission
thematicGuides.hook: The eleven were sent out while some still doubted, and the first to tell Greeks in Antioch about Jesus are never named.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went.
thematicGuides.intro: You can know perfectly well that you're meant to tell other people about Jesus and still say very little. It's hard to see how you'd bring Him up with a colleague or your sister-in-law without the conversation going stiff, and the command to make disciples of all nations sounds as if it was meant for braver people with plane tickets. It helps to look at who was standing there when Jesus gave it.
story: After the resurrection the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had told them to go. When they saw Him, "they worshiped him; but some doubted." Jesus came to them and began with Himself. All authority in heaven and on earth had been given to Him, and on that ground they were to go and make disciples of all nations, baptising and teaching them. The last sentence of Matthew's Gospel is His promise about where He would be, with them always, to the very end of the age.

Luke records the last conversation before Jesus was taken up, on the Mount of Olives outside Jerusalem. The apostles asked whether He was now going to restore the kingdom to Israel. He told them the times and dates were not theirs to know. They would be given power when the Holy Spirit came on them, and they would be His witnesses, in Jerusalem first and from there to the ends of the earth. Then He was taken up and a cloud hid Him. They were still looking up when two men in white asked them why they were standing there looking into the sky. The apostles walked back to the city, where He had told them to wait.

When the message about Jesus did leave Jerusalem, in Acts 8, the people carrying it were believers driven out by persecution. They told people about Him wherever they went. The apostles weren't among them, and a few verses on they were still in Jerusalem, hearing that Samaria had accepted the message. Luke picks the scattered believers up again in chapter 11. By then they had travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, speaking only to fellow Jews. In Antioch some of them, whom Luke identifies only as men from Cyprus and Cyrene, began telling Greeks about Jesus as well.

keyVerses.text: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

Some of them, however, men from Cyprus and Cyrene, went to Antioch and began to speak to Greeks also, telling them the good news about the Lord Jesus. The Lord's hand was with them, and a great number of people believed and turned to the Lord.

insights: The command rests on what is true of Jesus, His authority at the start and His presence at the end. The one thing the apostles were told to wait for was the Holy Spirit. Feeling sure was never made a condition.

Jesus calls them witnesses. A witness says what they have seen and heard, and the verdict is someone else's job. You weren't on the Mount of Olives, but you can tell a person who asks what you've come to believe about Jesus and why.

None of the believers in Acts 8:4 set out as a missionary. They were driven from home and talked about Jesus in the places they ended up, and Luke puts the many who believed in Antioch down to the Lord's hand. You're promised that Jesus will be with you in this, and no particular outcome.
reflectQuestions: Who in your own 'Jerusalem', the people you see most weeks, knows least about what you believe?
When a natural chance to mention your faith comes up and you let it pass, what is going on in you at that moment?
thematicGuides.practice: From Monday morning to Friday night, stop leaving the Christian part out of ordinary answers. When someone asks how your weekend was and church was part of it, say so. When a friend asks how you're coping and prayer is part of the honest answer, say that too. Keep it to one plain sentence and add nothing unless they ask.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I'd have been one of the ones on the mountain who doubted, and You'd have given me the job anyway. I keep quiet about You mostly because I don't want to be thought odd, and I call it tact. I'm not going anywhere this week except the usual places. Be with me there, as You said You would be. Give me one honest sentence when someone asks, and help me leave what happens next to You. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Saul, Ananias and the Damascus Road
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus stopped Saul outside Damascus, then sent a disciple Saul had come to arrest, who laid hands on him and called him brother.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Brother Saul, the Lord, Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.
thematicGuides.intro: Saul of Tarsus came into Damascus led by the hand. He had left Jerusalem with letters allowing him to arrest any followers of Jesus he found there, and he arrived blind. The story in Acts 9 is the one to read when something in your past makes you think God could have no use for you. Close to half of it belongs to a second man, a disciple called Ananias.
story: Saul had gone to the high priest and asked for letters to the Damascus synagogues. They covered women as well as men. Near the city a light from heaven flashed round him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" He asked who was speaking and was told it was Jesus. The only instruction Jesus gave him on the road in this chapter was to get up and go into the city, where he would be told what he must do. He got up unable to see and had to be taken the rest of the way. For three days he stayed blind and ate and drank nothing.

In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord called him in a vision and sent him to the house of Judas on Straight Street, to ask for Saul of Tarsus. Saul was praying, the Lord said, and had seen in a vision a man called Ananias come and place his hands on him. Ananias answered that he had heard many reports of the harm this man had done in Jerusalem, and that Saul had come with authority to arrest everyone who called on the Lord's name. That included Ananias. The Lord told him to go, because He had chosen this man to carry His name to the Gentiles, the non-Jewish peoples, and to Israel.

Ananias went. He entered the house, placed his hands on Saul and began with the words "Brother Saul". Jesus had sent him, he said, so that Saul could see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes. He got up, was baptised, ate, and spent several days with the disciples in Damascus, the people he had come to arrest. Years later Paul (the name Saul also went by) described that visit to a hostile crowd in Jerusalem. Ananias, he said, told him God had chosen him to be a witness, and then asked him, "And now what are you waiting for?"

keyVerses.text: 'Who are you, Lord?' Saul asked. 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,' he replied. 'Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.'

But the Lord said to Ananias, 'Go! This man is my chosen instrument to proclaim my name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel. I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.'

Here is a trustworthy saying that deserves full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst. But for that very reason I was shown mercy so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display his immense patience as an example for those who would believe in him and receive eternal life.

insights: Hardly anyone is stopped by a light on a road. The part of Saul's story most like other people's is the second half, where a believer came to the door and called him brother. What you know of God's purpose has probably reached you through other Christians. That puts you where Saul was, sent into the city to wait for a messenger.

Ananias objected with facts. The Lord let every one of them stand and answered with what Saul was going to become. When someone's record is all you can see of them, you're standing where Ananias stood. He went on the Lord's direct word, though, and nothing here asks you to put yourself back within reach of a person who has harmed you.

Paul never made his past smaller than it was. Writing to Timothy, he still calls himself the worst of sinners, in the present tense. He treats his record as evidence of how patient Christ is, and leaves it on show for whoever believes after him.
reflectQuestions: What in your past do you most often treat as the reason God couldn't have much use for you?
What does guilt or shame stop you from doing or offering?
thematicGuides.practice: Paul told Timothy he was once a blasphemer, a persecutor and a violent man, and that he was shown mercy. Tonight, on your own, write two sentences on that pattern. Start the first with 'I was once' and finish it truthfully. Start the second with 'I was shown mercy'. Read both aloud to God, then put the paper somewhere only you will find it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, You know what I did, and who it cost. I've half believed it puts me at the back of the queue with You for good. You had chosen Saul for Your work while he was still blind on Straight Street, so I'm asking You to have something for me. A light on the road would have suited me better, but send whoever You like and help me listen. And if You send me to the door of someone I've written off, let me say 'brother' and mean it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Poor Churches That Pleaded to Give
thematicGuides.hook: Before Paul wrote that God loves a cheerful giver, he described churches in extreme poverty who begged to take part.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
thematicGuides.intro: To most ears the line about God loving a cheerful giver sounds like two demands stacked together: hand it over, and look pleased while you do. That's a fair account of how it gets used, usually just before a collection. Paul wrote it towards the close of two chapters about a collection of his own, for poor believers in Jerusalem. Those chapters open with the givers he had least reason to expect anything from.
story: Paul starts with news from the churches of Macedonia. In the middle of a hard trial, and very poor, they had come up with a gift larger than they could afford. Nobody had pressed them for it. They pleaded with Paul to let them in on the collection. They also went further than Paul had hoped, giving themselves first to the Lord and then to him and his companions. Paul calls the whole thing a grace God had given them, and he puts their overflowing joy in the same sentence as their poverty.

The church in Corinth has a mixed record. The year before, they were the first to want to give and the first to begin, and Paul has been boasting about them in Macedonia, where their enthusiasm stirred most of the believers to act. But they have not yet finished. Now Paul is coming, perhaps with Macedonians beside him, and he admits he'd be ashamed to find them unprepared. He won't make it an order. "I am not commanding you," he writes, and reminds them of Christ, who was rich and for their sake became poor. A gift is acceptable, he tells them, "according to what one has, not according to what one does not have." Then he sends Titus and two other brothers ahead to finish the arrangements, so that when he arrives the money is waiting as a gift and nothing has to be wrung out of anyone on the day.

As Paul winds up his appeal he gives Corinth a farmer's rule, that whoever sows generously will reap generously, and leaves each of them to settle the amount in their own heart. We know how it turned out. Some time later he wrote to the church in Rome that he was on his way to Jerusalem with the money. Macedonia and Achaia, the province Corinth was in, "were pleased to make a contribution", he told them, and in his next sentence he said it again: "They were pleased to do it." He meant to see it safely delivered, and only then set out for Spain.

keyVerses.text: In the midst of a very severe trial, their overflowing joy and their extreme poverty welled up in rich generosity. For I testify that they gave as much as they were able, and even beyond their ability.
Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
And God is able to bless you abundantly, so that in all things at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.

insights: Paul says 'decided' before he says 'cheerful'. He puts the amount in your own hands, to be settled in private before anyone is standing in front of you. Nobody can order up a feeling, but you can decide early, and it's a good deal easier to be glad about a gift you chose yourself.

God is able, Paul says, to give you all you need, and the purpose he names is more good work. The verse says nothing about getting back what you gave. He measures a gift against what a person has, and doesn't want Corinth hard pressed so that others are relieved. By that measure a small sum out of a tight month, freely decided, is everything he asks for.
reflectQuestions: Think of a time you gave gladly and a time you gave because you felt cornered. What made the difference between the two?
Paul says God is able to give you all that you need for every good work. If you took that as true of this month, what would you do with what you have?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight or tomorrow, with your bank balance in front of you, decide on one amount you can give in the coming month without resenting it. Write the figure, the date and who it's for on a card, and keep the card next to your bank card. The next time an appeal puts you on the spot, the answer is already in your pocket.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, thank You for the Macedonians, who had nothing spare and begged to be allowed to give. I don't think I've ever begged for that. Most of what I give, I give because someone is standing there and it would be awkward to say no, and I mind about it all the way home. Help me decide in private what I can give, and then let go of it gladly. Thank You for Your Son, who was rich and for my sake became poor. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Widow Jesus Noticed at the Treasury
thematicGuides.hook: Having just warned about men who devour widows' houses, Jesus sat down and watched a widow put in her last two coins.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others.
thematicGuides.intro: This story is hard on you if you have plenty, and it has often been made hard on people who have little. If you give comfortably, Jesus says your large gift may have been the smaller one. If you're short of money, you may have had the widow held up to you as a reason to hand over what you can't spare. Mark sets her two coins straight after a warning about religious men who take widows' homes.
story: In the temple courts a large crowd was listening to Jesus with delight. He told them to watch out for the teachers of the law. They liked walking about in flowing robes and being greeted with respect in the marketplaces, and they liked the best seats in the synagogues and at banquets. They also prayed at length for show, and they swallowed up the houses of widows. The law these men taught warns that God will hear a widow's cry if she is wronged, and it forbids taking even her cloak as security for a loan. Jesus said the severest punishment was waiting for men like that.

Opposite the place where the offerings were put, Jesus sat down and watched the crowd putting their money into the temple treasury. Many rich people threw in large amounts. Then a poor widow came and put in two very small copper coins, worth next to nothing. Mark bothers to say there were two. She could have put in one and kept the other, and no one would have thought the less of her. She put in both, and that is the last we see of her. Nothing in the account suggests she knew anyone was watching.

Jesus called His disciples over and told them the widow had put in more than all the others. His reason was that the rich had given out of plenty and still had plenty, while she had given out of poverty, and those two coins were all she had to live on. That is the whole of what He said. He gave the disciples no instruction to do the same. As He was leaving the temple, one of the disciples said to Him, "Look, Teacher! What massive stones! What magnificent buildings!"

keyVerses.text: They devour widows' houses and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will be punished most severely.
Do not take advantage of the widow or the fatherless. If you do and they cry out to me, I will certainly hear their cry.
Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others. They all gave out of their wealth; but she, out of her poverty, put in everything, all she had to live on.

insights: The measure Jesus used that day was what each giver had left afterwards. By it the large donations came last and two small copper coins came first. If you give little because you have little, He has said how He counts it.

Jesus pointed the widow out and gave no command, and moments earlier He had condemned men who took widows' homes. Her two coins give no one the right to press a person who is struggling into giving what they can't afford.

Two chapters later a woman pours very expensive perfume over Jesus' head, and some of those present call it a waste of more than a year's wages. He answers, "She did what she could." One gift was two copper coins and the other a jar of pure nard, and Jesus measured each against the woman who gave it.
reflectQuestions: If you counted your giving over the past few months the way Jesus counted that day, by what it left you with, what would you find?
What could you give, in money or in time, that you would feel the loss of without leaving yourself or anyone who depends on you short?
thematicGuides.practice: One day this week, make a detour on your way home to a box nobody is standing over, the one at the back of a church or a charity tin on a quiet counter. Put in something you'll miss a little. If money is short just now, keep it small. Use coins or a note, so that it leaves your hand, and when you get home tell no one.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I notice the large gifts, and I like mine to be noticed too. Your Son sat and watched a poor widow put in two coins, and said they were more than all the others. I'd have kept one of those coins back. Thank You that He saw her in that crowd, and that You see what I give. When someone with very little is being leaned on for more, make me willing to speak up for them. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: A Tenth of Everything: What the Tithe Was For
thematicGuides.hook: In the Law of Moses the tithe was food, eaten by the family who brought it and stored for the Levite, the orphan and the widow.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: On the first day of every week, each one of you should set aside a sum of money in keeping with your income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will have to be made.
thematicGuides.intro: In Deuteronomy 14 the people who bring the tithe, a tenth of the year's harvest, are told to eat it. They carry the grain, wine and oil to the place of worship and feast there with their household. That is some way from the usual argument over whether Christians owe ten per cent, before tax or after. Churches answer that differently.
story: The first tenth in the Bible is Abram's. Four kings had raided Sodom and carried off his nephew Lot. Abram went after them with 318 men, attacked at night, and brought back Lot, the captives and the goods. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, came out with bread and wine and blessed him. "Then Abram gave him a tenth of everything." Genesis mentions no command to do it, and Hebrews 7 calls it a tenth of the plunder. The king of Sodom offered him the rest, and Abram wouldn't keep so much as a thread or a sandal strap.

Under the Law of Moses the tenth was food, with people waiting for it. Numbers 18 gives it to the Levites, who served at the sanctuary and had no land of their own, and every third year it was stored in the towns so that foreigners, orphans and widows could eat their fill too. After the return from exile in Babylon the people were holding it back. Through the prophet Malachi God asks them, "Will a mere mortal rob God?" They are to bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, so that there is food in His house, and test Him. The blessing He promises is more than they'll have room to store, with pests kept off the crops and vines that hold their fruit until it is ripe.

In the temple courts Jesus brings up the tithe while speaking about the teachers of the law and the Pharisees. They gave a tenth even of their kitchen spices, mint, dill and cumin. His charge is that they had neglected the more important matters of the Law, which He names as justice, mercy and faithfulness. Christians read His next sentence in two ways. "You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former." Some read it as Jesus keeping the tithe in place for His followers, others as said to Jews under the Law of Moses, before the cross. He goes straight on to call them blind guides who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel.

keyVerses.text: At the end of every three years, bring all the tithes of that year's produce and store it in your towns, so that the Levites (who have no allotment or inheritance of their own) and the foreigners, the fatherless and the widows who live in your towns may come and eat and be satisfied, and so that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands.

You give a tenth of your spices, mint, dill and cumin. But you have neglected the more important matters of the law, justice, mercy and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former.
On the first day of every week, each one of you should set aside a sum of money in keeping with your income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will have to be made.

insights: In Deuteronomy 14 Israel was under orders to set the tenth aside, and under orders to enjoy it. Families too far away to carry theirs sold it and bought whatever they liked on arrival, wine included, to eat before God and rejoice. The reason given is so that they would learn to revere Him. If giving has only ever felt like a bill to you, the tithe in that chapter is a feast.

When the tithe was held back, the people it fed went without. In Nehemiah 13 the Levites have left the temple and gone back to their fields, because their portions have stopped. Malachi's promise is made to that nation, about its harvests. Nobody should turn it into a rate of return, or use it to frighten someone who can't pay the rent.

Paul, writing to Corinth, leaves the figure open and asks for a sum put aside every week, in keeping with each person's income. Whichever side of the tithe argument you come down on, you can do that much.
reflectQuestions: How has what you were taught about tithing, or never taught, shaped the way you feel when giving comes up?
Where does the fear of not having enough decide what you do with your money?
thematicGuides.practice: Seven days running, when you sit down to your main meal, take one thing from the cupboard, a tin or a packet of rice, and put it in a bag by the door. On the seventh day carry the bag to a food bank, or to someone you know who is short.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've done the sum before tax and after it, and I know which answer I was hoping for. You spoke to men who counted out a tenth of their mint and missed justice, mercy and faithfulness, and I can be exact about money and careless about people in the same week. Show me what to set aside, and who it ought to feed. Keep me from treating any gift as a payment that leaves You owing me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: More Blessed to Give: Paul's Working Hands
thematicGuides.hook: Paul quoted Jesus on giving straight after speaking of his own hands and the work they had done.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: It is more blessed to give than to receive.
thematicGuides.intro: Your pay or your pension lands, and most of it goes where it always goes: rent, bills, a bit put by. Giving, if there is any, comes out of whatever is left. Paul had a different idea of what earning is for. Saying goodbye to the leaders of the church in Ephesus, he told them where his own wages had gone. One of the best-known sayings of Jesus comes from that speech.
story: On his way to Jerusalem, Paul sailed past Ephesus and sent for the church's elders to meet him at Miletus. He had spent three years with them, and now he said that none of them would see him again. The last thing he spoke about was money. He told them he had never coveted anyone's silver or gold or clothing. "You yourselves know that these hands of mine have supplied my own needs and the needs of my companions." He had worked like that, he said, to show them how the weak are to be helped, and he gave them a saying of Jesus that isn't in any of the four Gospels, that giving is more blessed than receiving. Then he knelt and prayed with them. They wept, and went with him to the ship.

The work Paul's hands did was tentmaking. When he reached Corinth he met Aquila and Priscilla, a couple newly arrived from Italy who were in the same trade. He stayed with them and worked alongside them, and every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue. He wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, among the people he would later say goodbye to at Miletus, and in it he describes how he and the other apostles were living. "To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are in rags, we are brutally treated, we are homeless. We work hard with our own hands." Later in the same letter he says he had every right to be paid for preaching, and had not used it.

In his letter to the Ephesians Paul speaks to anyone in the church who has been stealing. They are to stop, and work with their own hands at something useful, so as to have something to share with people in need. He also wrote to Timothy, whom he had asked to stay on in Ephesus, with orders for the wealthy there. They may enjoy what they have, since God provides everything "for our enjoyment". But wealth is uncertain, so their hope is to be in God, and they are to give freely.

keyVerses.text: In everything I did, I showed you that by this kind of hard work we must help the weak, remembering the words the Lord Jesus himself said: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'
Anyone who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing something useful with their own hands, that they may have something to share with those in need.

Command them to do good, to be rich in good deeds, and to be generous and willing to share. In this way they will lay up treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the coming age, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life.

insights: Paul was hungry and in rags while he lived by the saying he passed on, so being blessed and being well off are two different things. Proverbs does say a generous person will prosper, but a proverb tells you how things tend to go and is no guarantee.

Paul gives a thief and an apostle the same reason to work, which is to have something to give. That puts giving on the list of things your earnings are for, next to rent and food, and makes it something to plan before the money arrives.
The saying ranks two good things, and receiving is one of them. Paul took gifts from the church at Philippi more than once, and called them a fragrant offering.
reflectQuestions: What are you holding on to most tightly at the moment, whether that's money or time?
The last time you gave away something you'd worked hard for, how did it compare with being given something yourself?
thematicGuides.practice: Before your next pay or pension day, sit down for ten minutes with whoever shares your money, or with a friend you trust if you manage it alone. Put one question on the table: who is this money for, besides me and mine? Settle on one person or cause and an amount you can honestly manage, however small, and agree that it goes out first. If there is nothing spare, make it an hour of practical help for someone instead.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, thank You for what comes in each month and for the work behind it. Most of it is spoken for before it arrives, and I've been calling what's left over my giving. Paul could say his hands had kept other people as well as himself, and I want that to be true of mine. Show me who near me can't manage alone, and let part of my work be for them. Let me give without an eye on what comes back. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Barnabas and the Man Nobody Trusted
thematicGuides.hook: Barnabas sold a field for the church, then spent his good name on a convert every disciple in Jerusalem was afraid of.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles.
thematicGuides.intro: Somewhere you're trusted, perhaps in a family that listens when you speak or a workplace where people take your word for things. On the edge of that group there's often someone who isn't, because they're new or because of something they once did. Barnabas had that kind of standing in the first church in Jerusalem. This is what he did with it when Saul arrived.
story: In the early days of the church in Jerusalem, believers who owned land or houses would from time to time sell them and bring the money to the apostles. It was shared out to anyone in need, and nobody among them went without. One of those landowners was Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus. The apostles had given him a second name, Barnabas, which means "son of encouragement". He sold a field he owned and put the money at the apostles' feet. Luke, who wrote Acts, never calls him Joseph again.

Saul had gone from house to house in Jerusalem, dragging off men and women to prison. When he came back to the city and tried to join the disciples, they were all afraid of him and did not believe he was one of them. How Barnabas came to know Saul's story, or why he believed it, we aren't told. He took Saul to the apostles and did the talking, telling them what had happened to Saul on the road and how he had preached in Damascus since. Saul, whom Luke later calls "the chief speaker" of the pair, is given no words in this scene. Afterwards he moved about Jerusalem freely and spoke boldly in the name of the Lord.

Later, news reached Jerusalem that a great number of people in Antioch had turned to the Lord, and the church sent Barnabas. He saw what was happening, and then went to Tarsus himself to look for Saul, who had been sent there when his life was threatened in Jerusalem. He found him and brought him back, and the two of them taught in Antioch for a year. When a prophet warned of famine, the believers in Antioch sent a gift to the elders in Judea by Barnabas and Saul. The man who had laid his own money at the apostles' feet came back to Judea carrying a gift from a church that had not existed when he sold his field.

keyVerses.text: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles called Barnabas (which means 'son of encouragement'), sold a field he owned and brought the money and put it at the apostles' feet.

But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles. He told them how Saul on his journey had seen the Lord and that the Lord had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had preached fearlessly in the name of Jesus.
