When he arrived and saw what the grace of God had done, he was glad and encouraged them all to remain true to the Lord with all their hearts. He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord.

insights: By the time Saul arrived, the apostles knew Barnabas well enough to have given him a nickname. His word counted with them, and he used it for a man whose own word counted for nothing. Had Saul been lying, Barnabas would have been the one who brought him in.

The disciples are never blamed for being afraid. What Barnabas brought the apostles was an account they could weigh, of what had happened on the road and in Damascus. Speaking up for someone is saying what you know to be true about them, and that rules out calling a person safe while they're still doing harm.

Luke begins by writing "Barnabas and Saul". Partway through their first mission together it becomes "Paul and Barnabas" in most places. If you bring able people in, some of them will end up ahead of you.
reflectQuestions: Who do you know that others are still wary of and that a word from you would help?
When did you last go out of your way to speak up for someone, or to share work you could have kept to yourself?
thematicGuides.practice: Once this week, take someone who isn't trusted yet into a room where people trust you. It might be the team meeting or the Sunday service. The person might be a new colleague nobody has got to know, or someone back at church after years away. Introduce them to someone people there listen to, and say one specific, true thing you've seen in them while they're standing there to hear it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, someone has come to mind who is still on the edge of things. Help me stand beside them and say what I know is true of them. I like being trusted, and I've been careful not to spend it on anyone who might embarrass me. You speak to the Father for me, and I have never earned that. If they end up ahead of me, with their name said before mine, make me glad about it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Sowing, Reaping and the Farmer Who Slept
thematicGuides.hook: Paul's line about reaping what you sow is a warning, and then a word for people tired of doing good.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.
thematicGuides.intro: Paul told the churches in Galatia that when one of them was caught in a sin, the rest were to restore that person gently. A few lines later he wrote that a man reaps what he sows. The second line is the one that gets quoted, often to explain someone else's bad luck and sometimes as a way to get money back from God. What Paul wrote next is for anyone who has kept on doing good for a long time and seen little come of it.
story: Paul tells the Galatians that anyone being taught the faith should share all good things with their teacher. Then he warns them that God cannot be mocked. "A man reaps what he sows," he writes. Sow to please the flesh, a word he has just used for things like jealousy and selfish ambition, and the crop is destruction. Sow to please the Spirit and it is eternal life. He goes straight on to tell them not to tire of doing good, because the harvest will come at the proper time. So while there is the chance, he says, they are to do good to everyone.

Centuries before Paul, the prophet Hosea used the same picture on the northern kingdom of Israel. The land had prospered, he said, and as it did the people had built more altars and dressed up their sacred stones, which the LORD was going to demolish. He called the kingdom a trained heifer that loved to thresh, and said the LORD would put a yoke on her neck and drive her. They had planted wickedness and reaped evil, and because they had depended on their own strength and their many warriors, war was coming. In the middle of the charge Hosea told them to sow righteousness instead. The showers, he said, would be the LORD's to send.

Sitting in a boat just off the shore of Lake Galilee, Jesus told the crowd at the water's edge what the kingdom of God is like. A man scatters seed on the ground. The nights and days go by, the seed comes up and grows, and he couldn't tell you how. Between scattering and reaping, all the man does is sleep and get up. That evening Jesus and His disciples set off across the lake in the boat He had taught from, and a squall came up that nearly swamped it. Jesus was in the stern, asleep on a cushion.

keyVerses.text: Do not be deceived: God cannot be mocked. A man reaps what he sows. Whoever sows to please their flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction; whoever sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life.
Sow righteousness for yourselves, reap the fruit of unfailing love, and break up your unplowed ground; for it is time to seek the LORD, until he comes and showers his righteousness on you.
All by itself the soil produces grain, first the stalk, then the head, then the full kernel in the head. As soon as the grain is ripe, he puts the sickle to it, because the harvest has come.

insights: The sowing Paul names is doing good, the ordinary kind you do when the chance comes. The harvest he names is eternal life, and he puts no date on it beyond the proper time. Nothing in the passage says that money given comes back as money.

Job's friend Eliphaz used a version of this saying on a man who had lost his children and his health, telling him that those who sow trouble reap it (Job 4:8). At the end of the book God says Eliphaz had not spoken the truth about Him. If you're in hard times, this verse does not tell you why.
Paul writes "let us not become weary" and so counts himself among the tired. Doing good wears people out, apostles included. Not giving up can include going to bed and leaving the field alone.
reflectQuestions: Looking at where your time and money went over the past month, what would you say you've mostly been sowing?
Where are you closest to giving up on doing good because you can't see anything coming of it?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose one good thing you've kept up with little to show for it, such as the weekly call to a relative who never rings back, or praying for one person. Keep doing it, and until this day next week stop checking whether it's working. Don't look for the reply or the thank-you, and don't add up what you've put in. Each night, read Galatians 6:9 once and go to sleep.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I'm tired of doing some of the good I do. I've been keeping a tally of what I've given and who never thanked me, and some of it I did hoping You would pay me back. Thank You that the growing is Your work and goes on while I'm asleep. Break up the ground in me that I've left hard. Keep me from turning this saying on anyone who is suffering, myself included. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Guard Your Heart: Solomon and His Own Proverb
thematicGuides.hook: Solomon asked God for a discerning heart and got one, and in old age it was turned towards other gods.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.
thematicGuides.intro: "Guard your heart" is mostly quoted as advice about romance, a warning not to get attached too quickly or hand anyone the power to hurt you. There's sense in that, especially if you've been badly hurt. Proverbs 4 has something wider in view. In the Old Testament the heart is where you think and decide as well as where you feel.
story: Proverbs 4 is a father teaching his sons what his own father taught him. "For I too was a son to my father, still tender, and cherished by my mother." The book carries Solomon's name, which would make the father he learned from David. Towards the end of the chapter he works down through the body. His son is to turn his ear to these words and keep them within his heart, then watch his lips, his eyes and the paths his feet take. The heart comes second in the list, and it's the one item marked "above all else".

At Gibeon, early in Solomon's reign, the LORD appeared to him in a dream and told him to ask for whatever he wanted. Solomon asked for a discerning heart to govern the people. God was pleased and gave it, and in time the whole world came to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. The other end of the story is in 1 Kings 11. Solomon had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines, and he held on to them, though the law had warned that a king who took many wives would have his heart led astray. "As Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods." On a hill east of Jerusalem he built a shrine for Chemosh and for Molek, the gods of Moab and Ammon.

The Pharisees, the strictest of the Jewish religious parties, and some teachers of the law from Jerusalem saw Jesus's disciples eating with unwashed hands. Their tradition called for a ceremonial washing first, and they asked why His disciples didn't keep it. Jesus answered with Isaiah's words about people who honoured God with their lips while their hearts were far from Him. Then He told the crowd that nothing going into a person from outside can defile them. Indoors, the disciples asked what He meant. Food goes into the stomach and out again, He said. What makes a person unclean comes from within, out of the heart, and He gave a list that runs from evil thoughts and theft to envy, slander, arrogance and folly.

keyVerses.text: Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.
For wisdom will enter your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul. Discretion will protect you, and understanding will guard you.
Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.

insights: Proverbs uses the word guard in both directions. In chapter 4 you guard your heart. In chapter 2 wisdom enters your heart and then understanding guards you. So the first way to watch over your heart is to put something good in it and keep it there, which is where the father begins.
Solomon's wise heart was a gift from God, and it still needed guarding. The account in 1 Kings names no single bad day. It says he grew old, holding on to what turned him.

The Pharisees washed carefully before every meal, and Jesus said their hearts were far from God. So watching what goes in will only take you so far. For what's already inside, the prayer is Psalm 51. David, Solomon's father, wrote it after his adultery with Bathsheba, and in it he asks God for a pure heart.
reflectQuestions: Going by what you've read, watched and listened to this week, what is your heart mostly being filled with?
What one change this week, something dropped or something taken up, would do most to guard your heart?
thematicGuides.practice: After you've eaten this evening, walk once round the block on your own, or to the end of your road and back. As you go, think back over your day in the father's order from Proverbs 4: what you listened to, what you said, what your eyes rested on longest, where your feet took you. Spend longest on the one you'd least like to be asked about, and pray Psalm 51:10 before you go back indoors.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, create in me a pure heart, as David asked. I don't expect to manage one by being careful, when Solomon had more wisdom than I'll ever have and his heart was still turned. I've mostly taken guarding my heart to mean not letting people hurt me, and paid far less attention to what I keep in it. Some of what came out of it this week I wouldn't want played back to me. Keep watch where I've stopped watching. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Thomas Was Shown the Wounds
thematicGuides.hook: Thomas set his terms for believing, and a week later Jesus came back and met them, nearly word for word.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.
thematicGuides.intro: John covers a week of Thomas's life in three words: "A week later". For those seven days Thomas was the one among the disciples who hadn't seen Jesus alive. You may know something of that week. People you love are sure, you can't get there on their say-so, and the choice seems to lie between walking away and pretending. Thomas did neither.
story: In Matthew, Mark and Luke, Thomas is only a name in a list. John lets him speak, first in chapter 11. Jesus was across the Jordan when word came that Lazarus was ill at Bethany in Judea, where people had tried to stone Him a short while before. The disciples reminded Him of that when He said they were going back. Jesus told them Lazarus was dead and that He was going to him. Then Thomas spoke, to the other disciples and not to Jesus: "Let us also go, that we may die with him."

Thomas wasn't there on the evening of the day Jesus rose, when He came to the disciples and showed them His hands and side. When the others told him they had seen the Lord, he set a condition in three parts. He would have to see the nail marks in Jesus's hands, put his finger where the nails had been, and put his hand into the side a soldier had opened with a spear. Otherwise he would not believe. It was close to what the others had already been given. No argument follows in John's account, and nobody asks him to leave. The next thing we're told is that the disciples were in the house again, and Thomas was with them.

A week on, the doors were locked again. Jesus came and stood among them, greeted them all with peace, and then spoke to Thomas. He had not been there, so far as anyone could see, when Thomas laid down his terms, yet He went through them one by one, finger, hands and side, and told him to stop doubting and believe. John never says whether Thomas reached out. He gives Thomas's answer, "My Lord and my God!", which nobody else in the Gospels says to Jesus. Jesus replied that Thomas had believed because he had seen, and then blessed people who weren't in the room. In his next two sentences John turns to whoever is holding his book and says this is why he wrote it.

keyVerses.text: So the other disciples told him, 'We have seen the Lord!' But he said to them, 'Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.'
Then he said to Thomas, 'Put your finger here; see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe.'
Then Jesus told him, 'Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.'

insights: The disciple who asked for proof is the same one who, in chapter 11, was for going back to Judea to die with Jesus. A person can be that committed and still be unable to believe on someone else's word.
Jesus met Thomas's terms, and His next words were to stop doubting and believe. The doubt gets its answer, and it is also expected to end.

Jesus's blessing is for people who believe with no appearance in a locked room, which is nearly every Christian since. You haven't been promised an appearance. John wrote his book for those people. It is what the disciples saw, set down "that you may believe".
reflectQuestions: Thomas said what it would take for him to believe. What would it take for you?
Where could you say out loud what you can't yet believe and still be welcome the following week?
thematicGuides.practice: Find the next time Christians you know are meeting, a Sunday service or a few people round a friend's table, and go, without having settled anything first. Stay to the end. If a line in a song or a creed is more than you can mean, keep quiet for that line and join in after it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I wasn't there when the others saw You, and I can't believe it on their word alone. I've tried. You heard what Thomas said he needed, though he couldn't see You there, so You already know what I'd say. I wish I could be shown as he was, and I know You haven't promised me that. Give me what I need to believe, and keep me among Your people while I wait. I want to say what Thomas said and mean it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Whoever Watches the Wind Will Not Plant
thematicGuides.hook: The Teacher of Ecclesiastes says nobody can work out what God is doing, and then tells you to sow anyway.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Sow your seed in the morning, and at evening let your hands not be idle, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or whether both will do equally well.
thematicGuides.intro: A decision can sit for weeks as a form saved half-finished on your laptop, or as a straight question from someone that you still haven't answered. You've prayed, and you're holding off until you feel sure. Sometimes God does make a thing clear. Ecclesiastes has a passage for the times He doesn't, from a man who set out to understand everything done on earth and couldn't.
story: The Teacher of Ecclesiastes, a son of David and king in Jerusalem, set his mind to study everything done under the heavens. By his own account he had grown wiser than anyone who had ruled Jerusalem before him. He watched people work without sleep, day and night. He saw the righteous get what the wicked deserve, and the wicked get what the righteous deserve. His finding was that nobody can make sense of what goes on under the sun, however hard they search, and he made no exception for the wise who claim to know.

Send your grain off across the sea, the Teacher says, and after many days you may get something back. Spread what you have over seven ventures, or eight, because you don't know what disaster may come on the land. Both are pictures of letting something leave your hands before you can see how it ends. Then he turns to the weather. Full clouds will rain, and a tree lies where it falls, north or south, whatever anyone would prefer. A farmer who sowed by hand wanted a still day, and one with a crop to cut wanted a dry one. But whoever watches the wind, he says, won't plant, and whoever looks at the clouds won't reap.

In six verses of advice the Teacher gives his reason three times, and it is always the same one: you do not know. The farmer who held off planting was watching the wind, and the Teacher comes straight back to it. You don't know the path of the wind, he says, or how a body is formed in its mother's womb, and in the same way you can't understand the work of God, who made everything. So he tells his reader to sow in the morning and again in the evening. He sends the sower out twice in one day with the question of what will grow still open.

keyVerses.text: No one can comprehend what goes on under the sun. Despite all their efforts to search it out, no one can discover its meaning. Even if the wise claim they know, they cannot really comprehend it.
Whoever watches the wind will not plant; whoever looks at the clouds will not reap.

As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the body is formed in a mother's womb, so you cannot understand the work of God, the Maker of all things. Sow your seed in the morning, and at evening let your hands not be idle, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or whether both will do equally well.

insights: Not knowing is the Teacher's reason for acting. Because you can't tell what disaster may come, start seven things, or eight. Because you can't tell which sowing will succeed, sow twice. The usual reasoning takes the same not knowing as a reason to wait.

The Teacher makes no promise that what you choose will work out. He does rule out one hope, that you could have known if you had only waited longer. The farmer in verse 4 is being careful, and it costs him a field with nothing in it.

Jesus's picture of the kingdom of God has a farmer in it too, and he is no better informed. The man scatters seed, then sleeps and gets up while it sprouts and grows, "though he does not know how" (Mark 4:27).
reflectQuestions: What decision have you been holding back from until you feel sure about it?
Leaving the big decision aside, what good thing can you already see to do this week without knowing how it will turn out?
thematicGuides.practice: Seven mornings running, over breakfast, pick one small, good thing you can see to do that day whose result you can't know: send the enquiry, make the phone call, offer the lift. Do it before evening, and tell God the rest is His business. The big decision may be no clearer by the end of the week, but you'll have planted seven times.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I've been watching the wind. I told myself I was waiting on You, and part of that was true, and part of it was fear of choosing wrong and having nobody to blame but myself. You haven't told me how this turns out, and it seems You may not. If there's something You want me to see, show me. Where You're keeping it to Yourself, help me do the good in front of me this morning and again this evening, and leave what comes of it with You. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jonah Knew All the Right Answers
thematicGuides.hook: Jonah could recite the truth about God while running from Him, and the people who believed were the ones who knew least.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I knew that you are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger and abounding in love, a God who relents from sending calamity.
thematicGuides.intro: If you've been around church most of your life, you can say the right thing about God on demand. You know He made everything and that He's patient with people. All of that may feel like a set of facts you learned, with little in it you'd call trust. The prophet Jonah knew those same two things. He states each of them once in his book, accurately, while refusing to go along with the God he's describing.
story: God sent Jonah to preach against Nineveh, and Jonah went down to Joppa and paid his fare to Tarshish. In the storm that followed, each sailor cried out to his own god while Jonah slept below deck, and the captain had to wake the prophet and tell him to pray. When the sailors asked who he was, he said he was a Hebrew and worshipped the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land. He said it at sea, on a ship he had boarded to get away from that God. When they had thrown him overboard, as he told them to, and the sea went calm, it was the sailors who feared the LORD, offered Him a sacrifice and made vows.

After Jonah's three days inside a fish, the word of the LORD came to him a second time, and he went. He walked one day into a city that took three to cross, and all the book records of his preaching is one sentence: "Forty more days and Nineveh will be overthrown." It names no god and offers no way out. The Ninevites believed God. The king left his throne, took off his robes and sat in the dust in sackcloth, and his decree put the animals in sackcloth too. The decree's only stated hope was that God might yet relent. God saw them turn from their evil ways, and He did relent.

When God spared Nineveh, Jonah was angry, and told Him this was why he had run for Tarshish. He knew, he said, that God was gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love. That is how God had described Himself to Moses on Sinai (Exodus 34:6), after Israel made the golden calf and needed that mercy. Jonah recited it as a grievance and asked to die. He built a shelter east of Nineveh and sat down to see what would happen to the city. God grew a plant over him for shade, which made Jonah very happy, and at dawn sent a worm to kill it. God's last words to him are a question. Jonah cared about a plant he hadn't tended. Should God not care about a city of more than a hundred and twenty thousand people, and its animals?

keyVerses.text: He answered, 'I am a Hebrew and I worship the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.'
The Ninevites believed God. A fast was proclaimed, and all of them, from the greatest to the least, put on sackcloth.

He prayed to the LORD, 'Isn't this what I said, LORD, when I was still at home? That is what I tried to forestall by fleeing to Tarshish. I knew that you are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger and abounding in love, a God who relents from sending calamity.'

insights: The captain says maybe Jonah's god will notice them, and the king says "Who knows?" Jonah says "I knew". The two who were guessing acted at once. The one who knew slept through a storm and then sat outside a city to see what would become of it.

Everything Jonah knew was true, and he would have been no better off knowing less. He knew God was merciful and didn't want Him to be, at least to Nineveh. Trusting God includes wanting Him to be what you say He is.
God sent a storm, a fish, a plant, a worm and an east wind, all after one man whose answers were already right. To judge by His last question, He wanted Jonah to share His concern for the city.
reflectQuestions: Which true thing about God do you least want to be true?
What do you do, or avoid doing, only because of what you believe about God?
thematicGuides.practice: Have one conversation this week with someone whose faith is newer than yours, who came to believe as an adult or only lately. Ask what made them trust God and what they've done differently since. Give it twenty minutes, and don't supply the proper term for anything.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I know a lot about You, and I've let that stand in for trusting You. I can say You're gracious and slow to anger without feeling much, and there are people I'd rather You weren't so patient with. I could name them. Left to myself, I'll end up right about You and sitting outside the city. Take one thing I already believe and get me to act on it this week, before I file it with everything else I know. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: John the Baptist's Question From Prison
thematicGuides.hook: John had seen the Spirit come down on Jesus, and from Herod's prison he still sent to ask whether He was the one.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Blessed is anyone who does not stumble on account of me.
thematicGuides.intro: John the Baptist was in Herod's prison when he heard what Jesus was doing in the towns of Galilee. By Matthew's account he had been locked up since before Jesus began preaching there. He sent his disciples to Jesus with one question. It's a question you can come to yourself after years of believing, when God seems to be helping everyone else and you start to think you had Him wrong from the start.
story: John was baptising on the far side of the Jordan when he saw Jesus walking towards him and said, "Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" Then he explained how he knew. Twice he said, "I myself did not know him." The One who sent him to baptise had told him to look for the man on whom the Spirit came down and stayed, and John had seen the Spirit come down as a dove and stay on Jesus. The next day he pointed Jesus out again, and two of his own disciples left to follow Him.

Herod had locked John up for telling him it was not lawful to have his brother's wife, Herodias. When John's disciples came from the prison to ask Jesus whether He was the one who was to come, or whether they should expect someone else, He gave no yes or no. He told them to report what they heard and saw: the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, good news is preached to the poor. The list echoes Isaiah, where the verse about good news for the poor goes on to freedom for captives and release for prisoners (Isaiah 61:1). That line is not in the message John was sent, which ends with a blessing on anyone who does not stumble on account of Jesus.

As John's disciples were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowd about him. He asked what they had gone out into the wilderness to see, and ruled out a reed swayed by the wind and a man in fine clothes. They had gone to see a prophet, He said, and more than a prophet, and no one born of a woman had ever been greater. The man He was praising had only just asked whether to look for someone else, and the Gospels don't record that John ever heard a word of it. John was not released. On Herod's birthday, to keep an oath sworn in front of his dinner guests, Herod had him beheaded in the prison. John's disciples buried the body and went and told Jesus, who withdrew by boat to a solitary place.

keyVerses.text: I have seen and I testify that this is God's Chosen One.
When John, who was in prison, heard about the deeds of the Messiah, he sent his disciples to ask him, 'Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?'

Jesus replied, 'Go back and report to John what you hear and see: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, those who have leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is proclaimed to the poor. Blessed is anyone who does not stumble on account of me.'

insights: The evidence Jesus sent was all about other people, and it was still a true answer to what John had asked. Whether Jesus is who you took Him for is one question. Whether He will change the thing you are stuck in is another, and He may answer the first and leave the second.

Jesus thought no less of John for asking. Later, at the place across the Jordan where John had baptised, people said that all John had told them about Jesus was true (John 10:41). John hadn't got Him wrong.

Jesus raised other people's dead and left John in prison. Nobody should invent a reason for that, or for your situation either. The blessing He sent is for anyone who doesn't trip over Him, including over what He hasn't done.
reflectQuestions: Where does it look to you as though God is helping other people and passing you by?
If you could send Jesus one question, as John did from prison, what would it say?
thematicGuides.practice: Jesus sent His answer back to John in prison. Choose the place where your situation is hardest to forget, the desk where the job applications go out, say, or the kitchen once everyone else is in bed. Next time you're there alone this week, read verses 2 to 6 of Matthew 11 aloud, once, John's question and the answer he was sent. Then carry on with what you went there to do.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I've believed in You for a long time, and I didn't expect to be asking this. I hear what You're doing for other people. I'm glad for them, most days, and my own door is still shut. Are You the one I took You for? Show me enough to go on. If You leave me where I am, keep me from stumbling over You because of it, and let me believe the question hasn't counted against me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: How Can I Give You Up, Ephraim?
thematicGuides.hook: God asks how He can give up a people who keep leaving Him, and answers that He will not, because He is God and not a man.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: My heart is changed within me; all my compassion is aroused. I will not carry out my fierce anger, nor will I devastate Ephraim again. For I am God, and not a man, the Holy One among you.
thematicGuides.intro: People who drift from God and come back, again and again, tend to assume His patience is like theirs, only with more in the tank. Each return uses some up, and by the tenth time there can't be much left. Hosea 11 is God speaking about a people who had been walking away from Him for generations, and He starts with when they were small.
story: Hosea preached to the northern kingdom of Israel, which he often calls Ephraim. In chapter 11 God is the speaker, and He begins in Egypt. "When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son." But the more they were called, the further they went, off to sacrifice to the Baals, the local gods. Then He says what He did for them. He held Ephraim by the arms while they learned to walk, and He picked them up and bent down to feed them. Twice in one verse He says He was the one. He had healed them, and they never realised who had done it.

Earlier in the book God had called Ephraim a dove with no sense, calling to Egypt one moment and turning to Assyria the next. Now He uses the same two names to tell them where they are heading. They refuse to repent, so it will be Egypt again, and Assyria will rule over them. A sword will flash in their cities and put an end to their plans. "My people are determined to turn from me," He says. The Assyrians did come. In 2 Kings 17 their king lays siege to Samaria, the capital, for three years, takes it and deports the Israelites to Assyria.

Straight after warning them, God turns to questions. He asks how He can give Ephraim up, how He can treat them like Admah and Zeboyim. Those were two towns the LORD overthrew in fierce anger along with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29 lists the four together), so He is asking how He could make an end of His own child that way. He will not carry out His fierce anger, He says, "For I am God, and not a man." The speech ends with the LORD roaring like a lion and His children coming home trembling from Egypt and from Assyria, the two countries named in the warning a few verses earlier. The people He once called a senseless dove come back fluttering like doves, and He says He will settle them in their homes.

keyVerses.text: It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by the arms; but they did not realize it was I who healed them. I led them with cords of human kindness, with ties of love. To them I was like one who lifts a little child to the cheek, and I bent down to feed them.

How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel? How can I treat you like Admah? How can I make you like Zeboyim? My heart is changed within me; all my compassion is aroused. I will not carry out my fierce anger, nor will I devastate Ephraim again. For I am God, and not a man, the Holy One among you.
They will come from Egypt, trembling like sparrows, from Assyria, fluttering like doves. I will settle them in their homes.

insights: It's natural to think God's holiness makes Him quicker than we are to be done with someone. In verse 9 He calls Himself "the Holy One among you" in the very sentence where He explains why He will hold back. People run out of patience, and His reason is that He is God and not a man.

This chapter was spoken about a whole nation, and the nation still went into exile, so walking away had a cost. But the chapter lets you hear how God talks about people who keep walking off. He sounds like a parent who remembers teaching them to walk.

The ones who come home at the end of God's speech come trembling, and they are the ones He says He will settle. If you've come back yet again, nervous about how you'll be received, you are the kind of person He is describing.
reflectQuestions: When you come back to God after time away, what do you expect Him to say to you first?
Looking back, where were you being held up or fed without realising who was doing it, like the child God taught to walk?
thematicGuides.practice: Try a week without the waiting period, the stretch after you've drifted when you stay out of God's way until you feel fit to be seen. The first evening you realise a whole day has gone by without a word to Him, tell Him so in one sentence, before you do anything to make up for it. Then read Hosea 11:8 aloud.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I've lost count of how many times I've said I'm back, and I half expect You to have kept count for me. I can't tell how long You were holding me up while I thought I was managing alone. In Your place I'd have given up on me by now. You say You are God and not a man, so here I am again, about as bold as one of those sparrows. Settle me where You want me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Love Your Neighbour Began in Leviticus
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus was quoting Leviticus 19, where the command closes a list of rules about harvests, wages, gossip and grudges.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against anyone among your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.
thematicGuides.intro: On its own, 'love your neighbour' gives you nothing to do on an ordinary Wednesday, with bills to pay and someone you'd cross the road to avoid. When Jesus named it as the second greatest commandment He was quoting Leviticus 19. In that chapter the words come with instructions, and the instructions are for days like that Wednesday.
story: God told Moses to say to all Israel, "Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy." The instructions that follow soon reach the harvest. A farmer was to leave the edges of his field uncut and the dropped stalks and fallen grapes where they lay, for the poor and the foreigner. How wide to make the edge was up to him. Generations later a widow from Moab called Ruth, poor and a foreigner both, went out to pick up leftover grain behind the harvesters and found herself in a field belonging to a man named Boaz. He told his men to pull stalks out of their bundles and leave them for her.

After the harvest rule, Leviticus 19 moves quickly, one short line after another. A hired worker's wages are not to be held back overnight. Nobody is to curse the deaf or put a stumbling block in front of the blind. The deaf man would never hear the curse and the blind man would never see who had put the block there. You could get away with both, and that rule is the one that ends "but fear your God." Don't go about spreading slander. Don't hate a fellow Israelite in your heart, and when your neighbour is in the wrong, tell him so frankly. Then comes a sentence that starts by forbidding revenge and grudges and finishes, after a 'but', with the words everyone knows.

God gives the command to love a second time before the chapter ends, sixteen verses on, and this time it is about the foreigner living among them. The foreigner is to be treated as native-born and loved as yourself, because Israel had once been foreigners in Egypt. The very next rule is about honest scales and weights. Centuries later, asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus gave two, love for God from Deuteronomy and love for your neighbour from this chapter, and said all the Law and the Prophets hang on them. James called the second one the royal law, and three chapters on in the same letter he warned the rich that the wages they had failed to pay their harvesters were crying out against them.

keyVerses.text: When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. Do not go over your vineyard a second time or pick up the grapes that have fallen. Leave them for the poor and the foreigner.

Do not hate a fellow Israelite in your heart. Rebuke your neighbor frankly so you will not share in their guilt. Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against anyone among your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.

When a foreigner resides among you in your land, do not mistreat them. The foreigner residing among you must be treated as your native-born. Love them as yourself, for you were foreigners in Egypt. I am the LORD your God.

insights: The chapter opens with a call to be holy. In Leviticus 19 a holy person is someone whose workers are paid on the day and whose field has ragged edges.

Most of these rules are about what you do, whatever you feel. That helps on days when you can't find any warmth for someone. You can still pay what you owe them on time and keep their name out of your gossip.

The command to love your neighbour is the end of a sentence about grudges, and the verse before it sets frank speech against hatred kept in the heart. Where it was first said, love includes telling someone the hard thing to their face and then not holding it against them.
reflectQuestions: If your time and your money are your field, which edge of it could you leave for someone else to gather from?
What keeps you from saying to someone's face the thing you have been holding against them?
thematicGuides.practice: The foreigner in Leviticus 19 was to be treated as native-born. From the people you see regularly, at work or on your street, choose the one who arrived most recently from another country, or the newest arrival of any kind if nobody is from abroad. The next time you meet this week, ask what they still haven't been able to sort out here, a bus route, say, or an official letter. Then help with that one thing before the week is over, and go with them if that's what it takes.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I like this command best when it stays vague. You brought it down to the money I owe and the person I talk about once they've left the room. I have reaped right up to the edges of my field for years and called it being careful. Show me who is waiting on me. Help me say the frank thing kindly, and then drop it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Judas Was Still at the Table
thematicGuides.hook: Judas stayed for the foot washing and the bread, and Jesus had known all evening what he was going to do.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
thematicGuides.intro: The devil had already prompted Judas to betray Jesus before the towel came out, and Jesus knew who the betrayer was while He was washing feet. Both of those are in John 13, and Judas doesn't leave the room until verse 30. If you still have to sit down to meals or meetings with someone who has let you down badly, and who you expect will do it again, this is the evening when Jesus did that.
story: The evening meal was under way. Jesus knew that the Father had put all things under His power, and that He had come from God and was going back to God, "so he got up from the meal, took off his outer clothing, and wrapped a towel around his waist." He poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet. While He was doing it He told them they were clean, "though not every one of you," because He knew who would betray Him. Judas was still in the room.

After the washing Jesus went back to His place and quoted a psalm: "He who shared my bread has turned against me." Then, troubled in spirit, He told them that one of them was going to betray Him. The disciples stared at one another, at a loss to know which of them He meant. Asked who it was, Jesus said it was the one He would give a piece of bread to. He dipped the bread in the dish, gave it to Judas, and told him to do quickly what he was about to do. Judas looked after the group's money, so some thought he was being sent to buy something for the festival or to give to the poor. He took the bread and went out, and it was night.

When Judas had gone, Jesus told the others He would be with them only a little longer, and gave them what He called a new command, to love one another as He had loved them. That evening it had meant going round the room with a basin and a towel, knowing what one of them was about to do, while that man was still at the table sharing the meal. Judas went out anyway. Peter, who stayed, promised to lay down his life for Jesus, and was told he would disown Him three times before the rooster crowed.

keyVerses.text: Jesus knew that the hour had come for him to leave this world and go to the Father. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.
Jesus answered, 'It is the one to whom I will give this piece of bread when I have dipped it in the dish.' Then, dipping the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.

insights: Jesus got up to wash feet knowing who He was and where He was going, and what the men at the table deserved didn't come into it. The kindness didn't alter what Judas did next, and yours may not change the other person either.

Being civil doesn't require you to hide that you're hurt. Jesus was troubled, and said aloud that one of them would betray Him. He didn't name Judas to the room, though, and when Judas left, some of the others thought he was on an errand.

None of this means staying within reach of someone who is harming you. Jesus went to the cross by His own choice, for a purpose that was His alone, and earlier in John He would not entrust Himself to people because He knew what was in them. You can be courteous and keep your distance.
reflectQuestions: How do you usually behave around the person who let you down when you can't avoid being in the same room?
Where, for you, is the line between treating this person decently and trusting them with something they could use against you?
thematicGuides.practice: Before the next meal or meeting you can't get out of, take a small card and write two lines. First, one ordinary courtesy you will show the person who let you down, such as greeting them by name. Second, one thing you will not hand them, such as a confidence or time alone with you. Read the card before you walk in, and keep it for the next time.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, You knew about Judas before You picked up the towel. There is someone I can barely pass the salt to. You know what they did, and what I've said about them since. I'm not asking to feel warmly towards them. Help me be civil when I'm in the same room as them, and careful about what I trust them with. You were troubled that night, so I'll stop pretending I'm not. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: God Will Not Forget the Help You Give
thematicGuides.hook: Hebrews counts help given to God's people as love shown to God, and says it would be unjust of Him to forget it.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you have shown him as you have helped his people and continue to help them.
thematicGuides.intro: Take one drive to the hospital. You get someone to their appointment, sit two hours in the waiting room and bring them home, and the one remark in the car is that you took the wrong turning. Do that for years and you start to ask whether any of it registers anywhere. Hebrews was written to a church that had been helping people for a long time, and the writer keeps urging them not to give up.
story: The writer of Hebrews has been hard on his readers. He has told them they still need milk when by now they ought to be teachers, and he has warned them severely about falling away. Then his tone changes. "Even though we speak like this, dear friends, we are convinced of better things in your case." It is the only place in the letter where he calls them dear friends. He points to their record, the help they have given God's people and are still giving, and says it would be unjust of God to forget it. The writer wants each of them to show the same diligence to the very end.

Soon after they came to faith, the people this letter was written to went through a great conflict. They were insulted and persecuted in public, stood beside others who were, shared the suffering of people in prison, and took the seizure of their own property with joy. Most of what we know of what they did is in three verses of chapter 10, and those verses begin with the word "Remember". It was their own record, and the writer had to ask them to call it to mind.

By the last chapter of the letter the instructions get short, and the first ones are about love. The readers are to go on loving one another. They are to keep remembering people in prison as if they were in there with them, and they are not to forget hospitality to strangers. Some who took strangers in, the writer adds, entertained angels without knowing it. That recalls Abraham in Genesis 18, who saw three men standing near his tent in the heat of the day, hurried to have bread baked and a calf prepared, and stood by under a tree while they ate.

keyVerses.text: God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you have shown him as you have helped his people and continue to help them.

Sometimes you were publicly exposed to insult and persecution; at other times you stood side by side with those who were so treated. You suffered along with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, because you knew that you yourselves had better and lasting possessions.

Do not forget to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have shown hospitality to angels without knowing it. Continue to remember those in prison as if you were together with them in prison, and those who are mistreated as if you yourselves were suffering.

insights: In Hebrews 6:10 the help goes to God's people and the love is shown to God, so He was on the receiving end as well. The verse is about fellow believers, and the letter goes on to strangers. In Matthew 25 the people who fed the hungry and visited the prisoner had no idea they were doing it for the King until He told them.

Hebrews says God will remember His people's sins no more and will not forget their work, and it asks them in turn not to forget the stranger and to keep remembering the prisoner. The promise is about His memory. It doesn't extend to thanks from the person you care for, or to anyone else noticing.
The letter was written to a whole congregation, and the helping it describes was shared work. If you've been doing this alone and it has worn you down, ask someone to take a share.
reflectQuestions: What do you most wish someone would say to you about the care you give?
Which of the people you know does nobody else seem to be keeping in mind at the moment?
thematicGuides.practice: This one is small on purpose. Think of someone you know who looks after another person and rarely gets thanked for it. Within a week, take them something, a meal for their freezer or a bunch of flowers. Hand it over at the door and tell them in one sentence that you've seen what they do. It needn't cost much or take long.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I would like someone to notice. There have been more lifts and broken nights than I could list, and some days I do it with a bad grace and keep score as I go. You say You won't forget, and that it was love shown to You. I'll hold on to that, because there may be no other thanks coming. Give me what I need for tomorrow, and send someone to share it. And bring to mind the person I've forgotten. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Abigail Hurried, Then Waited Until Morning
thematicGuides.hook: David and Abigail were both in a hurry that day, and David himself said which of them had shown good judgment.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: May you be blessed for your good judgment and for keeping me from bloodshed this day and from avenging myself with my own hands.
thematicGuides.intro: Somebody needs to hear something from you, and neither of you is going to enjoy it. What you can't settle is when. Say it today and you may catch them at their worst. Leave it another month and it may be too late to do any good. In 1 Samuel 25 a woman called Abigail faces that choice twice in a day and a night, and she makes it differently each time.
story: Nabal was a rich man with three thousand sheep. David's men had lived in the wilderness alongside his shepherds and taken nothing from them, so at shearing time David sent ten young men to ask politely for whatever food he could spare. Nabal's answer was "Who is this David?" Plenty of servants, he said, were running away from their masters these days. David told his men to strap on their swords and set out with about four hundred of them. He swore that by morning not one male in Nabal's household would be left alive.

One of the servants told Abigail, Nabal's wife, what had happened, and said their master was such a wicked man that "no one can talk to him". Abigail wasted no time. She loaded donkeys with food and wine and set out, without a word to her husband. In a mountain ravine she met David and his men coming down towards her. She got down from her donkey, bowed with her face to the ground and asked to be heard. She called Nabal a fool, said it was what his name meant, and then talked about David's own future. The LORD was going to make him ruler over Israel, and when that day came he wouldn't want this killing on his conscience.

David praised God for sending her and blessed her for her good judgment. He accepted what she had brought, told her he had heard her and granted her request, and sent her home in peace. When she got there Nabal was holding a banquet like a king's, in high spirits and very drunk, and she told him "nothing at all until daybreak". In the morning, when he was sober, she told him all of it. His heart failed him and he became like a stone, and about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal and he died.

keyVerses.text: Abigail acted quickly. She took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five dressed sheep, five seahs of roasted grain, a hundred cakes of raisins and two hundred cakes of pressed figs, and loaded them on donkeys. Then she told her servants, 'Go on ahead; I'll follow you.' But she did not tell her husband Nabal.

When the LORD has fulfilled for my lord every good thing he promised concerning him and has appointed him ruler over Israel, my lord will not have on his conscience the staggering burden of needless bloodshed or of having avenged himself.
As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has kept me from harming you, if you had not come quickly to meet me, not one male belonging to Nabal would have been left alive by daybreak.

insights: Speed isn't what made Abigail wise, because David was moving just as fast. He was answering an insult, and Proverbs 12:16 says, "Fools show their annoyance at once, but the prudent overlook an insult." Abigail hurried because four hundred swords were on the road.

The word daybreak comes twice in the chapter. It's the hour by which David meant the killing to be over, and it's the hour Abigail's silence ended. She was waiting for one thing, a sober husband, and that took one night. If you decide to wait, know what you're waiting for and name the day.

Abigail chose her moment well, and by the end of that conversation the man nobody could talk to was like a stone. Waiting for morning got her a sober listener and settled nothing else. None of this is advice for living with someone who frightens you. If that's you, tell a friend or your GP what's been happening.
reflectQuestions: What exactly are you waiting for before you have the conversation you've been holding back?
Thinking of the last time you answered at once because you were stung, what would one night's wait have changed?
thematicGuides.practice: Each morning this week, take the one conversation you keep putting off and ask two things about it: whether anyone will be harmed if it waits another day, and whether the other person is in a state to hear it today. The first morning either answer is yes, have the conversation that day.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, there's something I need to say to someone, and I've called it waiting for the right moment for so long that I no longer believe myself. When I'm stung I'm as quick as David with his sword, and when it matters I drag my feet. If they can't hear me tonight, help me hold it until morning and then say all of it. And if I pick the moment well and it still goes badly, stay with me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Balaam and the Donkey That Saw First
thematicGuides.hook: Balaam's trade was seeing what others couldn't, and on the road to Moab his donkey saw the angel three times before he did.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Then the LORD opened Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with his sword drawn. So he bowed low and fell facedown.
thematicGuides.intro: Balaam once told his donkey that if he had a sword in his hand he would kill it. There was a drawn sword in the road ahead of him, in the hand of an angel he couldn't see. He was riding towards a handsome reward for a job God had first told him to refuse. If you have your answer already and keep going back to ask again, short-tempered with whatever gets in the way, you know something of the state he was in.
story: Balak, king of Moab, was frightened of the Israelites camped beside his land, and sent messengers with a fee for divination to bring Balaam to curse them. Balaam kept them overnight, God told him not to go, and in the morning he sent them home. Balak tried again with more distinguished officials and a promise to reward him handsomely. Balaam told them that all the silver and gold in Balak's palace couldn't take him beyond the LORD's command. Then he asked them to stay the night, so that he could find out what else the LORD would say. That night God told him to go with them, and to do only what He told him.

In the morning Balaam saddled his donkey and went with Balak's officials. The next verse begins, "But God was very angry when he went," and the angel of the LORD stood in the road to oppose him, sword drawn. The donkey saw the angel and turned off into a field, and Balaam beat it back onto the road. On a narrow path between vineyard walls it saw the angel again and pressed against the wall, crushing his foot, and he beat it again. The third time there was no room to turn, so the donkey lay down under him. Balaam was angry and beat it with his staff.

Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and it asked what it had done to deserve three beatings. Balaam answered that it had made a fool of him. It asked whether, in all the time he had ridden it, it had ever been in the habit of doing this. "No," he said. Then the LORD opened Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel with the drawn sword and fell face down. The angel told him his path was reckless, and that the donkey's turning aside had saved his life. Balaam said he had sinned, that he hadn't known the angel was there, and then, "Now if you are displeased, I will go back." He was told to go on with the men and speak only what he was given.

keyVerses.text: But God said to Balaam, 'Do not go with them. You must not put a curse on those people, because they are blessed.'

Why have you beaten your donkey these three times? I have come here to oppose you because your path is a reckless one before me. The donkey saw me and turned away from me these three times. If it had not turned away, I would certainly have killed you by now, but I would have spared it.

They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Bezer, who loved the wages of wickedness. But he was rebuked for his wrongdoing by a donkey, an animal without speech, who spoke with a human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.

insights: Balaam had just fallen face down before an angel with a drawn sword, and his offer to go back still began with 'if'. You can say every right thing about a no and still be holding the door open. Peter, writing long afterwards about false teachers, sums Balaam up as a man who loved the pay.

The second night gave Balaam an answer he could travel on. God let him go, and was very angry when he went. Numbers doesn't explain how those fit, and it's better not to guess. The angel's own word for the road he had been allowed onto was reckless.

When Balaam does prophesy over Israel, he introduces himself as "one whose eye sees clearly". On this road he never asked why an animal he had always ridden was acting so strangely. Most delays are only delays, but when everything that slows you down makes you furious, the fury is worth a second look.
reflectQuestions: Which decision have you already had a clear no about, and kept finding fresh reasons to reopen?
What do you stand to gain from the thing you keep going back to ask about?
thematicGuides.practice: By the weekend, go to the friend or relative who has been slowing you down over the thing you want, perhaps the one who keeps raising doubts. Ask them what they can see that you can't, and give them ten minutes without arguing your side. Thank them, and decide nothing that day.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I had my answer and I went back to ask what else You might say. I've been short with everyone who slowed me down, and I haven't once asked what they could see. I want this more than I've admitted to You or to anyone. Open my eyes before I go any further, and thank You for whatever has been lying down in the road in front of me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Synagogue That Checked Up on Paul
thematicGuides.hook: Luke calls the Jews of Berea noble because they heard Paul eagerly and then checked every day whether he was right.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
thematicGuides.intro: Believers are meant to believe, so you trust the person in the pulpit and leave the checking up to sceptics. There's something in that, since nobody learns much from a teacher they've decided to distrust. But there are now more people a tap away speaking in God's name than anyone could follow, and they contradict each other. The New Testament never asked you to believe them all. One of its warmest letters stops to tell Christians not to believe everything they hear.
story: John wrote his first letter to Christians he called his dear friends. People who had once been among them had walked out, and were now denying that Jesus is the Christ and trying to lead the rest astray. John told his friends not to believe every spirit, meaning every voice that claims to speak for God, but to test them. The test he gave was what a voice says about Jesus Christ, whether it acknowledges that He has come in the flesh, as a real human being. The letter that tells them to test every voice is the same one that, seven verses further down, says God is love.

The Sermon on the Mount was nearly over when Jesus told the crowd to watch out for false prophets. They come in sheep's clothing, He said, looking like part of the flock, and the way to know them is by their fruit. Nobody picks grapes from thornbushes or figs from thistles, and a bad tree can't bear good fruit. He went straight on to describe the last day, when many will come to Him calling Him Lord and listing the prophecies, the demons driven out and the miracles they did in His name. His answer to them will be "I never knew you."

In Thessalonica Paul reasoned from the Scriptures in the synagogue on three Sabbaths. Some were persuaded, and others raised a mob and went looking for him. The believers sent him and Silas away by night to Berea, where they went to the synagogue. Luke, who wrote Acts, says these Jews were of more noble character than the ones in Thessalonica. They received the message with great eagerness and "examined the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true". The man they were checking was an apostle, and what they checked him against was the Old Testament, the only Scriptures they had. The result was that many of them believed.

keyVerses.text: Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
Thus, by their fruit you will recognize them. Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.
Do not treat prophecies with contempt but test them all; hold on to what is good, reject every kind of evil.

insights: Luke counts the eagerness and the checking as one good quality, and so did Paul. Writing later to the church in Thessalonica, the city he'd had to leave by night, he told them not to look down on prophecies and to test every one. Sneering at everything is ruled out along with swallowing everything.

Confidence isn't one of the tests, and neither is a big following. John says of the false prophets that the world listens to them, and the people Jesus turns away have miracles to point to. Honest teachers will still disagree once you've applied all three tests, but you'll know which voices to drop.

Jesus's test needs a life you can see. You can check a stranger's podcast against Scripture and against what it says about Jesus, but you can't watch how that person treats people on a bad day. That's a reason to give most weight to teachers whose lives are open to people who know them.
reflectQuestions: Think of the person whose teaching about God you hear most. What do you know about how they live when they aren't teaching?
When you last heard something said about God that didn't sit right with you, what did you do with that unease?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose one thing you've heard a preacher or a podcast say about God lately that has stayed with you. This week, ask a friend for twenty minutes, someone who knows the Bible at least as well as you do. Look up together the verses the speaker used, read the paragraph on either side of each, and see whether the text says what you were told it says.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I listen to a lot of people talking about You, and mostly I judge them by whether they agree with me. There's one I wrote off a long time ago, and I never did open a Bible to find out whether they were wrong. I'd hate to turn into someone who sneers. Make me as eager as the people in Berea, and as willing to do the slow checking. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Egypt's Free Fish and the Good Old Days
thematicGuides.hook: The Israelites who remembered Egypt's fish as free had eaten it as slaves.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Do not say, 'Why were the old days better than these?' For it is not wise to ask such questions.
thematicGuides.intro: Missing the old days is hard to argue with, because the memory is usually true as far as it goes. The church really was fuller, and the friends really did live round the corner. What you can't see from inside is what the memory has left out, and what the comparing does to today. Ecclesiastes has one blunt line about it.
story: A little over a year after they left Egypt, the Israelites were wailing at the entrances to their tents. They wanted meat, and what they remembered aloud was the food of Egypt, beginning with fish that had cost them nothing. They had eaten that free fish as slaves. Exodus says the Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard labour in brick and mortar, and that they groaned and cried out for help. God's reply through Moses was that they would have meat for a whole month, until they loathed it, because in asking why they ever left Egypt they had rejected "the LORD, who is among you".

Centuries later, exiles came home from Babylon to rebuild the temple the Babylonians had burned. When the builders laid the foundation there were priests with trumpets and Levites with cymbals, and the people gave a great shout of praise. Many of the older priests, Levites and heads of families had seen the first temple, and at the sight of this foundation they wept aloud while many others shouted for joy. Then people living nearby bribed officials to frustrate the work, and it stood still for years, until the second year of King Darius.

In the second year of King Darius, after years at a standstill, the building started again, and less than a month in, God spoke through the prophet Haggai. He asked who was left that had seen this house in its former glory, and how it looked to them now. Then He asked the question for them: "Does it not seem to you like nothing?" He let the comparison stand, and told them He would shake all nations and fill this house with glory. Solomon had overlaid the whole interior of the first temple with gold. "The silver is mine and the gold is mine," God said, and the glory of this house would be greater than the first one's.

keyVerses.text: We remember the fish we ate in Egypt at no cost, also the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic. But now we have lost our appetite; we never see anything but this manna!
No one could distinguish the sound of the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people made so much noise. And the sound was heard far away.
'The glory of this present house will be greater than the glory of the former house,' says the LORD Almighty. 'And in this place I will grant peace,' declares the LORD Almighty.

insights: Ecclesiastes doesn't claim the present is as good as the past. The question it warns against, why the old days were better, has its verdict built in. The same chapter gives you something to do instead: be happy when times are good, and when they're bad, consider that God made the one as well as the other.

Both crowds were comparing something finished with something unfinished. For Israel, Egypt was over and could be remembered as a menu. The first temple stood complete in memory, gold and all, and what the elders had in front of them was a foundation. Whatever you're in the middle of will tend to lose that contest.

Ezra says nothing against the elders' tears, while God called the wailing for Egypt a rejection of Him. One group had come back to build and the other wanted to go back. Missing what's gone is no fault. The greater glory was promised to that temple, and nobody has promised that your church or your town will outdo its past.
reflectQuestions: What was hard about the time you now think of as the good old days?
What are you holding your heart back from now because it looks small beside what you remember?
thematicGuides.practice: Between now and this time next week, give up saying aloud that things used to be better. That covers 'It was better when' and 'Things aren't what they were'. When you catch a sentence like that starting, stop it halfway and name one thing about the present that you would miss if it were gone.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I remember the fish and forget the bricks. I've been telling myself, and anyone who'll listen, that things were better before, and some of them were. I miss them, and I can say that to You. But I've let the comparison make today look like nothing, and You made today as well. Show me what You've put in front of me while it's still here. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jehoshaphat: We Do Not Know What to Do
thematicGuides.hook: A prayer for when you can't stop what is coming and can't think what to ask for, from a king with an invasion on the way.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: For we have no power to face this vast army that is attacking us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.
thematicGuides.intro: Chronicles stops to say who was in the temple courtyard when King Jehoshaphat prayed. The men of Judah stood there with their wives, their children and their little ones. In front of all of them the king told God he didn't know what to do. If something is coming that you can't stop, such as a round of redundancies at work, and you've no plan of your own for God to bless, you are where Jehoshaphat was that day.
story: Word reached King Jehoshaphat that a vast army was on its way from the far side of the Dead Sea and had already got as far as En Gedi. Chronicles says he was alarmed. He turned to the LORD and called a fast for all Judah, and people came in from every town. He had soldiers of his own. Three chapters earlier the same book lists his fighting men, and the smallest of five divisions is 180,000 strong. In his prayer he would say that Judah had no power to face what was coming.

Jehoshaphat stood up at the front of the temple's new courtyard and began with God's rule over every kingdom. He recalled what the people had said when they built the sanctuary, that if disaster came they would stand before it and cry out, and God would hear and save. Jehoshaphat never told God how to deal with the army. The nearest he came to a request was a question, whether God would not judge these invaders, and his last words were, "We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you." When Solomon had finished that temple, God had told him that His own eyes would be open to the prayers offered there.

After the king's prayer, the Spirit of the LORD came on Jahaziel, a Levite standing in the assembly, and he told Judah not to be afraid, because the battle was God's. Tomorrow they were to march down, find the enemy at the end of a gorge in the Desert of Jeruel, take up their positions and stand firm. Early next morning, after consulting the people, Jehoshaphat appointed men to go out at the head of the army singing, "Give thanks to the LORD, for his love endures forever." As they began to sing, the LORD set ambushes and the invaders turned on one another. When the men of Judah reached the place that overlooks the desert, there was nobody left to fight.

keyVerses.text: Alarmed, Jehoshaphat resolved to inquire of the LORD, and he proclaimed a fast for all Judah. The people of Judah came together to seek help from the LORD; indeed, they came from every town in Judah to seek him.
Our God, will you not judge them? For we have no power to face this vast army that is attacking us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.

You will not have to fight this battle. Take up your positions; stand firm and see the deliverance the LORD will give you, Judah and Jerusalem. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged. Go out to face them tomorrow, and the LORD will be with you.

insights: Jehoshaphat's last line would do as a prayer on its own. It tells God what you can't do and where you're looking, and it asks for nothing in particular. If you've been putting off praying about something until you know what to ask for, you don't have to wait until then.

Judah was told a day ahead that they wouldn't have to fight. Nobody has told you that about what you're facing, and it may go badly. The part of Jahaziel's message that does carry over to you is its last line, that the LORD would be with them. Jesus said the same to His followers (Matthew 28:20).

The answer was a promise and one day's instructions: where to go in the morning and what to do there, with nothing about the week after. When you can't see how something will end, ask God for what tomorrow needs.
reflectQuestions: What is coming in the next few weeks or months that you can't stop and have no plan for?
Which one person could you tell this week that you don't know what to do, as Jehoshaphat told God with every family in Judah standing there?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, once you're on your own, stand up, as Judah stood, and tell God out loud what is coming. Give it two or three sentences and leave out any suggestion of how He might fix it. Then read Jehoshaphat's last line from 2 Chronicles 20:12 off the page, and stop there. Go to bed with the prayer as unfinished as his was.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I usually come to You once I've worked out what I'd like You to do. This time I haven't got that far. I haven't told anyone else that, and one or two people think I have it in hand. I don't know what to do. My eyes are on You. Show me what tomorrow needs, and be with me when I go out to face it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jesus Asked and the Cup Was Not Taken
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus prayed three times about the cup and it wasn't taken from Him, yet Hebrews says of His prayers that He was heard.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: During the days of Jesus' life on earth, he offered up prayers and petitions with fervent cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and he was heard
thematicGuides.intro: A message you sent goes a whole day without a reply, and already you're wondering whether it arrived. You kept asking God for something good, perhaps for someone to get well, and it didn't happen. After a while you stop asking why He said no and start asking whether anyone was listening. On one night Jesus prayed three times about what was coming, and it still came.
story: Jesus went with His disciples to a place called Gethsemane and told them to sit while He prayed. He kept three with Him, Peter and the two sons of Zebedee. He began to be sorrowful and troubled, Matthew says, and then He told them His soul was overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death. He asked them to keep watch with Him and went a little further alone. There He asked His Father to take the cup away if that could be done. The cup was His word for the death ahead of Him. He left the decision with His Father, and He prayed all of it with His face to the ground.

Jesus came back to find the three asleep, then went away and prayed a second time, and Matthew gives different words. The first prayer asked for the cup to be taken away if that were possible. The second supposes that it isn't, and asks, in a line from the prayer He had taught His disciples, that the Father's will be done. He prayed the same a third time, and Matthew records no reply. When Judas arrived with an armed crowd and one of His companions drew a sword, Jesus told him to put it back. "Do you think I cannot call on my Father, and he will at once put at my disposal more than twelve legions of angels?" He didn't ask for them.

The letter to the Hebrews gives one sentence to how Jesus prayed while He was on earth. He offered up prayers and petitions, the writer says, crying out and in tears, to the one who could save Him from death. The letter doesn't name the garden, though it seems to have that night in view. Hebrews is clear that He was not spared. Its next line says He learned obedience from what He suffered, and its closing blessing calls God the one who brought Him back from the dead. Of those prayers the writer says, "and he was heard".

keyVerses.text: Going a little farther, he fell with his face to the ground and prayed, 'My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will.'
He went away a second time and prayed, 'My Father, if it is not possible for this cup to be taken away unless I drink it, may your will be done.'

During the days of Jesus' life on earth, he offered up prayers and petitions with fervent cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission. Son though he was, he learned obedience from what he suffered

insights: Being heard and being given what you asked for were two different things even for Jesus. So a request that wasn't granted can't prove that God wasn't listening. At Lazarus's tomb Jesus had said to His Father, "I knew that you always hear me" (John 11:42), and the night in the garden falls inside that always.

Hebrews tells its readers to come to God's throne with confidence, for mercy and for help in their time of need (Hebrews 4:16). Both are there to be asked for when the thing you wanted was not given, and the high priest Hebrews points you to, Jesus, has prayed in tears Himself.

None of this explains why your prayer wasn't granted. Jesus knew why He had to drink the cup. You may never be given a reason, and the loss is no smaller for knowing you were heard. If you're grieving it, say so to a friend, as He told three friends how bad that night was.
reflectQuestions: Which prayer of yours that wasn't granted do you still think about most?
When the thing you asked for didn't happen, what did you conclude about God, or about how He sees you?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose an evening this week when you have ten minutes alone. On a sheet of paper, write at the top the thing you asked God for that didn't happen, as near as you can to the words you prayed. Leave a gap, then copy out Hebrews 5:7 underneath. Write nothing in the gap about why. Fold the sheet and keep it in the drawer by your bed.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I asked You for something good, and I went on asking for a long time. It didn't happen. Since then I've wondered whether I was talking to the ceiling, and some days I've prayed less so I wouldn't have to find out. I'd still like to know why You didn't give it.
