Your Son prayed three times and still drank the cup, and You heard every word. Help me believe You heard me as well, and keep me talking to You. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Psalm 42 for When God Feels Far Away
thematicGuides.hook: The writer of Psalms 42 and 43 keeps telling his own soul to hope in God, and the poem ends before the joy comes back.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Why, my soul, are you downcast? Why so disturbed within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise him, my Savior and my God.
thematicGuides.intro: You used to come away from praying with a sense that God was near. Lately He seems a long way off, you're low more days than not, and you've begun to wonder whether something is wrong with you. Psalms 42 and 43 were written by someone in that state. They're often read as one poem, and the same verse closes both. Whoever wrote it was in tears, with people taunting him, and the joy he remembered was gone.
story: The poem comes from the Sons of Korah, a family of temple musicians, and its writer remembers going up to the house of God in a crowd, shouting for joy. He begins with thirst, his soul panting for God as a deer pants for streams of water. His tears have been his food day and night, and all day long people ask him where his God is. At that point he turns and speaks to his own soul. He asks it why it is downcast, tells it to put its hope in God, and gives it a reason, "I will yet praise him". The praise is still ahead of him.

Straight after telling his soul to hope in God, the psalmist reports how that went. "My soul is downcast within me", he says. He is up by Mount Hermon, far to the north of the temple, and the water in the poem has changed. He began thirsty for a stream. Now waterfalls are roaring, and he tells God that all His waves and breakers have swept over him. Jonah uses the same words in his prayer from inside the fish. The psalmist goes on to ask God why He has forgotten him, and calls Him "God my Rock" as he asks. His foes are still asking where his God is, and he says to his soul a second time exactly what he said the first.

The psalmist's first requests come in Psalm 43. Up to that point he has told God how things are and asked Him why. Now he asks God to vindicate him and rescue him, and to send His light and His faithful care to lead him to the holy mountain. Once there he will go to the altar, to God, "my joy and my delight". He can still call God that with the joy itself missing. His question has sharpened, from why God has forgotten him to why God has rejected him. Then the sentence to his soul comes a third time, word for word, and the poem stops.

keyVerses.text: Why, my soul, are you downcast? Why so disturbed within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise him, my Savior and my God. My soul is downcast within me; therefore I will remember you
I say to God my Rock, 'Why have you forgotten me? Why must I go about mourning, oppressed by the enemy?'
Send me your light and your faithful care, let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy mountain, to the place where you dwell. Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my joy and my delight.

insights: These psalms don't treat feeling low and far from God as a fault. The writer never hunts for a sin to explain it, and the heading hands his poem to the director of music, for other people to sing.

The psalmist asks to be led. He wants God's light and faithful care to bring him back to the holy mountain, where he once stood in a crowd. If you've been this low for weeks, or you're not sleeping or eating properly, don't try to find the way back by yourself either. Your doctor ought to know, and so should one friend.

The writer tells his soul to hope while he is still low, and he is still low when the poem ends. His line about praising God is in the future tense, which is why you can say it honestly on a day when you can't praise at all.
reflectQuestions: What do you miss most about the way praying used to be for you?
The psalmist asked God why He had forgotten him. What question would you put to God if you were sure He wouldn't mind being asked?
thematicGuides.practice: One day this week, go to the nearest water you can get to, even if it's only the pond in a park. Take Psalms 42 and 43 with you and read them aloud there, from the stream in the first line to the end. Nothing has to happen while you're there.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I've carried on saying the words with nothing behind them, and I've let people think I'm fine. I miss how it used to be. I don't know why You seem so far away, and I'm asking You why. My soul is downcast, and telling it to hope hasn't lifted it. I will yet praise You. Send Your light and Your faithful care, and lead me back. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: We Prayed and Posted a Guard
thematicGuides.hook: Ezra would not ask for an armed escort, Nehemiah travelled with one, and both said the gracious hand of God was on them.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night to meet this threat.
thematicGuides.intro: By the Ahava Canal, with months of road ahead and children in the company, Ezra was ashamed to ask the king of Persia for soldiers. He had told the king that God's hand is on everyone who looks to Him, so he called a fast and they set out without an escort. If you've prayed about something and then also booked the appointment or changed the locks, you may wonder whether Ezra shows you up. The Bible's next book follows a man who took the road to Jerusalem with cavalry.
story: In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, Ezra, a priest and teacher of the Law, led a company of families from Babylon to Jerusalem. They carried the gifts for the temple, among them 650 talents of silver and 100 talents of gold, and because Ezra had been ashamed to ask for soldiers, no escort rode with any of it. They fasted and asked God for a safe road. Even so, Ezra weighed the treasure out to twelve of the leading priests and told them to guard it carefully until it was weighed again in Jerusalem. On the fourth day after they arrived, everything was accounted for by number and weight. Ezra put the safe road down to the hand of God, who had protected them from enemies and bandits along the way.

In the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, his cupbearer Nehemiah was given leave to go and rebuild Jerusalem, and he had more to ask. He wanted letters to the governors on his route, so that they would give him safe-conduct as far as Judah. The king granted his requests, and Nehemiah explains why in words Ezra had used, "because the gracious hand of my God was on me". In the next verse he mentions that the king had also sent army officers and cavalry with him. He passes no comment on them. He handed the letters to the governors and went on to Jerusalem.

The work on Jerusalem's wall drew mockery first. Speaking in front of his associates and the army of Samaria, Sanballat asked what those feeble Jews were doing, and Tobiah the Ammonite, at his side, said a fox climbing on the wall would knock it down. Nehemiah answered with a prayer and kept building. When the gaps in the wall began to close, Sanballat and Tobiah were joined by the Arabs, the Ammonites and the people of Ashdod, and they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem. This time Nehemiah wrote, "But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night to meet this threat."

keyVerses.text: I was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen to protect us from enemies on the road, because we had told the king, 'The gracious hand of our God is on everyone who looks to him, but his great anger is against all who forsake him.' So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and he answered our prayer.

And because the gracious hand of my God was on me, the king granted my requests. So I went to the governors of Trans-Euphrates and gave them the king's letters. The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me.
But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night to meet this threat.

insights: Ezra went without an escort because of something he himself had said to the king. He gives it as his own reason for that one road, and even he had the treasure weighed out and guarded. So if someone tells you that taking out insurance after you've prayed shows weak faith, these chapters don't back them.

When the plot came to nothing, Nehemiah wrote that God had frustrated it (Nehemiah 4:15), though his own sentries had been standing there day and night. Help that reaches you through a surgeon can be how God answers the prayer. Nothing here promises that every road will end as safely as these two did.
reflectQuestions: Where have you held back from sensible help or a precaution because taking it felt like not trusting God?
For the thing you're praying about most at the moment, what would posting a guard look like?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick one precaution you already take every day, such as fastening your seat belt. Each day for a week, as you do it, pray one sentence asking God to look after whatever the precaution is there for. That's praying and guarding together, seven days running.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I've prayed about this, and then I booked the appointment and checked the locks, and I've half wondered whether You took that as an insult. Nehemiah prayed and posted a guard in one sentence, and Your hand was on him. I'm relying on other people's help, and I thank You for them, whether or not they know You. Where I've used being careful as a way of not praying at all, show me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: David Afraid in Goliath's Home Town
thematicGuides.hook: The man who killed Goliath was later so frightened in Goliath's own town that he faked madness to get out alive.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: When I am afraid, I put my trust in you. In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust and am not afraid. What can mere mortals do to me?
thematicGuides.intro: The usual assumption is that someone who really trusted God wouldn't get properly frightened, and David walking out to meet Goliath is held up as the proof. He does look unafraid that day. Four chapters later, though, 1 Samuel says he was very much afraid. Psalm 56 is the prayer that goes with that later day, and by its third verse he is admitting as much to God.
story: David was on the run from King Saul, who meant to kill him. He came alone to the priest Ahimelek at Nob, who trembled when he saw him and asked why nobody was with him. David said the king had sent him on a secret errand. He had brought no weapon, and when he asked for a spear or a sword, the only one in the place was the sword of Goliath, the Philistine champion from Gath, kept there wrapped in a cloth. "There is none like it; give it to me," David said. He had once run at Goliath without a sword in his hand. Now he had Goliath's own, and that day he fled from Saul to Achish, king of Gath.

Achish's servants recognised him. They called him the king of the land and quoted the song the women of Israel had sung after Goliath fell, crediting Saul with thousands and David with tens of thousands. The song that had turned Saul against him gave him away in Gath. The words went home, and he was very much afraid of Achish. It's the first time the book says David was afraid of anyone. So while he was in their hands he acted like a madman, making marks on the doors of the gate and letting saliva run down his beard. "Am I so short of madmen that you have to bring this fellow here to carry on like this in front of me?" Achish asked his servants. David left Gath and escaped to the cave of Adullam.

Psalm 56 has a heading that places it in Gath, when the Philistines had seized David. Early on he says, "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you." In the very next line he says he trusts God and is not afraid, and asks what mere mortals can do to him. He goes straight on to list what they can do. They twist his words, they lurk, they watch his steps, hoping to take his life. He asks God to keep his tears on record. Then he says a second time that he trusts God and is not afraid.

keyVerses.text: When I am afraid, I put my trust in you. In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust and am not afraid. What can mere mortals do to me?
Record my misery; list my tears on your scroll, are they not in your record? Then my enemies will turn back when I call for help. By this I will know that God is for me.
In God, whose word I praise, in the LORD, whose word I praise, in God I trust and am not afraid. What can man do to me?

insights: The psalm says 'when', which assumes there will be a next time. David says he is not afraid one line after admitting that he is, and seven verses later he is saying it again. Being frightened doesn't mean you've stopped trusting God. David was both in one prayer.

The heading of Psalm 56 names a tune, 'A Dove on Distant Oaks', and marks the psalm for the director of music. David's prayer from Gath was set down for other people to sing. The words were meant to be borrowed.
David got out of Gath alive. The psalm makes no promise that you'll be spared the thing you dread. It gives you a God to tell, who keeps a record of your tears.
reflectQuestions: What are you frightened of at the moment that you'd rather nobody knew about?
When you're frightened, what do you usually do with it before you get round to telling God?
thematicGuides.practice: The priest's first words to David at Nob were, "Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?" David gave him a cover story. This week, give the real one to a friend or relative who'll keep it to themselves. Ring them or sit down with them and say in a few sentences what you're frightened of. They don't need to fix it. If the fear is there most days, or it's costing you sleep, have the same conversation with your doctor.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I'm frightened. I can't stop being afraid by deciding to, so I'm bringing it to You while it's still here. Keep a record of what it has cost me already, the way David asked You to list his tears. I've been telling people I'm fine, and You've heard every cover story. Please bring me through this, and stay with me if it goes the way I dread. Help me tell one person the truth about it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Nicodemus Came at Night
thematicGuides.hook: One man came to Jesus at night, another followed Him in secret, and on the day He died those two buried Him.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Joseph of Arimathea asked Pilate for the body of Jesus. Now Joseph was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly because he feared the Jewish leaders.
thematicGuides.intro: The trouble with keeping quiet about your faith is that it gets harder to undo the longer it runs. In your first week somewhere, mentioning church is a passing remark. Three years in, it's an announcement, and it comes with the awkward matter of why you never said. In John's Gospel, Nicodemus first came to Jesus at night, and Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple in secret because he was afraid.
story: Nicodemus was a Pharisee, a strict keeper of the Jewish law, and a member of the ruling council in Jerusalem. He came to see Jesus at night, and John gives no reason for the hour. He called Jesus Rabbi and said that he and others knew He was a teacher who had come from God, because of the signs He was doing. Jesus told him that no one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again, and Nicodemus asked how anyone could be born when they were old. The last thing he says in the scene is "How can this be?" Jesus called him Israel's teacher and asked if he did not understand these things.

Later the chief priests and Pharisees sent temple guards to arrest Jesus. The guards came back without Him, saying that no one had ever spoken the way He did. The Pharisees scoffed that not one ruler or Pharisee had believed in Him. Nicodemus was both, and he was there. He let that pass and raised a point of law, asking whether their law condemns a man without first hearing him. The question gave nothing away about himself, and they went for him anyway. "Are you from Galilee, too?" they said, and told him to look it up, because no prophet comes out of Galilee.

On the day Jesus was crucified, Joseph of Arimathea went to Pilate, the Roman governor, and asked for the body. John says Joseph was a disciple, but a secret one, because he was afraid of the leaders. With Pilate's permission he took the body away, and Nicodemus came with him, bringing about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes. The two of them wrapped the body with the spices in strips of linen and laid it in a new tomb in a garden, near the place where He had been crucified. Two evenings later the disciples who had followed Jesus openly were together behind locked doors. John says they were afraid of the leaders, which is the reason he had given for Joseph's secrecy.

keyVerses.text: Now there was a Pharisee, a man named Nicodemus who was a member of the Jewish ruling council. He came to Jesus at night and said, 'Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher who has come from God.'
Nicodemus, who had gone to Jesus earlier and who was one of their own number, asked, 'Does our law condemn a man without first hearing him to find out what he has been doing?'
On the evening of that first day of the week, when the disciples were together, with the doors locked for fear of the Jewish leaders, Jesus came and stood among them and said, 'Peace be with you!'

insights: At the tomb John still calls Nicodemus "the man who earlier had visited Jesus at night". He keeps the old history on the page next to the burial. You don't have to account for your quiet years before you're allowed to do something different.

John doesn't excuse hiding. He says in John 12:42-43 that many leaders believed and wouldn't admit it, because they loved human praise more than praise from God. Yet the one man he calls a secret disciple is the one who went to Pilate, and Mark 15:43 says he went boldly.
reflectQuestions: What do you expect would happen if the people you see every week found out you're a Christian?
Nicodemus began with a fair question in a room that was against Jesus. What is the smallest honest thing you could say where you are?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose one person you see most weeks who doesn't know you're a Christian. It might be a colleague, someone on your course, a neighbour or a friend at the club. The next time they ask what you did at the weekend, put church in your answer, in one ordinary sentence, and let the conversation go where it goes. It may cost you something. Nicodemus's careful question got him a sneer.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, give me an ordinary opening this week, and don't let me talk myself out of taking it. Most of the people I spend my days with don't know I belong to You, and I've let it stay that way because it was easier. I've laughed along with things so that nobody would guess, and I'm sorry. I've been coming to You after dark long enough, and I want to be known as Yours in daylight too. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Caleb at Eighty-Five
thematicGuides.hook: Outvoted at forty, Caleb waited forty-five years, then asked for the hill country whose people had terrified the other spies.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Now give me this hill country that the LORD promised me that day.
thematicGuides.intro: When the twelve men Moses sent to scout Canaan reached Hebron, Numbers 13 stops to name three men who lived there: Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai, descendants of Anak. People like them made ten of the twelve feel like grasshoppers. The three names turn up again in Joshua 15, some forty-five years on. If there's a hard thing you always meant to do and you suspect it's too late now, Caleb is the man to read about.
story: Moses sent twelve men, a leader from each tribe, to explore Canaan. They came back carrying a single cluster of grapes on a pole between two of them. All twelve agreed on the facts. The land flowed with milk and honey, the cities were fortified and very large, and Anak's descendants were there. Then Caleb silenced the people and said they should go up, because they could certainly take it. The others said the people there were too strong, and spread a bad report through the camp. Caleb was forty.

That night the whole community wept aloud, and there was talk of choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt. Caleb and one other spy, Joshua, tore their clothes and told the assembly that the LORD was with them and they shouldn't be afraid. The assembly talked about stoning them. God's verdict was forty years in the wilderness, until the adults who had grumbled were dead. Of Caleb He said that he had a different spirit and would be brought into the land. Caleb still had to turn back into the desert with everyone else, and he lived for forty years with the result of an argument he had lost.

Forty-five years later the land was being shared out at Gilgal, and Caleb came to Joshua, the only other one of the twelve still alive. He went back over the day Moses swore that the land his feet had walked on would be his, and the years the LORD had kept him alive since. "So here I am today, eighty-five years old!" he said, and told Joshua he was as strong as on the day Moses sent him out. He asked for the hill country he had been promised, Anakites and all. He reminded Joshua, who had heard it for himself, how large and fortified their cities were, and said that with the LORD helping him he would drive them out. Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron, and from Hebron Caleb drove out Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai.

keyVerses.text: Then Caleb silenced the people before Moses and said, 'We should go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly do it.' But the men who had gone up with him said, 'We can't attack those people; they are stronger than we are.'
But because my servant Caleb has a different spirit and follows me wholeheartedly, I will bring him into the land he went to, and his descendants will inherit it.

Now give me this hill country that the LORD promised me that day. You yourself heard then that the Anakites were there and their cities were large and fortified, but, the LORD helping me, I will drive them out just as he said.

insights: Caleb never argued with the facts. He saw the walls and the Anakites the other ten saw, and at eighty-five he lists them again while he is asking for the place. He counted what God had said among the facts, and they didn't.

Caleb had a sworn promise about one stretch of hills, and a body that had held up. You may not, and nothing here says what you have in mind will work. But some hard things God asks of everyone, such as ringing the friend you wronged years ago to say sorry, and nobody gets too old for those.
For forty-five years Caleb held on to a promise. In his speech to Joshua he gives the men who outvoted him one sentence, and he comes back to what the LORD said at least four times.
reflectQuestions: What do you already know about what God wants in the thing you once meant to do?
When you tell yourself it's too late now, what are you most relieved not to have to face?
thematicGuides.practice: Starting today, go a week without giving your age as the reason. Each time you're about to say 'at my age' or 'it's too late for that now', leave it unsaid and tell yourself what is really in the way. It may be your health, which is a real reason, or it may be fear of failing. Caleb gave his age to Joshua as proof that God had kept him alive.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, 'too late' has been a relief to me some days, because it means I don't have to try. Show me whether what I keep coming back to is something You have asked of me or something I only wanted. I don't have Caleb's strength, or a promise with my name on it about how it would turn out. If it's Yours, then with You helping me I'll start, at the age I am. If it isn't, help me put it down without bitterness. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Archangel Who Left the Verdict to God
thematicGuides.hook: Jude told his friends to fight for the faith, then pointed to Michael, who would not pass sentence even on the devil.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Keep yourselves in God's love as you wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you to eternal life. Be merciful to those who doubt.
thematicGuides.intro: Someone at work makes a crack about Christians and the table laughs. A relative sends you an article with 'explain this, then' typed above it. The two responses that come to hand are saying nothing and saying something sharp, and either can leave you ashamed by the evening. Jude wrote his short letter to friends who had people in their own church twisting the faith. He tells them to fight for it, and then he tells them how.
story: Jude began by calling his readers people who were loved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ. His greeting to friends he was about to send into an argument was, "Mercy, peace and love be yours in abundance." Then he told them he had been very eager to write a different letter, about the salvation they shared. But certain people had slipped in among them who were turning God's grace into permission for immorality and denying Jesus Christ. So he wrote instead to urge his friends to fight for the faith, which he said had been entrusted to God's people once for all.

The people troubling the church were free with their tongues. Jude said they heaped abuse on celestial beings and slandered whatever they didn't understand. Against that he set the archangel Michael in his dispute with the devil over the body of Moses. Even then, Jude said, Michael did not take it on himself to condemn the devil. All he said was, "The Lord rebuke you!" They are the words the LORD Himself speaks in Zechariah 3, when Satan stands ready to accuse the high priest Joshua.

After a run of warnings, in which he called the troublemakers clouds without rain and wandering stars, Jude reminded his friends that the apostles had told them to expect scoffers. Then he gave his orders, and they began at home. His friends were to keep themselves in God's love, building up their faith and praying in the Holy Spirit while they waited for the mercy of Jesus. Only then did he turn to other people, and in three short instructions he named mercy twice. He ended by giving glory to the God "who is able to keep you from stumbling".

keyVerses.text: Dear friends, although I was very eager to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt compelled to write and urge you to contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to God's holy people.
But even the archangel Michael, when he was disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not himself dare to condemn him for slander but said, 'The Lord rebuke you!'

But you, dear friends, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God's love as you wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you to eternal life. Be merciful to those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; to others show mercy, mixed with fear, hating even the clothing stained by corrupted flesh.

insights: The urge to hit back often comes from feeling that everything hangs on your answer. Jude opens by telling his friends they are kept and closes with the God who can keep them, and he says the faith was handed over once for all. It doesn't depend on your winning the exchange.

Michael had the devil in front of him and left the verdict to the Lord. Whoever is needling you is a good deal less than the devil. You can say firmly that something is false without passing sentence on the person who said it.

Jude is fierce about people who slipped into a church and twisted its faith, and for those who doubt, the word he uses is mercy. Across a lunch table you can't always tell a scoffer from a doubter, and mercy is where his orders about other people begin. He would rather have written the friendly letter and still wrote this one, so going quiet is not what he means by mercy.
reflectQuestions: When someone last mocked or twisted what you believe, what did you most want out of the next thirty seconds?
Whoever you argue with most about faith, what do you know about why they say what they say?
thematicGuides.practice: Tomorrow morning, before you leave your bedroom or say a word to anyone, read Jude 1:20-25 aloud, once. It's six verses. As you read verse 22, have in mind the person whose remarks about your faith get under your skin. Jude's orders to keep yourself in God's love and to be merciful will then be the first words you say that day, ahead of anything you say to that person.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, when someone laughs at what I believe, I either go quiet or I go for them, and I end up ashamed of both. There are arguments I've wanted to win more than I've wanted the other person to know You. Keep me in Your love when I'm needled, and give me one true thing to say kindly. Have mercy on the people I had written off. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Prayer of Judah's Worst King
thematicGuides.hook: Manasseh prayed as a prisoner in Babylon and the LORD listened, but some of what he had done was never undone.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: And when he prayed to him, the LORD was moved by his entreaty and listened to his plea; so he brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom.
thematicGuides.intro: You've done something you can't undo, and what it left behind is still there for anyone to see. Perhaps a person is worse off because of you, or a family no longer sits in the same room. You've said sorry and the damage hasn't gone anywhere, which makes it hard to pray. 2 Chronicles 33 is about a king who led his country into worse evil than the nations God had judged before it, and what happened when he prayed. It's frank about what his prayer didn't mend.
story: Manasseh became king of Judah at twelve and reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-five years. His father Hezekiah had demolished the high places, the local shrines on the hills, and Manasseh rebuilt them. He built altars to the stars in both courts of the LORD's temple and set an image he had made inside it. The LORD had said of that building, "My Name will remain in Jerusalem forever." In the Valley of Ben Hinnom, Manasseh sacrificed his children in the fire. The book of Kings says he shed so much innocent blood that it filled Jerusalem from end to end.

The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, and they paid no attention. So He brought the commanders of the Assyrian army against them, and they put a hook in Manasseh's nose and led him to Babylon in bronze shackles. There, in his distress, he humbled himself and prayed. Chronicles mentions that prayer three times and says other records had it in writing. All it passes on is the result. The LORD heard him, and Manasseh went home to Jerusalem as king. Long before, at the dedication of the temple, Solomon had prayed for any of God's people who sinned, were carried off captive and pleaded with Him from the land of their captivity. Manasseh had put an idol in that temple, and he was now the captive Solomon had described.

Back in Jerusalem, Manasseh went to work on what he had built. He took the image out of the temple and threw it out of the city, along with the foreign gods and every altar he had put up on the temple hill and around Jerusalem. With the LORD's altar restored, he told Judah to serve the LORD. The people kept sacrificing at the high places he had rebuilt, now to the LORD alone. After his death his son Amon reigned two years. He sacrificed to all the idols his father had made and, unlike his father, did not humble himself.

keyVerses.text: From heaven, your dwelling place, hear their prayer and their pleas, and uphold their cause. And forgive your people, who have sinned against you.

In his distress he sought the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his ancestors. And when he prayed to him, the LORD was moved by his entreaty and listened to his plea; so he brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God.

Then he restored the altar of the LORD and sacrificed fellowship offerings and thank offerings on it, and told Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel. The people, however, continued to sacrifice at the high places, but only to the LORD their God.

insights: Manasseh was heard as a prisoner, before he had put a single thing right. The clearing out came later and was partial: he could carry altars out of the city and could do nothing for the children he had sacrificed.
The LORD gave Manasseh his kingdom back. You may not get back what was lost. The promise in 1 John 1:9 is that God forgives those who confess.

The book of Kings tells this reign without the prayer. What passed between Manasseh and God in Babylon is in Chronicles alone. Some people who know your story will only ever have the Kings half, and they aren't wrong about the half they have.
reflectQuestions: When you look at the damage that's still there, what do you assume God is thinking as He looks at it?
The high places stayed in use, but Manasseh could carry his own altars out of the city. What is one thing you set up that is still yours to take down?
thematicGuides.practice: When you have ten minutes alone this week, take a sheet of paper. On one side write, in two or three sentences, what you did and what it damaged, then read it to God as it stands. On the other side copy out 2 Chronicles 33:13 and date it. Keep the paper somewhere private, such as inside your Bible, and on a day when the damage is all you can see, read both sides.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, this is the prayer I've been putting off. You know what I did, and what it cost people who never asked to be part of it. I can't give any of that back. I didn't come to You while things were going well. I'm here because I've run out of other places to go, and I'm asking to be heard the way Manasseh was. Show me what I can still put right. For the damage I can't reach, and the people living with it, I ask Your mercy. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Mark, Who Quit and Was Wanted Back
thematicGuides.hook: John Mark walked out on Paul and Barnabas partway through a mission, and Paul's last letter asks for him by name.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is helpful to me in my ministry.
thematicGuides.intro: At Perga in Pamphylia, with the work unfinished, John Mark left Paul and Barnabas and went back to Jerusalem. If you've let people down just when they were counting on you, you'll know how one day can become the first thing anyone remembers about you. With Paul, for a time, that is what happened to Mark. Paul's own letters name him three times after that, and not once as the man who left.
story: John, also called Mark, came from Jerusalem, where believers met to pray in his mother Mary's house. Barnabas and Paul brought him back with them to Antioch, and when the church there sent the two of them out, he went as well. "John was with them as their helper," writes Luke, the author of Acts. They crossed Cyprus, where the Roman governor believed, and sailed on to Perga. What happened there gets a single clause: "where John left them to return to Jerusalem." Paul and Barnabas went on inland without him.

Some time later Paul proposed going back to visit the believers in every town where they had preached. Barnabas wanted Mark along. Paul wouldn't take a man who had deserted them in Pamphylia. The disagreement became so sharp that the two of them parted company. Paul chose Silas and left through Syria and Cilicia. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus. It was Barnabas's home, and it was the one stretch of the first trip Mark had seen through to the end. That is the last Acts says of Mark. He leaves the book as the helper Paul and Barnabas fell out over.

When Mark's name next appears, it is in letters Paul wrote as a prisoner, and Mark is with him. Writing to Colossae, Paul passes on Mark's greetings and tells the church to welcome him if he comes. He counts him among three Jewish co-workers who "have proved a comfort to me." Peter ends a letter of his own with greetings from "my son Mark". How Mark and Paul were reconciled isn't recorded. In his last letter Paul expects to die soon. Demas has deserted him, and only Luke is still with him, the same Luke whose book records what happened at Perga. Paul asks Timothy to come quickly. He wants his cloak from Troas and his scrolls, and he wants Mark, because Mark is helpful to him in his work.

keyVerses.text: Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark, with them, but Paul did not think it wise to take him, because he had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not continued with them in the work.
My fellow prisoner Aristarchus sends you his greetings, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas. (You have received instructions about him; if he comes to you, welcome him.)
Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is helpful to me in my ministry.

insights: Mark set out as Paul and Barnabas's helper, and when Paul last mentions him it is to say he is helpful. In between, he went back to work with Barnabas while Paul still counted him a deserter. Paul's change of mind, whenever it came, came after Mark had already started again.

Paul had a reason for saying no, and Acts lets it stand, so someone you let down may be right not to rely on you yet. A person can have good reason to refuse you and later ask for you by name. You can't make that happen, and not everyone comes round as Paul did.
reflectQuestions: Where have you stopped offering your help because of the time you let people down?
Who could you take along again, as Barnabas took Mark, while other people are still wary of them?
thematicGuides.practice: Set tonight's alarm ten minutes earlier than usual. Tomorrow morning, use the extra time to be early at the first place you're expected, whether that's work, a lecture, the church hall or a relative's front door. Find one small job there that someone else would otherwise have to do, such as putting out the chairs or washing the mugs left in the sink, and do it without being asked. If you've held back from offering help since the day you let people down, count this as your first offer.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I walked away on a day when people were counting on me, and I've never given anyone a proper reason for it. I've assumed ever since that it's the first thing people think of when they hear my name, and with some of them I may be right. Changing their minds is out of my hands. Help me do the next piece of work in front of me whether or not anybody notices. If someone is willing to take me along again, give me the humility to say yes. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: God Sings Over the City He Rebuked
thematicGuides.hook: Zephaniah 3 begins with a city that accepts no correction and ends with God rejoicing over it with singing.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The LORD your God is with you, the Mighty Warrior who saves. He will take great delight in you; in his love he will no longer rebuke you, but will rejoice over you with singing.
thematicGuides.intro: The usual picture of God forgiving someone is a judge letting them off. The file is closed and nobody in the courtroom is smiling. There is truth in it, because the Bible does speak of a punishment being taken away. But the picture can't tell you how God regards you once that's done, and plenty of people assume He is putting up with them. Zephaniah, three chapters of mostly grim prophecy, ends with an answer, and it has singing in it.
story: Zephaniah prophesied while Josiah was king of Judah, and his book opens with God saying He will sweep away everything from the face of the earth. Chapter 3 begins with a woe on Jerusalem, the city of oppressors. Her officials are roaring lions and her priests profane the sanctuary. The LORD is within her all the while. Morning by morning He does justice there, and the unrighteous still know no shame. He had thought Jerusalem would surely fear Him and accept correction. But they were still eager, He says, to act corruptly in everything they did.

God says a day is coming when He will gather the nations and pour out His wrath on them. After the charges against Jerusalem, nobody could call that a surprise. But He goes on to describe a day beyond that one. He calls what Jerusalem did wrongs done to Him, and in the same sentence says she will not be put to shame for them. He will remove the arrogant boasters from the city Himself. The people He leaves in it are meek and humble, and they trust in His name. Of them He says, "They will eat and lie down and no one will make them afraid."

Zephaniah turns to Jerusalem and tells her to sing and shout aloud, because the LORD has taken away her punishment and turned back her enemy. On that day, he says, the city will be told, "Do not fear, Zion; do not let your hands hang limp." The reason given is that the LORD her God is with her, and He is called the Mighty Warrior who saves. The NIV has that title once before in this book, in chapter 1, where the Mighty Warrior shouts His battle cry on the day of wrath. Three verses after the city is told to sing, the singer is God. In the book's last verse He says, "I will bring you home."

keyVerses.text: She obeys no one, she accepts no correction. She does not trust in the LORD, she does not draw near to her God.
On that day you, Jerusalem, will not be put to shame for all the wrongs you have done to me, because I will remove from you your arrogant boasters. Never again will you be haughty on my holy hill.
The LORD your God is with you, the Mighty Warrior who saves. He will take great delight in you; in his love he will no longer rebuke you, but will rejoice over you with singing.

insights: The LORD whose verdict on Jerusalem fills the opening verses is singing over her by verse 17. Being welcomed by someone who doesn't know the worst about you is small comfort. Here the one who is glad listed the worst Himself.

These words were spoken to Jerusalem, about a day Zephaniah saw coming. Jesus says something very close about one person, that "there is rejoicing in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents."

The order not to let your hands hang limp comes straight before the singing. People who believe they are only tolerated tend to keep their heads down and attempt very little. Zephaniah tells the city to get its hands moving again because God is glad to have His people back.
reflectQuestions: When you picture God's face just after you've confessed something to Him, what expression do you see on it?
What have you stopped attempting because you assume God is only putting up with you?
thematicGuides.practice: Each day for a week, read Zephaniah 3:17 aloud, then sing one verse of a hymn or worship song you know by heart, somewhere nobody will hear you, such as the shower or the car. It may feel foolish, especially if you never sing.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I say sorry to You quickly and leave, the way I would with someone I've asked too many favours of. I've pictured You forgiving me with a sigh. Zephaniah says You sing, and I find that hard to believe about You and me. You named everything that was wrong before You took the shame of it away, so You were never fooled into being glad. Help me believe You could be glad about me. Lift my hands off my lap and put them back to work. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Knock at Laodicea's Door
thematicGuides.hook: The one letter in Revelation where Jesus praises nothing is the one where He knocks and offers to come in and eat.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Here I am! I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and eat with that person, and they with me.
thematicGuides.intro: A faith that has gone flat is hard to do anything about, because it doesn't hurt. Grief or guilt will at least send you looking for God. When the bills are paid, your health is holding and church is a pleasant habit, there's nothing pressing to bring Him, and after a while you stop expecting anything. Jesus sent a letter to a church in that condition, at Laodicea. It's a rough letter.
story: Laodicea is the last of the seven churches in the province of Asia that John was told to write to. Each letter opens with a title for Jesus, and in this one He is the faithful and true witness. In the other six He finds something to commend. Even in Sardis, which He calls dead, there are a few people He says are worthy. To Laodicea the witness says, "I know your deeds, that you are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were either one or the other!" Because they are lukewarm, He goes on, He is about to spit them out of His mouth.

Jesus quotes the Laodiceans' opinion of themselves. They say they are rich and don't need a thing. His complaint is that they have no idea of their real condition, which He gives in five words. They are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind and naked. "I counsel you," He says, and names what to buy from Him: gold for the poor, white clothes for the naked and salve for the blind. Buying is a strange thing to ask of people He has just called poor. God had spoken the same way through Isaiah centuries earlier, when He called people with no money to come and buy.

Only now does Jesus say why He has spoken like this. The people He loves are the ones He rebukes and disciplines. He says where He is. He is standing at the door, knocking. The letter is addressed to a church, so the people on the other side of that door are the same people who said they needed nothing. The offer is made to them one at a time. Anyone who hears His voice and opens the door will have Him in to eat. The letter's last promise, to whoever is victorious, is "the right to sit with me on my throne."

keyVerses.text: You say, 'I am rich; I have acquired wealth and do not need a thing.' But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind and naked.
Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost.

Those whom I love I rebuke and discipline. So be earnest and repent. Here I am! I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and eat with that person, and they with me.

insights: Nothing scandalous is charged against Laodicea. The fault Jesus names is their belief that they needed nothing, which comes on quietly when life is going well and is hard to see from the inside. He treats it as serious, and as something that can be put right, or He wouldn't be offering advice.

If you wonder whether He has lost interest in you, look at where He says He is standing. It is the door of the church He has just said He is about to spit out. And He offers to come in and eat, which is what you do with people whose company you want.
What Jesus asks for can be done by someone who feels very little: be earnest, repent, open the door. The letter says nothing about how soon the old warmth returns. It promises that He will come in.
reflectQuestions: If Jesus quoted back one sentence you say about your own life, as He quoted Laodicea's, which sentence would it be?
What did you last ask God for that you couldn't have arranged for yourself?
thematicGuides.practice: Ask one person whose faith you respect to have a meal or a coffee with you this week. Tell them the sentence you'd normally keep to yourself, that life is fine and you've stopped expecting anything from God. Then ask what they are expecting from Him at the moment, and hear the whole answer before you reply.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I've nothing urgent to bring You, and that is the trouble. I've been running my life without asking You for much. I still turn up on Sundays. I've stopped expecting You to. Jesus says He is at the door. I'd rather hear the knock than be left comfortable. I won't pretend to a warmth I don't feel, so I'm asking for what He offered. Give me eyes to see how I really am, and His company at my table. I'm opening the door as far as I know how. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Like a Weaned Child: Psalm 131
thematicGuides.hook: David tells God that some things are too wonderful for him, and his picture of a quiet mind is a weaned child with its mother.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But I have calmed and quieted myself, I am like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child I am content.
thematicGuides.intro: Psalm 131 says 'weaned' twice in one verse. The child David compares himself to is no baby at the breast. It's a picture for you if your mind keeps working at why something went the way it did, what somebody else is going to decide, or what next year holds. None of that is yours to settle, and your mind won't leave it alone. The whole psalm is three verses.
story: Psalm 131 is headed 'Of David'. He tells the LORD that his heart isn't proud, and that he doesn't concern himself with great matters. David had plenty of great matters that were his to deal with. The ones he leaves alone he calls too wonderful for him, and Job ends up using the same phrase. For most of his book Job asks God why, and when the LORD finally answers out of the storm it is with questions about the sea, the stars and the wild donkey. Job replies that he spoke of things he didn't understand, things too wonderful for him to know.

After Samuel was born, his mother Hannah stayed behind when the family went up to Shiloh for the yearly sacrifice. She would take the boy, she said, once he was weaned, and he would live there always. She nursed him at home until then, and afterwards she brought him, young as he was, to the house of the LORD and left him with Eli the priest. A child that age knows what it is to want milk and be refused. The child in David's psalm is past that and is with its mother. David says he is like that child, and he puts how it came about in the past tense: "I have calmed and quieted myself."

David's last line is for the whole nation. He turns from himself and tells Israel to put its hope in the LORD, now and for ever. Psalm 131 belongs to a run of fifteen psalms each headed 'A song of ascents', and the one before it could hardly be less calm. It opens with a cry out of the depths, and its writer waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning. Yet it turns to Israel with the same words, "Israel, put your hope in the LORD." Anyone going through the collection in order meets that line in two psalms running, first from someone shouting out of the depths and then from someone who has gone quiet.

keyVerses.text: My heart is not proud, LORD, my eyes are not haughty; I do not concern myself with great matters or things too wonderful for me.
But I have calmed and quieted myself, I am like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child I am content. Israel, put your hope in the LORD both now and forevermore.
Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know.

insights: Psalm 131 gives only one instruction, to hope in the LORD, and it comes in the last line. Everything before it is David describing himself to God, and he never turns it into an order for anyone else.

Some of what goes round in your head is yours to decide, and the psalm leaves that with you. The rest, the why and what other people will do, can be put down unanswered. Job never got his why, and the LORD still said he had spoken the truth about Him.

A child isn't weaned in an afternoon, so expect to put the same question down a good many times. If your mind runs like this most days, or it's costing you sleep, tell a doctor and somebody close to you. The child in the psalm has its mother there.
reflectQuestions: Which question have you gone over most this month that was never yours to settle?
What has helped you, in the past, to put a question down, even if only for an evening?
thematicGuides.practice: Within the next three days, pick a friend you can be honest with and ask them for five minutes. Tell them, as briefly as you can, the question you keep trying to work out and can't settle, and say you aren't after advice. Then ask them to read Psalm 131 aloud to you, which takes less than half a minute.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, there are things I keep trying to work out that were never mine to decide. I go over them most days and call it thinking it through. Why it happened and what they'll choose are Yours, and I'm leaving them with You, though I expect I'll have picked them up again by lunchtime. When I do, help me put them down again. And before any of it is settled, let me hope in You today. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Asaph, Who Envied the Arrogant
thematicGuides.hook: Asaph envied people who ignored God and stayed healthy and rich, until he went into the sanctuary and saw where their road ended.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Whom have I in heaven but you? And earth has nothing I desire besides you.
thematicGuides.intro: Someone you know has no time for God, bends whatever rule is in the way, and is doing very well on it. There's a new car on the drive and they haven't been ill in years. You've tried to do right, and this month you're putting off the dentist because of the bill. You start to think it has all been for nothing. Psalm 73 says that thought out loud. It carries the name of Asaph, the chief of the musicians David appointed to praise the LORD before the ark.
story: Asaph's first line is that God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. His second begins with himself. His feet had almost slipped, he says, and the cause he gives is envy. He had seen how the wicked prosper. They have no struggles, and their bodies are healthy and strong. The burdens other people carry pass them by. They wear pride like a necklace, their mouths lay claim to heaven, and they ask how God would know. Always free of care, they go on amassing wealth.

The conclusion Asaph came to was this: "Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure." His own days were full of affliction, and every morning brought new punishments. He never spoke out like that, he adds, because it would have betrayed God's children. Trying to understand it troubled him deeply. Then he went into the sanctuary of God. He doesn't say what he saw or heard there, only that he then understood where the people he envied were heading. The picture he began with changes sides. At the start the feet about to slip were his. Now he tells God that they are the ones set on slippery ground. Their ease ends suddenly, in ruin, and is gone like a dream when the sleeper wakes.

With his heart grieved and his spirit embittered, Asaph was by his own account senseless and ignorant, a brute beast before God. Then he says to God, "Yet I am always with you; you hold me by my right hand." Asaph was a Levite, one of the tribe given no territory of its own. Deuteronomy says of them that "the LORD is their inheritance." When he calls God his portion for ever, he is claiming what his tribe was told it had from the start. He claims none of what the arrogant have, and allows that his own flesh and heart may fail.

keyVerses.text: But as for me, my feet had almost slipped; I had nearly lost my foothold. For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
When I tried to understand all this, it troubled me deeply till I entered the sanctuary of God; then I understood their final destiny.
Whom have I in heaven but you? And earth has nothing I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

insights: Asaph ends the psalm owning nothing he didn't own at the start. God had hold of his right hand all the while he was adding up what other people had, and he says so with the word 'always'. Once he has seen where their road leads, what ends his envy is counting something he had left out.
Psalm 73 doesn't promise that living for God will pay in health or money, however long you wait. Asaph counts on God's hand now, His counsel, and glory afterwards.
reflectQuestions: When you look at the person whose easy life gets to you, what exactly is it of theirs that you want?
What do you already have from God that you've stopped counting?
thematicGuides.practice: Asaph says his envy came when he saw how well they were doing. Go a week without looking. Pick the one place you go to check on other people's good fortune, whether it's somebody's photos online or the property listings, and don't open it. Each time you'd have looked, tell God what Asaph told Him, that He holds you by your right hand.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I know roughly what their house is worth, because I looked it up. I've kept that kind of tally for as long as I've known them, and I've been angrier with You about it than I've admitted. Some days I think doing right has got me nothing, and I'm saying so to You, as Asaph did. You've had hold of my right hand all this while and I left that out of the sum. If my health and my money never match theirs, be my portion, and let me find it good to be near You. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Whitewash on a Flimsy Wall
thematicGuides.hook: God gave two pictures of prophets saying 'Peace' when there was none, and both fit a family where everyone says it's fine.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: They dress the wound of my people as though it were not serious. 'Peace, peace,' they say, when there is no peace.
thematicGuides.intro: In some families something happened, and the rule since has been that nobody mentions it. Everyone says it's fine. You say it too, because it keeps things calm and you can't see what else to do. The Bible's hardest words about saying 'peace' when there is none were spoken about a nation, Judah in the years before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem. A family is a long way from that. Even so, the two pictures those chapters use, a wound dressed as if it were nothing and a weak wall painted white, need very little translating.
story: Jeremiah preached in Jerusalem in the decades before the city fell. God told him an army was coming from the north, while the other prophets, and the priests, said the opposite. In Jeremiah 6 God says that everyone was greedy for gain, and that prophets and priests alike dealt in deceit. They dressed the wound of the nation He calls 'my people' as if it hardly mattered. Their word was 'Peace', said twice over, and God adds that these men didn't even know how to blush. Earlier in the chapter He has said that Jerusalem's sickness and wounds are always before Him.

Ezekiel was a priest living among the exiles in Babylon. God sent him to speak against prophets who prophesied out of their own imagination and saw visions of peace for Jerusalem. They had never gone up to the breaches in the wall to repair them, God says. When someone put up a flimsy wall, they covered it with whitewash. Rain would come in torrents, with hailstones and violent winds. The wall would fall, and people would ask the men who painted it, "Where is the whitewash you covered it with?" Not many years later the Babylonian army broke through the real wall of Jerusalem.

Isaiah 57 has the doubled word too, and there God is the one saying it. He describes Himself as living in a high and holy place and also with whoever is contrite and lowly in spirit, crushed and sorry. His people's sinful greed, the fault Jeremiah named, enraged Him. He punished them, and they kept on in their own way. Then He says He has seen their ways and will heal them. Only after that come the words "Peace, peace, to those far and near," followed at once by a second promise to heal.

keyVerses.text: They dress the wound of my people as though it were not serious. 'Peace, peace,' they say, when there is no peace.

Because they lead my people astray, saying, 'Peace,' when there is no peace, and because, when a flimsy wall is built, they cover it with whitewash, therefore tell those who cover it with whitewash that it is going to fall.

'I have seen their ways, but I will heal them; I will guide them and restore comfort to Israel's mourners, creating praise on their lips. Peace, peace, to those far and near,' says the LORD. 'And I will heal them.'

insights: In all three passages God is the one who refuses to call it nothing. In Ezekiel He adds that He never sent the prophets who did. If something was done to you and you were told it didn't matter, He has not agreed.

In Isaiah 57 God says He has seen His people's ways before He says 'Peace'. Keeping quiet and keeping the peace are different things. Quiet can keep a house calm, and sometimes it keeps a person safe, but where God says 'Peace' here, healing comes with it.

Telling the truth to God, and to one trusted person outside the family, is a step on its own. Nothing here obliges you to raise it with the family, and for some people that wouldn't be safe. If what happened was abuse, or anyone is still at risk, make that person someone who can act, such as a doctor, a counsellor or the police.
reflectQuestions: If you dropped the word 'fine' when you talk to God about your family, what would you say to Him in its place?
What would a person need to be like for you to trust them with the true account of what happened?
thematicGuides.practice: Once you're alone tonight, write one sentence that says what happened, the sentence nobody at home says. Make it as plain as you can manage, and leave off the part about it being fine now. Read it aloud to God, then read Isaiah 57:18-19 aloud after it. Nobody else needs to see it. Keep the paper or destroy it, whichever is safer.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I've said 'it's fine' so often that it comes out before I've thought. It isn't fine, and You've seen all of it, including the parts I leave out even when I'm on my own. Here is the true version, in the plainest words I have. I don't know yet what to do about it, and I'm not ready to say it to them. I'm asking for Your kind of peace, the kind that heals, and for one person I can safely tell. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Biting and Devouring Each Other
thematicGuides.hook: Eight of the fifteen acts of the flesh Paul lists are ways of falling out, and peace is in his other list, as fruit.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit. Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying each other.
thematicGuides.intro: Paul wrote to the churches of Galatia in the middle of a row. Some people were insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised, the churches were in confusion, and at one point Paul reached for words you would use of animals. If you bite and devour each other, he warned, you will be destroyed by each other. You probably know a quieter version. The people you're meant to be closest to, at church or round your own table, snipe at one another, and sometimes you join in. The second half of Galatians 5 is mostly about that.
story: Paul has spent most of the letter insisting that the Galatians are free, with no need to be circumcised to belong to God's people. Now he warns them against using that freedom to indulge the flesh, and says it is for serving one another humbly in love. The whole law, he tells them, is fulfilled in keeping one command, and the one he picks is the second half of a sentence in Leviticus 19: "Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against anyone among your people, but love your neighbor as yourself."

Further on in Galatians 5, Paul lists what he calls the acts of the flesh, and says they are obvious. He names fifteen. The list opens with sexual immorality and closes with drunkenness and orgies. In between, after idolatry and witchcraft, sit eight in a row that are all ways of falling out: hatred, discord, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, dissensions, factions and envy. A church could avoid everything at the two ends of that list and be living in the middle of it. Then comes a warning Paul says he has given them before, that those who live like this will not inherit the kingdom of God. It's a hard sentence, and he attaches it to the whole list, the quarrelling included.

Paul called his first list the acts of the flesh. He calls the second the fruit of the Spirit, and there are nine things in it. Peace comes third, after love and joy, with forbearance and kindness next and gentleness and self-control at the end. Then he asks them to keep in step with the Spirit, and in that sentence the 'you' he has used ever since telling them they were called to be free becomes 'us'. He includes himself. He is still saying 'us' in the last line of the chapter, about not becoming conceited, provoking and envying each other.

keyVerses.text: For the entire law is fulfilled in keeping this one command: 'Love your neighbor as yourself.' If you bite and devour each other, watch out or you will be destroyed by each other.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit. Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying each other.

insights: Paul files provoking and envying under conceit, and four verses on he tells each of them to test their own actions "without comparing themselves to someone else." Both habits start with comparing. Provoking is usually aimed at someone you feel ahead of, and envy at someone who seems ahead of you.

Deciding to be more peaceable rarely lasts, and Paul's choice of the word fruit suggests why. Peace grows, along with forbearance and self-control, in people who keep in step with the Spirit. Your part is the next step, such as the remark you leave out or the message you don't forward.
reflectQuestions: Think of the last sharp thing you said about someone at church or at home. What were you hoping it would do for you?
What is it about the person you most often snipe at that makes them hard for you to serve?
thematicGuides.practice: This Sunday, or at the next meal if the sniping is at home, give one thing of your own to the person you most often snipe at. Keep it small and ordinary, such as a coffee you've bought them or a book you've finished and think they'd like. Hand it over yourself, with no joke attached, and don't tell anyone else you did it. Before either of his lists, Paul tells the Galatians to serve one another humbly in love.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I join in. Some of it is the others, but I know which remark of mine got the laugh last week, and who it was aimed at. I've tried being more peaceable by gritting my teeth, and it has never lasted more than a few days. Grow in me what I can't force, and keep me in step with Your Spirit through the next conversation, the one where I'll want to say it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Rehoboam and the Advice He Didn't Want
thematicGuides.hook: Rehoboam asked two groups how to answer his people, and at forty-one he took the advice of the men he'd grown up with.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: If today you will be a servant to these people and serve them and give them a favorable answer, they will always be your servants.
thematicGuides.intro: The standard advice to anyone newly in charge is to start firm. Let people see early that you can't be pushed, since it's easier to ease off later than to tighten up. There's sense in it, and it's probably what your friends will tell you. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, was given a far harsher version of it at the start of his reign, and the opposite advice as well. He had three days to choose between them.
story: Rehoboam was forty-one, as 1 Kings 14 records, when all Israel gathered at Shechem to make him king. The people came with a request. Solomon had put a heavy yoke on them, and if his son would lighten the harsh labour, they would serve him. Rehoboam sent them away for three days and went to the elders who had served his father, the king the people were complaining about. They told him to serve the people that day and give them the answer they wanted, and they would be his servants for good.

Kings says Rehoboam turned the elders down before it says he asked anyone else. He "rejected the advice the elders gave him and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and were serving him." His question had changed too. He had asked the elders, "How would you advise me to answer these people?" To his friends it was "How should we answer these people". They told him to say that his little finger was thicker than his father's waist, and that where Solomon had used whips he would use scorpions.

Three days later the people came back and the king answered them harshly, in his friends' words. Israel replied that they had no share in David, and went home. Rehoboam sent out Adoniram, who was in charge of forced labour, to people whose complaint had been harsh labour, and they stoned him to death. The king got into his chariot and escaped to Jerusalem. Israel made Jeroboam king, and only the tribe of Judah stayed loyal to David's house. Kings says this turn of events was from the LORD, who had told Jeroboam through a prophet that it was coming. Two verses earlier it records, for the second time, that Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders.

keyVerses.text: If today you will be a servant to these people and serve them and give them a favorable answer, they will always be your servants.

The king answered the people harshly. Rejecting the advice given him by the elders, he followed the advice of the young men and said, 'My father made your yoke heavy; I will make it even heavier. My father scourged you with whips; I will scourge you with scorpions.'
The way of fools seems right to them, but the wise listen to advice.

insights: Rehoboam did ask. He took three days and consulted two groups. But he had turned the first answer down before he asked for the second, and once you know which answer you'll accept, asking more people only finds out who agrees with you.

The elders had served Solomon, and they told his son to lighten what Solomon had laid on the people. The friends worked for Rehoboam, and their answer made him a bigger man than his father. It's worth asking what it would cost any adviser of yours to tell you something you didn't want to hear.

Proverbs has Solomon's name in its first line, and it says the wise listen to advice. Growing up in the house those sayings came from didn't make Rehoboam a listener. It's an easy proverb to agree with until the day the advice is unwelcome.
reflectQuestions: Think of a decision you asked more than one person about. What was it about the advice you took that made you take it?
What would the people you now lead say about how you've started, if saying it cost them nothing?
thematicGuides.practice: Give your first conversation tomorrow morning to someone who knew the work before you did, whoever had the job last or has been there longest. Find them before you speak to the people you'd usually talk a decision over with, or ring them if they've moved on. Ask what they'd advise about one thing you haven't announced yet. Say their answer back to them so you know you've heard it, and leave it a day before you decide whether you like it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, send me someone who will tell me what I least want to hear, and keep me from brushing it off. I'm newly in charge and afraid of looking weak. I want people to say I'm tougher than whoever did this before me. When I ask for advice I already know which answer I'm hoping for, and I ask the people most likely to give it. Where I've already answered someone harshly to make a point, show me how to put it right. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Timothy, Too Young to Be Taken Seriously
thematicGuides.hook: After years of being sent to difficult churches, Timothy could still be looked down on for his age, and Paul told him what to do.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Don't let anyone look down on you because you are young, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith and in purity.
thematicGuides.intro: When you're the youngest in the room, both obvious responses make it worse. Push, and you confirm what they already think about people your age. Go quiet, and nobody finds out whether you had anything to say. Timothy was Paul's younger co-worker, trusted early with work Paul couldn't do himself, yet Paul could see that a church might write him off. He wrote about it twice, once to the church at Corinth and once to Timothy.
story: Paul, Silas and Timothy took the gospel to Thessalonica, and the visit ended in a riot, with Paul and Silas sent away by night. Paul tried to go back and was prevented. He was afraid the new church's faith had given way, and when he couldn't bear it any longer he sent Timothy, accepting that he'd be left in Athens without him. So Timothy went back into a city Paul had been hurried out of, to strengthen and encourage people who were being persecuted. He returned with good news about their faith and love.

A few years later Paul sent Timothy to Corinth, to a church where, by Paul's own account, some had become arrogant. Among the travel plans in the final chapter of 1 Corinthians, he tells them how to receive him. They must "see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you". No one is to treat him with contempt. Paul doesn't say what he expected to go wrong, and he doesn't mention Timothy's age. He gives one reason, that Timothy "is carrying on the work of the Lord, just as I am."

By the time Paul wrote 1 Timothy, Timothy had worked with him for years and was in Ephesus, left there to command certain people to stop teaching false doctrines. His age could still be held against him, and Paul wrote to him about it directly. He told Timothy not to neglect the gift he was given when the body of elders laid their hands on him. Nobody was to look down on him for being young, and his part in that was to set an example and keep at the work until everyone could see his progress. The next chapter opens with how he was to correct someone older. "Do not rebuke an older man harshly, but exhort him as if he were your father."

keyVerses.text: We sent Timothy, who is our brother and co-worker in God's service in spreading the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith.
Don't let anyone look down on you because you are young, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith and in purity.
Be diligent in these matters; give yourself wholly to them, so that everyone may see your progress.

insights: Paul was willing to ask a church for respect on Timothy's behalf, but he didn't tell Timothy to ask for it. Every instruction he gives him in 1 Timothy 4 is about what Timothy himself does, and all of them are to be done now, while he's young. The passage opens, "Command and teach these things."

Paul wanted everyone to see Timothy's progress, and progress is only seen by people who were watching before you'd made any. So the ones you want to take you seriously will be looking on while you're still not much good at it. It's slow, too. Years after going back into Thessalonica when Paul couldn't, Timothy could still be looked down on for being young.

If you're one of the people a newcomer is being sent to, notice who Paul wrote to in 1 Corinthians 16. Making sure Timothy had nothing to fear was the job of the church receiving him, and Paul told them so.
reflectQuestions: Paul names speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. Which of these have the people around you had least chance to see in you?
When someone last talked over you or waved away what you said, what did you do in the hour afterwards?
thematicGuides.practice: Once a day for a week, finish one thing you've been asked to do before anyone has to chase you for it, and say nothing about having done it. It can be small, like the reply you owe or the washing-up after the meeting. Don't expect one week to change how you're treated.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I'm sick of being talked over. I've rehearsed speeches that would put them in their place, and I've sat saying nothing and called it humility, and neither has helped. Give me real work and help me do it well where people can see. I'd like this to be quicker than it's going to be. Thank You for anyone who has spoken up for me when I wasn't in the room. And when I'm the older one, let me see to it that anyone younger has nothing to fear from me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Moses Did Not Get to Finish
thematicGuides.hook: Moses pleaded to cross the Jordan and was refused, and with the refusal came a last job, to get Joshua ready to go on without him.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But commission Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he will lead this people across and will cause them to inherit the land that you will see.
thematicGuides.intro: Deuteronomy's last chapter has a note on Moses's health. When he died at a hundred and twenty, "his eyes were not weak nor his strength gone." Handing over a business or a role you gave years to is hard when the work isn't finished, and harder if you still have the strength for it. Moses was stopped on the east side of the Jordan, in sight of the land he had spent forty years leading Israel towards, and another man took them in.
story: Not long before he died, Moses told all Israel about a prayer of his that God had refused. He had pleaded to go over and see the good land beyond the Jordan. As Moses tells it, the LORD was angry with him because of the people, and Numbers adds that he and Aaron had disobeyed God at the waters of Meribah. The answer was, "That is enough," with an order not to raise the matter again. He could climb Pisgah and look at the land, and that was all. God went straight on to Joshua, who would lead the people over. Moses was to commission him, and to encourage and strengthen him.

Numbers records what Moses said on being told he would see the land and then die. He asked the LORD to appoint someone over the community, so that the people wouldn't be left like sheep with no shepherd. He put no name forward, though Joshua had been his aide since youth. God named Joshua. Moses was to stand him before the priest and the whole assembly and give him some of his own authority, so that the community would obey him. Moses did so. He had been told to lay his hand on Joshua, and Numbers says he laid his hands on him.

Moses had been told to encourage Joshua, and he did it in front of all Israel. He told him to be strong and courageous, because he would go with this people into the land and the LORD Himself would go before him. Then Moses climbed Mount Nebo, and the LORD showed him the whole land, from Gilead to Dan and as far as the Mediterranean Sea. He was told, "I have let you see it with your eyes, but you will not cross over into it." He died there in Moab, and nobody knows where his grave is. Deuteronomy says the Israelites listened to Joshua, and traces it back to Moses having laid his hands on him.

keyVerses.text: Look at the land with your own eyes, since you are not going to cross this Jordan. But commission Joshua, and encourage and strengthen him, for he will lead this people across and will cause them to inherit the land that you will see.

May the LORD, the God who gives breath to all living things, appoint someone over this community to go out and come in before them, one who will lead them out and bring them in, so the LORD's people will not be like sheep without a shepherd.
Now Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. So the Israelites listened to him and did what the LORD had commanded Moses.
