insights: In Deuteronomy 1 and again in Deuteronomy 3, when Moses tells Israel about the refusal, an instruction follows at once, and both times the instruction is about Joshua. Getting Joshua ready was part of what Moses was to do with the time he had left.

Moses was kept out for something he had done himself, and the text names it. Nothing in these chapters says your work is unfinished because of something you did. Work that takes years is nearly always handed on part-done, because it outlasts one person's turn.
The handover was done in front of everyone, while Moses still had his strength and his authority to give. A successor you back only in private has to win that hearing alone, after you've gone.
reflectQuestions: Which unfinished part of the work is hardest for you to leave in someone else's hands?
What does the person who will carry this on most need to hear from you while you are still there to say it?
thematicGuides.practice: Sit down this week with whoever is taking over from you, at the shop or on the committee. Tell them one specific thing you've seen in them that makes you think they can do it, and ask what they need from you before you step back. If nobody has been named yet, go to whoever will make that choice and ask them to appoint someone, as Moses did.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, for the years I was given at this, thank You. I wanted to see it through, and I've gone on asking You to let me stay. If Your answer is that it's enough, help me to hear that without deciding I've failed. I half hope things wobble once I've gone, so that people notice, and I'm not proud of it. Look after the work, and the one who has it now. It was Yours before it was mine. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Paul Could Have Pulled Rank
thematicGuides.hook: Paul tells the Thessalonians he could have given them orders, then compares himself to a child, a mother and a father.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Just as a nursing mother cares for her children, so we cared for you. Because we loved you so much, we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God but our lives as well.
thematicGuides.intro: Somebody asks why the hall has to be set out your way, or why they have to be in by ten, and you hear yourself say that you're the one in charge. It works, in that the chairs get moved, and you may have every right to say it. Paul had more right than most. He was an apostle of Christ, and in his first letter to the church at Thessalonica he mentions that he could have done the same. Then he reminds them what he did with his time there.
story: Paul and Silas arrived in Thessalonica from Philippi, where they had been beaten with rods and put in the stocks. With Timothy, they preached in the face of strong opposition and a church began. Writing to it afterwards, Paul goes back over how the three of them behaved, and six times in twelve verses he appeals to what the Thessalonians themselves know, remember or saw for themselves. They never used flattery or put on a mask to cover up greed, and they weren't looking for praise from anyone. He adds that as apostles of Christ they could have asserted their authority.

In Thessalonica Paul and his companions paid their own way. They worked night and day so as not to be a burden to anyone while they preached, and in his second letter to the church Paul says they never ate anyone's food without paying for it. They had a right to be supported and didn't use it, so that the Thessalonians would have a model to imitate. Looking back on how they had lived among these people, Paul says they were like young children, and like a mother nursing her own.

Paul says they dealt with each of the Thessalonians as a father deals with his own children. The stay was cut short. He and Silas were forced out of the city, and the church they left was new and already suffering at the hands of its own people. A few verses after comparing himself to their father, Paul writes that being separated from them left him "orphaned". When news of the church reached him at last, it was that they were standing firm, had pleasant memories of him and longed to see him.

keyVerses.text: We were not looking for praise from people, not from you or anyone else, even though as apostles of Christ we could have asserted our authority.

Instead, we were like young children among you. Just as a nursing mother cares for her children, so we cared for you. Because we loved you so much, we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God but our lives as well.
For you know that we dealt with each of you as a father deals with his own children, encouraging, comforting and urging you to live lives worthy of God, who calls you into his kingdom and glory.

insights: Paul was forced out of Thessalonica and the church stood firm without him. An order tends to hold for as long as the person who gave it is standing there. These people had something else to go on. Paul could appeal six times to what they already knew of how he lived, and the letter says they became imitators of him and of the Lord.

Paul still asked things of them. The father he compares himself to urges his children, and later in this letter Paul reminds them of instructions he gave by the authority of the Lord Jesus. He took the slow way and dealt with each of them, when telling all of them at once would have been quicker.

Years later Paul wrote to a man named Philemon, "although in Christ I could be bold and order you to do what you ought to do, yet I prefer to appeal to you on the basis of love." He wanted what Philemon did to be voluntary and not forced.
reflectQuestions: What did the person whose lead you've followed most willingly do that made you willing?
What have the people you're responsible for seen of your life apart from the times you were telling them what to do?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick one person you're in charge of, a child or someone on your team, and this week spend an hour doing their job alongside them, at their pace and without correcting anything. Stack the chairs with them, or sit through the homework. If they ask why you're there, say you wanted to see what their end of it is like.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I reach for 'because I said so' when I'm short of patience, mostly because explaining would take time I'm not willing to spend. Help me not to lead with the authority You've given me. There's at least one person I've only ever given orders to, and I don't know what their days are like. Help me find out. And when there's a hard thing to say, let me say it to the one who needs to hear it, and not to the whole room. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Naaman Wanted Something More Impressive
thematicGuides.hook: A general with leprosy was told to wash in the Jordan, and was so insulted that he nearly went home without doing it.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: My father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it? How much more, then, when he tells you, 'Wash and be cleansed'!
thematicGuides.intro: You've been asking God to step in, and what you've had back so far is advice. Someone at church said the obvious thing, which you'd already thought of and set aside. None of it feels much like an answer to prayer. In 2 Kings 5 a general arrived for his cure with a fortune in silver, and a messenger came out and told him to go and wash.
story: Naaman commanded the army of Aram, the country later called Syria, and he had leprosy. A young Israelite girl, carried off by Aramean raiders, served his wife, and she spoke of a prophet in Samaria who would cure him. Naaman told his king, who wrote a letter and addressed it to the king of Israel, a man the girl had never mentioned. Naaman set out with the letter, ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold and ten sets of clothing. The king of Israel read it, tore his robes, and said Aram's king was trying to pick a quarrel. Elisha heard and sent word to have the man come to him.

Naaman drew up at the door of Elisha's house with his horses and chariots. Elisha sent a messenger out to tell him to wash seven times in the Jordan, and his flesh would be restored. Naaman was angry. He had expected the prophet himself, he said, with a prayer to his God and a hand waved over the spot. Damascus, he added, had the Abana and the Pharpar, better than all the waters of Israel. He went off in a rage, taking his leprosy and his silver with him.

His servants went to him. They called him 'my father' and pointed out that he'd have done some great thing if the prophet had asked for one, and this was only washing. Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, and his flesh became clean like a young boy's. He went back and this time stood in front of Elisha. "Now I know that there is no God in all the world except in Israel," he said. Elisha would take no gift. The man who had rated Israel's rivers below his own then asked for as much of Israel's earth as a pair of mules could carry, and said he would never again sacrifice to any god but the LORD.

keyVerses.text: She said to her mistress, 'If only my master would see the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy.'
But Naaman went away angry and said, 'I thought that he would surely come out to me and stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, wave his hand over the spot and cure me of my leprosy.'
And there were many in Israel with leprosy in the time of Elisha the prophet, yet not one of them was cleansed, only Naaman the Syrian.

insights: One king writes to the wrong man and the other tears his robes. The cure reaches Naaman through servants at every step. A captive girl starts it, a messenger delivers it and his own servants talk him into it, and not one of them is named.

Naaman would have done some great thing, as his servants said. He objected to a small thing, delivered without ceremony. He did have a prophet's word that it would work. The advice you've had carries no such promise, and it may be wrong. Being ordinary doesn't make it wrong.

Jesus mentioned Naaman once, in the synagogue at Nazareth where He grew up. People there were asking, "Isn't this Joseph's son?" No prophet is accepted in his home town, He told them, and He gave them Naaman, the foreigner who was cleansed when nobody with leprosy in Israel was. They drove Him out of the town.
reflectQuestions: Think of the plain advice you've heard a few times now about the thing you're praying over. What has kept you from taking it?
Naaman had the scene of his healing worked out before he reached Elisha's door. What does your own picture of God answering you look like?
thematicGuides.practice: Until this day next week, pray about the thing that's weighing on you without saying what the help should look like. Ask for help and stop there. If the same sensible suggestion comes round again in that time, take it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I had it worked out. You'd do something nobody could miss, and I'd have a story to tell. Instead I've had a suggestion from someone I wasn't planning to listen to, and I've been put out about it. I'd have done something hard for You. It's the small thing I keep refusing. I don't know whether it's Your answer, but don't let me turn it down for being plain. Help me go down to the water. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Blind Man Jesus Touched Twice
thematicGuides.hook: After Jesus first touched him, a blind man at Bethsaida saw people who looked like trees, and Jesus touched him again.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Once more Jesus put his hands on the man's eyes. Then his eyes were opened, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly.
thematicGuides.intro: Jesus took a blind man by the hand, led him out of Bethsaida and put His hands on him, and the man's sight came only part of the way back. Jesus touched him a second time. No other healing in the Gospels is told with a half-finished stage in the middle, and Mark places this one between two scenes of disciples who only half understand. If you do believe, and a good deal of it is still a blur, you may have decided it hasn't worked.
story: The disciples were crossing the lake with Jesus and had forgotten to bring bread. There was one loaf in the boat. When Jesus warned them about the yeast of the Pharisees and of Herod, they decided He meant the bread they hadn't brought. He asked whether they had eyes but failed to see, and then how many basketfuls of pieces they had picked up after the five loaves for the five thousand. Twelve, they said. And after the seven loaves for the four thousand, seven. They had the figures right. "Do you still not understand?" He said.

They came to Bethsaida, where some people brought a blind man and begged Jesus to touch him. Jesus took him by the hand and led him outside the village. He spat on the man's eyes, put His hands on him, and asked whether he could see anything. The man looked up and said, "I see people; they look like trees walking around." That was more than he had arrived with and a long way short of sight. Jesus put His hands on the man's eyes once more, and the man saw everything clearly. Jesus sent him home and told him not to go into the village.

On the way to the villages around Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked the disciples who people said He was, and then who they said He was. Peter answered that He was the Messiah, God's promised king. Then Jesus began to teach them that He must suffer, be rejected and killed, and after three days rise again. Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him. Jesus turned, looked at His disciples, and rebuked Peter: "Get behind me, Satan!" Peter could see who Jesus was. A Messiah who would be killed was still beyond him. Six days later Jesus took him, with James and John, up a high mountain.

keyVerses.text: Do you still not see or understand? Are your hearts hardened? Do you have eyes but fail to see, and ears but fail to hear?
When he had spit on the man's eyes and put his hands on him, Jesus asked, 'Do you see anything?' He looked up and said, 'I see people; they look like trees walking around.'
'But what about you?' he asked. 'Who do you say I am?' Peter answered, 'You are the Messiah.'

insights: The man could have said yes. It had half worked, and people had begged for it. He described the trees, and the second touch followed. You can tell Jesus what your own faith looks like without dressing it up.

Mark tells of two blind men healed, this one and Bartimaeus at Jericho two chapters on. On the road between them Jesus says three times that He'll be killed and rise, and each time the disciples miss it. He goes on teaching the same men.

This man saw clearly at the second touch. You may wait far longer, and the passage doesn't promise full sight in this life. Paul, who had met the risen Jesus, wrote that "now we see only a reflection as in a mirror", with face to face still to come. The first touch was real, though, and Jesus was still there after it.
reflectQuestions: If Jesus asked you today what He asked at Bethsaida, what would you say you can see now that you once couldn't?
What makes it hard to tell other Christians how much of your faith is still unclear?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, somewhere you won't be overheard, answer the question Jesus asked outside Bethsaida. Say out loud one thing about Him you're sure of, and then one thing that is still a blur, in the simplest words you have. Don't tidy either of them up. Then ask Him, in one sentence, to put His hands on you again.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, You asked the man what he could see, so here is my answer. I can see that You're real, and that I'm not who I was. A lot of the rest is trees walking. I've told other people I could see when I couldn't, because it sounded better, and I'm not going to do that with You. Put Your hands on me again, and keep me near You while it's still unclear. Thank You for not leaving after the first touch. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Bronze Snake They Kept Too Long
thematicGuides.hook: Moses made a bronze snake that saved lives, and centuries later a good king broke it because people were burning incense to it.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.
thematicGuides.intro: When God has done something for you that you can't explain away, it seems right to keep going back to it. You tell the story again, return to the place, and try to feel what you felt then. There's sense in that, and the Bible often tells people to remember. The trouble comes when the old day becomes the place you go to find God, and ordinary prayer feels thin beside it. Israel got into trouble of that kind over a bronze snake.
story: In the wilderness, on the way round Edom, the Israelites lost patience. They spoke against God and against Moses, and said they detested the food they had. The LORD sent venomous snakes among them, and many people died. The people came to Moses, admitted they had sinned, and asked him to pray that the LORD would take the snakes away. Moses prayed. The LORD told him to make a snake and set it up on a pole, where anyone who had been bitten could look at it and live. Moses made one out of bronze. From then on, anyone who was bitten and looked at the bronze snake lived.

Centuries later Hezekiah became king of Judah at twenty-five, and did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. He removed the hilltop shrines, smashed the sacred stones and cut down the poles set up to the goddess Asherah. He also broke into pieces a bronze snake, the one Moses had made. It had been kept all that time, and the Israelites had been burning incense to it. By then it had a name, Nehushtan. The next verse says Hezekiah trusted in the LORD.

One night Nicodemus, a member of the Jewish ruling council, came to talk with Jesus, and Jesus brought up the bronze snake. He went back to the day it was made: "Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up," so that everyone who believes may have eternal life in Him. Son of Man was His name for Himself. Days before the crucifixion, with a festival crowd around Him, He spoke again of being lifted up from the earth, and John adds that He said this to show the kind of death He was going to die.

keyVerses.text: The LORD said to Moses, 'Make a snake and put it up on a pole; anyone who is bitten can look at it and live.' So Moses made a bronze snake and put it up on a pole. Then when anyone was bitten by a snake and looked at the bronze snake, they lived.
He broke into pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, for up to that time the Israelites had been burning incense to it. (It was called Nehushtan.)
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.

insights: The snake Hezekiah broke was the real one. God had ordered it, and people had lived because of it. Something can come from God and still end up in the place that belongs to Him alone, and that includes a day you keep going back to.

The people asked for the snakes to be taken away, and were given somewhere to look once they'd been bitten. The bronze did nothing of itself. It worked because God had said to look there. When Jesus used the story, He put Himself in the snake's place, and where Numbers speaks of looking He spoke of believing. You can do that today, whether or not the old feeling comes back.

The Bible commands remembering, so the memory isn't the problem. The line Kings draws is at the incense. Thanking God for the day He helped you is remembering. Feeling you can't pray until that day comes back is nearer to what Israel was doing in front of the snake.
reflectQuestions: When you go back to the time God was most real to you, what are you hoping to find there?
What do you need from God this week that has nothing to do with that day?
thematicGuides.practice: One evening this week, write the memory down once, so you no longer have to rebuild it in your head. On one page, put the date as near as you can, where you were and what God did. Slip it into an envelope, and on the front finish the sentence 'Today I'm looking to You for'. Prop the envelope on a shelf, and when you reach for the old day, read the front first.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, thank You for what You did for me that day. I've never forgotten it. But I've been going back to it more than I've been coming to You. I've tried to work the feeling up again, as if You had stayed behind there and I had to go and fetch You. Today's troubles aren't the ones I had then, and I need You for these. Help me look to Jesus today. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Friend Paul Left Sick in Miletus
thematicGuides.hook: Paul saw the sick of Malta cured and later left his friend Trophimus ill in Miletus, and he blamed nobody's faith.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Erastus stayed in Corinth, and I left Trophimus sick in Miletus.
thematicGuides.intro: Praying for someone who is ill is hardest afterwards, if they don't get better. The person stays ill, or dies, and you go back over your prayers looking for the fault. Maybe you didn't believe enough as you prayed, and somebody may have hinted as much. Before you settle on that, look at how Paul wrote about two sick friends of his own.
story: Paul reached Malta as a prisoner, from a ship that had broken up in the surf. At the fire the islanders built, a viper fastened on his hand, and they said he must be a murderer. When he came to no harm they changed their minds and said he was a god. Publius, the chief official of the island, had an estate nearby and put the travellers up for three days. His father was in bed with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to see him, prayed, placed his hands on him and healed him. After that the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured.

Timothy had been one of Paul's helpers at Ephesus, the city where, Acts says, people took handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched Paul to the sick, and they were cured. Later Paul urged him to stay on there, and wrote to him as his true son in the faith. Among instructions about church elders he added a word about Timothy's own health. He was to stop drinking only water and take a little wine, because of his stomach and his frequent illnesses. So Timothy was often unwell, in the same city where those cloths had been taken to the sick.

Trophimus came from Ephesus, and travelled with Paul to Jerusalem. Some men there saw the two of them together in the city and assumed Paul had taken him, a Greek, into the temple, and the riot that followed ended with Paul in chains. As 2 Timothy closes, among greetings and news of where people are, this old companion gets half a line. Paul has left him sick in Miletus. That is all he says. There's no word of blame for Trophimus or for himself, and we aren't told whether Trophimus recovered.

keyVerses.text: God did extraordinary miracles through Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, and their illnesses were cured and the evil spirits left them.
Stop drinking only water, and use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.
Erastus stayed in Corinth, and I left Trophimus sick in Miletus.

insights: Paul, who had seen the sick cured, met Timothy's illnesses with a line of practical advice and set down Trophimus's as a piece of news. If the man who was there left it at that, it's wiser not to supply a reason yourself, or to accept one from somebody else.
A stranger on Malta was healed, and a friend who had shared Paul's travels was left ill. So someone else's recovery is no measure of how much the person you prayed for was loved, by you or by God.

Paul prayed for the sick, and he also expected Timothy to look after his stomach. If you or someone close to you is ill, keep asking God for healing, keep seeing the doctor, and tell one good friend how things really are.
reflectQuestions: Since the prayer wasn't answered as you asked, what have you been telling yourself about why?
What has someone said about your faith, or about the faith of the person who was ill, that has stayed with you?
thematicGuides.practice: Some day this week, go in person to someone who has been ill for months, or to someone who misses the person you prayed for. Ask first when would suit them. Take something you've made or bought, a loaf or a pot of soup, and stay half an hour. Offer no reasons for the illness. If they'd like you to pray, ask God straight out for what you both want.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I asked You to heal someone I love, and it didn't happen as I asked. Since then I've gone back through my prayers looking for the weak one. I've found it hard to be glad when other people's prayers are answered, and I'm not proud of that. Thank You that Trophimus is in Your book, still sick, with no blame beside his name. However things are now with the one I prayed for, I leave them in Your hands. Keep me praying for the sick. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jeremiah 29:11 and the Seventy Years
thematicGuides.hook: One prophet said the exiles would be home in two years, and the letter with Jeremiah 29:11 in it told them seventy.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: 'For I know the plans I have for you,' declares the LORD, 'plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.'
thematicGuides.intro: Jeremiah 29:11 begins with the word 'For', so it's finishing a thought, and the sentence before it has a number in it, seventy years. Both come from a letter Jeremiah sent to captives taken from Jerusalem to Babylon. People quote the verse as a promise that things will work out, which is hard to hear when they haven't. In the chapter before, a prophet called Hananiah had said those captives would be home within two years.
story: Jeremiah had been wearing a wooden yoke, a sign that Judah would have to serve the king of Babylon. In the temple, in front of the priests and all the people, the prophet Hananiah announced in the LORD's name that within two years the exiles would be home. Jeremiah's first word in reply was Amen. He hoped the LORD would do it, he said, but a prophet who promises peace is known to be sent by the LORD only when his words come true. Hananiah took the yoke off Jeremiah's neck, broke it and said two years again, and Jeremiah went on his way. Later God sent him back to tell Hananiah, "The LORD has not sent you, yet you have persuaded this nation to trust in lies." Hananiah had spoken in the fifth month. He died in the seventh.

Jeremiah's letter went to Babylon with two of King Zedekiah's envoys, addressed to everyone Nebuchadnezzar had taken. It told them to build houses, plant gardens, see their children married, and pray for Babylon itself, because if it prospered so would they. It warned them about the prophets among them, who were prophesying lies in God's name, and gave their hearers a share of the blame, telling them, "Do not listen to the dreams you encourage them to have." One of those prophets, Shemaiah, wrote to the priest in charge of the temple to ask why Jeremiah hadn't been reprimanded. His summary of the letter was, "It will be a long time."

Jeremiah's letter told the exiles how long. When seventy years are completed for Babylon, God says, He will come and keep His good promise to bring them back, for He knows the plans He has for them, plans to prosper them and to give them hope and a future. That is said to all the exiles together, and seventy years was more than most of the adults listening had left. The letter adds that they will then call on God and pray, and He will listen. Decades later Daniel, taken to Babylon as a young man, read Jeremiah's seventy years and did just that, with fasting. Ezra says that when King Cyrus let the exiles go home, it was to fulfil the word the LORD had spoken through Jeremiah.

keyVerses.text: Seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you into exile. Pray to the LORD for it, because if it prospers, you too will prosper.

'When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will come to you and fulfill my good promise to bring you back to this place. For I know the plans I have for you,' declares the LORD, 'plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.'
Then you will call on me and come and pray to me, and I will listen to you. You will seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart.

insights: Verse 11 was a promise to a whole people about one homecoming, with a date on it. The plans it speaks of are God's, and His good plan for them included seventy years in Babylon. So a life that isn't going to plan is no proof that God means you harm.

Hananiah spoke in the temple, as a prophet, and even Jeremiah said Amen to the wish. How welcome a promise is tells you nothing about whether God made it. The exiles were given a number. You haven't been, so be wary of anyone who tells you in God's name when your trouble will end.
reflectQuestions: Where did you get the timetable for the thing you thought would be sorted out by now?
If you were to be where you are now for years, what good would you ask God to do there?
thematicGuides.practice: Every day for a week, pray one sentence for the place you'd most like to get out of, such as an office, a flat, a ward or a town. Name it and ask God to prosper it, the word the letter uses for Babylon. Do it when the kettle goes on. You can pray for a place and still leave it, and if it isn't safe for you there, leaving comes first.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've held Jeremiah 29:11 up to You like a receipt, as if You owed me the life I had planned. I would have believed Hananiah, because two years is what I'd have wanted to hear. You haven't told me how long this will go on. Help me pray for the place I'm in as well as praying to get out of it, and let me find You here before anything is settled. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Obadiah and the Brother Who Stood By
thematicGuides.hook: Edom kept its distance while Jerusalem was looted, and God called it violence against a brother.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: On the day you stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were like one of them.
thematicGuides.intro: A colleague is being pushed out by a manager who wants them gone. You've never much liked this colleague, speaking up would cost you, and so you keep your head down. When they finally leave you feel a small satisfaction you wouldn't admit to. Nobody could say you did anything. Obadiah, the shortest book in the Old Testament, is addressed to the nation of Edom, which began by watching while its brother Judah was invaded.
story: Edom and Judah were family. The Edomites came from Esau and Judah from his twin brother Jacob, and the law of Moses told Israel not to despise an Edomite, because they were related. Edom lived high in the hill country of Seir. In Obadiah's vision God says to it, "The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rocks and make your home on the heights." Edom has been telling itself that no one can bring it down. God answers that if it soared like an eagle and nested among the stars, He would bring it down from there.

The charge against Edom is violence against its brother Jacob, and the first thing listed under it is something Edom didn't do. On the day strangers carried off Judah's wealth and cast lots for Jerusalem, Edom stood aloof, and God tells it, "you were like one of them." Edom, the vision goes on, should not gloat over its brother or boast, should not march in through his gates and seize his wealth. It should not wait at the crossroads to cut down people running for their lives, or hand over the survivors. Psalm 137 remembers the Edomites on the day Jerusalem fell, calling for the city to be torn down to its foundations.

Seven times in three verses Obadiah says "in the day of", and each time it is the day of Judah's trouble. Then he announces another day, the day of the LORD, which is near for every nation. What Edom has done, he says, will be done to Edom. The nation that turned on its brother will be deceived by its own allies and trapped by people who eat its bread, and it won't see the trap. On Mount Zion, though, there will be deliverance. Jacob will possess his inheritance, and the kingdom, Obadiah says, will be the LORD's.

keyVerses.text: Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame; you will be destroyed forever. On the day you stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were like one of them.
You should not gloat over your brother in the day of his misfortune, nor rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their destruction, nor boast so much in the day of their trouble.
The day of the LORD is near for all nations. As you have done, it will be done to you; your deeds will return upon your own head.

insights: Obadiah's charges begin with the one who watched. Nobody was attacking Edom that day. It's charged as a brother who stood aloof and then gloated, so if someone hurt you and you were relieved when they were stopped, you're not the person this book is addressing.

On the first count Edom did nothing, and God files it under violence. From there the list runs through enjoying it to profiting from it. Hardly anyone sets out to hand over survivors. The private pleasure at seeing someone taken down comes early, and that's the easiest place to stop.

Obadiah gives Edom no way back, and it's hard reading if you see yourself in it. The rest of Scripture does give one. John writes that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just and will forgive us. Confessing this one starts with giving up 'I didn't do anything'.
reflectQuestions: What would it cost you to speak up for someone you can see being treated badly now?
Thinking of a time you stayed out of it, what were you protecting by keeping your distance?
thematicGuides.practice: Name one person you watched being treated badly and did nothing for. This week, speak to them, face to face if you can. Tell them you saw what happened and that you're sorry you kept out of it. Leave out the reasons, and don't ask them to tell you it's all right. If it's still going on, ask them what would help. If they've died, or you can't find them, say the same words to God and use their name.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I told myself it was none of my business. You saw that it was, and You saw the part of me that enjoyed watching. I never lifted a hand against anyone, and I've been hiding behind that. Forgive me for the distance I kept. Make me go to them and say so. The next time someone is being stripped of what is theirs in front of me, move me towards them before I've worked out what it will cost. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Nahum and the Fall of a Cruel City
thematicGuides.hook: Nahum is three chapters about one cruel empire being stopped, written for the people it had crushed.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The LORD is slow to anger but great in power; the LORD will not leave the guilty unpunished.
thematicGuides.intro: Someone has done real harm for years and nothing has happened to them. They've kept their good name, and the people they hurt have been told to move on. You may be one of those people, and you may have begun to wonder whether God has let it go. The prophet Nahum had one subject, Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian empire, and one audience, Judah, a country Assyria had overrun.
story: Assyria had taken Samaria after a three-year siege and deported the people of Israel. Later its king Sennacherib captured the fortified cities of Judah, and King Hezekiah paid him in silver from the temple and gold stripped from its doors. Nahum the Elkoshite's vision is about Nineveh, and it has a word for Judah. God says He will break Assyria's yoke from Judah's neck and tear their shackles away. Then Nahum points to the mountains, where a messenger is coming with good news of peace. Judah is told to celebrate its festivals and fulfil its vows, and that is the whole of its part.

An attacker advances on Nineveh in Nahum's vision. The river gates are thrown open and the palace collapses. The city empties like a pool draining away, and no one turns back when they're told to stop. Nahum calls it "the city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder, never without victims". His last words are for the king of Assyria. The king's shepherds are asleep, his people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them, and his wound is fatal. Everyone who hears the news claps their hands, "for who has not felt your endless cruelty?" The people clapping are the ones who had felt it.

Nahum describes God before he describes Nineveh, and he does it in words God had used about Himself to Moses on Mount Sinai. He is slow to anger, and He does not leave the guilty unpunished. Generations earlier Jonah had walked into Nineveh announcing that it would be overthrown, the Ninevites had turned from their evil ways, and God had relented. So the city Nahum speaks against had been warned once and spared once. In his vision the mountains quake, the rocks are shattered, and no one can withstand God's anger. The same God, he says, is good, a refuge in times of trouble, and cares for those who trust in Him.

keyVerses.text: Look, there on the mountains, the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace! Celebrate your festivals, Judah, and fulfill your vows. No more will the wicked invade you; they will be completely destroyed.
The LORD is slow to anger but great in power; the LORD will not leave the guilty unpunished. His way is in the whirlwind and the storm, and clouds are the dust of his feet.
The LORD is good, a refuge in times of trouble. He cares for those who trust in him.

insights: Slow to anger and unwilling to leave the guilty unpunished are two halves of one sentence about the same God. The slowness is what had once spared Nineveh itself, in Jonah's day.

Many of the people Assyria crushed never saw it fall. The Israelites deported from Samaria were long dead by then. You may not see the person who did the harm answer for it in this life. Nahum's claim is that God will not leave it unanswered.

Judah is given nothing to do to Nineveh. The people Assyria hurt may clap when it's over, but the judging is God's, which takes revenge out of your hands. Reporting a crime, or getting yourself to safety, isn't revenge, and nothing in Nahum tells you to keep quiet.
reflectQuestions: What wrong, done to you or to someone you love, are you still waiting to see answered?
Nahum calls the LORD slow to anger and, four verses later, a refuge in times of trouble. Which is harder for you to believe at the moment?
thematicGuides.practice: In daylight one day this week, sit on your doorstep, or at a window, where you can see the sky. Set a timer for five minutes and put the phone face down. Read Nahum 1:3 aloud, where the clouds are the dust of His feet, and tell God in one sentence the wrong you keep coming back to. Then keep still and look up until the timer goes. If you start planning how to get your own back, hand that part to Him. Finish with Nahum 1:7. If the harm is still going on, tell someone who can help stop it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, You are the judge of this and I am not. You know what was done and who did it, and that they seem to have got away with it. Some days I want it stopped and some days I want them to suffer, and You can tell those apart better than I can. I've taken Your slowness for not caring. Be my refuge until You act, and show me what is mine to do. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Peter on Why Jesus Hasn't Come Back Yet
thematicGuides.hook: Peter wrote down what people would say about the promise that Jesus will return, and answered that the delay is patience.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise, as some understand slowness. Instead he is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance.
thematicGuides.intro: Shortly before he died, Peter wrote down a question he expected his readers to hear: "Where is this 'coming' he promised?" The wait for Jesus to return had then lasted a few decades. It's now about two thousand years. If you've wondered, perhaps without saying so in church, whether He is still coming, Peter had the question on paper long before you asked it, and he gave an answer.
story: Peter was on the Mount of Olives the day Jesus was taken up. The disciples had just asked Him whether He was now going to restore the kingdom to Israel, and been told, "It is not for you to know the times or dates the Father has set by his own authority." A cloud hid Him, and two men in white said He would come back the same way they had seen Him go. Years later Peter's second letter warns that scoffers will come, following their own evil desires, and ask where the promised coming has got to. Our ancestors have died, they will say, and everything goes on as it always has. They deliberately forget, he replies, that the world was once destroyed by a flood.

With the Lord a thousand years are like a day, and a day like a thousand years. The thought is from Psalm 90, a prayer of Moses, and Peter asks the readers of his second letter, whom he calls dear friends four times in its last chapter, not to forget it. What some call slowness, he writes, is the Lord being patient, and his word for the people the Lord is patient with is 'you'. The Lord wants no one to perish and everyone to come to repentance, which means turning back to Him. No date is given. The Lord's patience, he says again, means salvation.

Jesus once told His disciples about the owner of a house who wouldn't have let it be broken into if he had known what hour the thief was coming, and said the Son of Man would come at an hour they didn't expect. Peter, Luke records, asked whether the parable was meant for them or for everyone. In his letter the thief is back. The day of the Lord will come "like a thief", and this time the question is Peter's own, "what kind of people ought you to be?" People who live holy lives, he answers, who look forward to a new heaven and a new earth and make every effort to be found at peace with God. Peter wrote all this expecting to die before the day came.

keyVerses.text: But do not forget this one thing, dear friends: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.
The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise, as some understand slowness. Instead he is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance.

But in keeping with his promise we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells. So then, dear friends, since you are looking forward to this, make every effort to be found spotless, blameless and at peace with him.

insights: Everyone who has turned to God since Peter wrote has done so inside the delay. Had Jesus returned when the first scoffers thought He was overdue, there would have been no time for you. The wait that makes the promise look doubtful is how you came to hear it.

The scoffers deliberately forget, Peter says, and then he asks his own friends not to forget. So he knows believers lose hold of this too, and wondering about it doesn't put you with the scoffers. He calls both his letters reminders.

The picture of a thief rules out a date. Christians have long disagreed about how the last things will unfold, and you can leave that open. Peter's question for the meantime is what kind of person you ought to be.
reflectQuestions: Peter says the Lord's patience is with you. What has that patience given you time for so far?
What do you honestly expect when you hear that Jesus will come again?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick the one thing you'd least like the Lord to find you in the middle of, such as the scrolling after midnight or the way you talk about one particular person, and go without it from today until this time next week. If you slip, read 2 Peter 3:9 aloud and start the day again.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, two thousand years is a long time, and some days I think the people who laugh at this have a point. I say in church that You will come again, and then I plan as though You won't. The delay suits me more than I like to admit, because nothing of mine has to change yet. Thank You that it had room in it for me. Use the time for the people I love who haven't turned to You yet, and make me ready. Come when You choose. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Lord, If You Had Been Here
thematicGuides.hook: Two sisters each told Jesus their brother would not have died if He had been there, and He rebuked neither.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Jesus wept. Then the Jews said, 'See how he loved him!'
thematicGuides.intro: When someone dies after you've prayed for them, people tend to assume there's nothing more to say to God about it. He knows best, they say, meaning it kindly. Telling Him you think He let you down sounds like the start of losing your faith, so you keep quiet. In John 11 two sisters sent word to Jesus that their brother was ill, and had buried him by the time He came. Each met Him with the same sentence about where He had been.
story: Lazarus and his sisters, Martha and Mary, lived in Bethany, less than two miles from Jerusalem. When he fell ill they sent a message to Jesus, who was staying across the Jordan. All the message said was, "Lord, the one you love is sick." John writes that Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus, and then that when He heard Lazarus was sick He stayed where He was two more days. By the time He reached Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days.

Martha heard that Jesus was coming and went out to meet Him, while Mary stayed at home. Martha's first words to Him were that if He had been there, her brother would not have died. Even now, she went on, God would give Him whatever He asked. Jesus told her that her brother would rise again. "I know he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day," she said. He answered that He Himself is the resurrection and the life, and asked whether she believed it. She did. He was the Messiah, she told Him, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.

Martha went back and told Mary the Teacher was asking for her. Mary got up quickly and went, and the mourners in the house followed. She found Jesus still outside the village, fell at His feet, and said the very sentence her sister had said. She added nothing to it. When Jesus saw her weeping, and the people with her weeping too, He was deeply moved and troubled. He asked, "Where have you laid him?" They told Him to come and see, and He wept. Then He went on to the tomb and called Lazarus out of it alive.

keyVerses.text: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So when he heard that Lazarus was sick, he stayed where he was two more days.
'Lord,' Martha said to Jesus, 'if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But I know that even now God will give you whatever you ask.'
Jesus said to her, 'I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die; and whoever lives by believing in me will never die. Do you believe this?'

insights: The same sentence got two different answers. Martha said it and went on to talk about what she knew, and Jesus gave her a promise to believe, that whoever believes in Him will live even though they die. Mary said it and wept, and He asked where the grave was and wept as well.

Psalm 22 opens with a complaint of the same kind, and on the cross Jesus prayed its first line Himself: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" If Jesus could ask His Father that, you can ask God where He was.

Martha and Mary had their brother back that day, and you have not been given back the person you lost. You do have the promise He gave Martha. He wept after giving it, so it was never meant to stop the hurting. The sisters grieved in a house full of people who had come to comfort them. If grief is keeping you from sleeping or coping, tell a friend and your doctor.
reflectQuestions: If you told God exactly where you think He was when it happened, what would your first sentence be?
Martha went out to meet Jesus, and Mary stayed in the house until He asked for her. What has your loss done to the way you approach God?
thematicGuides.practice: Do this tonight, somewhere you won't be overheard. Say Martha's sentence to God out loud, putting the name of the person you lost in place of her brother. Add whatever else is true, or add nothing, as Mary did. Then read John 11:33-35 and go to bed.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I asked You to step in and You didn't, not in time. If You had, I think the person I love would still be here, and I've been afraid to tell You so. I've nodded when people said God knows best, and gone home angry. I'm not asking You to explain it tonight. Keep hold of me while it hurts, and help me believe what Jesus told Martha about Himself. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Psalm That Ends in the Dark
thematicGuides.hook: Psalm 88 is a prayer that never cheers up, and it was kept in the Bible for anyone who can't either.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But I cry to you for help, LORD; in the morning my prayer comes before you.
thematicGuides.intro: Praying gets harder the longer you've been low, because you run out of hopeful things to say. Thanking God starts to feel like lying. Most prayers you hear, in church and in the Psalms, end on a brighter note, and you can come to think that until you manage that turn you aren't praying at all. Psalm 88 is eighteen verses spoken to God in which the writer never manages it.
story: The heading of Psalm 88 calls it a song, gives it to Heman the Ezrahite and marks it for the director of music. Its first line is its warmest. Heman calls the LORD the God who saves him, and cries out to Him day and night. After that he is overwhelmed with troubles, and his life is drawing near to death. He is counted among those who go down to the pit, like the dead "whom you remember no more". It is God, he says, who has put him in the lowest pit, and God whose anger lies heavily on him.

Heman's closest friends are gone. God has taken them from him, he says, and made him repulsive to them. His eyes are dim with grief, and still he calls to the LORD every day and spreads out his hands to Him. He names God's love once and His faithfulness once, in a single question, which asks whether either is declared among the dead. After one more question the next line begins with 'But'. He cries for help, and in the morning his prayer is in front of God again, asking why the LORD rejects him and hides His face.

Heman tells God, "From my youth I have suffered and been close to death." He has borne God's terrors and is in despair. He comes back to the friends and neighbours God has taken from him, and his last words are that darkness is his closest friend. Most psalms that begin with a cry for help turn before they finish. Psalm 13 asks God four times how long, and by its sixth verse it is singing. Psalm 88 ends lower than it began, and it went into Israel's songbook as it stood.

keyVerses.text: LORD, you are the God who saves me; day and night I cry out to you. May my prayer come before you; turn your ear to my cry.
But I cry to you for help, LORD; in the morning my prayer comes before you. Why, LORD, do you reject me and hide your face from me?
You have taken from me friend and neighbor, darkness is my closest friend.

insights: Heman says three times how often he prays: day and night, every day, in the morning. The darkness still hasn't lifted by the last verse, so nothing here suggests you'd be better if you prayed more. A low that lasts for months can be an illness, and seeing a doctor about it is no lack of faith.
Every line of the psalm is spoken to God. Heman blames Him and questions Him, and all the way through he says 'you'. What makes it a prayer is who it's said to.

Twice Heman tells God that his friends are gone, and both times he sets it down as a loss, alongside the rest. His loneliest words were handed to a director of music, for other people to sing. If there's anyone you can still reach, nothing in the psalm asks you to stay away from them.
reflectQuestions: What have you been leaving out of your prayers because it doesn't sound hopeful enough?
What makes it hard to tell the people closest to you how low you have been?
thematicGuides.practice: On a card, write the name of one person you could tell how long you've been low, a friend or somebody from church. Under it copy Psalm 88:13, and leave the card where you'll see it when you get up. This week, ring or message them and say you've been struggling and would like to talk. If you can't face it today, the card will be there in the morning, which is when Heman prayed. If you've had thoughts of ending your life, don't wait. Tell a doctor or a crisis line today.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I've run out of hopeful things to say to You, so I won't make any up. I'm tired in a way that sleep doesn't mend, and some days Your name is all I manage. Help me tell one other person how bad it has been. Heman told You that darkness was his closest friend, and You kept his prayer, so I'm trusting You'll take mine as it comes. I'm still talking to You, so hear me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: What Job's Friends Got Right
thematicGuides.hook: The best comfort Job's friends ever gave him came before any of them said a word.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was.
thematicGuides.intro: Before Job's three friends said any of the things they're remembered for, they sat on the ground beside him for a week and said nothing at all. If someone you care about has had terrible news and you've put off going because you don't know what to say, what the book of Job has to tell you comes as a relief.
story: Job had lost his herds, his servants and all ten of his children, and then his health. He was sitting among the ashes, scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, set out from their homes and met by arrangement to go and comfort him. When they saw him from a distance they could hardly recognise him. They wept aloud, tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads. Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights, and in all that time none of them spoke to him. It was Job who spoke first.

Job curses the day he was born, and Eliphaz is the first of his three friends to answer. He begins by asking whether Job will be impatient if someone ventures a word, and adds, "But who can keep from speaking?" Five verses on he asks who, being innocent, has ever perished. All three press the same case for chapter after chapter. Suffering like this must have a cause, they say, and the cause must be in Job, though the book opens by calling him blameless and upright. Bildad tells him his children sinned and paid the penalty. Job tells them he has heard many things like these, and calls all three "miserable comforters". If they were the ones suffering, he says, his mouth would encourage them.

The one consolation Job asks of his three friends is to be listened to carefully. He tells them to look at him and clap a hand over their mouths. They go on arguing, and at the end the LORD tells Eliphaz He is angry with him and his two friends, because they have not spoken the truth about Him. The last comforters in the book are Job's brothers and sisters and everyone who had known him before. They come to his house and eat with him, and each brings a piece of silver and a gold ring.

keyVerses.text: Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was.
If only you would be altogether silent! For you, that would be wisdom.
Listen carefully to my words; let this be the consolation you give me.

insights: If you go and can't think of a thing to say, you haven't failed. Job told his friends that their silence would have been wisdom, and the week they spent saying nothing is the one part of their visit nobody in the book complains about.

The friends' visit went wrong when they started explaining. They had a theory about why Job was suffering, and no way of knowing. God's verdict at the end falls on what they said. You're free to tell your own friend that you don't know why this has happened to them. It's true, and it's kinder than a guess.

Job didn't want silence for ever. He wanted to be listened to, and he said himself that words can bring relief when they encourage. So ask how they are and let them tell you, five times over if they need to.
reflectQuestions: When you were last in real trouble yourself, what is one thing somebody did or said that you still remember gratefully?
What are you most afraid of getting wrong if you go and sit with the person you have in mind?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick a day this week and go to the person you've been thinking of, having asked first when would suit them. Take something that asks nothing of them: soup in a tub they needn't return, or a loaf and some milk. Sit down, ask how today has been, and listen for as long as they want to talk. If you feel an explanation or a silver lining coming, keep it to yourself. For someone too far away to visit, post something and ring.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, there is one person on my mind, and they are carrying a great deal. Get me to their door this week. I've stayed away because I didn't know what to say, and I've been rehearsing lines that would mostly make me feel useful. I can't mend this for them and I can't explain it. Help me sit down, keep quiet and hear what they tell me, and stop me when I start to explain. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Tower That Fell in Siloam
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus refused to treat a massacre or a fallen tower as proof that the dead were worse than anyone else.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Those eighteen who died when the tower in Siloam fell on them, do you think they were more guilty than all the others living in Jerusalem? I tell you, no!
thematicGuides.intro: A neighbour's house is burgled, and the first thing people ask is whether they'd left a window open. We like bad things to have a reason, preferably one that was the victim's doing, because then it needn't happen to us. When the bad thing happens to you, the same habit turns round and goes through your own past for the cause. Some people once brought Jesus news of a massacre, and His reply went straight to that habit.
story: Some people in the crowd told Jesus about a group of Galileans. Pilate, the Roman governor, had killed them, and their blood had been mixed with their sacrifices. Jesus replied by asking whether they thought these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans because they suffered this way. He answered His own question with a flat no. Then He told the people who had brought the news, "But unless you repent, you too will all perish." To repent is to turn back to God.

Jesus had just been told about Galileans killed by Pilate, and He raised a second case Himself. Eighteen people had died in Jerusalem when the tower in Siloam fell on them. The first deaths were a governor's doing, and these, as far as Luke tells it, were nobody's. Jesus asked whether those eighteen were more guilty than everyone else living in the city. He gave the same no, and after it the same warning to His hearers. He never said why the tower fell, or why those people were the ones beneath it.

After speaking of the massacre and the tower, Jesus told a parable. A man had a fig tree growing in his vineyard. For three years he had looked for fruit on it and found none, and he told his gardener to cut it down. "Why should it use up the soil?" The gardener asked him to leave it alone for one more year. He would dig round it and feed it. If it bore fruit next year, good. If not, it could come down then. The parable ends there, on the gardener's request.

keyVerses.text: Jesus answered, 'Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans because they suffered this way? I tell you, no! But unless you repent, you too will all perish.'

Or those eighteen who died when the tower in Siloam fell on them, do you think they were more guilty than all the others living in Jerusalem? I tell you, no! But unless you repent, you too will all perish.
'Sir,' the man replied, 'leave it alone for one more year, and I'll dig around it and fertilize it. If it bears fruit next year, fine! If not, then cut it down.'

insights: Jesus takes one disaster that was a ruler's doing and one that just happened, and both times He refuses to say the dead were worse than anyone else. His no leaves room for trouble that does follow from wrongdoing. It rules out working backwards from a disaster to the guilt of the people it fell on.

Jesus leaves both disasters unexplained, and nobody else is in a position to hand you a reason for yours. The next person Luke shows Him with is a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years. Nobody can promise you her healing. You can see, though, that it was Jesus who called her over, and that He healed her without a word about anything she had done.

The warning to repent went to people talking about someone else's death, and it applies to everyone alike. If there are things you know you need to turn from, the gardener in the parable is asking for more time, and offering to do the digging himself. What you need to turn from and why the tower fell are two separate matters, and Jesus never joins them.
reflectQuestions: When you go back over your past looking for what you did to deserve this, where does your mind usually stop?
If you were given the year the gardener asked for, what would you most want to do with it?
thematicGuides.practice: Each evening for seven days, read Luke 13:4 aloud and carry on into verse 5 as far as "I tell you, no!" That is Jesus's answer to the idea that what happened proves you are worse than other people. Say those four words a second time and stop there. If the blame keeps coming back, tell a friend what you've been thinking, or a minister if you know one.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, since it happened I've been going back through my life looking for the thing I did. I have a list. I've done the same with other people's troubles, and felt a little safer each time. Jesus looked at people killed by a governor and by a falling tower and said they were no worse than anyone else. I want to hear that said about me. Show me what I do need to turn from, and thank You for time to do it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Naboth's Vineyard and the King's Seal
thematicGuides.hook: The elders of Naboth's own town condemned him in proper form, and God sent Elijah to call it murder.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: This is what the LORD says: Have you not murdered a man and seized his property?
thematicGuides.intro: Something that belonged to you or your family has gone to someone with more money and better connections, and nobody broke a rule doing it. The papers were signed, so there's nobody you can call a thief without sounding bitter. In 1 Kings 21 a vineyard changes hands by sealed letters and a public hearing, and the chapter records what God called it.
story: Naboth had a vineyard in Jezreel, close to the palace of Ahab, king of Israel. Ahab wanted the ground for a vegetable garden and offered a better vineyard or the price in money. Naboth told him, "The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my ancestors." God's law said the land was His and must not be sold permanently. Ahab went home, lay on his bed sulking and wouldn't eat. When his wife Jezebel asked why, he gave her Naboth's answer with the reason taken out, "I will not give you my vineyard." Jezebel said she would get it for him.

Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name, under his seal, to the elders and nobles of Naboth's own town. They were to proclaim a fast and seat Naboth in a prominent place, with two scoundrels opposite him to say he had cursed both God and the king, and then stone him. The law of Moses forbade cursing God or the ruler, and it required two or three witnesses before anyone was put to death. The letters ordered two. The elders did as they were told. Naboth was stoned outside the city, and word went back to Jezebel. She told Ahab to go and take the vineyard, and he got up and went.

The word of the LORD sent Elijah down to meet Ahab in Naboth's vineyard, where he had gone to take possession. Elijah was to charge him with murder and with seizing a man's property. Ahab had written no letter and thrown no stone, and the charges were addressed to him. "So you have found me, my enemy!" he said. Elijah announced disaster on Ahab's house. The king tore his clothes and fasted, and God put it off until his son's day. Years later a commander called Jehu, who had been riding behind Ahab when the prophecy was given, killed Ahab's son Joram and had the body thrown onto Naboth's plot. He quoted the LORD's words, "Yesterday I saw the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons." Only there do we learn that Naboth's sons were killed too.

keyVerses.text: The land must not be sold permanently, because the land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers.

Then two scoundrels came and sat opposite him and brought charges against Naboth before the people, saying, 'Naboth has cursed both God and the king.' So they took him outside the city and stoned him to death.

Go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who rules in Samaria. He is now in Naboth's vineyard, where he has gone to take possession of it. Say to him, 'This is what the LORD says: Have you not murdered a man and seized his property?'

insights: Naboth was put to death with the forms of the law kept, and God called it murder. Whether a thing went through the right process and whether it was right are two questions, and the one God put to Ahab was the second.

Naboth never got his vineyard back, and nothing here promises you'll get back what was taken. God saw Naboth's blood the day it was shed and refused the town's verdict, and He is no more bound by paperwork now.

The trial of Jesus has many of the same parts. The council went looking for evidence against Him and two witnesses came forward. He was condemned for blasphemy on His own answer to the high priest, and was crucified outside the city. The one you pray to has been through a court like Naboth's.
reflectQuestions: God told Ahab to his face what he had done to Naboth. If He described what was done to you or your family, what would He call it?
What have you gone along with because it came with the right signatures and objecting would have cost you?
thematicGuides.practice: Elijah was sent to say out loud what had been done. You may never get to say it to the people who did it, so this week tell a friend who wasn't involved the whole of what was taken, in the words you've stopped using. Ask them to hear you out and tell you honestly how it looks. If there may still be a lawful way to challenge it, ask them to help you find out.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, a court went looking for witnesses against You, so You know what it is to be wronged by the people running the hearing. You saw what was taken from my family and how tidily it was done. I've been told it was legal so often that I've half stopped calling it wrong. I'd like it put right, and I'd like them to pay. I won't pretend otherwise. Don't let this harden me, and keep me from ever doing the same to someone smaller. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Lazarus at the Rich Man's Gate
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus never says what the rich man did wrong, only how he lived and who was lying at his gate.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: At his gate was laid a beggar named Lazarus, covered with sores and longing to eat what fell from the rich man's table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.
thematicGuides.intro: A beggar called Lazarus lay at the gate of a rich man's house, and Jesus's story leaves him there until he dies. You may know a place like that gate, the spot by the station where the same person sits most mornings. If you never know what to do there, this is the passage that comes nearest, and it gives very few instructions.
story: Jesus told this story to some Pharisees, strict religious men who, Luke says, loved money and had been sneering at Him. He names only the beggar. The rich man dressed in purple and fine linen and lived in luxury every day. Lazarus was covered with sores. He "was laid" at the gate, so somebody had put him there, and he longed to eat what fell from the rich man's table. Jesus adds that even the dogs came and licked his sores. The rich man ate, and Lazarus was outside.

Both men died. Angels carried Lazarus to Abraham's side. The rich man was buried, and in torment he looked up and saw Abraham a long way off with Lazarus beside him. He called out, "Father Abraham, have pity on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue." So he knew the beggar's name, though he spoke about Lazarus to Abraham and never to Lazarus. Abraham called him 'Son' and named no crime. He told him to remember that in his lifetime he had received his good things while Lazarus received bad things. Now Lazarus was comforted, and a great chasm lay between them.

The rich man tried again. He asked Abraham to send Lazarus to his family instead, because he had five brothers who needed warning. It was the second time he had asked for Lazarus to be sent somewhere for him. Abraham answered, "They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them." He meant the Scriptures the brothers already had. The rich man argued that someone from the dead would make them repent, and Abraham said it would not. In those Scriptures Moses tells Israel not to be hard-hearted or tight-fisted towards a poor person in any of their towns, and Isaiah speaks of sharing your food with the hungry. From the first line of the story to the last, Lazarus says nothing.

keyVerses.text: At his gate was laid a beggar named Lazarus, covered with sores and longing to eat what fell from the rich man's table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.
If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.

If anyone is poor among your fellow Israelites in any of the towns of the land the LORD your God is giving you, do not be hardhearted or tightfisted toward them. Rather, be openhanded and freely lend them whatever they need.

insights: Jesus sets a daily feast and a hungry man at the same address and tells us what became of each. If you go to the story for the rule the rich man broke, so as to be sure you haven't broken it, all it gives you is the gate.

Jesus's story doesn't settle whether to hand over money or buy a sandwich, and Christians land in different places on that. Abraham's point about the five brothers was that they needed no new sign. They'd already been told enough to act on.
Lazarus longed for what fell from the table, food that was on its way to the floor anyway. He was hoping for very little.
reflectQuestions: When you pass someone begging, what do you tell yourself in the few seconds it takes to walk by?
Who is the person in need nearest to your own front door, the one you didn't choose and keep coming across?
thematicGuides.practice: Here's one way to start. Next time you reach the person you usually walk past, stop. Ask whether you can get them something to eat or drink and what they'd like, then go and get it. When you hand it over, tell them your name and ask theirs. If nobody sits on your route, take a meal to the neighbour whose need you've known about longest.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, there's someone I pass and have trained myself not to see. I get my phone out before I reach them so I don't have to decide anything. I've got Moses and the Prophets on that same phone, so I can't say nobody told me. I don't know what the right help is, and I've let that excuse me from giving any. Slow me down next time, and show me what to do once I've stopped. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Five Sisters Who Asked Moses Why
thematicGuides.hook: When Zelophehad's five daughters asked for their father's land in front of all Israel, God said they were right.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: What Zelophehad's daughters are saying is right. You must certainly give them property as an inheritance among their father's relatives and give their father's inheritance to them.
thematicGuides.intro: Early on we learn that when an arrangement leaves you out, the wise course is to keep quiet, because whoever points it out gets known as difficult. So we say nothing in the room and plenty afterwards, to people who can't change it. There's sense in the caution. The book of Numbers is full of people complaining to Moses, and it rarely ends well for them. Then, late in the book, five sisters stand up in front of everybody and ask Moses why, and it goes another way.
story: On the plains of Moab Moses had just counted the men of Israel, and the land across the Jordan was to be shared out by the names on that count. Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh, had died in the wilderness leaving five daughters and no son. So Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milkah and Tirzah came forward and stood before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the leaders and the whole assembly. They said their father had died for his own sin and had been no follower of Korah, who led a revolt against Moses. "Why should our father's name disappear from his clan because he had no son?" they said, and they asked outright for land among their father's relatives.

Moses took their case to the LORD, whose reply began by saying the sisters were right. They were to have their father's inheritance, and from then on, if any man in Israel died without a son, his inheritance was to go to his daughter. Later the heads of their clan came to Moses with a worry. If the five married into other tribes, the land would go with them. The ruling, given at the LORD's command, began the same way, by saying these men were right. The sisters could marry anyone they pleased within their father's clan. They married their cousins on their father's side, and the land stayed in the clan.

By the time the land was divided, Moses had died and Joshua was leading Israel. The book of Joshua writes out all five names once more, the fourth time the Bible lists them in full, and has them raise the matter again. They went to Eleazar the priest, to Joshua and to the leaders, and reminded them what the LORD had commanded Moses. Joshua gave them their land alongside their father's brothers. Manasseh's share came to ten tracts of land, besides its territory east of the Jordan, "because the daughters of the tribe of Manasseh received an inheritance among the sons".

keyVerses.text: What Zelophehad's daughters are saying is right. You must certainly give them property as an inheritance among their father's relatives and give their father's inheritance to them.

What the tribe of the descendants of Joseph is saying is right. This is what the LORD commands for Zelophehad's daughters: They may marry anyone they please as long as they marry within their father's tribal clan.

They went to Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders and said, 'The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our relatives.' So Joshua gave them an inheritance along with the brothers of their father, according to the LORD's command.

insights: Korah, whom the sisters mention, had put a 'why' to Moses as well: "Why then do you set yourselves above the LORD's assembly?" He came with 250 men to oppose Moses. The sisters came with a case, and a request that could be refused.

You're unlikely to be told in so many words that you're right, and the people you ask may say no. You can still ask the way the sisters did. Go to the people who can change it, in the open, and ask for one thing.

The second 'is right' in this story goes to the clan leaders who saw a problem with the first. The sisters kept their land and accepted a limit on whom they could marry. Asking for what's fair to you may mean finding out what's fair to someone else.
reflectQuestions: Which arrangement in your family or your workplace leaves you or someone else out, and has done for so long that nobody asks why?
If you had one minute in front of the people who could change it, what exactly would you ask them for?
thematicGuides.practice: Before you raise your own case, give one thing back. There's probably an arrangement at home or at work that suits you and leaves another person out. Perhaps you always get first pick of the holiday dates, or the car on Saturdays. This week, go to the person who loses by it and hand it over, face to face, without waiting to be asked. When God told Moses the sisters were right, His next words were an order to give them the land.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I've told nearly everyone about the thing I think is unfair, except the people who could change it. I'm not certain I'm right. Show me whether this is a fair question or a grudge I've grown fond of. If it's fair, give me one plain sentence and let me say it in the right room. If the answer is no, don't let me turn into Korah. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Good Seat and the Floor
thematicGuides.hook: To James, showing one visitor to a good seat and telling another to sit on the floor is sin.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, 'Love your neighbor as yourself,' you are doing right. But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as lawbreakers.
thematicGuides.intro: Favouritism never feels like a decision. You're warmer to the person who is good company or might be useful, and you haven't been rude to the one you didn't quite register. They just end up at the edge of the room, and you don't see it happen. The letter of James takes one small case of this, a matter of who was offered which seat, and the words it uses belong in a courtroom.
story: James is writing to believers scattered among the nations, and he asks them to suppose that two men come into their meeting. He describes them by what they have on. One wears a gold ring and fine clothes, and the other is a poor man in filthy old clothes. James has his readers say to the first, "Here's a good seat for you." The poor man is told to stand where he is, or else, "Sit on the floor by my feet." James asks whether people who do this have not discriminated among themselves and become judges with evil thoughts.

After the scene with the two seats, James turns on his readers. "But you have dishonored the poor." It is the rich, he reminds them, who are exploiting them and dragging them into court, and the man they'd save the good seat for is a rich man. Next comes the law he calls royal, love your neighbour as yourself. Favouritism breaks it and is sin, and James won't have it counted as a small one. Whoever keeps the whole law and stumbles at one point is guilty of breaking all of it, and the two commands he sets beside this one are those against adultery and murder.

One Sabbath Jesus went to eat at the house of a prominent Pharisee, one of a group devoted to keeping the law of Moses in every detail, and He was being carefully watched.
