He did some watching Himself, and noticed how the guests picked the places of honour at the table. Then He spoke to the man who had invited Him. When you give a lunch or a dinner, He said, don't invite your friends, your brothers and sisters, your relatives or your rich neighbours, because "they may invite you back and so you will be repaid." Invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, who can't repay you, and you will be blessed. He said this as a guest, at the man's own table.

keyVerses.text: Do not pervert justice; do not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the great, but judge your neighbor fairly.
If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, 'Love your neighbor as yourself,' you are doing right. But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as lawbreakers.
But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed. Although they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.

insights: James quotes 'love your neighbour as yourself' from Leviticus 19. Three verses before it, the same chapter tells Israel to judge a neighbour fairly, with no favouritism to the great and no partiality to the poor either. The man with the ring is welcome to a seat. What James objects to is the difference between the two welcomes.
In James's scene the judging is over before either visitor has said a word. Your next chance to choose differently is the next room you walk into, and it'll involve nothing bigger than where you sit.
reflectQuestions: In the rooms you're in every week, who has never once had your full attention?
What do you hope to get back from the people you make the most effort with?
thematicGuides.practice: This evening, by yourself, go back over the last gathering you walked into, a church service or a family meal. Write down who you went to first and who you didn't speak to at all. Beside each person put the honest reason in as few words as you can. Fold the paper into your wallet or your bag, and read it before you next walk into that room.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I can size up a room in seconds, and I usually know whose attention I want before I've sat down. I've always called that being sociable, and James has a harder word for it. There are people I see every week whose names I couldn't give You. Thank You for not sizing me up by what I could offer. Bring one of them to mind now, and next time put me in the seat beside them. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Here Is Your Mother: When Parents Grow Old
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus took the command to honour your parents to mean helping them, and from the cross He found His own mother a home.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: 'Here is your mother.' From that time on, this disciple took her into his home.
thematicGuides.intro: When Jesus quotes the command to honour father and mother in Mark 7, nobody in the conversation is a child. He's talking about adults and what they could have used to help a mother or father. That is where the command reaches many of us: a mother who can't manage the stairs, a father who has started repeating himself, and more needed from you each year than you can give alone. On the day He died, Jesus made sure His own mother had somewhere to go.
story: Pharisees and teachers of the law asked Jesus why His disciples ate without the hand-washing their tradition required. He told them, "You have a fine way of setting aside the commands of God in order to observe your own traditions!" His example was the command to honour your father and mother. The teachers had ruled that a person could declare Corban, which means devoted to God, over whatever might have been used to help their parents. From then on they would not let that person do anything for father or mother. Jesus called it cancelling the word of God.

The soldiers who crucified Jesus divided His clothes into four shares and cast lots for the undergarment. His mother was standing near the cross with other women, and the disciple He loved was close by. Jesus saw them and gave them to each other. She was to have the disciple as her son, and he was to have her as his mother. From that time on the disciple took her into his home. The next thing John writes is that Jesus knew everything had now been finished.

Timothy was looking after the church in Ephesus when Paul wrote to him about its widows. The church helped them, and there was a list a widow's name could be put on. Paul wants that help kept for the widow who is really in need and left all alone. Where a widow has children or grandchildren, they come first. Caring for her is something they are to learn, and Paul calls it repaying their parents and grandparents. A believing woman with widows in her care should go on helping them, he adds, so that the church can help "those widows who are really in need."

keyVerses.text: But you say that if anyone declares that what might have been used to help their father or mother is Corban (that is, devoted to God), then you no longer let them do anything for their father or mother. Thus you nullify the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down.

When Jesus saw his mother there, and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to her, 'Woman, here is your son,' and to the disciple, 'Here is your mother.' From that time on, this disciple took her into his home.

But if a widow has children or grandchildren, these should learn first of all to put their religion into practice by caring for their own family and so repaying their parents and grandparents, for this is pleasing to God.

insights: In Mark 7 the test of honouring a parent is whether you helped them. Jesus says nothing there about a grown adult obeying a parent, or about going back within reach of one who harmed you. His target is a religious ruling that let a person who could help do nothing. If keeping your distance is how you stay safe, He isn't describing you.

Jesus kept the command by arranging care He couldn't give in person, and the home His mother went to was somebody else's. If you've found a carer for the mornings, or chosen a care home and kept visiting, you've done the kind of thing He did.

Paul's word for looking after a parent is religion, put into practice. The Corban ruling had used religion to get out of that very thing, and a full diary at church can be used the same way. Neither Jesus nor Paul sets an amount, so nobody can tell a worn-out carer from these passages that they ought to be doing more.
reflectQuestions: What does your mum or dad need from you now that they didn't need a few years ago?
What stops you from asking another person to take on part of looking after your parent?
thematicGuides.practice: Sit down one evening this week with a sheet of paper and write down who does what for your mum or dad: the shopping, the lifts to hospital, the bills, the phone calls. Put a name against each job, your own included, and a carer's or a neighbour's if that's who does it. Circle one job nobody is covering and write beside it who you'll ask. Keep the sheet with their paperwork.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I'm praying about one of my parents, and what they need now is more than I've got. Some evenings I've seen it was them calling and let the phone ring out, and been ashamed afterwards. Show me which of my reasons are real limits and which are my own Corban. Give me people to share this with, as You gave Your mother the disciple You loved, and the humility to let them. On the days I can't be there, let my mum or dad know they haven't been left. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Single, and Not a Dry Tree
thematicGuides.hook: A man who could never have children called himself a dry tree, and God gave him an answer.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I will give within my temple and its walls a memorial and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that will endure forever.
thematicGuides.intro: A wedding invitation arrives with 'plus one' printed on it, and you spend longer on those two words than on the date. Then there's the form that asks for a next of kin, and the relative who asks every Christmas whether there's anyone yet. After enough of it you can start treating your life as a waiting room for the real one. Isaiah 56 speaks to men who could never have children, and Paul wrote about marriage as a man without a wife.
story: A eunuch was a man who had been castrated. The law in Deuteronomy 23 kept him out of the assembly of the LORD, and he would never have a child to carry on his name. In Isaiah 56 the prophet gives the complaint in the man's own words: "I am only a dry tree." Then the LORD answers it. To the eunuchs who hold fast to His covenant He will give a memorial inside His temple and its walls, and an everlasting name, better than sons and daughters. He is the one who calls it better.

Christians in Corinth had written to Paul with questions, some of them about marriage. The man who answered had no wife. Later in the same letter he asks, "Don't we have the right to take a believing wife along with us, as do the other apostles and the Lord's brothers and Cephas?" Cephas is Peter. The others took their wives from town to town, and Paul had none to take. He tells the Corinthians he wishes they were all as he is, adds at once that each has their own gift from God, and calls it good for the unmarried and the widows to stay as he is. Those who marry, he says, have not sinned. For people who have never married he has no command from the Lord, and gives his judgment as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy.

Paul had not yet visited Rome when he wrote to the Christians there, and the last chapter of his letter is mostly names. He greets more than twenty people one by one. First come Priscilla and Aquila, the married couple he had stayed and made tents with in Corinth, who risked their lives for him. Andronicus and Junia have been in prison with him. Four people he calls his dear friend. Then, partway down the list: "Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me, too."

keyVerses.text: To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose what pleases me and hold fast to my covenant, to them I will give within my temple and its walls a memorial and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that will endure forever.

I wish that all of you were as I am. But each of you has your own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that. Now to the unmarried and the widows I say: It is good for them to stay unmarried, as I do.
Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my co-workers in Christ Jesus. They risked their lives for me. Not only I but all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them.

insights: The eunuch's complaint is quoted before the LORD answers it, so what he says about himself had been heard. The answer leaves the loss where it is, and nothing in it promises you a husband or wife. The name and the place with God that he is given don't depend on having a family.

Paul calls staying unmarried good and marrying no sin. So you don't have to marry in order to count, and you don't have to be glad you haven't. Wanting to be married is no fault anywhere in that chapter.

Friends are not a marriage. Even so, by the end of Romans unmarried Paul has more than twenty people to greet by name in a city he had never visited, a married couple first and somebody's mother partway down. That was his real life, and it was already going on.
reflectQuestions: What have you been putting off until there's someone to do it with?
Who has been a mother, a father, a brother or a sister to you without being related to you?
thematicGuides.practice: Make or buy something small this week, a loaf or a plant, for someone who has been family to you: the friend with your spare key, or the older couple who feed you on Sundays. Take it to their door and tell them in one sentence what they have been to you, as Paul did for Rufus's mother. If nobody comes to mind, take it to someone you know who lives alone and say you thought of them.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I don't know whether I'll ever marry, and nobody can tell me. There are weeks I mind so much that I can't be glad for my friends, and other weeks I hardly think about it. I dread being asked. When I start calling myself a dry tree, remind me what You said to the man who did. Don't let me spend these years waiting for my life to begin, and show me whose list of dear friends I belong on. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jesus's Brothers Did Not Believe in Him
thematicGuides.hook: His family said He was out of His mind, and after the resurrection His brothers were praying with the disciples.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: For even his own brothers did not believe in him.
thematicGuides.intro: You're the only Christian in your family. They think it's a phase, or that you've gone a bit strange, and there are things you no longer mention at the table because of the look that follows. They're also the people you most want to understand you. Jesus's own family once set out to take charge of Him, and the Gospels show how He lived with relatives who weren't persuaded.
story: Jesus had gone into a house, and such a crowd gathered that He and His disciples were not even able to eat. When His family heard, they went to take charge of Him. They said, "He is out of his mind." His mother and brothers arrived, stood outside and sent someone in to call Him. When He was told, He looked at the people seated in a circle around Him and said that they were His mother and His brothers, and so was anyone who does God's will. Mark doesn't record that He went out to them, or that He sent them away.

Jesus was keeping to Galilee, because the Jewish leaders in Judea were looking for a way to kill Him. With the Festival of Tabernacles near, His brothers told Him to go to Judea, so that His disciples there could see the works He was doing. Nobody who wants to be a public figure acts in secret, they said. They knew about the works, and they did not believe in Him. Jesus answered that His time had not yet come and told them to go up to the festival themselves. He stayed in Galilee. After they had left He went too, "not publicly, but in secret."

After the resurrection Jesus was taken up from the Mount of Olives, and the apostles walked back to Jerusalem and went upstairs to the room where they were staying. All eleven were there. With them, praying constantly, were the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and His brothers. No Gospel tells how the brothers got from standing outside a house sending for Him to praying in this room. Paul gives one clue. Among those the risen Jesus appeared to he lists a James, and in another letter he mentions meeting "James, the Lord's brother" in Jerusalem.

keyVerses.text: Then he looked at those seated in a circle around him and said, 'Here are my mother and my brothers! Whoever does God's will is my brother and sister and mother.'

Jesus' brothers said to him, 'Leave Galilee and go to Judea, so that your disciples there may see the works you do. No one who wants to become a public figure acts in secret. Since you are doing these things, show yourself to the world.' For even his own brothers did not believe in him.
They all joined together constantly in prayer, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.

insights: Jesus neither cut His family off nor changed course to please them. They came to take charge of Him and He carried on. He went to the festival in His own time, and He still answered His brothers when they spoke. You can decline to be managed by your family and go on being part of it.

His brothers knew about the works He was doing and still didn't believe in Him. If that could happen in Jesus's own family, your family's doubts are no verdict on how well you've put things. He answered what His brothers said and left it there, so you needn't treat every meal as a debate to win.

Acts records that Jesus's brothers ended up praying with the disciples, and makes no promise that your family will come round. Jesus knows what it is to be thought odd at home, and He calls whoever does God's will His brother and sister. The church is meant to be that family to you while you go on loving your own.
reflectQuestions: What is the hardest part of being around your family now that you believe and they don't?
Where have you been trimming what you say or do so that your family will approve?
thematicGuides.practice: Pray one sentence for one member of your family, by name, each day for the next seven. Once or twice in the week, when there's a real reason, get in touch with one of them about something that matters to them, the job interview or the bad knee. You needn't steer the talk towards faith. If they ask, answer the question they asked and stop there.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, Your own family said You were out of Your mind. I get that look across the table too, and it's lonely being the odd one. Some days I want to win the argument more than I want them to know You, and I'm sorry for that. I can't make them believe, and You haven't promised me they will. Keep me from hiding You to keep the peace, and from preaching at them to prove a point. I'd give a great deal to pray in the same room as them one day. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: No One to Comfort Her: A Chapter for the Lonely
thematicGuides.hook: A ruined city asks God and the passers-by to look at her, and in Isaiah 40 God orders someone to go and comfort her.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: No one is near to comfort me, no one to restore my spirit.
thematicGuides.intro: Lamentations begins in Jerusalem after the city has fallen. The city once so full of people lies deserted, and the poet pictures her as a widow weeping at night, tears on her cheeks, with nobody coming. If you're lonely in a way that advice about joining a club doesn't touch, this chapter is about that. It says one sentence five times, that there is no one to comfort her, and lets it stand.
story: Jerusalem was queen among the provinces and has become a slave. Her friends have betrayed her and become her enemies, and of all the allies she once counted on, the ones the poem calls her lovers, not one comforts her. The roads to Zion mourn, because nobody travels them to her festivals any more. In her affliction Jerusalem remembers all the treasures that were hers in days of old, and that when her people fell into enemy hands there was no one to help her. Her enemies looked at her and laughed.

For the first eleven verses of Lamentations 1 the ruined city is described by someone else. Twice she breaks in with a single line, both times speaking to God. The second is "Look, LORD, and consider, for I am despised." From there she does most of the talking, and she turns to the people walking past: "Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look around and see." She says for herself what had been said about her, that no one is near to comfort her, no one to restore her spirit. Her last words are that her groans are many and her heart is faint. The chapter ends there, without a reply.

Isaiah 40 is about the same city, and its first word is the one Lamentations 1 kept saying was missing. "Comfort, comfort my people, says your God." It is an order, given to someone other than Jerusalem, and in Hebrew the verb is plural, so it goes to more than one person. They are to speak tenderly to her and tell her that her hard service has been completed and her sin has been paid for. A few verses on, someone is sent up a high mountain to shout to the towns of Judah, "Here is your God!", and He is pictured as a shepherd carrying lambs close to His heart.

keyVerses.text: Bitterly she weeps at night, tears are on her cheeks. Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her.
This is why I weep and my eyes overflow with tears. No one is near to comfort me, no one to restore my spirit.
Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her that her hard service has been completed, that her sin has been paid for.

insights: The sentence stands five times, three in the narrator's mouth and two in her own, and it is never corrected. Nobody tells her it could be worse, or that with God she ought not to need people. Scripture counts having no one to comfort you as a real loss, and gives you the words for it.
Three times she asks the LORD to look at her, and the first two times that is the whole request. A prayer that short can be prayed on a day when you have nothing else in you.

The poem says Jerusalem's ruin was a judgment for her many sins. That is her history. It doesn't make your loneliness a punishment, and Isaiah's promise to her is not a promise that yours will end. God heard her complaint, and His answer was to send people to speak to her.
reflectQuestions: What is it about the worst hour of your week that makes the loneliness heavier then?
What would you say if someone asked how you are and wanted the true answer?
thematicGuides.practice: Tell one person this week that you've been lonely, and for how long. Zion asked the people passing only to look around and see, and you aren't asking anyone to solve it either. Choose someone likely to listen without hurrying to fix it: your minister, your doctor, a relative you rarely ring. You can begin by saying you've had a lonely few months and wanted someone to know.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, look. That is most of what I have to say. The evenings are long, and I've told people I'm fine so many times that nobody asks twice. You let it be said five times that she had no one to comfort her, so I'm saying it to You now, about me. You gave the order to speak tenderly to Jerusalem. Send someone to speak to me, and until they come, don't let me decide that nobody would. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Ezekiel and the Room Behind the Wall
thematicGuides.hook: God had Ezekiel dig into a wall and walk in on seventy elders who were saying the LORD did not see them.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, purifies us from all sin.
thematicGuides.intro: The assumption behind a private habit is that it stays where it's put. You keep what you look at late at night, or what you do when you're away from home, in one room, and church and the people who think well of you in another. Not everything is everyone's business, so the arrangement can seem reasonable. Ezekiel was once shown a hidden room behind a wall at the temple in Jerusalem. God told him what the men inside it were saying.
story: Ezekiel was living among the exiles in Babylon when God took him in a vision to the temple in Jerusalem. At the entrance to the court he saw a hole in the wall, was told to dig into it, found a doorway, and was sent in to see the wicked things being done there. The walls were covered with pictures of crawling things, unclean animals and idols. Seventy elders of Israel stood before them in the dark, each holding a censer of incense, each at the shrine of his own idol. God told Ezekiel what these men were saying: "The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land." They said it in a room He had just opened up to a visitor from Babylon.

Luke describes a crowd of many thousands gathering around Jesus. He spoke first to His disciples, and the first thing He warned them against was hypocrisy. Nothing is concealed that won't be disclosed, He said, and what was whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed from the roofs. With His next words He called these same people His friends. He told them to fear God more than anyone who could kill them, and then that this God doesn't forget a single sparrow and has numbered the hairs of their heads. "Don't be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows."

John's first letter puts what he had heard from Jesus into a single line: "God is light; in him there is no darkness at all." He works out what follows in a run of sentences that each begin 'If we'. The first is about claiming to have fellowship with God, a shared life with Him, while walking in the darkness. John's word for that is lying, and his 'we' counts himself in. Another of the sentences is about confessing. We own up to our sins, and God, who is faithful and just, forgives them.

keyVerses.text: Son of man, have you seen what the elders of Israel are doing in the darkness, each at the shrine of his own idol? They say, 'The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land.'

There is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, or hidden that will not be made known. What you have said in the dark will be heard in the daylight, and what you have whispered in the ear in the inner rooms will be proclaimed from the roofs.

If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, purifies us from all sin. If we claim to be without sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.

insights: In John's letter the people walking in the light are still being purified from sin, so being in the light can't mean having none. The cleaning happens in the light, and there's no use waiting in the dark until you're presentable.
John says walking in the light gives you fellowship with one another, where you might have expected him to say with God. A secret means your friends know only part of you.

A secret life needs the elders' sentence to be true. Jesus told His friends that nothing stays hidden, and then that God had counted the hairs on their heads. Telling God what you've kept from everyone else tells Him nothing He doesn't know, and it ends the pretence that He can't see.
reflectQuestions: The elders had a sentence that let them carry on. What do you tell yourself that keeps the door of your own room shut?
When you think about telling one trusted person the thing nobody knows, what are you most afraid would happen next?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose one person who can keep a confidence, such as an old friend, or your minister or priest. Within the week, ask them for half an hour in private. Tell God first, in plain words, what you've kept hidden. Then tell them in those same words, without tidying it up. You needn't say everything at once.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, You have seen the room all along, and I've carried on as if You hadn't. I've kept what I look at and where I go from everyone who thinks well of me. I've been more afraid of people finding out than of You seeing, which is the wrong way round. I'm telling You now, by its name. Forgive me and make me clean. Give me the courage to tell one person, and let them be kind. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Sin Crouching at Cain's Door
thematicGuides.hook: We usually start fighting temptation much later than the moment God chose to warn Cain.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you do not do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires to have you, but you must rule over it.
thematicGuides.intro: What makes a repeated sin so hard is that you have already tried. You've fought it at the last second more times than you could count, lost, felt terrible and promised yourself it was over. After enough rounds of that you begin to suspect you're a person who can't. Genesis 4 and Proverbs 7 each describe a fall, and both start the account well before the last second.
story: Cain worked the soil and his younger brother Abel kept flocks. Each brought an offering, and the LORD looked with favour on Abel and his offering and not on Cain and his. Cain was very angry, and his face was downcast. That was when God spoke to him, before he had done anything to Abel. He asked why Cain was angry and warned him, in the Bible's first use of the word sin, that it was crouching at his door, wanting to have him, and that he must rule over it. Cain's next words are to Abel: "Let's go out to the field." There he attacked his brother and killed him.

In Proverbs 7 a father tells his son what he once saw from his window, looking down through the lattice. A young man was walking down the street towards a married woman's house. The father says exactly where, near her corner, and gives the hour three ways, as twilight, as the day fading and as the dark of night setting in. All of that came before she appeared or anyone said a word. Then she came out, took hold of him and talked, and it was over quickly: "All at once he followed her like an ox going to the slaughter." The father's lesson for his sons, when it comes, is not to let their hearts turn her way or stray into her paths.

Paul reminded the church in Corinth that all Israel came through the sea and God was still not pleased with most of them, and he warned anyone who thought they were standing firm to be careful not to fall. God is faithful, he went on, and when they were tempted He would provide a way out so that they could endure it. For the Corinthians the pull came from meals in the temples of idols, which Paul had written about in chapter 8. The sentence that follows the promise starts with 'Therefore' and tells them to flee from idolatry.

keyVerses.text: Then the LORD said to Cain, 'Why are you angry? Why is your face downcast? If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you do not do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires to have you, but you must rule over it.'
He was going down the street near her corner, walking along in the direction of her house at twilight, as the day was fading, as the dark of night set in.

No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to mankind. And God is faithful; he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, he will also provide a way out so that you can endure it.

insights: God's warning reached Cain before he had lifted a hand. By the time you're fighting a temptation, a good deal has usually been settled by where you are and what time it is, and an earlier, smaller choice is easier to make. That's help for next time, and no extra charge against you for last time.
Temptation, Paul says, is common to mankind, so you are not a special case. The way out he promises is there so that you can endure, which is a word for holding out while the pull is still there.

Paul's promise of a way out was written to a whole church. A pattern you keep losing to alone usually needs another person in it, and if you can't stop when you want to, it may need a doctor or a recovery group as well. More willpower is rarely what's missing.
reflectQuestions: Think back to the last time it happened. What were you doing an hour before the moment you count as losing?
If one person knew your street and your hour, what would you want them to do for you?
thematicGuides.practice: Work out your own street and hour, the thing that nearly always comes shortly before. It may be the phone coming to bed with you, or the drive home past a certain shop, or the second drink. Starting today, go a whole week without that one earlier thing. Ask a friend who knows you well to check with you when the week is up.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, You spoke to Cain while he was still only angry, so You know where this starts in me. I've asked You for strength at the last second and said nothing about the hour before, because I still wanted that road left open. Show me my street and my hour, and the way out while it's still easy to take. Cain's answer isn't written down. Mine is that I want to rule over this, and I haven't managed it on my own. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Abraham's Half-Truth About Sarah
thematicGuides.hook: Sarah really was Abraham's half-sister, and because he said so she was twice taken into another man's house.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: LORD, who may dwell in your sacred tent? Who may live on your holy mountain? The one whose walk is blameless, who does what is righteous, who speaks the truth from their heart
thematicGuides.intro: When Abraham said Sarah was his sister, the statement was accurate. She was his father's daughter by another mother, and he says so himself, once he has been found out and a king wants an explanation. You can mislead someone the same way, by saying something true and letting them draw the wrong conclusion, and afterwards claim you never lied. Genesis tells the sister story three times, and each time it shows who else was put in danger.
story: A famine sent Abram down to Egypt. On the way in he told his wife Sarai that she was beautiful, and that the Egyptians, seeing she was his wife, would kill him and let her live. So he asked her to say she was his sister. She was taken into Pharaoh's palace, and Abram, treated well for her sake, acquired livestock and servants. What Sarai said to any of this we aren't told. Then the LORD struck Pharaoh's household with serious diseases because of her, and Pharaoh sent for Abram. One of his questions was about the part left out: "Why didn't you tell me she was your wife?" He gave her back and sent them away.

Years later, in Gerar, Abraham said the same thing about Sarah, and the king, Abimelek, sent for her and took her. God warned Abimelek in a dream that she was married. Abimelek had not gone near her, and when he protested that both of them had called themselves brother and sister, God agreed that he had acted with a clear conscience. In the morning the king asked Abraham why. Abraham said he had assumed there was no fear of God in the place and that he'd be killed. Besides, she really was his sister. And it was a standing arrangement: he had asked her to say this everywhere they went, as the way to show her love to him. Abimelek returned Sarah, telling her he was giving a thousand shekels of silver to "your brother".

Abraham's son Isaac, in another famine, went to Abimelek, king of the Philistines, in Gerar. When the men of the place asked about his wife Rebekah, he said, "She is my sister," because he was afraid they might kill him on account of her. Rebekah was the granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor, so Isaac could not have made the defence his father made. He had been there a long time when Abimelek looked down from a window and saw him caressing her. The king sent for him, and once more it was an outsider who said what the lie could have led to. One of the men might well have slept with her, and Isaac would have brought guilt on them all.

keyVerses.text: Say you are my sister, so that I will be treated well for your sake and my life will be spared because of you.
Besides, she really is my sister, the daughter of my father though not of my mother; and she became my wife.
The one whose walk is blameless, who does what is righteous, who speaks the truth from their heart; whose tongue utters no slander, who does no wrong to a neighbor, and casts no slur on others

insights: Psalm 15 says the person who may live with God "speaks the truth from their heart". Abraham's words were true, and he chose them so that the men of Gerar would think Sarah unmarried. You don't owe everyone every fact about yourself, but if you pick your words so that someone will believe what isn't so, you have deceived them, however accurate the words were.

The plan worked, and that is part of why this kind of lie is hard to give up. Abraham came through both episodes alive and richer than he went in. The cost fell on Sarah, taken first by Pharaoh and then by Abimelek, and each time it was God who stepped in for her.
reflectQuestions: Where have you recently said something accurate in the hope that the other person would get the wrong idea?
Sarah was the one taken into the palace. In your own half-truth, who has been carrying the cost you avoided?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, when you're on your own, pick one conversation where what you said was accurate and misleading at once. Say out loud what you told them, and straight after it what you wanted them to believe. If a call or a message tomorrow could put it right, decide before bed what its first line will be.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I chose my words carefully, and I've been quite pleased that none of them was false. I meant them to mislead, and they did. I was afraid of what the whole story would cost me, and I let someone else carry it. I'm sorry. Let me go back and say the part I left out to the person who should have heard it, and teach me to speak the truth from my heart. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Pay It Back and Add a Fifth
thematicGuides.hook: After Jesus came to his house, Zacchaeus offered anyone he had cheated four times the amount back.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: They must make full restitution for the wrong they have done, add a fifth of the value to it and give it all to the person they have wronged.
thematicGuides.intro: Say you borrowed money from a friend years ago, during a bad patch, and never paid it back. Nobody mentions it now. You've told God you're sorry and you believe He has forgiven you, but your friend is still out of pocket, and it crosses your mind whenever you see them. Numbers 5 has a few verses of law on this. Being sorry is where they start.
story: God gave Moses a rule for any man or woman who wrongs another person in any way. The rule calls this being "unfaithful to the LORD", so a wrong done to another person counts as a wrong done to God as well. The guilty person has to confess it, then pay the whole amount back to the one they wronged, with a fifth added. The law has even thought of the case where there is no one left to repay, because the wronged person has no close relative to receive it. Then the payment belongs to the LORD and is handed to the priest. Whoever receives it, it leaves the wrongdoer's hands.

Samuel had led Israel since his youth. Old and grey, with the people's first king now in place, he stood in front of all Israel and asked them to testify against him before the LORD and their new king. He asked whose ox he had taken and whose bribe, and before anyone could answer he promised that if he had done any of it he would make it right. His own sons were there among the people, and 1 Samuel 8 says they had accepted bribes. About Samuel the people said, "You have not taken anything from anyone's hand."

Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, and wealthy. Too short to see Jesus over the crowd, he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree. Jesus reached the spot, looked up and called him by name: "I must stay at your house today." Zacchaeus came down at once and welcomed Him gladly, and the people muttered that Jesus had gone to be the guest of a sinner. Then Zacchaeus stood up and made his offer: half of what he owned to the poor, and four times over to anyone he had cheated. Jesus said salvation had come to the house that day.

keyVerses.text: If that person has no close relative to whom restitution can be made for the wrong, the restitution belongs to the LORD and must be given to the priest, along with the ram with which atonement is made for the wrongdoer.

Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated? Whom have I oppressed? From whose hand have I accepted a bribe to make me shut my eyes? If I have done any of these things, I will make it right.

But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, 'Look, Lord! Here and now I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have cheated anybody out of anything, I will pay back four times the amount.'

insights: Numbers lists two separate things, a repayment to the person and a ram for atonement, the sacrifice that put the wrongdoer right with God. Christians believe Jesus has done for good what the ram stood for. Nothing has taken the place of the repayment.

Jesus invited Himself to Zacchaeus's house before a penny was offered, and the repayment followed unasked. Zacchaeus set it at four times the amount, the Exodus 22 rate for a sheep stolen and then killed or sold, where Numbers asked for a fifth. God's forgiveness did not wait for the money, but the person you wronged still hasn't had it back, and that is reason enough to pay.
Samuel asked about particular things, an ox, a donkey and a bribe. Repayment is for the one or two wrongs you already know about, so there's no need to comb through your whole past.
reflectQuestions: Which one wrong, with a real cost to someone else, came to mind first as you read this guide?
What has made going back to that person harder for you than saying sorry to God?
thematicGuides.practice: Before Sunday, take one sheet of paper and write the person's name, what you took or what it cost them, and a fair figure for it today with something on top, as the law adds a fifth. Underneath, write how you'll repay it and by what date. If contact wouldn't be welcome or safe for them, or they can't be found, write the church or charity it will go to instead, as Numbers sends it to the priest. Keep the sheet in your Bible until it's done.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, each time this has come back to me I've said sorry to You and left it there, as if that settled it with them too. I've been hoping enough years had gone by to write it off, and they haven't, because someone is still short of what I took. Thank You that You came to me before I'd put anything right, as Jesus went to Zacchaeus's house. Help me pay it back with something added, in a way that is good for them. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Paul Was Stopped Twice
thematicGuides.hook: Paul was stopped from preaching in Asia, then barred from Bithynia, and learned where to go only once he had run out of land.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: After Paul had seen the vision, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
thematicGuides.intro: You've tried more than one thing by now, a course you didn't finish, a job that went to someone else, and none of them has held. After a few of those it's hard not to suspect there was a right road and you missed the turning. Acts 16 has a stretch of Paul's life that looks, from the outside, a good deal like that. Luke, who wrote Acts, gets through it in three verses, and in them Paul is stopped twice.
story: The trip had started as something modest. Paul wanted to go back round the towns where he had preached and see how the believers were getting on. He took Silas with him, and Timothy joined them on the way. The churches they visited grew stronger in the faith and larger by the day. Then the Holy Spirit kept them from preaching in the province of Asia, so they travelled on. They tried to enter Bithynia next, and the Spirit of Jesus would not allow that either. They went on down to the coast, to the port of Troas.

During the night at Troas, Paul had a vision of a man from Macedonia, the country across the water. The man stood and begged him, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." The next verse is the first in Acts where the narrator says 'we', so the writer seems to have joined them at Troas and to be telling this part from the inside. They got ready at once to leave, "concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them." The vision was Paul's, and the conclusion was everybody's.

They sailed across and went on to Philippi, a Roman colony and the leading city of its district. Several days passed. Luke mentions no man coming to meet them. On the Sabbath they walked out through the city gate to the river, looking for a place where people prayed, and found a group of women there. They sat down and talked with them. One was Lydia, who dealt in purple cloth, and the Lord opened her heart to what Paul was saying. She and her household were baptised, and she persuaded them to stay at her house. She came from Thyatira, which Revelation lists among the seven churches of Asia, the province Paul had been kept from preaching in.

keyVerses.text: Paul and his companions traveled throughout the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching the word in the province of Asia. When they came to the border of Mysia, they tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them to.

On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer. We sat down and began to speak to the women who had gathered there. One of those listening was a woman from the city of Thyatira named Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth. She was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul's message.

He took the disciples with him and had discussions daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. This went on for two years, so that all the Jews and Greeks who lived in the province of Asia heard the word of the Lord.

insights: Luke names the Spirit as the one who closed those two roads. You may never be told which of your own disappointments were God's doing and which were a firm that was never going to hire you. Paul tried two places he wasn't meant to go and still arrived in Philippi. If you're scared you've already missed your turning, notice that two wrong tries didn't cost him the right place.

Neither place was closed for good. Paul later taught daily in Ephesus for two years, and by the end the whole province of Asia had heard. Peter's first letter is addressed to believers in five provinces, and Bithynia is one of them. As far as we know, someone else had taken the message there.
reflectQuestions: If you wrote down your last few years the way these verses record Paul's, as a bare list of what you tried and where you ended up, what would be on it?
Paul and his companions set off on a conclusion they had reached together. Who would you trust to help you reach one about your own next step?
thematicGuides.practice: At some point this week, walk out from your front door for fifteen minutes, then turn round. On the way out, tell God about each thing that has fallen through, by name. On the way home, decide on one thing you could still try (an application, a phone call, a visit) and do it within three days.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I'm tired of guessing which of my closed doors were You and which were only doors. I have no Luke to tell me. I'm afraid I took a wrong turn years ago and it's too late to go back. Even so, I'll keep walking. Show me the next place to go, and give me people to decide it with. If what's waiting is a few people by a river, let me sit down and start there. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Bezalel Was Good With His Hands
thematicGuides.hook: The first person the Bible says God filled with His Spirit was a craftsman, and his altar outlasted him by centuries.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills.
thematicGuides.intro: On Mount Sinai, after six chapters of instructions for a tent, its furnishings and its priests, God gave Moses the name of the man who was to make it. He was Bezalel, of the tribe of Judah, and everything God said about him concerned his work. If what you're good at is practical, a trade, or any job where the thing either works when you've finished or it doesn't, you may have wondered whether God takes much interest in it.
story: God named him in full, Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, and said He had filled him with His Spirit and with skill in metal, stone and wood. Before Bezalel, the Bible describes nobody as filled with the Spirit of God. The first is a craftsman. God gave him a helper from another tribe, Oholiab of Dan, and said that every skilled worker on the job had their ability from Him. Then He went through what they were to make, from the ark and the altar for burnt offerings to the priests' woven clothes and the incense.

Moses later repeated this to the whole community, almost word for word, with one addition. God had also given Bezalel and Oholiab "the ability to teach others." Theirs wasn't the only skill in the camp. The women who could spin had already brought in their yarn and goat hair. Once the work began, the people kept bringing materials, morning after morning, until the craftsmen stopped what they were doing and went to tell Moses there was more than enough. He had to send an order round the camp to stop the giving. Most of the next four chapters go through what they made, down to the bronze tent pegs, with a note that Bezalel made everything the LORD commanded Moses.

Bezalel is named again a long way on in the Bible. Early in his reign Solomon took Israel's leaders to the high place at Gibeon, where the tent of meeting from the wilderness stood. David had already moved the ark to Jerusalem, but the bronze altar was still in front of the tent, and Chronicles calls it the altar that Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on it. By the count in 1 Kings, Solomon's fourth year was the 480th after Israel left Egypt, so the altar was getting on for five centuries old. It was acacia wood overlaid with bronze, made in a desert camp.

keyVerses.text: I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills, to make artistic designs for work in gold, silver and bronze, to cut and set stones, to work in wood, and to engage in all kinds of crafts.
By wisdom the LORD laid the earth's foundations, by understanding he set the heavens in place; by his knowledge the watery depths were divided, and the clouds let drop the dew.

But the bronze altar that Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made was in Gibeon in front of the tabernacle of the LORD; so Solomon and the assembly inquired of him there. Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the LORD in the tent of meeting and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.

insights: God put wisdom, understanding and knowledge into Bezalel. Proverbs 3 uses the same three words, in the same order, for how He made the world, laying the earth's foundations and setting the heavens in place. A craftsman's skill is described in the words the Bible uses for God's own work.

God cared how the stones were set and the wood was joined, and He picked a man by name to do it. That was for His own tent, and Exodus stops short of saying every trade today is a gift of the Spirit. Even so, the God you pray to is the one who thought good workmanship worth giving His Spirit for.
reflectQuestions: What are you good at, in your work or with your hands, that you have never thought of as something God gave you?
What was it like the last time you tried to teach someone something you do well?
thematicGuides.practice: For a week, at the point each day when you put your tools away or shut the laptop, look at one thing you made or mended that day. Say one sentence of thanks to God for the particular skill it took, and name the skill, whether it was an eye for a level line or patience with a tangled set of accounts. On a day with nothing to show for it, name the skill you used anyway.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, You filled a man with Your Spirit so that he could cut stone and work wood. I had assumed You were mainly interested in people who preach and pray well, and I've been a little embarrassed that what I'm best at is something else. I've never once thanked You for it, and have treated it as mine, or as luck. Thank You for it now. Help me do it properly on the days when nobody will check, and make me patient in teaching it to someone slower than I am. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Haggai and the People Who Said Not Yet
thematicGuides.hook: Back from exile to rebuild God's house, the people left it for years, said the time hadn't come, and panelled their own.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Is it a time for you yourselves to be living in your paneled houses, while this house remains a ruin?
thematicGuides.intro: We tend to assume that anyone who keeps putting off something important can't care much about it, and sometimes that's fair. It doesn't fit the people Haggai was sent to. They had left Babylon to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, and had laid its foundation to trumpets and cymbals. Then the site went quiet. If there's something you already know you should be doing, and you keep telling yourself the time isn't right, you'll recognise them.
story: Once the temple's foundation was laid, the peoples living round about set out to discourage the builders and make them afraid to go on. They bribed officials to work against the project, and kept it up through the whole reign of Cyrus, the king who had sent the exiles home to build, and down to the reign of Darius. The work on the house of God came to a standstill, and it stayed that way until Darius's second year. By the usual dating of those kings, that is about sixteen years.

On the first day of the sixth month in Darius's second year, the prophet Haggai brought a message to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. It began with the people's own words, "The time has not yet come to rebuild the LORD's house." Nobody in that sentence is refusing to build. God's question picked up their word 'time' and turned it round: "Is it a time for you yourselves to be living in your paneled houses, while this house remains a ruin?" Panelling goes on after the walls and the roof are done. The message then gave them a first job, to go up into the mountains, bring down timber and build.

Zerubbabel, Joshua and the whole remnant of the people obeyed. Before the work started Haggai was given another message for them, four words long in English: "I am with you." On the twenty-fourth day of that month, twenty-three days after he first spoke, they came and began to work. Official trouble arrived all over again. Tattenai, the governor of the province, came to ask who had authorised the building and what the builders' names were. This time the building went on while the question went to Darius, and his answer was to leave the builders alone. The temple was completed in the sixth year of his reign, roughly four and a half years after they began.

keyVerses.text: 'Go up into the mountains and bring down timber and build my house, so that I may take pleasure in it and be honored,' says the LORD.
Then Haggai, the LORD's messenger, gave this message of the LORD to the people: 'I am with you,' declares the LORD.
But the eye of their God was watching over the elders of the Jews, and they were not stopped until a report could go to Darius and his written reply be received.

insights: Their reason for stopping was real on the day they stopped. By Haggai's time the talk was all of timing, and they had found time for their own houses. A reason that was true once can go on being given long after it stopped being true. If you must say 'not yet', put a date on it.

Read on in Haggai 1 and you'll find God tying that community's drought and poor harvests to the unbuilt house. That was a prophet's word to one people about one drought. It's no rule for reading your own bank balance, and no promise to you that doing the right thing brings in money.

The first job God gave them was a small one, to go and fetch wood, and He told them He was with them before any of the work was done. The house they had put off for about sixteen years took four and a half to build.
reflectQuestions: What reason have you been giving, to yourself or to other people, for not yet starting the thing you already know you should be doing?
What has had your time and energy while you've been saying not yet?
thematicGuides.practice: Tell a friend this week what you've been putting off, and for how long. Choose the one who's hardest to make excuses to. Between you, work out what your equivalent of fetching the timber would be, the first small job, and fix a day for it within the next twenty-three days. Ask them to ring you that evening to find out whether you went.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I've been telling You 'not yet' for so long that it has begun to sound like good sense. In that time I've repainted the hall and kept up with a great deal of television. I haven't touched the thing itself, and I've always had a reason ready. Some of those reasons were true once. I can't face the whole of it, so show me the first load of timber and get me up the hill for it this week. And say to me what You said to them, that You are with me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Man Jesus Sent Home
thematicGuides.hook: In Mark 5 Jesus grants what the demons ask and what the frightened town asks, and refuses the man who begs to go with Him.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.
thematicGuides.intro: It's hard to feel you're following Jesus properly when your life looks much as it always has, in the same town and the same job. The Christians who get talked about tend to be the ones who left, for a mission overseas or the ministry, and next to them staying put can look like the lesser thing. Mark tells of a man who begged to go with Jesus. He was refused, and given something else to do.
story: Jesus crossed the lake to the region of the Gerasenes, and a man who lived among the tombs came out to meet Him. He had been put in chains and leg irons many times and had broken them all, and by now nobody was strong enough to hold him. Day and night he was out among the graves and on the hills, shouting and gashing himself with stones. When he saw Jesus from a distance he ran and fell on his knees. The spirits in him, who gave their name as Legion, begged to be allowed into a large herd of pigs on the hillside. Jesus gave them permission. The herd, about two thousand animals, rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

The herdsmen ran off and told the town and the countryside, and people came out to see. They found the man nobody could hold sitting there, dressed and in his right mind, "and they were afraid." They were told what had happened to him, and to the pigs, and they began to plead with Jesus to leave their region. He had crossed the lake through a squall to get there, and one man is all Mark shows Him attending to on that shore. The next sentence has Him getting into the boat.

Jesus was already climbing into the boat when the man begged to go with Him. Jesus did not let him. He sent him home to his own people instead, and home was the district that had just asked Jesus to leave. The man was told to say how much the Lord had done for him. What he told the Decapolis, a district of ten towns, was how much Jesus had done, and everyone was amazed. Two chapters later Jesus is back in the Decapolis, and this time people bring Him a deaf man and beg Him to put His hand on him. Mark draws no line between the two visits.

keyVerses.text: The demons begged Jesus, 'Send us among the pigs; allow us to go into them.' He gave them permission, and the impure spirits came out and went into the pigs.
Then the people began to plead with Jesus to leave their region. As Jesus was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged to go with him.

Jesus did not let him, but said, 'Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.' So the man went away and began to tell in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him. And all the people were amazed.

insights: Peter and Andrew were called away from their nets. This man was told to go home, to people who had seen him at his worst. Each of them was following Jesus by doing what he was told. None of that is a reason to stay in a home that isn't safe.

Jesus said yes to the demons and yes to a town that wanted Him gone, and no to the man He had just set free, so a yes from Him is no measure of what He thinks of the one asking. If you've asked to be sent somewhere and the answer seems to be no, this story won't let you read that as being passed over.
When Jesus chose the Twelve, He appointed them "that they might be with him and that he might send them out to preach." The man from the tombs asked for the first half and was handed the second.
reflectQuestions: Who are your own people, the ones who have known you longest and remember what you were like before?
What would have to change about where you live or what you do before you'd count yourself as really following Jesus?
thematicGuides.practice: Your own people are probably already in your phone. Pick one who has known you a long time, a parent or an old friend, and message them today, at lunchtime or from the sofa this evening. In two or three sentences, tell them one particular thing God has done for you, something you know first-hand. Leave out the sermon. If they write back with a question you can't answer, say you don't know.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I've wondered whether I'd count for more with You if I had gone somewhere. I'd still like to be sent away, mostly because the people here remember what I was like at seventeen, and strangers would be easier. If home is where You want me, help me stop treating it as second prize. Thank You for the mercy You've shown me. Give me one honest sentence about it and one person to say it to this week. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Women Who Paid Jesus's Way
thematicGuides.hook: If you hate being helped, look at Jesus, Elijah and Paul, who each lived for a time on what other people gave them.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: These women were helping to support them out of their own means.
thematicGuides.intro: Luke spends one sentence on who paid for Jesus and the Twelve as they went from town to town. A group of women did, out of their own pockets. Keep that sentence in mind if you've always been the helper, and now you're ill, or out of work, or getting old, and other people are paying for you and doing what you used to do yourself.
story: Jesus was going from one town and village to another, announcing the kingdom of God, with the Twelve alongside Him. Thirteen men on the road have to eat. The ones who saw to it, Luke says, were women who had been cured of evil spirits and diseases. He names Mary called Magdalene, then Joanna, whose husband Chuza managed Herod's household, then Susanna, and says there were many others. Luke mentions Joanna once more. She was among the women from Galilee who prepared spices for Jesus's body, took them to the tomb on the first day of the week and found it empty.

During a drought God kept Elijah alive beside a brook, where ravens brought him bread and meat. Then the brook dried up. God sent him to Zarephath, outside Israel, and said He had directed a widow there to feed him. Elijah found her at the town gate gathering sticks, and asked her for water and a piece of bread. She had a handful of flour and a little oil, she said, enough for one last meal for herself and her son. Elijah told her not to be afraid, and to make a small loaf for him first, because God had said the flour and oil would last until the rain came. She did, and from then on there was food every day for Elijah, for her and for her family. He lodged in her upper room.

Paul made a point of earning his keep, and he reminded the elders of Ephesus that his own hands had supplied his needs. From the church at Philippi, though, he took help, as far back as his time in Thessalonica. He was in chains when their latest gift arrived, and Epaphroditus, the man who carried it, fell ill on the errand and almost died. Writing back, Paul says he has learned to be content, and then adds, "Yet it was good of you to share in my troubles." His phrase for what lay between them is "the matter of giving and receiving", and the receiving was his. The gifts themselves he calls an offering made to God.

keyVerses.text: Joanna the wife of Chuza, the manager of Herod's household; Susanna; and many others. These women were helping to support them out of their own means.
Go at once to Zarephath in the region of Sidon and stay there. I have directed a widow there to supply you with food.

I have received full payment and have more than enough. I am amply supplied, now that I have received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent. They are a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.

insights: The women who supported Jesus were women He had healed. If He could let people He had helped pay for Him, you can take a lift to the hospital from someone you once helped move house.

It was Paul who passed on Jesus's saying, "It is more blessed to give than to receive." The same Paul took the Philippians' gifts and called them pleasing to God. Had he sent them back, the Philippians would have had no offering to make.

God could have kept the ravens coming. He sent Elijah to a widow with one meal left. Nobody who helps you has been promised a jar that never empties, and carrying Paul's gift nearly killed Epaphroditus, so it's right to care what your need costs them. But help through people, whether a neighbour, a carer, a doctor or a benefits office, is the kind God chose for His own prophet.
reflectQuestions: When someone pays for you or does a job you used to do yourself, what is it that stings most?
Who has shared in your troubles lately without ever hearing from you what it meant?
thematicGuides.practice: See if you can get through a week without the sentences you use to push help away or pay it off, such as 'I'm fine' and 'I'll make it up to you'. When someone offers a lift, a meal or an hour of their time, and you need it, say yes and thank you, and tell them one thing it will let you do.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, You let other people pay Your way, and I can hardly let anyone pay for my lunch. I'd rather be the one carrying the bags, and I keep a tally of everything I now owe people. Thank You for the ones who drive me, cook for me and cover what I can't. Let what they give me be an offering You're pleased with. Teach me to say thank you and stop there. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Gaius and the Strangers at His Door
thematicGuides.hook: John wrote to praise a man for putting up travelling believers he had never met, and called it working for the truth.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: We ought therefore to show hospitality to such people so that we may work together for the truth.
thematicGuides.intro: Say a friend's cousin needs somewhere to sleep on Friday, and what you have is a sofa in a flat you share with three other people and enough pasta for two. It's natural to think that's too little to offer. One of the shortest books in the Bible is a letter to a man called Gaius, and the one thing it reports him doing is taking in travellers who were strangers to him.
story: Some believers had been on the road, and Gaius had taken them in, though he didn't know them. They went back and told the church about his love, and John writes to say he has heard. He asks Gaius to send the travellers on their way in a manner that honours God. They had set out for the sake of the Name, meaning Jesus, and accepted no help from the pagans. That left people like Gaius. Whoever takes such people in, John says, is working alongside them for the truth.

John had already written to the church, and a man called Diotrephes would have nothing to do with him. Diotrephes was spreading malicious talk about John, and he went further. He refused to welcome the travelling believers, stopped anyone else who wanted to, and put those people out of the church. In that congregation, giving a stranger a bed could cost you your place. What the travellers reported of Gaius was his love, and what John reports of Diotrephes is that he "loves to be first". John says that when he comes he will call attention to what Diotrephes is doing.

John tells Gaius to copy what is good, and then puts in a word for a man called Demetrius, who is well spoken of by everyone. He doesn't explain why. A traveller arriving at a stranger's door needed a good word from someone the host trusted, and this may be his. John has much more to say, but he would rather say it face to face than with pen and ink, and he hopes to see Gaius soon. Until then he passes on greetings from the friends where he is, and his last instruction is "Greet the friends there by name."

keyVerses.text: Dear friend, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers and sisters, even though they are strangers to you. They have told the church about your love. Please send them on their way in a manner that honors God.
We ought therefore to show hospitality to such people so that we may work together for the truth.
And if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones who is my disciple, truly I tell you, that person will certainly not lose their reward.

insights: John calls what Gaius did faithful. Nothing in the letter says what the food was like or whether Gaius had a spare room or any money, and what counts with John is that he welcomed people he didn't know. The one shut door in the letter belongs to Diotrephes, and John describes him as a man who loves to be first.

Jesus had said much the same before John did. Whoever welcomes a prophet, He told the Twelve, will receive a prophet's reward, and He set the lowest gift that counts at a cup of cold water. A sofa and a plate of pasta are a good way above that.

Gaius's guests were strangers to him, but the church knew them, and John adds his own word for Demetrius. In his second letter John tells his readers not to take in anyone who comes without the teaching of Christ. So a welcome leaves room for asking who sent someone and, if you share a flat, for asking the people you live with.
reflectQuestions: What do you remember about the last time someone gave you a bed or a meal when you needed one?
What do you tell yourself your home would need before you could have someone round?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, send one message. Pick someone who is new, or passing through, or who eats alone most evenings, and offer a meal on a particular day at your place as it is, something like 'I'm cooking pasta on Thursday, come at seven'. If you share a flat, ask the people you live with before you send it. Leave out any apology for the state of the place.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I've been waiting until I had a place worth inviting someone to, and I could be waiting for years. What I have is a small table, one decent pan and most evenings free. Part of why I don't invite people is that money is tight, and part is not wanting anyone to see how I live. Use what I've got as You used what Gaius had. Bring to mind someone who needs a meal this week, and help me remember their name. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Family Quarrel Behind the Bigger Barns
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus told the story of the bigger barns just after a man asked Him to settle a row over an inheritance.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Watch out! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; life does not consist in an abundance of possessions.
thematicGuides.intro: Your family is falling out over a will. You want what's fair, and you may well be right about what that is, but the argument has got into everything. Jesus was once asked to step into a quarrel like it by a man who wanted a ruling against his brother. He wouldn't give one. He told a story about a rich man's harvest, and it ends with a question about who gets the estate.
story: A crowd of many thousands had gathered, so many that people were treading on one another. Jesus was teaching His disciples when a man in the crowd said, "Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me." He didn't ask Jesus to hear both sides. He had the verdict ready and wanted Jesus to hand it down. Jesus answered, "Man, who appointed me a judge or an arbiter between you?" Then He warned the whole crowd to be on their guard against every kind of greed, because a person's life isn't made up of what they own.

The story He told them begins with a man who was rich already. His ground gave an abundant harvest, and the only difficulty was where to put it. He talked it over with nobody but himself, and settled on a plan to pull down his barns, build bigger ones and store the surplus there. In the few lines he speaks he says 'I' six times, and the crops, the barns and the grain are each 'my'. There's no family in his plans and no neighbour, and he says nothing to God about a harvest the ground gave him. He has even worked out what he'll say to himself when it's done: take life easy, eat, drink and be merry.

God is the only other voice in the story, and He speaks that same night. He calls the man a fool, tells him his life is being demanded of him, and ends with a question, "Then who will get what you have prepared for yourself?" The parable stops there, with the bigger barns unbuilt and the question unanswered. The man in the crowd had come about that question, because someone had died and left property, and two brothers were at odds over who should have it. The story Jesus told in reply looks at an inheritance from the dead man's side.

keyVerses.text: Watch out! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; life does not consist in an abundance of possessions.
This is how it will be with whoever stores up things for themselves but is not rich toward God.
Surely everyone goes around like a mere phantom; in vain they rush about, heaping up wealth without knowing whose it will finally be.

insights: Jesus never said the man was wrong about his share. The law of Moses had rules for dividing an estate, and a solicitor or mediator can do the job Jesus turned down. You can be right about the will and still find yourself adding up, when you should be asleep, what your sister has already had.

God's question to the rich man is an old one. In Psalm 39 David says people rush about heaping up wealth without knowing whose it will finally be. Whatever share reaches you, you'll hold it for a while, and then other people will be asking who gets it.

The rich man never asks how much is enough. He had barns already, and his one idea for the extra was bigger ones. Ask yourself what the money in dispute would be for once you had it. Jesus calls the alternative being "rich toward God", and later in the same chapter He links treasure in heaven with giving to the poor.
reflectQuestions: If the money were shared out tomorrow exactly as you think is fair, what would still be unsettled between you and the others?
What has this argument already cost you that no share of the estate would pay back?
thematicGuides.practice: While the will is still being argued over, write one sentence on a card: what you want to be true between you and your family ten years from now, whatever happens to the money. Keep the card on top of the solicitor's letters, or wherever the paperwork lives. Read it each time before you answer a message about the estate.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I'd have asked You for the same thing that man did. I want You on my side. I think I'm right about what's fair, and I may be, but I can't think about my own family now without doing sums. Keep me on my guard. Don't let what one person left behind cost me the people who are still here. Let me find out what being rich toward You means, and want it more than winning. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Tenants on God's Land
thematicGuides.hook: Leviticus calls Israel foreigners and strangers on God's land, and David, after giving away a fortune, says the same of himself.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The land must not be sold permanently, because the land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers.
thematicGuides.intro: At Mount Sinai, in the desert, God gave Moses the rules for buying and selling land. The people they were for had been slaves in Egypt and didn't own a single field. Before they had anything to sell, God told them whose it would be. That's where to start if you give, and every time it still feels like losing something you earned.
story: God's instructions in Leviticus 25 begin, "When you enter the land I am going to give you". Each family would have fields of its own, and the chapter calls them that family's property. Even so, God says the land must never be sold for good, because it is His and His people live on it as foreigners and strangers. We would say tenants. So a field could change hands only until the jubilee, the year when every field went back to the family it came from. What was really being sold, He says, was a number of crops.

If an Israelite became poor and had to sell some of his land, his nearest relative was to come and buy it back. The book of Ruth shows the rule at work. At the gate of Bethlehem, with ten elders seated as witnesses, Boaz offers Naomi's field to the relative who has first claim, and the man says he will buy it. When he hears that Ruth, the widow of Naomi's son, comes with the land, he backs out, saying, "I might endanger my own estate." Boaz buys the field and marries Ruth. Leviticus goes on to a neighbour who has sunk further and can no longer support himself. He is to be lent money without interest and sold food without profit, and God tells Israel to help him as they would "a foreigner and stranger". It is the phrase He had just used of them.

David was old when he gathered Israel's leaders in Jerusalem. God had told him he would not be the one to build the temple, and David gave to it anyway. He handed over his own treasure, three thousand talents of gold and seven thousand of silver. The leaders followed, and the people rejoiced, the king with them. Then David prayed in front of everyone. He asked who he was to be able to give like this, when they had only given God what came from His hand. And the king, in his own capital, called himself and his people foreigners and strangers in God's sight. Their days on earth, he said, were like a shadow.

keyVerses.text: The land must not be sold permanently, because the land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers.
If any of your fellow Israelites become poor and are unable to support themselves among you, help them as you would a foreigner and stranger, so they can continue to live among you.

But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? Everything comes from you, and we have given you only what comes from your hand. We are foreigners and strangers in your sight, as were all our ancestors.

insights: You did earn it, and Leviticus doesn't argue. The Israelite farmer sowed and reaped his own field, and the ground under him was still God's. If giving feels like a loss, that is how it feels to an owner, and it would be strange never to feel it. Chronicles says David rejoiced greatly, and his prayer says whose he thought the gold was.

Twice in two verses Leviticus gives the aim of the help, which is that the neighbour can go on living among you. So the measure is whether they can stay, and that can cost more than a donation does. The relative at Bethlehem's gate said yes to the field and no once his own estate was at risk.
These were laws for Israel's fields, and they give you no figure for your salary. What carries over is whose it was to begin with. David gave on that footing, and no law told him how much.
reflectQuestions: What do you have that feels least like something lent to you?
Which person near you is closest to going under and hasn't asked you for anything?
thematicGuides.practice: On your next food shop, fill a second bag with the same things you're buying for yourself. Carry it to a food bank, or to the door of someone you know is short this month.
