As you put it down, say David's words under your breath: "Everything comes from you, and we have given you only what comes from your hand."
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I worked for what I have, and when I give some away I feel the gap and check the balance afterwards. You told Israel the land was Yours while they were still in the desert without a field between them. I find that easier to believe about their land than about my wages. Help me hold my money as someone staying on Your ground. Let me notice the neighbour who is going under, and give them some of what You've given me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: We Had Hoped: The Road to Emmaus
thematicGuides.hook: Two disciples told a stranger on the road that they had hoped in Jesus, past tense, and the stranger was Jesus.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: We had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel.
thematicGuides.intro: When something you were sure God was behind falls apart, the natural conclusion is that you misread Him. You stop mentioning it and try to get on. Often that's fair, because sincere people do get God's intentions wrong. The two followers of Jesus in Luke 24 had come to the same conclusion about Him. It was the third day since the crucifixion. They were walking out of Jerusalem when He joined them, and they didn't know Him.
story: On the day the women found the tomb empty, two of Jesus's followers set out for Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem. Jesus came up and fell into step with them, and Luke says they were kept from knowing who He was. He asked what they were talking about, and they stopped in the road, downcast. One of them, Cleopas, asked whether He was the only visitor to Jerusalem who didn't know what had happened. "What things?" He asked. They told Him about Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet their own chief priests and rulers had handed over to be crucified. They added, "we had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel", the one who would set it free. They said it to His face, and He let them tell Him the story of His own death.

Cleopas and his companion had more to tell. That morning some of their women had gone to the tomb, found no body, and come back saying angels had told them He was alive. Others went to look and found it as the women said, "but they did not see Jesus". The two had heard all this and left Jerusalem anyway. Jesus told them they were slow to believe their own prophets, and that the Messiah had to suffer first and come to His glory afterwards. Then He started with Moses and went on through the Prophets, showing them what the Scriptures said about Himself, and they still didn't know who was speaking.

As the two disciples came up to Emmaus, Jesus made as if to go on down the road. They pressed Him to stay, because it was nearly evening, and He went in. At the table it was the guest who took the bread, gave thanks and broke it. As He handed it to them they knew Him, and He was gone. They got up at once and went the seven miles back to Jerusalem, at the end of a day they had just told Him was almost over. They found the Eleven and the others already saying, "It is true! The Lord has risen and has appeared to Simon."

keyVerses.text: As they talked and discussed these things with each other, Jesus himself came up and walked along with them; but they were kept from recognizing him.
How foolish you are, and how slow to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Did not the Messiah have to suffer these things and then enter his glory?
In his great mercy he has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

insights: The two on the road had the right person and a hope with no room in it for a Messiah who suffers. Yours may be a different case. The job or the relationship may really be over, and nothing in this chapter says God was in it after all, or that something better is coming. Jesus did walk with two disappointed people, and He heard them out before He corrected them.

The Simon the Lord appeared to that day is Peter, and 'a living hope' is his phrase. He hangs it on the resurrection of Jesus, whom he had seen alive for himself. That hope won't give back what you lost. It rests on Jesus being alive, so losing the job or the person hasn't taken it away.
reflectQuestions: What did you once hope God was going to do that you now only talk about in the past tense?
If Jesus walked beside you this week and asked what had happened, which part would be hardest to tell Him?
thematicGuides.practice: Walk for ten minutes every day this week, on your own. As you go, tell Jesus the next part of what fell apart, aloud if nobody is near, picking up where you stopped the day before. If walking is hard for you, sit by a window for the same ten minutes. Take the whole week to tell it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I was sure You were in it, and I told people so. Now it's over, and I've gone quiet about it with them and with You. I've started talking about You in the past tense as well. You don't have to tell me I was right. Hear the whole story, as Your Son heard those two on the road, and stay when I've finished. Whatever else has ended, don't let me walk away from You. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jeremiah Buys a Field in a Falling City
thematicGuides.hook: With Babylon's army at the walls, Jeremiah paid seventeen shekels for a field and had the deed stored in a clay jar.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: This is what the LORD Almighty, the God of Israel, says: Houses, fields and vineyards will again be bought in this land.
thematicGuides.intro: It's hard to train for a job or plant a tree when each year's news is worse than the last. Both assume a future, and the people who say things are getting worse are sometimes right. Jeremiah was one of them. He had told Jerusalem for years that it would fall, and while the Babylonian army was besieging it, God told him to buy a field.
story: In the tenth year of King Zedekiah, with Babylon's army around Jerusalem, Jeremiah was confined in the courtyard of the guard. The king had put him there for saying in the LORD's name that the city would be taken. God told him his cousin Hanamel would come and ask him to buy a field at Anathoth, Jeremiah's home village, outside the besieged city. As nearest relative, Jeremiah had the right and the duty to buy it. Hanamel came into the courtyard, as the LORD had said, and asked. "I knew that this was the word of the LORD," Jeremiah says. He bought the field and weighed out seventeen shekels of silver.

Jeremiah's own account of buying his cousin's field leaves out none of the paperwork. He signed and sealed the deed and had it witnessed. There were two copies, one sealed and one open. He handed both to Baruch son of Neriah in front of Hanamel, the witnesses, and all the Jews sitting in the courtyard. So the purchase was made in public, by the man who had said the city would be captured. God's instruction was for Baruch to put the documents in a clay jar "so they will last a long time". The reason He gave was one sentence about property: houses, fields and vineyards would be bought in that land again. No date came with it.

Only once the deed was in Baruch's hands did Jeremiah pray. He began by telling God, "Nothing is too hard for you". Then he came to the siege. "See how the siege ramps are built up to take the city," he said. The prayer ends by setting two things side by side. The city is about to fall to the Babylonians and God has told him to buy a field. It stops there, without a request. God's answer turns Jeremiah's own words into a question. He confirms that the city will burn. After that, He says, fields will again be bought for silver, with deeds signed, sealed and witnessed, and the first place He names is the territory of Benjamin, where Anathoth was.

keyVerses.text: Ah, Sovereign LORD, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and outstretched arm. Nothing is too hard for you.
Though the city will be given into the hands of the Babylonians, you, Sovereign LORD, say to me, 'Buy the field with silver and have the transaction witnessed.'
I am the LORD, the God of all mankind. Is anything too hard for me?

insights: From Hanamel's arrival to the clay jar, Jeremiah's account is a list of things he did. Hope here is a purchase, made with real silver and proper paperwork on God's word, before he understood it.
Jeremiah's hope never needed the bad news to be wrong. The grimmest forecast in the city was his own, and God's answer confirmed it. The field was bought for what God would do after the fire.

Jeremiah was later taken to Egypt, and the book never records him using the field. He had God's word about that one plot, and you have none about your savings or your plans. Paul does tell the Corinthians that, because Christ was raised, what they do for the Lord is not in vain. A repair can be done for Him, and a tree planted. Whether either pays is left open.
reflectQuestions: What have you stopped doing, or decided against starting, because you expect things to get worse?
What would you be willing to start that only the people who come after you might enjoy?
thematicGuides.practice: On the first dry day this week, sit still for five minutes on a park bench or a low wall, in sight of a full-grown tree. Somebody planted it years before it gave any shade. Jeremiah told God about the siege ramps and then about the field, and stopped. Do the same: tell God what you think is getting worse, then the one thing you've put off starting because of it. Stay until the five minutes are up.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I read the news and decide there's no point starting anything. I call it realism, and there's comfort in it, because if nothing lasts I needn't try. I'm quicker to point at the siege ramps than to sign anything. But nothing is too hard for You, and You were talking about deeds and vineyards while the ramps were still going up. Help me do one ordinary thing properly this week, and trust You with what I won't live to see. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Paul Had More Than He Could Bear
thematicGuides.hook: The saying about God never giving you more than you can handle is not in the Bible, and Paul's own experience contradicts it.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Indeed, we felt we had received the sentence of death. But this happened that we might not rely on ourselves but on God, who raises the dead.
thematicGuides.intro: Two of Paul's letters to Corinth survive, and each has a line about how much a person can take. The first says God "will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear". The saying that God never gives you more than you can handle comes from there, though the verse is about temptation, and what it promises is a way out. The second, to the same church, says Paul himself had been pushed past what he could stand. If what you're carrying is more than you can manage, you haven't got faith wrong.
story: Paul was only a few lines into his second letter to Corinth when he told the church there how bad things had been. He didn't want them to be uninformed about the troubles he and his companions had met in the province of Asia. He left out what the troubles were and gave only their weight. The pressure was great, more than they could bear, until they gave up expecting to come through alive. It felt to them like a death sentence already passed. Looking back, he said it had happened so that they would rely on "God, who raises the dead" and stop relying on themselves.

By the time Paul wrote to Corinth about his troubles in Asia, the danger was behind him. God had delivered him and his companions, he wrote, and he didn't stop there. God would deliver them again, and their hope was set on Him to go on delivering them, so Paul didn't expect this rescue to be the last he would need. He gave the Corinthians a part in it, since their prayers would help. This was a church he was on strained terms with. A little further on he explained that he had stayed away to spare them another painful visit. These were the people he told how bad it had been, and whose prayers he counted on.

Paul wrote to the church at Philippi in chains, with his case still undecided. The whole palace guard knew he was held for Christ, and his imprisonment, he told the Philippians, had made most of his fellow believers bolder. Again he looked to a church's prayers. Through them, and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, he expected what had happened to him to turn out for his deliverance. Then he wrote down what he hoped for himself: that he would not be ashamed, and would have enough courage for Christ to be honoured in his body "whether by life or by death". His hope covered either ending.

keyVerses.text: No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to mankind. And God is faithful; he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, he will also provide a way out so that you can endure it.
We were under great pressure, far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired of life itself.
He has delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us again. On him we have set our hope that he will continue to deliver us, as you help us by your prayers.

insights: Paul called Him the God who raises the dead, so his hope had already taken the worst into account. When he says the trouble came so that he would rely on God, he is looking back on what happened to him. Nobody can tell you that is why yours has come.

If things have reached the point where you don't want to be alive, tell someone today: a doctor, a crisis line, or the friend or relative you find easiest to talk to. Paul's own despair was that he expected to die, and he told people about it. He put it in a letter for a whole church to read, and let them help him by praying.
reflectQuestions: What are you carrying at the moment that is more than you can bear, whatever you have been telling people?
How much do the people who would pray for you know about what this has been like?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick one person this week. Tell them how bad it has been, without rounding it down, and ask them to pray for you. If saying it aloud is too much, send a message, something like: 'This has been more than I can cope with. Would you pray for me?' If nobody comes to mind, ask a minister or a chaplain. It is part of what they are for.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, someone told me You would never give me more than I could handle, and I've worn myself out trying to make that true. This is beyond me. I've been saying 'fine' at church because I thought anything else would show how thin my faith is. Your Father raised You from the dead, so nothing I'm dreading is out of His reach. Deliver me, as Paul was delivered. Either way, give me enough courage for tomorrow, and one person I can tell. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Waiting Like a Night Watchman
thematicGuides.hook: Psalm 130 ends with its writer still waiting for a morning he can't hurry and doesn't doubt.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I wait for the LORD, my whole being waits, and in his word I put my hope. I wait for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, more than watchmen wait for the morning.
thematicGuides.intro: You sent the application a fortnight ago, or had the scan last Tuesday, and since then there's been nothing useful left for you to do. You've prayed about it every night. Most of the day now goes on checking your phone and trying not to. The middle of Psalm 130 is written from inside a wait like this. Its writer gives one picture of what the waiting is like, a watchman on the night shift.
story: Psalm 130 starts at the bottom, with "Out of the depths I cry to you, LORD". In eight verses its writer names God eight times and asks Him for one thing only, to listen to his cry for mercy. The one trouble he names is sin, and he counts himself in. If God kept a record of sins, he says, nobody could stand. In the very next line he says what he knows about God, that with Him there is forgiveness, and that because of it people can serve Him with reverence.

Having asked God to listen, the psalmist waits. For four verses he has spoken to God, and now he speaks about Him. His whole being waits for the LORD, he says, and his hope is in God's word, in what God has said. For a picture of it he chooses the men who kept watch through the night. A watchman can't bring the dawn one minute sooner. He also has no reason to wonder whether it will come, because no night he has worked has failed to end. The psalmist says he waits for the Lord more than that. Then he says the line a second time, word for word.

In the last two verses of Psalm 130 the writer turns to his own people. He tells Israel to put their hope in the LORD, because with Him there is unfailing love and full redemption, the word for buying someone back out of debt or slavery. The psalm ends in the future tense: "He himself will redeem Israel from all their sins." No verse says the morning came, so the man urging everyone else to hope is still waiting as he says it. Centuries later an angel told Joseph in a dream what to name the child Mary was carrying. He was to be called Jesus, "because he will save his people from their sins."

keyVerses.text: If you, LORD, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, so that we can, with reverence, serve you.
I wait for the LORD, my whole being waits, and in his word I put my hope. I wait for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, more than watchmen wait for the morning.
Israel, put your hope in the LORD, for with the LORD is unfailing love and with him is full redemption. He himself will redeem Israel from all their sins.

insights: When you've done all you can, waiting can feel like a job you're doing badly. The watchman's whole job is to be at his post when the light comes. Nobody on watch is asked to produce it.

The watchman is sure of the morning, and the psalmist is sure of God: His forgiveness, His unfailing love, a full redemption. The psalm makes no promise about the result or the reply you're waiting for. Its writer says he is waiting for the Lord, and that is a wait he is sure will end.
You may have to tell yourself tonight exactly what you told yourself last night. The psalm does that inside a single verse, and the second time its writer adds nothing new.
reflectQuestions: What are you waiting for at the moment that you can do nothing more to bring about?
The psalmist said one line twice. If you picked one thing God has said to repeat during this wait, what would it be?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick the thing you keep checking for news, whether that's your inbox, the hospital's patient portal or a tracking page. For one evening this week, from six o'clock until you get up the next morning, don't open it. Each time you catch yourself going to look, say the first five words of Psalm 130:5 instead, "I wait for the LORD". If you're expecting an urgent call, leave the ringer on. In the morning, look out of the window before you look at the screen.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I've done what I can about this, and I don't like having nothing left to do. I've checked for news more times today than I'd admit to anyone, as though looking could bring it sooner. You haven't told me how this will go, and I wish You would. You've said that with You there is forgiveness and unfailing love, so that's where I'm putting my hope tonight. I wait for You. I'll probably need to say it again tomorrow, so I will. Keep me at my post until morning. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Grieving, but Not Without Hope
thematicGuides.hook: Paul didn't tell the Thessalonians to stop grieving, and Luke calls the men who mourned Stephen godly.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Brothers and sisters, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope.
thematicGuides.intro: Someone you love has died. You believe what Christians believe about resurrection, and it still hurts far more than you expected, perhaps more than you think it should. People mean well when they say 'they're at peace now', and you can come away feeling that real faith would be coping better. One verse about a burial in Acts speaks to that, and so does a paragraph Paul wrote to a young church whose members had begun to die.
story: Stephen was stoned to death outside Jerusalem while a young man named Saul stood by and approved. Luke, who wrote Acts, records that Stephen saw heaven open before he died, and his phrase for the death itself is that he fell asleep. That same day a great persecution broke out and the Jerusalem church, all but the apostles, was scattered. Luke gives one verse to the burial, with Saul in the verses on either side: "Godly men buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him."

The Saul who approved of Stephen's killing is better known as Paul. Years later he wrote to the church in Thessalonica, which he'd had to leave in a hurry. Since then some of its members had died. He writes so that the others will not "grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope." The sentence could have ended at the word grieve, and it doesn't. He rules out one kind of grief, the kind with nothing at the end of it. His reason is that Jesus died and rose again, and so God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him. Three times in these few verses he calls their death sleep, the word Luke uses for Stephen's death.

Paul goes on to tell the Thessalonians that the dead in Christ will rise, and he ends on being with the Lord for ever. Then he tells them what to do with this: encourage one another with these words. Paul would have grieved too, by his own account. From prison he told the church at Philippi how close their messenger Epaphroditus had come to dying. God had mercy on the sick man, he wrote, and on Paul as well, sparing him "sorrow upon sorrow". That is the letter in which he says that to die is gain.

keyVerses.text: Godly men buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him.

Brothers and sisters, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope. For we believe that Jesus died and rose again, and so we believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in him.
And so we will be with the Lord forever. Therefore encourage one another with these words.

insights: The loss is as large with hope as without it. The people the Thessalonians had buried were still gone. Because Jesus died and rose, death is not the last thing that happens to those who are His.

Paul is writing about a particular group, "those who have fallen asleep in him", people who died trusting Jesus. If you don't know where the person you've lost stood with God, these verses don't say, and nobody else can tell you either. You can leave that with God, who knew them better than anyone did. Whoever you are mourning, grieving hard is no failure of faith.

Paul ends this paragraph by telling them to encourage one another, and that can't be done alone. Let a friend, or someone at your church, see how you are. If weeks pass and you still can't sleep or eat, tell your doctor as well.
reflectQuestions: What have you picked up, from other people or from yourself, about how a Christian is supposed to grieve?
Since the person you love died, who have you been honest with about how you are?
thematicGuides.practice: Find a quarter of an hour today when you can be alone. Sit with a photograph of them, or something that was theirs, and say their name out loud. Then tell God one thing you miss about them, in the words you'd use to a friend. If you cry, let it come. Before you get up, read Acts 8:2 aloud. It is one sentence long, and it is about people doing what you have just done.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, You died and rose again. I believe that, and I still miss them more than I know how to say. I keep picking up my phone to tell them something before I remember. I'd half expected that trusting You would make this hurt less, and I've been ashamed that it hasn't. Thank You that the men who buried Stephen mourned him hard and are still called godly. Let me grieve as someone who has hope. On the days I can't feel any, hold on to me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Don't Raise My Hopes
thematicGuides.hook: A woman in Shunem told Elisha not to raise her hopes, and when the worst came she went straight back to him.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: 'Did I ask you for a son, my lord?' she said. 'Didn't I tell you, 'Don't raise my hopes'?'
thematicGuides.intro: A woman stood in the doorway of the room she'd had built on her roof for the prophet Elisha, and he told her that in a year she would be holding a son. She objected, "Please, man of God, don't mislead your servant!" If you've had your hopes up before and been badly hurt, you'll recognise that answer. It can seem safer to want nothing. She says it to him again later in 2 Kings 4, with far more cause.
story: The woman of Shunem was well-to-do, and she fed Elisha whenever he passed through. The room on the roof was her idea, down to the bed, the table, the chair and the lamp. When he offered to speak to the king for her in return, she answered that she had a home among her own people. His servant Gehazi pointed out that she had no son and that her husband was old. Elisha called her back and promised her a son within the year, and she asked him not to mislead her. The boy was born the next year, as Elisha had said.

One day, out among the reapers with his father, the boy complained of his head. A servant carried him to his mother, and he sat on her lap until noon and then died. She laid him on Elisha's bed, shut the door and asked her husband for a donkey. When he asked why she was going to the prophet on an ordinary day, she said it was all right. At Mount Carmel Gehazi ran out to ask if all was well, and she gave him the same answer. Then she took hold of Elisha's feet. Gehazi moved to push her away, and Elisha stopped him, saying she was in bitter distress and that the LORD had not told him why. "Did I ask you for a son, my lord?" she said. "Didn't I tell you, 'Don't raise my hopes'?" Nowhere in the chapter does she say that the boy is dead.

Elisha sent Gehazi ahead with his staff, but the mother swore she would not leave Elisha himself, so he went with her. The staff brought no response. Elisha went in alone, shut the door and prayed to the LORD, then twice stretched himself out on the boy, who sneezed seven times and opened his eyes. She bowed to the ground, took her son and went out. That is how it ended for this one woman. Most parents who have lost a child, in the Bible and since, were not given the child back.

keyVerses.text: 'About this time next year,' Elisha said, 'you will hold a son in your arms.' 'No, my lord!' she objected. 'Please, man of God, don't mislead your servant!'

When she reached the man of God at the mountain, she took hold of his feet. Gehazi came over to push her away, but the man of God said, 'Leave her alone! She is in bitter distress, but the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me why.'
But the child's mother said, 'As surely as the LORD lives and as you live, I will not leave you.' So he got up and followed her.

insights: She tells God's prophet she never wanted her hopes raised, first in the doorway and again at his feet. Neither time is she corrected, and the only person rebuked is Gehazi, for trying to move her on. If you're afraid to hope, you can tell God exactly that.

Hebrews 11 remembers mothers like her, "Women received back their dead, raised to life again", and the same verse goes on to people who were tortured. All of them, it says, were commended for their faith. A loss that was never reversed says nothing against the faith of whoever bore it, and nor does a longing that was never met.

There may be days when you can't bring yourself to ask God for anything. At Carmel she asks Elisha for nothing. When he sends his servant ahead with a staff, she swears she will not leave the prophet himself, and he gets up and follows her.
reflectQuestions: What is the thing you've stopped hoping for because hoping began to cost too much?
What would you tell God about the thing you keep telling other people you're fine about?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, take a card and write one sentence to God beginning 'Don't raise my hopes about', finished with the thing you've stopped letting yourself want. Date it and keep it in your wallet, or in a paper Bible at 2 Kings 4. Writing it commits you to nothing beyond telling God where you stand, which is all she did in the doorway.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, there's something I've stopped asking You for, and it has been easier that way. I tell people I'm content, and some days it's true. What I haven't told You is that I'm afraid to want it again. I'd sooner You gave me nothing than gave and took away, and I know that isn't a brave thing to pray. I can't promise to hope. I can take hold of You, as she did, and I will not leave. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Habakkuk's Joy on Shaking Legs
thematicGuides.hook: Habakkuk says he will rejoice in the LORD two verses after admitting that his legs are trembling.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will be joyful in God my Savior.
thematicGuides.intro: Joy is usually thought of as the feeling you get when something has gone well, and most of the time that's what it is. You're glad when the person you were worried about finally rings. That leaves you with very little in the months when the news is bad and likely to get worse. The prophet Habakkuk prayed at a time like that, and joy is where his short book ends.
story: Habakkuk looked at the violence all round him, with the law paralysed, and took it to God as a complaint. "How long, LORD, must I call for help, but you do not listen?" God did answer, and the news was worse, because He was raising up the Babylonians, who laughed at fortified cities. God Himself called them guilty people "whose own strength is their god". Habakkuk argued, then said he would stand on the ramparts and watch for a reply. The reply was that the plunderers would be plundered in their turn, at an appointed time, and that he was to wait for it however slow it seemed.

With an invasion coming, Habakkuk prayed. He asked God to do in his own day what He had done before, and in wrath to remember mercy. For most of the prayer he described God coming out to deliver His people and trampling the sea. Then he came to his own body. What he had heard, he said, set his heart pounding, his lips quivering and his legs trembling. Before the verse was out he said he would wait patiently for the day of calamity to come on the nation invading his own. So the invasion hadn't been called off. What he was waiting for lay on the far side of it.

When his prayer had three verses left, Habakkuk went through a farm, from the fig tree down to the cattle stalls, six things and every one of them failed or empty. He put 'though' in front of all of it and 'yet' after it. He would rejoice in the LORD, who was his strength and gave him feet like a deer's. Those were the legs that had been trembling a moment before. David has almost the same line in Psalm 18, which he sang when the LORD had delivered him from all his enemies. Habakkuk used it with his enemy still on the way. His last line hands the prayer to the director of music, for stringed instruments.

keyVerses.text: I heard and my heart pounded, my lips quivered at the sound; decay crept into my bones, and my legs trembled. Yet I will wait patiently for the day of calamity to come on the nation invading us.

Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will be joyful in God my Savior.
The Sovereign LORD is my strength; he makes my feet like the feet of a deer, he enables me to tread on the heights.

insights: Habakkuk says what he will rejoice in, and it is God Himself. Every item on his list is something God gives, and he has just faced losing them all. When the six go, what he is glad of is still there.

Arguing with God, Habakkuk had said that the invader "rejoices and is glad" as well, over a full net, and goes on to burn incense to the net. Habakkuk finishes the other way round, with the pen empty, glad of the LORD and calling Him his strength.
Habakkuk put his pounding heart into a prayer meant for the director of music, and didn't take it out. If dread is with you most days, tell a doctor and a friend as well as God.
reflectQuestions: If you wrote your own verse 17, with 'though' in front of each thing you've lost or are afraid of losing, what would be on the list?
What do you know about God that would still be true if everything on that list went?
thematicGuides.practice: Go for a twenty-minute walk on your own this week, without headphones. On the way out, tell God what has gone and what you're afraid will go next, one thing at a time, as Habakkuk did. Where you turn for home, stop and say Habakkuk 3:18 aloud. On the way back, tell Him what is still true of Him with all of that gone. If walking is hard, do the same from a chair.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I'd rather have the figs back. When I say I want joy I mostly mean I want the stalls full again, and You know that. My heart is going fast about what's coming and I can't slow it down. I can't promise You a glad mood. I can say that You are still my God and my Saviour with the pen empty, and that I'm glad of You. Be my strength, and steady my legs for tomorrow. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Ten Were Healed and One Came Back
thematicGuides.hook: All ten men with leprosy did what Jesus told them, and only one turned round on the road to thank Him.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: One of them, when he saw he was healed, came back, praising God in a loud voice. He threw himself at Jesus' feet and thanked him, and he was a Samaritan.
thematicGuides.intro: Thanking God is harder than asking Him, and the reason is a dull one. By the time a prayer is answered you're busy with what the answer has made possible: the job starts on Monday, or the all-clear means you can book the trip. From the inside, forgetting to say thank you feels like getting on with things. Luke tells a story about ten men who all got what they asked Jesus for.
story: Jesus was on His way to Jerusalem, travelling along the border between Samaria and Galilee. As He went into a village, ten men who had leprosy met Him. They stood at a distance, as the Law of Moses required of people with such a disease. "Jesus, Master, have pity on us!" they called out in a loud voice. When Jesus saw them, all He said was that they should go and show themselves to the priests, which is what the Law asked of someone whose disease had already cleared. All ten set off with it still on them. As they went, they were cleansed.

One of the ten saw that he was healed, and he turned round. The road he left led to a priest, and through the priest to home. In Leviticus the inspection and the rites that follow take eight days, and at the end a person who has been living outside the community belongs to it again. This one came back praising God, and he was as loud about it as all ten had been when they called for pity. Then the man who had stood at a distance threw himself at Jesus' feet and thanked Him. Luke holds one fact back until the end of the sentence, that he was a Samaritan.

With the man still at His feet, Jesus asked whether all ten had not been cleansed, where the other nine were, and whether no one had come back to give praise to God except this foreigner. No answer to any of the three is recorded. The man had thanked Jesus, and Jesus called it giving praise to God. The others had set off down the road He sent them on, and that is the last we see of them. Then Jesus told the man to rise and go. His faith, He said, had made him well. The nine had clean skin by then as well. They weren't there to hear Him speak.

keyVerses.text: One of them, when he saw he was healed, came back, praising God in a loud voice. He threw himself at Jesus' feet and thanked him, and he was a Samaritan.
Jesus asked, 'Were not all ten cleansed? Where are the other nine? Has no one returned to give praise to God except this foreigner?' Then he said to him, 'Rise and go; your faith has made you well.'
Praise the LORD, my soul, and forget not all his benefits.

insights: What the nine left out was coming back, and Jesus noticed. Gratitude in this story is an interruption. You stop on the way to something good and go back to the One who gave it.

Jesus had spoken of a foreigner with leprosy before. At Nazareth He recalled Naaman the Syrian, the only one cleansed, He said, out of many with leprosy in Elisha's day. Naaman was healed at a distance too, washing in the Jordan as he'd been told, and 2 Kings says he "went back to the man of God" to say what he now knew about Israel's God.
reflectQuestions: Think of the last thing you prayed hard for and then received. What did you do in the first hour after you knew?
What are you on your way to at the moment that makes stopping to thank God feel like a delay?
thematicGuides.practice: Every day this week, the first time something goes the way you hoped (the bus comes, the awkward call goes better than you feared), stop before you do the next thing. Stand still for ten seconds and thank God for it, out loud if you're alone. Psalm 103 tells the soul to "forget not all his benefits", and this way one a day doesn't get forgotten.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I'm loud when I need something and quiet once I have it. There are things I begged You for that I now file under things that worked out. One of them is on my mind now, and I thank You for it, late as this is. When the next answer comes, stop me on the road before I've gone far, and turn me round. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Joy of the Lord and a Crowd in Tears
thematicGuides.hook: The famous line about joy was first spoken to people in tears, who were then sent off to eat.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Go and enjoy choice food and sweet drinks, and send some to those who have nothing prepared. This day is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
thematicGuides.intro: The people who first heard "the joy of the LORD is your strength" were crying when it was said to them. They had been listening to God's Law read aloud since daybreak. If you've lately seen how far you've drifted from God and feel wretched about it, you're nearer to that crowd than most people who quote the line. Nehemiah said it on a feast day, and the feast was why he asked them to dry their eyes.
story: The people gathered in the square in front of the Water Gate, and it was they who told Ezra the priest to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses. Men and women came, and anyone else able to understand. A high wooden platform had been built for the occasion. When Ezra opened the book on it the whole crowd stood up, and when he praised the LORD they answered Amen and bowed with their faces to the ground. He read from daybreak until noon, while thirteen Levites went through it with the people, making it clear and giving the meaning, so that they understood what was being read.

The people had wept as they listened. Nehemiah the governor, Ezra and the Levites told them all not to mourn or weep, because of what day it was. "This day is holy to the LORD your God." It was the first day of the seventh month, which in the Law of Moses was a festival, a day of rest and trumpet blasts. So Nehemiah sent them off to eat and drink well and to send some to anyone who had nothing prepared, and it was then that he said the joy of the LORD was their strength. The Levites calmed the people and told them to be still. Then they all went and ate and drank and sent food out, and celebrated with great joy, because they now understood the words they had wept through that morning.

The next day the heads of families gathered round Ezra to study the Law, and found in it a festival due that same month. For seven days Israel was to live in shelters made of branches, as their ancestors had after Egypt. So people fetched branches of olive, myrtle and palm and built shelters on their roofs and in the city squares. The festival hadn't been kept like this since the days of Joshua, and their joy was very great. Then, on the twenty-fourth of that month, they gathered again, fasting, in sackcloth, with dust on their heads. They read the Law for a quarter of the day and spent another quarter confessing and worshipping. In their prayer that day they called God forgiving, gracious and compassionate.

keyVerses.text: Go and enjoy choice food and sweet drinks, and send some to those who have nothing prepared. This day is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
Then all the people went away to eat and drink, to send portions of food and to celebrate with great joy, because they now understood the words that had been made known to them.
But you are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love. Therefore you did not desert them.

insights: Three times in three verses the crowd is told not to grieve, and each time the reason is the day. Nobody says the tears were wrong. Once the festival was over, sorrow had a day of its own, with sackcloth and hours of confession. If you are grieving, nothing in this chapter tells you to stop.

The feast came before the confession. On the day they were sent off to eat, these people hadn't yet fasted or confessed or promised anything. The feast had been in the Law since long before any of them were born, and Nehemiah told them the joy of the LORD was their strength that day, as they were.
reflectQuestions: When you last saw clearly that you had drifted from God, what did you assume He wanted from you first?
If you gave your sorrow a day of its own, as Jerusalem did on the twenty-fourth, what would you do on it?
thematicGuides.practice: Ask a friend you can talk to about God to eat with you this week, and make it food you both enjoy. During the meal, tell them, in a couple of sentences, the thing you've seen lately about yourself and God that made you feel worst. Then read Nehemiah 8:9-12 together and ask what they notice. They don't have to fix anything.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've seen how far I've drifted, and part of me thinks I should stay miserable for a good while before I come near You, to prove I mean it. That crowd was sent off to eat on the very day they wept. I do need to say sorry properly, and I'll give it the time it deserves. Today let me be glad that You are still speaking to me, and that this time I understood what I heard. Let Your joy be my strength. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Singing Songs to a Heavy Heart
thematicGuides.hook: Paul told a whole church he was sorrowful, and one proverb warns whoever tries to sing the sadness away.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Like one who takes away a garment on a cold day, or like vinegar poured on a wound, is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.
thematicGuides.intro: Someone at the church door asks how you are, and you've said 'Good, thanks' before you've thought about it. It's easier than the true answer. Everyone else in the room looks glad to be there. After enough Sundays of that, you start to suspect a real Christian would feel what the songs say. Proverbs has a saying about songs and heavy hearts, and it doesn't side with the songs.
story: Nehemiah was cupbearer to the king of Persia when word came from Judah that Jerusalem's wall was broken down and its gates burned. He sat down and wept, and for some days he mourned, fasted and prayed. About four months later he took the king his wine. "I had not been sad in his presence before," he writes. The king asked why his face looked so sad when he wasn't ill. Nehemiah says he was very much afraid. He still gave the true answer, that the city where his ancestors were buried lay in ruins. The king asked, "What is it you want?"

In Proverbs 25, the person who sings songs to a heavy heart is like someone who takes your coat away on a cold day, or pours vinegar on a wound. The saying just before it is about relying on an unfaithful person in a time of trouble, which is like a broken tooth or a lame foot. The one before that is about a false witness against a neighbour, who is like a club, a sword or a sharp arrow. So the singer is listed with the liar and the friend who lets you down.

Some people in the church at Corinth doubted that Paul was a true apostle. In his second letter to them he listed what commended him as a servant of God. He began with hardship: beatings, imprisonments, riots, sleepless nights, hunger. He ended with a run of pairs joined by 'yet', and one of them is "sorrowful, yet always rejoicing". The sorrow goes on the list with the beatings and the hunger, as part of what commends him. His next sentence is, "We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians, and opened wide our hearts to you." He asks them to open theirs in return.

keyVerses.text: Even in laughter the heart may ache, and rejoicing may end in grief.
Like one who takes away a garment on a cold day, or like vinegar poured on a wound, is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.
sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything.

insights: The saying about songs gives the heavy heart no instruction. Its warning is for the person doing the singing. If a breezy 'cheer up' has ever left you feeling colder than before, Proverbs expected that. Back in chapter 12, a heart weighed down by anxiety is cheered up by a kind word.

Paul told the Romans he had great sorrow and unceasing anguish over his own people. He also told the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord always. Rejoicing in the Lord, as Paul meant it, left him free to say he was sad.

The king saw the sadness in Nehemiah's face and asked. Yours may not show. Proverbs 14 says a heart can ache even in laughter, and that may be true of people who look glad on a Sunday too. If the heaviness has gone on for weeks, or you can't sleep or get through a day's work for it, a doctor should hear about it, and so should a friend.
reflectQuestions: What did the last person who really helped you when you were low do differently from the people who tried to cheer you up?
Paul put sorrow and rejoicing into one sentence about himself. If you wrote a sentence like that about this week, what would go in each half?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick someone who has been kind to you before and, by next Sunday, tell them how you've been, without the smile. Two sentences will do, over a cup of tea or in a message. Say at the start that you aren't asking to be cheered up or fixed, and that you'd just like someone to know. If they offer to pray with you, let them.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I've said I'm fine so many times that it comes out before I can stop it. On Sundays I've mouthed the songs and gone home as heavy as I came. So here is the true answer. I'm sad, and I'm tired of covering it. I'm glad Paul could be sorrowful and still be Yours. Show me one person I can tell the truth to, and help me get the words out. I do want to be glad in You as well, and for it to be real. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Ecclesiastes Says Enjoy Your Dinner
thematicGuides.hook: The Bible's bleakest book calls being able to enjoy a meal a gift from God, and its writer saw people who weren't given it.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: A person can do nothing better than to eat and drink and find satisfaction in their own toil. This too, I see, is from the hand of God.
thematicGuides.intro: You can go a long time without enjoying anything. Either the next task is already pulling at you while you eat, or the meal is good and you feel faintly guilty, as if you ought to be doing something more useful. Ecclesiastes opens by calling everything meaningless and keeps returning to death, and five times it stops to commend eating, drinking and enjoying your work. It also has a man in it who never stops working and asks why he is depriving himself of enjoyment.
story: The writer calls himself the Teacher, a king in Jerusalem. He once set out to test himself with pleasure, building houses and planting vineyards. He owned more herds and flocks than anyone in Jerusalem before him and refused his heart no pleasure. Then he looked over it all and found nothing gained. He came to hate life, and wrote that work is grief and pain and that even at night the mind doesn't rest. The very next verse says a person can do nothing better than eat, drink and find satisfaction in their work. He says he built the houses for himself. The meal, he says, is from the hand of God.

The Teacher saw a man who was all alone, with no son and no brother. There was no end to the man's work, and his eyes were never content with his wealth. He asked who he was toiling for and why he was depriving himself of enjoyment. The Teacher calls it a miserable business. A chapter later he writes that when God gives someone wealth and also the ability to enjoy it, that is a gift of God. He had seen people with wealth, possessions and honour, lacking nothing their hearts desired, whom God had not granted the ability to enjoy any of it. Strangers enjoyed it instead.

In chapter 9 the Teacher says the dead know nothing and even their name is forgotten. Two verses later he comes to eating and drinking for the fifth time, and this time it's an order: "Go, eat your food with gladness, and drink your wine with a joyful heart, for God has already approved what you do." He is talking about the meal. God gave it, so enjoying it needs no further permission, though the book's last verse still says every deed will be judged. The next lines are written to a married man, and tell him to enjoy life with the wife he loves.

keyVerses.text: A person can do nothing better than to eat and drink and find satisfaction in their own toil. This too, I see, is from the hand of God, for without him, who can eat or find enjoyment?
When God gives someone wealth and possessions, and the ability to enjoy them, to accept their lot and be happy in their toil, this is a gift of God.

So I commend the enjoyment of life, because there is nothing better for a person under the sun than to eat and drink and be glad. Then joy will accompany them in their toil all the days of the life God has given them under the sun.

insights: In Ecclesiastes, having something and being able to enjoy it are separate gifts. If you can taste tonight's dinner, you have both, and the second deserves thanks as much as the first. If you haven't been able to enjoy anything for weeks, tell a doctor.

In chapter 8 the Teacher complains that good people get what the wicked deserve, and his next verse begins, "So I commend the enjoyment of life". Two verses on he says no one can comprehend what goes on under the sun. He commends the meal with the question still open, so you needn't settle it before you eat yours.

If dinner feels like time you ought to be spending on something more useful, look at how Jesus described Himself. "The Son of Man came eating and drinking", He said, and He quoted the people who called Him a glutton for it.
reflectQuestions: Which ordinary good thing in your week do you most often rush through or feel guilty about enjoying?
What are you waiting to have finished or sorted out before you let yourself enjoy what's already in front of you?
thematicGuides.practice: Go without a screen at one meal a day, from today until the same day next week. Put your phone in another room and leave the television off. Before you eat, thank God in a sentence for the food and for whoever is eating with you, or for the quiet if you're alone. Then eat slowly enough to taste it.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, You came eating and drinking, and people held it against You. I've treated enjoyment as something I earn once the work is finished. The work is never finished. I ate lunch today and couldn't tell You what it was. The food, the work and the people I eat with all came from You. I've hardly said so. Teach me to take them from Your hand without guilt, and to do some good with the strength they give me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Seventy-Two Came Back with Joy
thematicGuides.hook: Jesus heard how well the seventy-two had done, agreed, and then gave them a safer thing to be glad about.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: However, do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.
thematicGuides.intro: Seventy-two people came back to Jesus from the towns He had sent them to, and the word Luke uses for their mood is joy. If things are going well for you at the moment (a good set of results, or kind words about something you did at church), you'll know the feeling. What Jesus said to them can sound as though He wanted them less happy. That's hard to square with the next verse, where Jesus Himself is full of joy.
story: Jesus was on His way to Jerusalem when He appointed seventy-two others and sent them ahead in pairs to every town He was about to visit. They were to take no purse, bag or sandals. He told them He was sending them out like lambs among wolves. In a town that welcomed them they were to heal the sick and say that the kingdom of God had come near. In a town that didn't, they were to go into its streets, wipe its dust from their feet, and say it again. He went on to speak of Chorazin and Bethsaida, towns where miracles had already been performed and the people had not repented.

The seventy-two came back with joy and told Jesus about something their instructions hadn't mentioned. Even the demons, they said, submitted to them in His name. Jesus answered that He had seen Satan fall like lightning from heaven, and that He had given them authority to overcome all the power of the enemy. Then He said 'however'. They were to rejoice that their names were written in heaven, and not that the spirits submitted to them. In the chapter before, a man in a crowd had called out to Jesus to look at his only son, whom a spirit kept seizing. He told Jesus, "I begged your disciples to drive it out, but they could not."

At that time, Luke says, Jesus was full of joy through the Holy Spirit, and He praised His Father aloud. The prayer doesn't mention demons. His joy was over a gift from the Father to people nobody would have called wise or learned. He called them little children. Then He turned to His disciples and said privately, "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see." Many prophets and kings, He told them, had wanted to see what they were seeing and hear what they were hearing, and never did.

keyVerses.text: The seventy-two returned with joy and said, 'Lord, even the demons submit to us in your name.'
However, do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.

At that time Jesus, full of joy through the Holy Spirit, said, 'I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this is what you were pleased to do.'

insights: Jesus had just confirmed their success in the strongest terms, so 'do not rejoice' can't mean it was nothing. A good month is worth thanking God for. Jesus is telling them which to rest their joy on, the spirits that obeyed them or their names written in heaven. He chooses the one that was done for them.

Jesus allowed for bad results before anyone set off. His instructions cover the town that refuses, and the towns He named had seen most of His own miracles, Matthew says, without repenting. So a pair could do everything He asked and come back with nothing to report. If your joy this month rests on how things went, it will go the month things go badly.

Hebrews later describes the whole church as people "whose names are written in heaven". So every Christian has the thing Jesus told the seventy-two to rejoice in. It comes with trusting Him, which is why the newest believer has it in full and nobody gets more of it by having a good year.
reflectQuestions: How would the last month have felt if the thing that's going best for you had gone badly?
When did you last feel glad to belong to Jesus on a day when nothing in particular had gone well?
thematicGuides.practice: The seventy-two were sent to tell people the kingdom of God had come near, and somebody once told you about Jesus. Today, on the way home or once you've eaten, send that person one message. Leave this month's good news out. Say you're glad to belong to Jesus, and thank them for their part in it. If you can't reach them, send it to someone who has kept you going since.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, it has gone well lately, and I've told the story a few times now. It gets a little better with each telling. It came from You, and I'm grateful. I know that if it had gone badly I'd think less of myself tonight, and perhaps less of You. Thank You that my name is written in heaven and that this month's results didn't put it there. Make that the thing I'm most glad about. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Forgiving Someone Who Never Said Sorry
thematicGuides.hook: With no apology in sight, Stephen and Paul left the matter with God, and Paul still told Timothy to be on his guard.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: When they hurled their insults at him, he did not retaliate; when he suffered, he made no threats. Instead, he entrusted himself to him who judges justly.
thematicGuides.intro: Forgiveness is usually pictured as a scene with two people in it. One says sorry and means it, the other forgives, and something between them is mended. That is the best ending there is. But the person who hurt you may never say it. Jesus, Stephen and Paul were each wronged by people who offered no apology, and each left the judging to God.
story: When Jesus was arrested, Peter drew a sword and cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant, Malchus. Jesus told Peter to put the sword away. Later, while the high priest was questioning Him, an official slapped Jesus in the face. Jesus told the man to say what He had said wrong, then asked, "But if I spoke the truth, why did you strike me?" The man who drew that sword went on to write a letter. In it he tells slaves, some of them under harsh masters, to follow in the steps of Jesus, who didn't hit back when He was insulted and made no threats when He suffered, trusting God to judge fairly.

Stephen told the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, that they had betrayed and murdered the Righteous One, and that he could see Him standing at God's right hand. At that they covered their ears, rushed at him, dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses left their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen fell on his knees and cried out, asking the Lord not to hold this sin against them. Sin was his own word for it, with the stones still coming. That prayer was the last thing he said. No one there is recorded as being sorry, and Saul, who approved of the killing, began dragging men and women from their houses to prison.

The young man who minded the coats at Stephen's stoning became the apostle Paul. In a letter to Timothy he says that Alexander the metalworker did him a great deal of harm, and that the Lord will repay Alexander for it. He leaves it there, except to add that Timothy too should be on his guard against the man. So Paul was on his guard already. Then he turns to his first defence in court, where everyone deserted him, and writes, "May it not be held against them." Stephen had asked much the same for the men who killed him, with Saul standing by.

keyVerses.text: When they hurled their insults at him, he did not retaliate; when he suffered, he made no threats. Instead, he entrusted himself to him who judges justly.

While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.' Then he fell on his knees and cried out, 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them.' When he had said this, he fell asleep.
Alexander the metalworker did me a great deal of harm. The Lord will repay him for what he has done. You too should be on your guard against him, because he strongly opposed our message.

insights: None of them said it didn't matter. Jesus asked the man who slapped Him why, Stephen called the stoning a sin, and Paul put the harm Alexander did him in writing. Handing the case to God keeps the wrong on the record, and what you give up is collecting on it yourself.

You can give up revenge without trusting the person again. Paul left Alexander to the Lord and, in his next sentence, warned Timothy about him. The slaves Peter wrote to couldn't walk away, but if you can, nothing here asks you to stay within reach of someone who harms you, or to keep a crime from the police.

Jesus says in Luke 17, "if they repent, forgive them", and Christians differ over whether full forgiveness waits for that. On either view, a mended relationship needs both of you. Leaving them with God needs only you.
reflectQuestions: If you handed the whole case to a judge who gets it right, what would you most want Him to know?
What form does hitting back take for you at the moment, even if it only ever happens in your head?
thematicGuides.practice: Set aside twenty minutes this week and write the case out on one sheet of paper: what they did and what it cost you. Don't tidy it up. At the bottom write 'Handed to God' and the date. Fold the sheet and keep it somewhere private. When the anger comes back, take it out and read the last line.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, You saw what was done to me, and that they have never said sorry. In my head I've put them on trial a hundred times. I win every time, and I'm no better for it. I'm handing the case to You, because You judge justly. I may never see what You do with it, and I still want to watch. I'm giving up my turn at paying them back. When I reach for it again, take it out of my hands. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Peter Asked How Many Times to Forgive
thematicGuides.hook: The answer Jesus gave Peter was seventy-seven times, the figure a man in Genesis had claimed for his revenge.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant just as I had on you?
thematicGuides.intro: Forgiving somebody once is hard enough. The fourth time, for the same thing, is harder, because by then the last apology has turned out to be worth very little. Forgiving starts to feel like giving permission, and like being taken for a fool. Peter put the question to Jesus as arithmetic and got a number back.
story: After Cain killed his brother Abel, God said that anyone who killed Cain would suffer vengeance seven times over, and put a mark on him so that no one would. Five generations down Cain's line comes Lamech, and Genesis gives him a short poem, spoken to his two wives. He has killed a man for wounding him, he says, a young man for injuring him. If Cain is avenged seven times, Lamech will be avenged seventy-seven. God's seven had been a protection placed on a guilty man. Lamech multiplies it by eleven and awards it to himself.

Jesus had been telling His disciples what to do when a brother or sister sins. Peter asked how many times he should forgive, and suggested seven, which as it happens was the figure God set for Cain. Jesus answered with Lamech's. In the NIV the phrase "seventy-seven times" comes in those two places and nowhere else. Some other Bibles give Jesus' number as seventy times seven. Then Jesus told a story about a servant brought before his king owing ten thousand bags of gold, each one about twenty years of a labourer's wages. The king ordered him sold, with his wife and children. The servant fell on his knees and begged for time to pay. The king took pity, cancelled the whole debt and let him go.

On his way out, the forgiven servant found a fellow servant who owed him a hundred silver coins, about a hundred days' wages. He grabbed him and began to choke him. The man fell to his knees and said, "Be patient with me, and I will pay it back", almost exactly what the forgiven servant had said to the king. He was refused, and thrown into prison. The other servants told the king. He called the forgiven servant wicked, reminded him of the debt he had been let off, and in anger handed him to the jailers to be tortured until he paid everything. Jesus then said, "This is how my heavenly Father will treat each of you unless you forgive your brother or sister from your heart."

keyVerses.text: Lamech said to his wives, 'Adah and Zillah, listen to me; wives of Lamech, hear my words. I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for injuring me. If Cain is avenged seven times, then Lamech seventy-seven times.'

Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, 'Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother or sister who sins against me? Up to seven times?' Jesus answered, 'I tell you, not seven times, but seventy-seven times.'

Then the master called the servant in. 'You wicked servant,' he said, 'I canceled all that debt of yours because you begged me to. Shouldn't you have had mercy on your fellow servant just as I had on you?'

insights: Lamech counted the revenge he was due, and Peter counted the forgiveness he owed. Jesus answered the request for a limit with a reason, the size of what you yourself have been let off. A hundred days' pay is a real debt, as what you're owed may be, and He sets it beside ten thousand bags of gold.
The servant the king condemns has just been let off a fortune, and he has his hands on another man's throat. Someone being hurt, who finds forgiving slow and hard, is not doing what he did.

Forgiving again doesn't oblige you to let it happen again, or to stay where it will. Just before Peter's question, Jesus says to raise a wrong with the person and, if they won't listen, to bring others in. If raising it alone isn't safe, go to someone else first.
reflectQuestions: If you know how many times one person has wronged you, what has carrying that number been doing to you lately?
What would forgiving the person who keeps doing it look like if it didn't mean letting it happen again?
thematicGuides.practice: Somebody probably owes you something small, the tenner you lent or the book that never came back. This week, go and see them, or ring them, and tell them it's theirs to keep and they owe you nothing. Then never raise it again. Leave the person who keeps hurting you out of this, and find out what cancelling feels like when the amount is one you can manage.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I know the number, and the dates of the worst ones. I've kept the account because I was afraid that dropping it would mean it was all right, and it wasn't. You wrote off more for me than anyone will ever owe me. Help me forgive this again from my heart, and give me the courage to say what needs saying so that it stops. Show me who to ask for help with that. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Still Feeling Guilty: The Priest Who Sat Down
thematicGuides.hook: Hebrews says four times that Jesus sat down, a detail for anyone who keeps confessing what God has already forgiven.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: If our hearts condemn us, we know that God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.
thematicGuides.intro: Hebrews 10 bothers to say what position Israel's priests worked in. They stood. That matters if you've asked God to forgive the same thing more times than you can count, believe He has, and still feel the weight of it. Guilt that stays on after you've confessed is common, and the New Testament writers knew about it.
story: Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the day for dealing with the whole people's sins, Israel's high priest sacrificed a bull for himself and his household and a goat for the people. Then he laid both hands on the head of a second, live goat, confessed the people's sins over it, and had it led away into the wilderness. Leviticus says that on that day they would be clean from all their sins. A year later he did it all again. Hebrews 10 calls those sacrifices "an annual reminder of sins." If they had finished the job, it points out, they would have stopped, and the worshippers "would no longer have felt guilty for their sins."

In Hebrews 10 every priest of Israel is on his feet, offering the same sacrifices day after day, though they can never take sins away. Jesus offered one sacrifice for sins, for all time, and sat down at the right hand of God. The letter says so four times, the first in its opening lines. Then comes God's promise, given through Jeremiah: "Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more." Where sins are forgiven, no further sacrifice is needed. The offering for the thing you keep confessing has been made, and the priest who made it is sitting down.

Early in his first letter John says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just and will forgive us. Two chapters later he comes to the case where our hearts condemn us. He says 'our', counting himself in, and tells his readers how to set their hearts at rest: God is greater than our hearts, and knows everything. John's Gospel has Peter say something very like it. Peter had disowned Jesus three times. After the resurrection Jesus asks him three times whether he loves Him. The third time Peter is hurt, and says, "Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you."

keyVerses.text: Day after day every priest stands and performs his religious duties; again and again he offers the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God.
For by one sacrifice he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy.
This is how we know that we belong to the truth and how we set our hearts at rest in his presence: If our hearts condemn us, we know that God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.

insights: Hebrews 10:14 says of the same people that they have been made perfect for ever by one sacrifice and are still being made holy. What had to be offered for your sins is complete, while you yourself are unfinished. The feeling of being forgiven often arrives long after the fact, and its lateness doesn't mean you lack faith.

That God knows everything could sound like a threat. John offers it as comfort. Your heart knows what you did, and God knows that too, along with what His Son did about it, so when the two disagree His verdict is the one that stands.

Some of what people carry was done to them, and blame for that was never theirs. What you still owe a person, an apology perhaps, is a different debt from the one Jesus dealt with. It may well be right to pay it, but that adds nothing to what He finished.
reflectQuestions: When you bring the same thing back to God again, what are you hoping will happen that didn't happen the last time?
On the days your heart condemns you, what does it say, in its own words?
thematicGuides.practice: Once a day this week, the first time the old thing comes to mind, sit down, wherever you are. Say one sentence to Jesus, thanking Him that this was dealt with before He sat down. Then get up and carry on. For these seven days, thank Him and don't ask again. You may feel no lighter by the end, and that's all right.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've asked You to forgive this so many times that I've started praying as if You didn't hear me the first time. You offered one sacrifice and You sat down. I keep getting up to add something, a bit more regret, one more apology, as though that could top it up. I have nothing to add. My heart still says guilty. You are greater than my heart, and nothing it condemns me for is hidden from You. So tonight I won't ask again. Thank You that it's done. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jacob and Esau After Twenty Years
thematicGuides.hook: Esau ran to meet the brother he had once planned to kill, and that same day the two went their separate ways.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: But Esau ran to meet Jacob and embraced him; he threw his arms around his neck and kissed him. And they wept.
thematicGuides.intro: Say a family wedding is coming and your brother will be there. You haven't talked in years, and you'll spend the day keeping track of where he is in the room. You can't see the two of you ever being close again, so you wonder whether it's worth trying. Genesis tells of twin brothers meeting after twenty years apart, from the side of Jacob, the one in the wrong.
story: Jacob's messengers came back saying his twin brother Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men. Dressed in Esau's clothes, Jacob had once tricked their blind father into giving him the blessing meant for his brother. Esau planned to kill him, so their mother sent Jacob to her brother Laban for a while. He stayed twenty years. Now, in great fear, he split his people and animals into two camps, in case one was attacked. Then he prayed to be saved from his brother. He had crossed the Jordan with only a staff, he told God, and now he was two camps. He sent more than five hundred and fifty animals ahead as a gift, and spent the night in the camp himself.

Jacob looked up and there was Esau with his four hundred men. He went ahead of his family and bowed to the ground seven times as he came near. The blessing he had taken said he would be lord over his brothers and they would bow down to him. Now Jacob bowed, and kept calling Esau his lord. Esau ran to meet him, threw his arms round his neck and kissed him, and they wept. When Jacob said the herds were for him, Esau answered, "I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what you have for yourself." Jacob pressed him until he took them. The last time he asks, the word translated 'present' is the Hebrew word for a blessing. Neither of them, in what Genesis records, speaks of what happened twenty years before.

Esau offered to travel on with him. Jacob said the children and the nursing animals couldn't be driven hard, and that he would follow slowly to Seir. Esau then offered to leave him some of his men, and Jacob turned that down too. Esau set off for Seir that same day. Jacob went to Sukkoth instead, and built there. Genesis never shows him arriving in Seir. It does show the brothers together once more. Years before, Esau had told himself that when the days of mourning for their father came, he would kill Jacob. When Isaac died, "his sons Esau and Jacob buried him."

keyVerses.text: Save me, I pray, from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am afraid he will come and attack me, and also the mothers with their children.
But Esau ran to meet Jacob and embraced him; he threw his arms around his neck and kissed him. And they wept.
So that day Esau started on his way back to Seir. Jacob, however, went to Sukkoth, where he built a place for himself and made shelters for his livestock.

insights: Peace with someone you've fallen out with may come out as it did for these two, with the dread gone and your lives still separate. Theirs held well enough for the two of them to bury their father together. If someone has been a danger to you, distance may be the only safe form peace can take.

God had promised to be with Jacob and had told him nothing about what Esau would do. The most Jacob could tell himself was "perhaps he will receive me", and you have no guarantee of an Esau who runs either. His part was to go. The night before, he sent his herds ahead and stayed in camp. When the day came he walked out in front of his family.
reflectQuestions: When you picture meeting the person you fell out with, what is the worst thing you expect them to say or do?
If the two of you could be at peace and still live quite separate lives, what would that peace need to include?
thematicGuides.practice: Have one short conversation this week with the person you've been avoiding, by phone if a visit is too much. Say you'd like to be on speaking terms. If you owe an apology, make it briefly and leave the rest for another day.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, You know who I've been avoiding. I've rehearsed that meeting, and in every version I'm more in the right than I was. I'm afraid of what I'll see in their face. I can't make them run to meet me. Help me to go first, and to go without my excuses. If the most that comes of it is peace at a distance, let me be thankful for that much. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Haman and the One Man Who Would Not Kneel
thematicGuides.hook: Haman had wealth, sons and the king's favour, and said none of it satisfied him while Mordecai sat at the gate.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God and that no bitter root grows up to cause trouble and defile many.
thematicGuides.intro: Someone slighted you. They talked over you, or left you off the list. You know it's small, but you keep going back to it, and it has started to spoil things that have nothing to do with them. Haman, the villain of the book of Esther, was in that state. What he did with his anger was monstrous, but one speech he makes at home sounds uncomfortably familiar.
story: Mordecai, a Jew who sat at the king's gate, would not kneel to Haman, the highest noble in Persia. Haman had answered with a decree to kill every Jew in the empire. One day Haman left the queen's banquet in high spirits and passed Mordecai, who neither stood up nor showed any fear of him. Haman was filled with rage, held it in and went home, where he boasted to his wife and friends about his vast wealth, his many sons, his rank and the queen's invitation. Then he said all of it gave him "no satisfaction" as long as he saw Mordecai sitting at the king's gate. They told him to set up a pole fifty cubits high (about seventy-five feet), ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai impaled on it, and then enjoy the banquet. Haman had it built.

That night the king could not sleep, and the records read to him told how Mordecai had once exposed a plot against his life and gone unrewarded. Haman had just arrived to ask for Mordecai's death when the king asked him what should be done for a man he wanted to reward. Haman thought to himself, "Who is there that the king would rather honor than me?" He suggested a royal robe, the king's own horse and a parade through the city, and was told to go at once and do all of it for Mordecai. So Haman led Mordecai's horse through the streets, calling out that this was what the king did for a man he delighted in. Afterwards Mordecai went back to the king's gate. Haman rushed home with his head covered in grief.

The same day Haman was hurried off to the queen's second banquet. There Esther, herself a Jew, told the king that she and her people had been sold to be destroyed, and named Haman. The king went out to the garden in a rage and came back to find Haman falling on the couch where Esther was reclining, begging for his life. A eunuch mentioned the pole by Haman's house, and who it had been set up for. The king had Haman impaled on it. His estate went to Esther that day, and she put Mordecai in charge of it.

keyVerses.text: But all this gives me no satisfaction as long as I see that Jew Mordecai sitting at the king's gate.
So they impaled Haman on the pole he had set up for Mordecai. Then the king's fury subsided.
