Make every effort to live in peace with everyone and to be holy; without holiness no one will see the Lord. See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God and that no bitter root grows up to cause trouble and defile many.

insights: If good things in your life have gone flat since the snub, one person is outweighing everything else you have. Haman made his speech with the money, the sons and the seat of honour all still his, and he could enjoy none of it.

Mordecai had not robbed Haman or lied about him. He had refused to kneel, and the injury was to Haman's pride. Real harm, such as abuse or a betrayal, is a different thing and needs more help than a story about a snub can give.

The letter to the Hebrews tells a church to make every effort to live in peace with everyone, and to see that nothing bitter takes root among them. That is said to all of them together, so your grudge is something other people are meant to help you catch. Your own effort can start with greeting that person properly next time you pass.
reflectQuestions: Which good thing in your life have you enjoyed less since this person snubbed you?
When you tell other people what this person did, what do they usually say back?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick one person who is likely to be straight with you, and this week tell them what happened. Haman took his grievance home to people who agreed with him. Give yourself two minutes to say it, then ask how big it looks from where they sit, and hear the answer out without arguing.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, it would sound so small if I said it out loud, and I've carried it for weeks anyway. You've been kinder to me than I've earned, and I'm still keeping accounts on somebody else. Pull this up before it spreads. I don't need them to stand when I walk in. Help me to want good things for them, or at least to start wanting to. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Charge It to Me: Paul's Letter to Philemon
thematicGuides.hook: Caught between two people he loved, Paul asked instead of ordering and offered to pay whatever was owed.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: If he has done you any wrong or owes you anything, charge it to me.
thematicGuides.intro: Paul was an old man and a prisoner when he sent Onesimus back to Philemon with a letter of twenty-five verses. Onesimus had been a slave in Philemon's household, and Paul had come to call him his son. Philemon was Paul's dear friend. If two people you love have fallen out and you're stuck between them, unsure whether to step in or how to do it without making things worse, it's worth watching how Paul went about it.
story: Paul would have liked to keep Onesimus with him, to help while he was in chains. He sent him back, because he didn't want to do anything without Philemon's consent, and this letter went with him. In it Paul writes that he could be bold and order Philemon to do what he ought to do. He appeals to him instead, on the basis of love. The name Onesimus means useful, and Paul plays on it, writing that Onesimus was once useless to Philemon and is now useful to them both. He is sending back, he says, his very heart.

Onesimus was Philemon's slave, and what happened to him when he came back through the door was Philemon's to decide. It's hard to read about one man being sent back to another who owned him. Paul puts his whole weight on the side of the weaker man. He asks Philemon to have him back for good, "no longer as a slave", and to welcome him as he would welcome Paul himself. Onesimus, he writes, is very dear to him and dearer still to Philemon, as a fellow man and as a brother in the Lord. In Colossians, a letter meant to be read aloud to the church, Onesimus is "our faithful and dear brother".

Paul doesn't rule on what had happened between the two men. He writes, "If he has done you any wrong or owes you anything, charge it to me." His 'if' allows that nothing may be owed, and his offer covers whatever is. He adds that he is writing this with his own hand and will pay it back, a signed promise from a man in chains. He also mentions that Philemon owes him his very self, and tells him to get a guest room ready, because he hopes to come. The choice is still Philemon's.

keyVerses.text: But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that any favor you do would not seem forced but would be voluntary.
Perhaps the reason he was separated from you for a little while was that you might have him back forever, no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a dear brother.
If he has done you any wrong or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand. I will pay it back, not to mention that you owe me your very self.

insights: Each of them will want you to say they were right, and you may know less about what happened than you think. Paul's 'if' is a way through. He didn't accuse Onesimus, and he didn't declare that nothing was owed. You can take someone's hurt seriously without giving a verdict on it.

Getting involved will cost you something, most likely a phone call you'd rather not make, or both of them being cross with you for a while. Paul's offer could have cost him money, and he put it in writing. If you aren't willing to carry anything, it may be better to stay out of it.

Paul leaned hard, on behalf of the man who had no say in what happened next. The two you're caught between are probably equals, which gives you less reason to lean on either. You can still do what he did, which was to ask even though he could have ordered, and leave the last word with them. Paul couldn't make the peace for those two, and neither can you.
reflectQuestions: How much of what you believe about their falling-out comes from only one of them?
If you helped these two make peace, which cost would you be least willing to pay?
thematicGuides.practice: Stop giving verdicts until this time next week. When either of them tells you their side, don't say who you think was right, and don't pass on anything one has said about the other. If you need to say something, say one good thing you know to be true about the one who isn't in the room.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I love them both, and I'm worn out with hearing each side. I want this mended, partly for their sake and partly because birthdays would be easier for me. I don't know everything that happened, and I've been talking as if I did. If there's a cost here that's mine to carry, show me what it is. Keep me from taking over. The choice is theirs, so be with them both while they make it. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Hagar and the God Who Sees Me
thematicGuides.hook: Abram and Sarai never say Hagar's name in Genesis, and the first voice to use it is the angel's, at a desert spring.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: She gave this name to the LORD who spoke to her: 'You are the God who sees me,' for she said, 'I have now seen the One who sees me.'
thematicGuides.intro: It's fair to assume God's attention goes first to the people at the centre of what He's doing, and Genesis seems to agree. For chapters it follows Abram, the man with the promise, and his wife Sarai. If you're the one nobody asks about, it's a short step to thinking you're in the background for God as well. Then Genesis 16 leaves the couple at home and follows their slave into the desert.
story: After ten years in Canaan, Abram had God's promise of descendants, and he and Sarai had no child. Sarai had an Egyptian slave named Hagar, and she told Abram to sleep with the slave, hoping to build a family through her. Abram agreed. When Hagar knew she was pregnant she began to despise her mistress, and Sarai blamed Abram. He answered, "Your slave is in your hands." Neither of them uses her name anywhere in the chapter, and Sarai has already called her "my slave" twice. Sarai mistreated her, and Hagar ran away.

She had got as far as a spring beside the road to Shur when the angel of the LORD found her. His first word was her name, and he asked where she had come from and where she was going. She answered only the first question. He told her, "Go back to your mistress and submit to her." Genesis gives no reason. The angel promised her descendants too many to count, and told her to name her son Ishmael, which means God hears, "for the LORD has heard of your misery." Then the slave whose owners never use her name gave the LORD a name. She called Him the God who sees her.

Years later Sarah, as she was now called, had a son of her own. She saw Hagar's son mocking and told Abraham to get rid of that slave woman and her son. God told Abraham to do as she said, and promised to make the boy into a nation too. Early next morning Abraham set some food and a skin of water on Hagar's shoulders and sent her off with the boy. In the Desert of Beersheba the water ran out. She put the boy under a bush, sat down a bowshot away because she couldn't watch him die, and sobbed. The angel of God called to her from heaven, and again he used her name. God had heard the boy crying, he said. When God opened her eyes she saw a well, and she filled the skin and gave the boy a drink.

keyVerses.text: The angel of the LORD found Hagar near a spring in the desert; it was the spring that is beside the road to Shur. And he said, 'Hagar, slave of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?' 'I'm running away from my mistress Sarai,' she answered.
She gave this name to the LORD who spoke to her: 'You are the God who sees me,' for she said, 'I have now seen the One who sees me.'
God heard the boy crying, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, 'What is the matter, Hagar? Do not be afraid; God has heard the boy crying as he lies there.'

insights: Hagar heard her name from an angel. You have Jesus's description of Himself as the shepherd who calls His own sheep by name (John 10:3). That is how He knows you on the days when to everyone else you're the new one at work or somebody's mother.

Hagar was seen before anything was settled. She gave God that name while pregnant, on the run and about to go back, and in neither desert is she recorded asking Him for anything. Her promise about Ishmael was hers alone, and what carries over to you is the God who had heard, both times, before He was asked.

The angel's order to go back was given to Hagar, and to nobody else. If someone is harming you, nothing here tells you to stay with them or return to them, and it's right to let a friend or your doctor know, or to ring a helpline.
reflectQuestions: Where do people know your role better than they know you?
What would you want God to see about your life this week, before any of it is sorted out?
thematicGuides.practice: Tonight, when nobody else is about, say out loud to God your answers to the two questions the angel asked Hagar: where you have come from, and where you are going. Take a few minutes over each. She answered only the first, and if you've nothing for the second, tell Him so. Finish by reading Genesis 16:13 aloud and saying her sentence to Him as your own.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I can get through a whole day without anyone asking how I am, and I've half assumed You weren't asking either. I want to be found the way Hagar was, before she had asked for anything. I don't know where I'm going any better than she did. See me tonight, and hear what I haven't told anyone. Open my eyes as You opened hers, in case there's a well nearer than I think. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Loved at the Jordan Before the Work Began
thematicGuides.hook: The Father's words of love at the Jordan came before Jesus had preached a sermon or healed anyone.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: And a voice came from heaven: 'You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.'
thematicGuides.intro: What makes it hard to believe God loves you is that almost nothing else in your week is given to you first. Pay follows the work, and so does praise. Even at home you can feel only as welcome as you were useful today. So you carry the same sums into prayer and try to turn up with something to show. Mark tells the baptism of Jesus in three verses, and what the Father says there comes earlier than you'd expect.
story: Mark's Gospel has no Christmas story. Jesus first appears in it as a grown man, coming from Nazareth to be baptised by John in the Jordan. As He came up out of the water He saw heaven being torn open and the Spirit coming down on Him like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, "You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased." At that point in Mark, Jesus has preached no sermon and called no fisherman from his nets. His first sentence is still four verses off.

From the river the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, where He fasted forty days and forty nights and was hungry. Then the tempter came. Of his three tests, the first two open with the same words, "If you are the Son of God". The first asked for stones turned into bread. Jesus answered from Deuteronomy that man does not live on bread alone but on every word that comes from the mouth of God, and He made no bread. For the second the devil stood Him on the highest point of the temple and told Him to throw Himself down, quoting a psalm about angels who would catch Him. Jesus answered from Deuteronomy again, and did not jump.

At the cross the tempter's words came back. Jesus was crucified between two rebels, and people passing by shook their heads and shouted, "Come down from the cross, if you are the Son of God!" The chief priests and elders joined in. They said, "Let God rescue him now if he wants him", because He had claimed to be God's Son. The voice at the river had said He was loved, and the taunt here was that God might not want Him. Jesus did not come down. He stayed until He died, and when the earth shook, the centurion and those on guard with him were terrified. Surely, they said, He was the Son of God.

keyVerses.text: Just as Jesus was coming up out of the water, he saw heaven being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: 'You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.'
The tempter came to him and said, 'If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.'
See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are!

insights: Jesus is God's Son as nobody else is, and the New Testament still calls you God's child if you trust Him. John writes that we are God's children now, while what we will be hasn't yet been made known (1 John 3:2). The name comes before there's anything finished to show for it.

Each 'if' asked Jesus to prove with a miracle what God had already said. His first answer was that people live on what God says, and in Matthew the last thing God had said was at the river. A thought of your own that begins 'if you were any good, you would' is asking for the same kind of proof.
Being loved didn't keep Jesus out of the wilderness. Mark says the Spirit sent Him there at once. A hard week straight after a good one doesn't mean God has taken back the name He gave you.
reflectQuestions: What are you working hardest to prove about yourself at the moment, whether at work, at home or to God?
If you began tomorrow already sure that you are God's child, which part of the day would go differently?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose one person you love, a brother perhaps, or a friend you've known for years. In the next two days, ring them or go and see them, and before either of you has asked how the week is going, tell them you love them. Don't attach it to anything they've done or to anything you need from them. At the Jordan the Father spoke before Jesus had preached a sermon, and your sentence can come before the news.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I bring You my week like a report and wait to hear how I did. I think I'd still rather be marked, because then I'd know where I stood. You spoke to Jesus at the river before He had done any of it, and You've called me Your child while I'm still unfinished. Let me start tomorrow from there and do the work afterwards. On the days I get it wrong, keep me from deciding You've changed Your mind. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Lord, What About Him?
thematicGuides.hook: Saul measured himself against David over one line of a song, and when Peter asked about John, Jesus told him to follow.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: When Peter saw him, he asked, 'Lord, what about him?' Jesus answered, 'If I want him to remain alive until I return, what is that to you? You must follow me.'
thematicGuides.intro: The song that made Saul so angry was sung in his honour, and its first line was about him. What he heard was the second line, which gave a younger man a bigger number. Anyone who has heard a friend's good news and come away feeling worse about a life that was fine an hour earlier knows how that goes. The first book of Samuel follows where the habit took him, and John's Gospel records what Jesus said when Peter started on it.
story: King Saul sent David on missions, and David did so well that Saul gave him a high rank in the army. When the men were coming home after David had killed Goliath, women came out from all the towns of Israel to meet the king with timbrels and lyres, singing as they danced, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands." Saul was very angry. He thought that David had been credited with ten times his own figure and had only the kingdom left to get. From that day on, Saul kept a close eye on David.

The next day an evil spirit came on Saul. David was playing the lyre for him, as he usually did, and Saul had a spear in his hand. He threw it, meaning to pin David to the wall, and David got clear of him twice. So Saul sent him away to command a thousand men, and David did well at that too. Three times the chapter says Saul was afraid of him: because the LORD was with David and had left Saul, then when he saw David's success, and still more when he realised his own daughter Michal loved David. He stayed David's enemy for the rest of his days.

Beside the Sea of Galilee, the risen Jesus gave Peter the care of His sheep. He also told him how his life would end, as an old man led by someone else where he did not want to go. Then Jesus said, "Follow me!" and the next two words in the Gospel are "Peter turned". Behind them was the disciple Jesus loved, John by long tradition, and Peter asked, "Lord, what about him?" Jesus would not say. If He wanted that disciple to stay alive until He returned, that was nothing to Peter, whose part was to follow. Later, in Acts 3, Peter and John are going up to the temple together at the time of prayer.

keyVerses.text: Saul was very angry; this refrain displeased him greatly. 'They have credited David with tens of thousands,' he thought, 'but me with only thousands. What more can he get but the kingdom?' And from that time on Saul kept a close eye on David.
When Peter saw him, he asked, 'Lord, what about him?' Jesus answered, 'If I want him to remain alive until I return, what is that to you? You must follow me.'
Each one should test their own actions. Then they can take pride in themselves alone, without comparing themselves to someone else, for each one should carry their own load.

insights: The song took nothing from Saul. He came home a king, with thousands to his name and Israel's most successful officer under his command, and the comparison alone turned a victory into an insult. Your own job and home are what they were before you looked at someone else's.

Jesus told Peter nothing about John, and didn't say things would even out. Peter had just heard he would die a death he wouldn't choose. The road you're given may be shorter or harder than the next person's, and all Jesus says about that is to follow Him along it.
Paul's version in Galatians 6:4 is to test your own actions. Whether you did what was yours to do today is a question you can answer without knowing how anyone else got on.
reflectQuestions: What is the 'tens of thousands' in someone else's life that you keep counting against your own?
Leaving other people's lives to one side, what do you think Jesus has given you in particular to get on with at the moment?
thematicGuides.practice: Peter was walking with Jesus when he looked round, so do this one walking. Some day this week, leave your phone at home and walk for ten minutes in one direction. On the way out, tell God about the person you measure yourself against most and what they have that you want. Then turn for home, and all the way back talk to Him only about the next thing that is yours to do.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've been checking one person's life against mine. I know their news better than I know what You've asked of me this week. I can have thousands of my own and still feel robbed by someone else's tens of thousands. You didn't tell Peter what You had planned for John, and You haven't told me what You have planned for them. Turn me back round to face You, and tell me again to follow. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Once You Were Not a People
thematicGuides.hook: Two names God gave Hosea's children, 'not loved' and 'not my people', come back in Peter's letter with the 'not' taken off.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
thematicGuides.intro: After church you read the noticeboard a second time, coffee in hand, because everyone else seems to have someone to talk to. It can be much the same at work, or at your own family's table. After enough years of it you begin to ask whether there's anywhere you do belong. Peter's first letter was written to Christians who didn't fit where they lived, and he answers that question for them without pretending they'll soon feel at home.
story: Hosea was a prophet in Israel when the nation had gone after other gods. God told him to marry, and as each child was born gave him the name, so that every name was a message to the country. The second child, a girl, was Lo-Ruhamah, which means 'not loved', or shown no mercy. She had carried that name long enough to be weaned before her brother was born and named Lo-Ammi, 'not my people'. God gave the reason: "you are not my people, and I am not your God." The next word He says is 'Yet'. In the place where they were told they weren't His people, He says, they will be called children of the living God.

In Hosea 2 God speaks about Israel as a wife who has left Him for other gods. He sets out what that will cost her, with her path blocked by thornbushes and her festivals stopped. Then He says He will lead her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her, and the promises that follow keep coming back to names. She will call Him 'my husband' and no longer 'my master'. He will take the names of the Baals, the gods she ran after, off her lips, never to be called on again. The last promise in the chapter is about Hosea's daughter and son, the children He had named 'not loved' and 'not my people'. The one who gave those names takes the 'not' off them.

Peter's letter went to believers scattered across five provinces, and it opens by calling them "God's elect, exiles", chosen by God and strangers where they lived. In chapter 2 he tells them they were once not a people and had not received mercy, which are the names of Hosea's son and daughter, and that neither name fits them now. His very next sentence calls them foreigners and exiles. He goes on to tell them how to live among neighbours who accuse them of doing wrong. Nowhere in the letter does he promise they will come to feel at home in those towns.

keyVerses.text: I will show my love to the one I called 'Not my loved one.' I will say to those called 'Not my people,' 'You are my people' and they will say, 'You are my God.'

But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's special possession, that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
Dear friends, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles, to abstain from sinful desires, which wage war against your soul.

insights: Peter's readers didn't fit because they had stopped living as their neighbours did, and the neighbours were surprised and abusive about it. Your reasons may be different, like shyness, or a family that never made room for you, but the names were given because God had shown mercy. Nobody had to fit in first, and Peter's readers still didn't.

Peter calls Jesus a living Stone, "rejected by humans but chosen by God and precious to him", and says his readers are being built, like stones, into a house with Him as the cornerstone. The first stone of the house you belong to was one the builders turned down.
reflectQuestions: In the place where you feel most like an outsider, what is it that tells you that you don't belong?
Peter called the same people God's own and exiles. Which of the two do you find harder to believe about yourself?
thematicGuides.practice: Every day this week, just before you walk into the place where you fit least (it might be the staff room, or your own kitchen), stop at the door. Say the first half of 1 Peter 2:10 under your breath: "Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God". You aren't trying to feel different, and you may well go in still feeling like a stranger.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I've got good at looking busy in rooms where I've nobody to stand with. Some days I decide the fault is mine, and other days that it's everybody else's. Peter says I'm one of Your people, out of mercy and not for anything I've managed. Most days I don't feel it. Help me believe it on those days too. Where I'm still a stranger, keep me from going sour, and show me who else is standing on their own. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Man Who Asked If Jesus Was Willing
thematicGuides.hook: A man covered with leprosy was sure Jesus could heal him and unsure He'd want to, and Jesus answered with His hand first.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Jesus reached out his hand and touched the man. 'I am willing,' he said. 'Be clean!'
thematicGuides.intro: Plenty of people are sure God helps others and just as sure that, in their own case, He'd rather keep His distance. If that's you, the reason may be something you did, last month or twenty years ago. Or it's something that was done to you, which was never your fault and has left you feeling marked anyway. Luke 5 has a man who put that doubt to Jesus in one sentence.
story: Luke says Jesus was in one of the towns when a man came along who was covered with leprosy. Under the law of Moses a priest pronounced anyone with such a disease unclean, and they lived alone outside the camp for as long as it lasted. When this man saw Jesus he fell with his face to the ground and begged, "Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean." There's no 'if' on the 'can', and what he asks to be made is 'clean', the word a priest pronounces.

Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. He said, "I am willing", and told him to be clean, and immediately the leprosy left him. So the hand was on him while he was still covered. Under the law, anyone who touched human uncleanness became unclean themselves, and Jesus had no need to touch him in order to cure him. In Luke 17, when ten men with leprosy call out to Him from a distance, He sends them to the priests with a single sentence and they are cleansed as they go. This man He touched.

Jesus then ordered the man to tell no one, and to go and show himself to the priest with the offerings Moses commanded. Leviticus 14 sets out what that meant. A priest would come out of the camp to examine him and, finding the disease gone, pronounce him clean. He would wash, shave off all his hair and come back into the camp, but stay outside his own tent for seven days and bring his offerings on the eighth. For a man healed in a moment, the way back among people still took over a week, and it went through someone who had to look at him and say the word aloud. Luke doesn't record whether he went.

keyVerses.text: Anyone with such a defiling disease must wear torn clothes, let their hair be unkempt, cover the lower part of their face and cry out, 'Unclean! Unclean!' As long as they have the disease they remain unclean. They must live alone; they must live outside the camp.

When he saw Jesus, he fell with his face to the ground and begged him, 'Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.' Jesus reached out his hand and touched the man. 'I am willing,' he said. 'Be clean!' And immediately the leprosy left him.
Then Jesus ordered him, 'Don't tell anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the sacrifices that Moses commanded for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.'

insights: Unclean in the law of Moses was a ritual state, used just as much of someone who had touched a dead body, and it laid no blame on the man. Jesus says nothing to him about sin. If your shame comes from what someone did to you, it did not make you unclean, and the fault lies with the person who did it.

If it's what you've done that makes you sure He'd keep back, look earlier in the same chapter. Simon Peter fell at Jesus' knees and told Him to go away, because he was a sinful man. Jesus told him not to be afraid and took him on as a disciple.

The man was healed at once, and you may not be. Luke 5 makes no promise that an illness will lift or that shame will go quickly. It does show which way Jesus moved when a man the law called unclean asked whether He wanted to.
reflectQuestions: What do you assume Jesus sees first when He looks at you?
The man got his doubt into one sentence. If you did the same, what would your sentence to Jesus be?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick one person who can keep a confidence, a friend or an older Christian you know, and this week tell them one true sentence about why you think God would keep His distance from you. You don't owe them the whole story. Do it on a walk or over the phone, where you can stop when you want to. If what you're carrying is harm someone did to you, a counsellor or your doctor is a good person to choose.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I believe You can. What I've doubted is whether You'd want to, for me. I've kept back from You to save You the trouble of keeping back from me. So I'm saying what the man with leprosy said, as my own words: Lord, if You are willing. Let me hear Your answer to him as Your answer to me, and help me tell one other person. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Carried to Old Age and Grey Hairs
thematicGuides.hook: Isaiah sets gods that have to be carried beside a God who says He'll still be carrying you when your hair is grey.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Even to your old age and gray hairs I am he, I am he who will sustain you. I have made you and I will carry you; I will sustain you and I will rescue you.
thematicGuides.intro: Isaiah 46 opens with two gods being carted away on the backs of animals. The chapter is about who carries whom. You may have spent years as the one who carried other people, and now you've retired, or your health has gone, or they no longer need you to, and you're asking what you're for. What God says in this chapter runs from birth to grey hair.
story: Bel and Nebo were two of the chief gods of Babylon, the empire that took Judah into exile. Isaiah pictures them on the day they are taken away themselves. Bel bows down and Nebo stoops low. Bowing was what people did in front of them, and now the gods are the ones doing it, as their statues are loaded onto beasts of burden, "a burden for the weary". They can't rescue their own images, and they go off into captivity. The chapter also has people paying a goldsmith to make a god, lifting it onto their shoulders, carrying it to its place and setting it down. There it stays, because it can't move itself.

With the gods of Babylon loaded onto animals, God turns to His own people. He calls them the remnant of Israel, the ones who are left, and asks one thing of them, which is to listen. The word 'carried' comes back pointing the other way. He tells them He has upheld and carried them since they were born. Then He goes to the far end of life, to old age and grey hairs, and says He will still be the one carrying. He is speaking to a whole nation as if it were one person growing old.

In Psalm 71 one person prays for what Isaiah 46 promises a nation. The writer has relied on God from birth, since God brought him out of his mother's womb. He asks, "Do not cast me away when I am old; do not forsake me when my strength is gone." He says 'when', so he expects his strength to go. His enemies are already saying that God has forsaken him and no one will rescue him. Later he asks again not to be forsaken when he is old and grey, until he has told the next generation what God has done.

keyVerses.text: They lift it to their shoulders and carry it; they set it up in its place, and there it stands. From that spot it cannot move. Even though someone cries out to it, it cannot answer; it cannot save them from their troubles.

Listen to me, you descendants of Jacob, all the remnant of the people of Israel, you whom I have upheld since your birth, and have carried since you were born. Even to your old age and gray hairs I am he, I am he who will sustain you. I have made you and I will carry you; I will sustain you and I will rescue you.

Since my youth, God, you have taught me, and to this day I declare your marvelous deeds. Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, my God, till I declare your power to the next generation, your mighty acts to all who are to come.

insights: A newborn does nothing useful for anybody, and nobody in the house asks what it's for. God starts His sentence there, with the carrying He did when you could do nothing for Him, and ends it at grey hairs. The years in between, when other people relied on you, get no special mention, and He was carrying you through those as well.

In both of Isaiah's pictures the maker does the carrying. People who make a god have to lift it, and the God who made you says He will lift you. A god who needed you to stay useful would be one more load on your shoulders.

Your strength may not come back. God's promise in Isaiah 46 is to carry you, and saying yes to help, from God or from a neighbour with a car, is one way of believing it. If low days have run into weeks, being carried includes telling your doctor and someone close to you.
reflectQuestions: Which part of being needed do you miss most now that it has gone?
Looking back, when were you being carried while you thought you were doing the carrying?
thematicGuides.practice: Ring or sit down this week with one person younger than you, a grandchild perhaps, or someone from church. Tell them about one time you can now see that God carried you, and give the year and the place. Keep it to ten minutes and don't turn it into advice. The writer of Psalm 71 asked God not to forsake him until he had done this.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I used to know what I was for. People needed me, and I liked being needed more than I ever let on. Now I can do less, and I've been wondering what's left. You say You carried me before I could do a thing for You, and that You'll carry me on into old age and grey hair. I don't take well to being carried. Teach me to let You, and to let other people. Don't cast me away now my strength is going, and give me someone younger to tell what You've done. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: David Danced and Michal Watched
thematicGuides.hook: Three months after a man died beside the ark, David danced as it came into his city, and his wife Michal despised him for it.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: I will celebrate before the LORD. I will become even more undignified than this, and I will be humiliated in my own eyes.
thematicGuides.intro: In church we take it for granted that we can tell how much someone means it by watching them. For some the proof is raised hands and a loud voice, and others trust only the person standing still. The first group quotes David's dancing. But in 2 Samuel 6 a man also dies beside the ark, David is too afraid to take it home, and the dancing ends in a quarrel at his own door.
story: David gathered thirty thousand men to bring the ark of God, the chest that stood for His throne in Israel, up to Jerusalem. They put it on a new cart, and David and all Israel celebrated before the LORD with all their might, with harps, timbrels and cymbals. At the threshing floor of Nakon the oxen stumbled. Uzzah, who was guiding the cart, took hold of the ark, and God struck him down beside it. The writer calls it an irreverent act and says no more. David was angry that it had happened, and then afraid of the LORD. He would not have the ark in his own city, and left it at the house of Obed-Edom for three months.

Then David heard that the LORD had blessed Obed-Edom's whole household because of the ark, and he went to fetch it. Nobody used a cart this time. In 1 Chronicles David says what had gone wrong: the Levites should have carried it, and no one had asked God how He wanted it done. So it went on their shoulders, and after six steps David sacrificed a bull and a fattened calf. Wearing a linen ephod, the garment priests served in, he danced before the LORD with all his might, among the shouting and the trumpets.

Michal, whom this chapter calls daughter of Saul and never David's wife, watched David from a window as the ark came in, and despised him in her heart. She had loved him, and once let him down through a window to escape the men her father had sent to kill him. Saul then gave her to another man, Paltiel. Years later David made her return a condition of a political deal, and Paltiel followed her weeping until he was ordered home. Now she came out to meet David and said the king had been going around half-naked in full view of his servants' slave girls, like any vulgar fellow. David's answer was sharp too, and brought up her father. Twice in it he said who the dancing had been for: "It was before the LORD", and then, "I will celebrate before the LORD."

keyVerses.text: David was afraid of the LORD that day and said, 'How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?'
Wearing a linen ephod, David was dancing before the LORD with all his might, while he and all Israel were bringing up the ark of the LORD with shouts and the sound of trumpets.
As the ark of the LORD was entering the City of David, Michal daughter of Saul watched from a window. And when she saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, she despised him in her heart.

insights: Both processions were loud, so the noise neither caused the first disaster nor cured it: David changed how the ark was carried and kept the music. Uzzah's death is still hard to read. The chapter records that David was angry about it before he was afraid, and that the same man danced three months later.

If you hold back because of who might notice, your attention is where Michal's was, on the room. It's in the same place when you think less of the person along the row, whether their hands are in the air or by their sides. You can be facing God while standing quite still.

Before she looked out of that window, Michal had been given to another man by her father and taken back by David as part of a deal. The person near you has a history too, which is a reason to be slow in deciding why they worship the way they do.
reflectQuestions: Whose opinion of you are you most aware of when you worship with other people?
What is it about the way some people worship, louder or quieter than you, that most tempts you to judge them?
thematicGuides.practice: At the next service you go to, stop looking around during the singing and the prayers. Keep your eyes on the words, or keep them shut, so you can't see what anyone near you is doing or who is noticing you. If you catch yourself glancing up, say "before the LORD" under your breath and look down again. How still or loud you are is up to you.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I can tell You who sat near me last Sunday and hardly a line of what I sang. I hold back in case someone thinks me odd, then look down on the people who don't, and either way my mind is on them. It's You I've come to. Make me careful how I come, as David learned to be, and glad enough in You to forget who's looking. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The Man Who Prayed to Half a Log
thematicGuides.hook: Isaiah's idol is the unburnt half of a log, and Psalm 115 says the people who trust such things end up like them.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Those who make them will be like them, and so will all who trust in them.
thematicGuides.intro: The Bible's warnings on idols are hard to take personally, because they seem meant for somebody else. You've never carved a god or knelt to one, and when a preacher says your idol is your phone or your salary it can sound like a stretch. Isaiah 44 is a good place to test that, because Isaiah keeps his eye on the man who made the statue and on what he did with the rest of the wood.
story: Isaiah follows an idol back to where it came from. A carpenter marked out the wood, roughed it out with chisels and gave it a human shape. Before that he had cut down a cedar or an oak, or planted a pine and let the rain grow it. Half of the tree went on the fire. He baked bread over it, roasted his meat, ate his fill and said, "Ah! I am warm; I see the fire." From what was left he made a god, bowed down and prayed to it to save him. Nobody stopped to think, Isaiah says. The man could not look at what he was holding and say, "Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?"

The nations kept asking Israel where their God was, and Psalm 115 is the answer Israel sang. He is in heaven, it says, and does whatever pleases Him. Then the song turns on the nations' own gods, which are silver and gold, made by human hands. They have mouths and can't speak, eyes and can't see, ears and can't hear, and so on down to feet that can't walk. Last come the makers. Those who make such gods will be like them, and so will everyone who trusts in them. Isaiah says as much of his carpenter and the rest of the trade: their eyes are plastered over so they cannot see.

When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, his face was shining because he had been speaking with the LORD, and he did not know it. Aaron and the Israelites were afraid to come near him. After that he wore a veil, and took it off whenever he went in to speak with the LORD. Paul picks the story up in a letter to Corinth. Whenever anyone turns to the Lord, he writes, the veil is taken away. All of us who look on the Lord's glory with unveiled faces are being changed, more and more, into His likeness, and the changing is the Lord's doing. Early in the next chapter he says where that glory is seen, "in the face of Christ".

keyVerses.text: From the rest he makes a god, his idol; he bows down to it and worships. He prays to it and says, 'Save me! You are my god!'
Those who make them will be like them, and so will all who trust in them. All you Israelites, trust in the LORD, he is their help and shield.
And we all, who with unveiled faces contemplate the Lord's glory, are being transformed into his image with ever-increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

insights: Nothing was wrong with the wood, which gave the man a fire and a hot meal. Half of it became an idol when he asked it to save him. Money is good for paying the rent and a phone for ringing your sister. By Isaiah's test either becomes an idol once you look to it to save you.

Neither man could see what was happening to him. The carpenter had become as blind as the thing he carved and could not say it was a lie, and Moses did not know his face was shining. What you give your attention to is changing you whether you feel it or not, and someone who knows you well may see it before you do.
reflectQuestions: On a bad day, what do you reach for first, before it occurs to you to pray?
Who or what would the person who knows you best say you have come to resemble over the past few years?
thematicGuides.practice: Shut a door behind you some time today, and say out loud what you turned to first the last time you were low or afraid. Then say one thing it's good for, as the log was good for a fire, and one thing you've been asking of it that it can't give. Finish by reading Isaiah 44:21-22 aloud, the next thing God says in the chapter. It ends, "Return to me, for I have redeemed you."
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, I've never made a god and prayed to it, and I'd quietly ticked that commandment off. But I know what I go to first when I'm frightened, and most days You come second. It's good in its place, and I've been asking it to save me. I can't see what that is doing to me, so show me, and be gentle about it. You told Israel You had made them and would not forget them. Don't forget me. Turn my face back towards You. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: The God Who Says He Isn't Hungry
thematicGuides.hook: In Psalm 50 God says He needs nothing His people bring Him, then asks them to thank Him and to call on Him in trouble.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Sacrifice thank offerings to God, fulfill your vows to the Most High, and call on me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will honor me.
thematicGuides.intro: Psalm 50 has Asaph's name at the top. He was the man David put in charge of the thanks and praise sung before the ark, and in the psalm under his name God tells Israel He has no need of anything they bring Him. If you've wondered why God wants praise at all, when in a person that would look needy or vain, this is where God takes up the subject Himself.
story: The psalm is set out as a trial. God summons the whole earth, and comes with fire ahead of Him and a storm around Him. He has His people gathered to hear Him testify against them, and then says, "I bring no charges against you concerning your sacrifices." But He has no need of a bull from their stalls, because every animal of the forest is His already, with the cattle on a thousand hills and the insects in the fields. If He were ever hungry, He adds, He wouldn't be telling them. "Do I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?"

The man who wrote Psalm 116 had been close to death, called on the name of the LORD, and been saved. He asks what he can give back for all the LORD's goodness to him. His answer is to sacrifice a thank offering, keep his vows (the promises he had made to God), and go on calling on the LORD's name. Those are the three things God asks for in Psalm 50, straight after saying He isn't hungry. A burnt offering went up in smoke on the altar and nobody ate it. A thank offering, by the rule in Leviticus, was shared: the fat was burnt, the priest took his portion, and the people who brought it ate the rest that same day. So the sacrifice God asks for is one the worshippers ate.

In Athens, a city Luke describes as full of idols, Paul was taken before its council, the Areopagus, to explain his teaching. He started from an altar he had found, inscribed "to an unknown god". The God who made the world, he told them, doesn't live in temples built by human hands, and human hands don't serve Him as though He were short of anything. He gives everyone life and breath, and made the nations so that people would seek Him and perhaps find Him. When Paul came to the resurrection, some sneered and some asked to hear more. Some believed, among them a council member called Dionysius and a woman named Damaris.

keyVerses.text: If I were hungry I would not tell you, for the world is mine, and all that is in it.
Sacrifice thank offerings to God, fulfill your vows to the Most High, and call on me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will honor me.
And he is not served by human hands, as if he needed anything. Rather, he himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.

insights: If someone says a God who wants praise sounds needy, the Bible got there first. The thank offering He asks for was a meal the worshipper ate, and the call in the day of trouble ends with the caller rescued. In Psalm 50 the worshippers go home with more than they brought.

A vain person wants to be admired. In verse 15 God asks to be sent for when you're in trouble, and the honour comes afterwards, from someone He has helped. Nobody calls a lifeboat crew vain for wanting the call.
Verse 15 promises deliverance and gives no date. Psalm 77, also under Asaph's name, is the prayer of someone still waiting, who cried out to God at night and would not be comforted.
reflectQuestions: When you sing or pray to God, what do you think He gets out of it?
Thinking of the last time you were in real trouble, what made it easy or hard to call on God about it?
thematicGuides.practice: Go for one walk in daylight this week, to the nearest park or patch of trees, and stop there for five minutes. In Psalm 50 God says He knows every bird in the mountains. Find five living things you can see or hear that you neither made nor feed. Then, before you turn for home, thank Him out loud for one thing you were given today, and ask His help with one thing that's troubling you.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, the breath I'm praying with was Yours before it was mine. I've sung to You as if You were short of something and my singing made it up. I've said thank You as a sort of payment, to keep the next request moving. You don't need paying. So here is what You asked for. Thank You for what was on my plate today. And there's something I can't sort out alone, so I'm asking for Your help. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: John Looked for a Lion and Saw a Lamb
thematicGuides.hook: In Revelation 5 all heaven sings to a Lamb that had been killed, and the first song gives the reason.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and praise!
thematicGuides.intro: A child asks what people do all day in heaven, and the only answer that comes to you is that they sing. You say it, and privately think it sounds like a service that never finishes. Read Revelation and heaven can seem frightening instead, with lightning coming from a throne and creatures covered in eyes. Chapter 5 is where John says who the singing is for, and where the singers give their reason.
story: In his vision John had been shown a throne in heaven with twenty-four elders seated round it, and four living creatures who never stop saying that God is holy. In the right hand of the One on the throne he saw a scroll, written on both sides and sealed with seven seals. A mighty angel called out in a loud voice, asking who was worthy to break the seals and open it. But no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth could open it, or even look inside. John writes, "I wept and wept."

John was still weeping when one of the elders told him to stop and look. The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, had triumphed and could open the scroll. Both names belong to the king promised from Judah's tribe and David's family. John looked, and at the centre of the throne he saw a Lamb, "looking as if it had been slain". It had been killed, by the look of it, and yet it was standing. Then the Lamb went and took the scroll from the right hand of the One on the throne.

When He had taken it, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down in front of the Lamb, holding harps and gold bowls of incense, which John says are the prayers of God's people. They sang a new song, and it answered the angel's question. The Lamb was worthy to open the scroll because He had been killed, and with His blood had bought men and women for God from every tribe, language, people and nation. Then John heard angels all round them, thousands upon thousands, calling the slain Lamb worthy in a loud voice. After that he heard every creature in heaven, on earth and under the earth, the three places where no one worthy had been found, and every creature on the sea with them. Their song was to the One on the throne and to the Lamb together. The four living creatures said, "Amen", and the elders fell down and worshipped.

keyVerses.text: Then one of the elders said to me, 'Do not weep! See, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed. He is able to open the scroll and its seven seals.' Then I saw a Lamb, looking as if it had been slain, standing at the center of the throne, encircled by the four living creatures and the elders.
You are worthy to take the scroll and to open its seals, because you were slain, and with your blood you purchased for God persons from every tribe and language and people and nation.

Then I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and on the sea, and all that is in them, saying: 'To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power, for ever and ever!'

insights: Lion and Lamb are one person, and He won by dying. If the singing sounds like a service that never finishes, notice that the new song starts the moment He takes the scroll, just after John was in tears because nobody could. The first song says what He did, and for anyone among the people He bought, joining in is thanks.

John's Gospel says the risen Jesus showed the disciples His hands and His side, and told Thomas to reach out and touch them. In Revelation He stands at the centre of God's throne and His death still shows on Him. If thunder and creatures covered in eyes make heaven sound frightening, this is who is in the middle of it.
reflectQuestions: What picture do you have of Jesus as He is now, in heaven?
The new song says "You are worthy" and then gives its reason. What reason would you give from your own life?
thematicGuides.practice: Go to the nearest church building this week, your own or any other, and find the cross on it or in it. If there's none outside and the door is locked, go back when it's open. Stand where you can see it for a couple of minutes, then read Revelation 5:9 and 5:12, aloud if nobody's about. Of everything Christians could have put on their buildings, they chose the thing that killed Him.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, thank You for letting John see that the one at the centre of heaven is Jesus, alive, with the marks of His death still on Him. He was killed for people of every language, and I am one of them. When I picture the place myself I'm mostly bored or a bit afraid, and I've never admitted that to You. I've sung the word worthy without ever asking what question it answered. Next time I sing it, let me mean it. Add my Amen to theirs. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: When Every Cooking Pot Is Holy
thematicGuides.hook: The words engraved on the high priest's gold plate turn up again on horses' bells, and Paul takes them into an ordinary week.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Therefore, I urge you, brothers and sisters, in view of God's mercy, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, this is your true and proper worship.
thematicGuides.intro: For an hour on Sunday God seems close. Then it's work, washing and emails until the next one, and from Monday to Saturday you may not do a single thing you'd call worship. That leaves most of your life happening somewhere He seems to have little to do with. The Bible has an inscription, "holy to the Lord", that starts out in one very small place, on a gold plate tied to one man's forehead.
story: At Sinai God gave Moses instructions for the clothes of the high priest, Moses' brother Aaron. There was a blue robe with gold bells round its hem, and a linen turban. For the front of the turban God ordered a plate of pure gold, engraved the way a seal is cut, with the words "holy to the Lord", and tied on with a blue cord. It was to be on Aaron's forehead continually. Wearing it, Aaron would bear the guilt involved in the sacred gifts the Israelites brought, whatever they were, so that they would be acceptable to the LORD. Exodus describes nothing else with those words written on it.

Centuries later Zechariah was a prophet in Jerusalem while the temple was being rebuilt. His book ends by looking ahead to a day when the LORD will be king over the whole earth. On that day, he says, the words from Aaron's plate will be inscribed on the bells of the horses. The bells on Aaron's robe were heard when he went into the Holy Place. These ones are on horses. Every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD Almighty, and anyone who comes to sacrifice will take one and cook in it. Leviticus gave the priests the job of telling the holy from the common. In Zechariah's picture a cooking pot from anyone's house is on the holy side of that line.

In Corinth Paul met a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, who had left Rome when all Jews were ordered out of the city. They were tentmakers, as he was, and he stayed and worked with them. By the time he wrote his letter to the Christians in Rome the two were back there, with a church meeting in their house, and he sends them his greetings. For eleven chapters that letter sets out what God in His mercy has done. Then Paul turns to what his readers should do about it, and he uses the words of the temple: offer, sacrifice, holy, pleasing. They are to offer their bodies, the part of a person that makes tents, cooks, carries things and sleeps. He calls this worship, the word he used three chapters earlier for the service of the temple. The rest of the chapter is about serving, giving, sharing with people in need and practising hospitality. A page later he has got to paying taxes.

keyVerses.text: Make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it as on a seal: holy to the Lord. Fasten a blue cord to it to attach it to the turban; it is to be on the front of the turban. It will be on Aaron's forehead, and he will bear the guilt involved in the sacred gifts the Israelites consecrate, whatever their gifts may be. It will be on Aaron's forehead continually so that they will be acceptable to the LORD.

On that day holy to the Lord will be inscribed on the bells of the horses, and the cooking pots in the LORD's house will be like the sacred bowls in front of the altar. Every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD Almighty, and all who come to sacrifice will take some of the pots and cook in them.
Therefore, I urge you, brothers and sisters, in view of God's mercy, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, this is your true and proper worship.

insights: Aaron wore the plate because even gifts set apart for God needed making acceptable, and he carried whatever was wrong with them. Peter says Christians bring offerings "acceptable to God through Jesus Christ". A distracted, ordinary Tuesday can be offered on those terms.
Paul calls the offered body worship without a word about how it feels. A day can be given to God, and count with Him, when you feel nothing in particular.
reflectQuestions: Which part of an ordinary week seems least like something you could offer to God?
What happens in that hour on Sunday that you would most like to take with you into Monday morning?
thematicGuides.practice: Pick the pan you cook in most, or the mug you use if you don't cook. Every evening for a week, when you wash it up, hold it for a moment before you put it away and offer God, in one sentence, one thing your body did that day, the plainer the better (drove, typed, lifted, stood in a queue). It takes about as long as drying your hands.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, I've treated You as someone I visit on Sundays. The rest of the week is bills and laundry, and I'd assumed none of it interested You much. I can't offer You six days of prayer. I do have a body that will carry the shopping home and stand at the sink, so I'm offering You that. You are the priest who makes what I bring acceptable, and I'm counting on it, because by Thursday the offering will mostly be tiredness. Take it anyway. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Can't Get to Church: David Without the Ark
thematicGuides.hook: David remembered God on a bed in the desert, and Jesus told a woman at a well that the Father is looking for worshippers.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: On my bed I remember you; I think of you through the watches of the night. Because you are my help, I sing in the shadow of your wings.
thematicGuides.intro: When King David fled Jerusalem he sent the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest at the centre of Israel's worship, back into the city and went on without it. If illness, shift work or someone who can't be left has kept you out of church for months, you may have wondered whether a prayer said in bed, or a hymn half remembered in the kitchen, counts as worship at all.
story: David's son Absalom had won the hearts of the people, and David left Jerusalem in a hurry. The whole countryside wept aloud as he crossed the Kidron Valley towards the wilderness. Zadok the priest was there with the Levites, carrying the ark, and David told him to take it back. If he found favour in the LORD's eyes, he said, the LORD would bring him back to see it and His dwelling place again. If not, he was ready for whatever seemed good to Him. The ark went back in, and David climbed the Mount of Olives barefoot, his head covered, weeping.

The heading of Psalm 63 puts David in the Desert of Judah, and its last verse speaks of the king, which fits his flight from Absalom. Early in the psalm he says he has seen God's power and glory in the sanctuary, and that God's love is better than life. Then he comes to his bed. He remembers God on it and thinks of Him through the watches of the night, the shifts a sentry kept. Because God is his help, he says, he sings in the shadow of His wings. He clings to God, and God's right hand holds him up.

Jesus was sitting alone by Jacob's well in Samaria, at about noon, when a woman came to draw water. When she found He knew about her five husbands she called Him a prophet, and put to Him the old quarrel between her people and His. Her ancestors, she said, had worshipped on this mountain, and the Jews said the place was Jerusalem. Jesus told her, "a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem." That time, He said, had already come, and the worshippers the Father is looking for worship in the Spirit and in truth. She left her water jar and went back to tell her town.

keyVerses.text: Take the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the LORD's eyes, he will bring me back and let me see it and his dwelling place again. But if he says, 'I am not pleased with you,' then I am ready; let him do to me whatever seems good to him.

I have seen you in the sanctuary and beheld your power and your glory. Because your love is better than life, my lips will glorify you. I will praise you as long as I live, and in your name I will lift up my hands.

Yet a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in the Spirit and in truth, for they are the kind of worshipers the Father seeks. God is spirit, and his worshipers must worship in the Spirit and in truth.

insights: In the psalm David speaks of the sanctuary before he speaks of the bed, and on the bed he remembers. The hymns and prayers you learned in church came home with you, and you can worship with them where you are.

Asked which place was the right one, Jesus named neither. He said the Father is the one looking for people who worship in the Spirit and in truth, and nothing in that needs you to be able to leave the house. David, on the run from Absalom in Psalm 3, calls out where he is, and God answers "from his holy mountain", the hill he could no longer get to.

David did get back, though when he spoke of seeing the ark again he couldn't know he would. Nobody can promise you the same. If you don't get back, that is no sign God is displeased with you: in Psalm 63 David is still in the desert, and he is sure of God's love and help there.
reflectQuestions: What do you miss most about being in church, now that you can't get there?
If you were awake tonight with no book to hand, which hymn, prayer or Bible passage could you say from memory?
thematicGuides.practice: Before Sunday, ring one person from your church. Tell them you can't get there for now, and ask them to let you know each week what was read and what was sung, so that someone there on Sunday knows you're worshipping too. Then read the same passage where you are, at whatever hour you can manage.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I'd be there if I could, and it's been months now. I've started to feel like someone who used to belong, and I've wondered whether a psalm read in bed reaches You, or half a hymn before I lose the words. David remembered You on his bed, so I'm remembering You on mine. If You mean to bring me back, bring me back. If I'm to stay where I am, help me say what he said, that I'm ready for whatever seems good to You. Either way, You are the one who goes looking for worshippers, so come and find me here. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Elijah Under the Broom Bush
thematicGuides.hook: When Elijah asked God to let him die, what he was given first was sleep, bread and a jar of water.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: The angel of the LORD came back a second time and touched him and said, 'Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you.'
thematicGuides.intro: A worn-out Christian usually gets told to pray longer and read more. Often that's good advice. It's hard to hear when you've already done everything you were supposed to do and praying has become one of the things you can't manage. Elijah reached that point a day's walk into the desert, under a broom bush.
story: On Mount Carmel Elijah had prayed and fire had fallen on his altar. The drought broke, and he ran ahead of King Ahab's chariot all the way to Jezreel. Then Ahab's wife Jezebel sent word that by the same time next day he would be as dead as the prophets of Baal he had killed. Elijah was afraid and ran for his life, to Beersheba in Judah. He left his servant there and walked on alone for a day into the wilderness, where he sat down under a broom bush and prayed that he might die.

Elijah fell asleep under the bush. An angel woke him with a touch and told him to eat, and by his head were a jar of water and bread baked over hot coals. He had asked for those two things once before. During the drought God sent him to Zarephath, where he called out to a widow at the town gate for a little water in a jar and a piece of bread, and she fed him from her last handful of flour. Now the same two things were beside him, and this time all he had asked for was to die. The angel said nothing about that prayer and nothing about Jezebel. Elijah ate and drank and lay down again.

The angel of the LORD came back and touched him a second time. The instruction was the same, and now a reason came with it: "the journey is too much for you." Elijah ate and drank, and on the strength of that food he travelled forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God. He spent the night in a cave there, and only then did the word of the LORD come to him, as a question: "What are you doing here, Elijah?" God did have things to say to him. They came after two sleeps, two meals and nearly six weeks on the road.

keyVerses.text: He came to a broom bush, sat down under it and prayed that he might die. 'I have had enough, LORD,' he said. 'Take my life; I am no better than my ancestors.'

Then he lay down under the bush and fell asleep. All at once an angel touched him and said, 'Get up and eat.' He looked around, and there by his head was some bread baked over hot coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank and then lay down again.
As a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD has compassion on those who fear him; for he knows how we are formed, he remembers that we are dust.

insights: Under the bush Elijah prayed once, to ask for death, and no other word from him is recorded until Horeb. What got him back on his feet was food, and the writer says it gave him strength for forty days. If you're too spent to pray much, sleep and eat first.

'Too much for you' is the angel's phrase, and it's given as the reason for a second meal. The LORD, Psalm 103 says, remembers that we are dust. Admitting you've reached your limit tells Him nothing He hadn't allowed for.

Elijah asked to die. If that prayer is close to your own thoughts, tell a friend or your doctor today, and ring a crisis line if it can't wait. Elijah was alone when he prayed it, and help came from outside him, as a touch and food he hadn't made. You aren't promised an angel. A person can cook for you and put a hand on your shoulder.
reflectQuestions: If an angel told you this week that the journey is too much for you, what would he be talking about?
Who have you most avoided telling how tired you really are?
thematicGuides.practice: Ask one person to eat with you this week. Send the message today, before you talk yourself out of it. It can be soup at a kitchen table or sandwiches on a bench. While you're eating, tell them how worn out you are, in as few words as you like. You don't have to explain it or know what you want from them, and if they offer to cook, let them.
thematicGuides.prayer: Father, I've got nothing left. I did what I thought I was supposed to do and it has emptied me, and I've been ashamed that I can't pray my way back. This is about as much praying as I can manage. You fed Elijah before You asked him anything. Tonight I'm going to eat something and go to bed early, and I'm trusting that's allowed. Send me help I can recognise, and make me willing to take it from someone else's hands. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: A Day Off for People Who Used to Be Slaves
thematicGuides.hook: Pharaoh called his slaves lazy when they asked for leave, and the God who freed them gave them a day off every week.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Remember that you were slaves in Egypt and that the LORD your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.
thematicGuides.intro: Nothing stops you working on a day off except you, and that's the difficulty, because you don't trust your own reasons. You sit down, and within the hour you're calling yourself lazy and looking for a job to do. In Exodus that is Pharaoh's word, said to slaves who had asked leave to go out into the wilderness and worship.
story: Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh with a message from God, that he should let the people go to hold a festival to Him in the wilderness, three days' journey away. Pharaoh asked why they were taking the people from their work. That same day he stopped the supply of straw for making bricks and kept the number of bricks the same. His reason was that they were lazy. The people scattered all over Egypt gathering stubble, and when the count fell short their overseers were beaten. When the overseers went to Pharaoh to protest, he said it again and sent them back to work.

About a month out of Egypt the Israelites were living on manna, gathered from the desert floor each morning. On the sixth day they gathered twice as much, and Moses explained that the next day was to be a day of sabbath rest, so they should keep the extra overnight. This is the first time the word sabbath appears in the Bible. On the seventh morning some of the people went out to gather anyway and found none. Through Moses, God asked how long they would refuse His instructions, and told them to bear in mind that the Sabbath was something He had given them. "So the people rested on the seventh day."

Forty years after Egypt, east of the Jordan, Moses stood in front of the generation about to enter the land and went through the Ten Commandments again. When he came to the Sabbath he named everyone it covered: sons and daughters, male and female servants, the foreigner living in their towns, even the ox and the donkey. Their servants, he said, were to rest as they did. At Sinai the command had looked back to creation, when God rested on the seventh day. This time it looked back to Egypt. "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt", Moses told them, and that the LORD their God had brought them out.

keyVerses.text: Pharaoh said, 'Lazy, that's what you are, lazy! That is why you keep saying, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.' Now get to work. You will not be given any straw, yet you must produce your full quota of bricks.'
Bear in mind that the LORD has given you the Sabbath; that is why on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Everyone is to stay where they are on the seventh day; no one is to go out.

Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your male or female servant, nor your ox, your donkey or any of your animals, nor any foreigner residing in your towns, so that your male and female servants may rest, as you do.

insights: Proverbs is hard on people who won't work, and this command includes six days of labour. But in Exodus the charge of laziness comes from the man counting bricks, and the day off comes from God, who sent two days' bread ahead of it. It's fair to ask which of them your guilt sounds like.

If you care for small children or an ill parent, or work shifts, a whole day may be out of reach. The command has people like you in view. Its stated purpose is rest for servants, who couldn't stop unless someone let them, and it is addressed to the people who could let them.

Christians have long disagreed about how, or whether, the Sabbath command applies to them, and Paul was already dealing with arguments about special days in Romans 14. Whichever view you hold, the command tells you something about God. He freed slaves, and one of the first things He gave them was a day when nobody could make them work.
reflectQuestions: When you feel on a day off that you ought to be getting something done, who do you imagine is keeping count?
Which person near you most needs a few hours off that you could give them this month?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose a stretch of time this week that you can manage, a whole day if your life allows it and two hours if it doesn't, and put it in the diary. For that stretch, go without your to-do list. Leave the chores and the work email and whatever else you'd tick off afterwards. When you catch yourself getting up to do a job, sit back down. It will keep.
thematicGuides.prayer: Heavenly Father, when I get a free afternoon I fill it with jobs, and feel guilty about the one hour I sat down. Nobody is counting my bricks except me. I don't know how to stop, and it's time I learned. Help me take rest the way the slaves You freed were told to, as something You've given, and show me whose day off depends on me. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Three Psalms for a Sleepless Night
thematicGuides.hook: David slept with an army after him, Asaph couldn't close his eyes, and Psalm 121 says the LORD never sleeps.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: He will not let your foot slip, he who watches over you will not slumber; indeed, he who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
thematicGuides.intro: Psalm 3 has a heading above its first line, saying David wrote it when he fled from his son Absalom. It comes from a time when he had every reason to keep one eye open. To sleep you have to leave everything unguarded for hours, and after midnight that is exactly what you can't bring yourself to do, however tired you are.
story: David's son Absalom had won over the people of Israel, and David fled Jerusalem. He went up the Mount of Olives barefoot and weeping, and further on a man named Shimei kept pace along the hillside, throwing stones and shouting that the LORD was repaying him. Psalm 3 comes from that flight. It reports what many were saying about David: "God will not deliver him." Then, in the middle of the psalm, he says that he lies down and sleeps, and wakes again, because the LORD sustains him. Before the psalm ends he is asking God to rise up and rescue him, so the danger was still there when he woke.

Psalm 77 carries the name of Asaph. At night he stretches out his hands to God and will not be comforted. He remembers God and groans. And he puts the sleeplessness down to God Himself: "You kept my eyes from closing; I was too troubled to speak." Six questions follow, among them whether God has forgotten to be merciful. Nobody answers them. Asaph makes up his mind to remember what the LORD has done, and the rest of the psalm goes back over the crossing of the sea, when God's path led through the water and His footprints were not seen.

Psalm 121 is one of the songs of ascents, which pilgrims are thought to have sung on the road up to Jerusalem. A traveller looks towards the mountains and asks where help is going to come from, then answers that it comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth. After that the traveller says nothing more. The rest is spoken to the traveller, as 'you', and what it says five times is that the LORD is watching. It names the moon by night as well as the sun by day, so the watch covers the dark hours too. And the one keeping it, the psalm says, never dozes off.

keyVerses.text: I lie down and sleep; I wake again, because the LORD sustains me. I will not fear though tens of thousands assail me on every side.
I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your miracles of long ago. I will consider all your works and meditate on all your mighty deeds.
He will not let your foot slip, he who watches over you will not slumber; indeed, he who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.

insights: David slept and Asaph didn't, and both prayers were kept in the Bible. Psalm 77 never treats the bad night as a failure of trust. Asaph prayed with his hands stretched out and still lay awake, and said so to God. If your own bad nights have run into weeks, that's worth a doctor's appointment as well.

What Asaph chose to go back over happened at night. Exodus says "all that night the LORD drove the sea back", and that it was in the last watch before dawn that He looked down on the Egyptian army and threw it into confusion.

None of these psalms promises you sleep. Psalm 121 says that someone else is awake, and in the psalm that is something the traveller is told. Reading verses 3 and 4 aloud is a way of having it said to you. The watch isn't yours to keep.
reflectQuestions: What do you most fear would go wrong if you left your biggest worry alone until morning?
From the Bible or your own life, what has God done that you could go back over on a night you can't sleep?
thematicGuides.practice: When you lock the front door tonight, stop there for a minute. Say out loud the thing you're most reluctant to leave unwatched until morning (the unanswered email, perhaps, or next week's scan). Then read Psalm 121:3-4 aloud and go to bed. If you're awake later on, you haven't done it wrong. Do what Asaph did, and go slowly back over one thing God has done.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord Jesus, You slept on a cushion in a boat that was nearly swamped, and I can't sleep in a quiet room with the door locked. You also spent a night awake praying, out on a mountainside. I've been keeping watch over things I can do nothing about before morning, and I'm handing the watch over to You until it's light. If sleep comes, thank You. If it doesn't, keep me company, and bring to mind what You have done. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Jesus Offers the Tired a Yoke
