thematicGuides.hook: The rest Jesus promised was first offered through Jeremiah, to people who were told to find the good road and walk it.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
thematicGuides.intro: You take a week off, sleep late most days, and on Monday morning you're as tired as you were when you stopped. More hours in bed don't shift tiredness like that, and by now you may be wondering what would. In Matthew 11 Jesus makes an offer to tired people. He promises them rest, and then He holds out a yoke.
story: About six hundred years before Jesus, God warned Jerusalem through the prophet Jeremiah that an attack was coming, and that He had ordered the siege ramps Himself. Partway through that warning He told the people to stop where the roads meet, ask for the old paths and the good way, and take it. The promise that went with it, rest for their souls, was made to people on their feet and walking. Jeremiah wrote down the answer God got, which was that they would not walk in it.

In the last week of His life Jesus was in the temple courts, telling the crowds and His disciples about the teachers of the law and the Pharisees, a group strict about keeping God's law. He said they tied heavy loads on other people's shoulders and wouldn't lift a finger themselves, and that everything they did was done to be seen. They wore the tassels on their clothes long, and they loved the place of honour at banquets, the best seats in the synagogue, and being called 'Rabbi'. His own followers were not to take that title, He told them, because they had one Teacher.

In Galilee, well before His last week in Jerusalem, Jesus prayed aloud. He praised His Father for hiding these things from the wise and learned and showing them to little children. Then He called everyone who was weary and burdened to come to Him, and promised to give them rest. Next He spoke of a yoke, the wooden bar laid across the shoulders of working animals so they can pull a plough. The weary were to take His yoke and learn from Him, and the reason He gave was Himself, gentle and humble in heart. The promise that followed, "you will find rest for your souls", was the one God had made through Jeremiah, in the same words. His last line was that His yoke is easy and His burden is light.

keyVerses.text: Stand at the crossroads and look; ask for the ancient paths, ask where the good way is, and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls. But you said, 'We will not walk in it.'
They tie up heavy, cumbersome loads and put them on other people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them.

Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.

insights: In Matthew 11 Jesus speaks of rest twice. First it is given, to anyone who comes. Then it is found, after the yoke and the learning, while you're doing what He teaches. In Jeremiah the rest lay along a road. Jesus repeats the promise and puts Himself where the road was.

In Matthew's Greek, the loads the teachers tied on and the burden Jesus calls light are the same word. So Jesus, the one Teacher, has something for you to carry too. The weight is different, and so is the one handing it over. Some of what tires you now may have come from someone else's idea of a proper Christian or a good son or daughter.

Jesus was speaking about rest for the soul. A body can be worn out for reasons of its own, so if you've been exhausted for weeks whatever you do, see a doctor about it, and let someone close to you know.
reflectQuestions: What were you doing the last time you felt at rest in yourself?
Jesus calls Himself gentle and humble in heart. How does that compare with the way you picture Him looking at you when you're behind with everything?
thematicGuides.practice: Set aside twenty minutes this week with a sheet of paper. List whatever is weighing on you, one line each. Beside every line write where it came from: something Jesus taught, something you put on yourself, or another person, and if it's a person, write their name. Don't decide anything yet. Keep the sheet where you'll find it, inside a Bible at Matthew 11 if you have one, and read it again in a month.
thematicGuides.prayer: God, I'm tired in a way sleep hasn't touched, and I keep expecting the next day off to fix it. A lot of what I'm carrying was handed to me by people I didn't want to disappoint, and I never asked You whether it was mine. I'm half afraid that coming to Jesus means one more thing on the list. He says what He gives is light, and I want to know that for myself. Let me find the rest He promised while I'm still on my feet. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Everyone Is Looking for You
thematicGuides.hook: The morning after a whole town came to His door, Jesus went out in the dark to pray, and then left for other villages.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, left the house and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed.
thematicGuides.intro: If people depend on you, the day has no natural end. There's always one more person who needs feeding, driving, lifting or listening to, and stopping while any of them is still waiting feels like letting them down. Mark's Gospel records a morning when Jesus was in that position, with a whole town asking for Him and His own friends out searching for Him.
story: It was the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, in Capernaum. Jesus taught in the synagogue, and from there He went to Simon and Andrew's house. Simon's mother-in-law was in bed with a fever. Jesus took her hand and helped her up, the fever went, and she was soon looking after them. The Sabbath ended at sunset, and that was when the town came. People brought everyone they had who was ill or demon-possessed, until the whole of Capernaum was gathered at the door. Jesus laid His hands on the sick one at a time and healed them, and He drove out many demons.

After an evening given to a whole town's sick, Jesus was up before it was light and out of the house, somewhere He could be alone, and He was praying. He did this often, even with crowds coming to hear Him and to be healed. That morning Simon and his companions went to look for Him, and when they found Him their news was that everyone was looking for Him. Luke adds that the people came out to where He was themselves, and tried to keep Him from leaving them.

When Simon and the others found Him that morning, Jesus said it was time to go somewhere else. There were other villages nearby, and He meant to preach in those as well. "That is why I have come," He told them. He went through Galilee, preaching in the synagogues and driving out demons, with Capernaum still looking for Him. A man with leprosy came to Him on his knees and was healed, and then talked about it so freely that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly. He stayed outside in lonely places, and people came to Him there from everywhere. A few days later He was back in Capernaum, and so many gathered that there was no room left, "not even outside the door".

keyVerses.text: Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, left the house and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed.
When they found him, they exclaimed: 'Everyone is looking for you!' Jesus replied, 'Let us go somewhere else, to the nearby villages, so I can preach there also. That is why I have come.'
The news about him spread all the more, so that crowds of people came to hear him and to be healed of their sicknesses. But Jesus often withdrew to lonely places and prayed.

insights: Nobody could do more for a sick person than Jesus could, and He still left a town that was asking for Him. If He had waited until nobody in Capernaum needed Him, He would never have left. You won't reach the end of what people need from you either. Leaving cost something, because the people who came out to keep Him there were told no.

Jesus decided by what He had come to do, and He had been praying before He said so. You won't have His certainty. You probably do know the two or three things that are yours to do and nobody else's. Start the day with those, before the list of who is asking.

Some people can't be left, like a baby, or a parent with dementia. Then stopping means handing over to someone for a while. Jesus didn't keep the work to Himself. In Mark 3 He appointed twelve to be sent out preaching and driving out demons, the things He had been doing. So pick one person and ask them to take a turn.
reflectQuestions: What do you tell yourself when you stop for the night and someone is still waiting for something from you?
If you had to say in one sentence what this week is for, what would you put?
thematicGuides.practice: Choose one morning this week. Before you look at your phone or anyone has asked you for anything, go out of the house to somewhere you'll be alone, a bench down the road, or the back step if you can't go further. Stay fifteen minutes. Ask God one thing, what you're here to do today, then keep quiet until the time is up.
thematicGuides.prayer: Jesus, there are people at my door too, and I've been a little proud of never keeping any of them waiting. You left a whole town asking for You, and I can't leave one message unanswered overnight. Tell me what I'm here to do tomorrow. There will still be a queue when I stop tonight, and I mean to stop. Look after the ones I've left waiting while I'm away. Amen.

thematicGuides.title: Martha Was Worried About Many Things
thematicGuides.hook: Martha told Jesus she'd been left with all the work, and at a later dinner in John 12 she is serving at His table again.
thematicGuides.anchorVerse: 'Martha, Martha,' the Lord answered, 'you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed, or indeed only one.'
thematicGuides.intro: Martha walked up to Jesus, who was a guest in her house, and told Him to make her sister help. If you're the one at home or at work who does what needs doing while other people sit, you'll know how she got there. The story is usually remembered as Jesus picking the quiet sister over the busy one. Luke's wording is more careful than that.
story: A woman named Martha opened her home to Jesus when He came to her village, on the road with His disciples. His travelling depended on people doing that. Earlier in the same chapter He had sent seventy-two followers ahead with no purse or bag, to stay in whichever house welcomed them and eat what they were given. Once He was inside, Martha's sister Mary sat down at His feet to listen, and Martha, with all the preparations to see to, was distracted. When she complained, it was to Jesus. Luke gives no word of hers to Mary.

Jesus began His answer to Martha with her name, twice over. In Luke's Gospel He spoke to one other person that way, Simon Peter, at the Last Supper on the night Peter would deny knowing Him, and that was to tell Peter He had prayed for him. Then He told her she was worried and upset about many things, and that few were needed, or indeed only one. Mary had chosen what was better, He said, and it would not be taken away from her. He didn't send Mary to help.

Martha and Mary appear again in John's Gospel, in Bethany, with a brother called Lazarus. The account of his illness stops for one sentence: "Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus." In that sentence Martha is the one named, and Mary is only her sister. Later, six days before the Passover at which Jesus would die, a dinner was given in His honour. Lazarus was reclining at the table. Mary poured about a pint of expensive perfume on Jesus' feet and wiped them with her hair. Someone objected to Mary this time too. It was Judas, and Jesus told him to leave her alone. Martha served.

keyVerses.text: Martha was distracted by all the preparations that had to be made. She came to him and asked, 'Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to do the work by myself? Tell her to help me!'

'Martha, Martha,' the Lord answered, 'you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed, or indeed only one. Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her.'
Here a dinner was given in Jesus' honor. Martha served, while Lazarus was among those reclining at the table with him.

insights: Martha was upset about many things, and by Jesus' count few were needed. The serving itself He left alone, and so did everyone at the dinner in John 12. You can ask of your own list how much of it is needed today, and keep that apart from the question of who should be helping.

Jesus never says Martha was wrong about being left to it, and you may be carrying more than your share too. You can say so. Martha said it bluntly, to His face, and the first thing that came back was her own name. You can also ask the people around you for help, and tell them which job you want them to take.

Jesus did turn Martha down on one point. He would not settle it by taking something from Mary. If you've been hoping He will make the others pull their weight, that part is hard, and Luke's story stops before it is resolved.
reflectQuestions: When you're working and other people are sitting down, what do you find yourself saying about them in your head?
What have you said so far, and to whom, about being left to do the work on your own?
thematicGuides.practice: Every day this week, leave one job undone on purpose. Pick something only you would miss, like the ironed tea towels or the reply nobody is waiting for. Spend the ten minutes it would have taken sitting down, with Luke 10:38-42 open or with nothing at all. At the end of the seventh day, count how many of the seven anybody noticed.
thematicGuides.prayer: Lord, I've wanted to ask whether You care that I'm doing all this on my own, so now I'm asking. I could tell You who hasn't helped and how many times, because I've been keeping count. Some of it really is unfair. Say my name the way You said hers. Show me the few things that are needed today, and help me do them without the running total in my head. Amen.
